### [Printed Leaves]

[z CCXXXIII]
[Margin: Concerning principles self-evident: and first concerning the definitions of the same.]

**The most illustrious book of the elements of Euclid, the most perspicacious, begins most happily into the art of Geometry:**

**A point** is that which has no part. ¶ **A line** is length without breadth, the extremities of which are indeed two points. ¶ **A straight line** is the shortest extension from one point to another, receiving each of those [points] into its own extremities. ¶ **A surface** is that which has length and breadth only: the boundaries of which are indeed lines. ¶ **A plane surface** is an extension from one line to another receiving [them] into its own extremities. ¶ **A plane angle** is the mutual contact of two lines, the expansion of which is upon a surface and the application [of which] is not direct. ¶ But when two straight lines contain the angle, it is named a **rectilinear angle**. ¶ When a straight line stands upon a straight line and the two angles on either side are equal, each of them shall be a **right [angle]**. ¶ And the line standing upon the line it stands over is called **perpendicular**. ¶ An angle indeed which is greater than a right angle is called **obtuse**. ¶ An angle indeed smaller than a right angle is called **acute**. ¶ **A boundary** is that which is the end of anything. ¶ **A figure** is that which is contained by a boundary or boundaries. ¶ **A circle** is a plane figure contained by a single line, which is named the **circumference**: in the middle of which is a point, from which all straight lines going out to the circumference are equal to one another. And this point indeed is called the **center** of the circle. ¶ **A diameter** of a circle is a straight line which, passing over its center and applying its extremities to the circumference, divides the circle into two halves. ¶ **A semicircle** is a plane figure contained by the diameter of the circle and half of the circumference. ¶ **A portion [segment]** of a circle is a plane figure contained by a straight line and part of the circumference: either greater or smaller than a semicircle. ¶ **Rectilinear figures** are those which are contained by straight lines: of which some are **trilateral**, which [are contained] by three straight lines; some **quadrilateral**, which by four straight lines; some **multilateral**, which are contained by more than four straight lines. ¶ Of trilateral figures: one is a **triangle** having three equal sides. Another is a triangle having two equal sides. Another is a triangle of three unequal sides. ¶ Of these again, one is **orthogonal [right-angled]**, having one right angle (namely). Another is **ambligonium [obtuse-angled]**, having a certain obtuse angle. Another is **oxigonium [acute-angled]**, in which there are three acute angles. ¶ Moreover, of quadrilateral figures: one is a **square**, which is equilateral and rectangular. Another is a **long tetragon [oblong]**, which is a rectangular figure, but is not equilateral. Another is the **helmuaym [rhombus]**, which is equilateral, but is not rectangular.

---

[page number: 3]

¶ Another is **similar to the helmuaym [rhomboid]**, which has equal opposite sides and equal opposite angles: it is not, however, contained by right angles nor by equal sides. ¶ Moreover, besides these, all quadrilateral figures are named **helmuariphe [trapezia]**. ¶ **Equidistant [parallel] lines** are those which, being located in the same surface and drawn out in either direction, do not meet, even if they are extended to infinity.

**Postulates** [*Petitiones*] are five: ¶ To draw a straight line from any point to any point, and to extend a defined line continuously and straight as far as one wishes. ¶ To describe a circle upon any center by occupying any amount of space. ¶ That all right angles are equal to one another. ¶ If a straight line falls upon two straight lines and the two angles on one side are less than two right angles, those two lines being drawn out in that same direction will without doubt go to a meeting point. ¶ That two straight lines enclose no surface.

**Common notions of the mind** [*Axioms*] are these: ¶ Things which are equal to one and the same thing are also equal to one another. ¶ And if equals are added to equals, the wholes will also be equal. ¶ And if equals are taken away from equals, those which remain will be equal. ¶ And if you take away equals from unequals, those which remain will be unequal. ¶ And if you add equals to unequals, they themselves will also be unequal. ¶ If there be two things equal to one, they themselves will be equal to one another. ¶ If there be two things of which each is half of one and the same thing, each shall be equal to the other. ¶ If any thing be placed upon another and applied to it, and the one does not exceed the other: they shall be equal to one another. ¶ Every whole is greater than its part.

**It should be known** however that besides these conceptions of the mind, or common [notions], Euclid passed over many others which are incomprehensible in number: of which this is one. ¶ If two equal quantities are compared to any third of the same kind, both together will be either equally greater than that third, or equally smaller, or together equal. ¶ Likewise another: As great as any quantity is to any other of the same kind, so great is any third to some fourth of the same kind in continuous quantities; this is universally true whether the antecedents were greater than the consequents or smaller. For magnitude decreases to infinity. But in numbers it is not so: but if the first be a submultiple of the second, any third will be equally a submultiple of some fourth, since number increases to infinity just as magnitude is diminished to infinity.

**Proposition 1.**
**To construct an equilateral triangle upon a given straight line.**
¶ Let the given straight line be **a.b.** I wish to constitute an equilateral triangle upon it. Upon one of its extremities, at point **a.**, I shall place the fixed foot of the compass; and I shall extend the other movable foot as far as **b.** and describe, according to the quantity of the given line itself through the second postulate, the circle **c.b.d.f.**

***

### Scholarly Notes & Vocabulary
*   **Proper Nouns:** *Euclides* (Euclid), *Ratdolt* (the printer).
*   **Helmuaym / Helmuariphe:** These terms are transliterations from the Arabic (*al-mu’ayyan* and *al-munharif*), reflecting the medieval transmission of Euclid through Arabic sources into Latin. They correspond to the Rhombus and the Trapezium/Trapezoid respectively.
*   **Orthogonis / Ambligonium / Oxigonium:** Traditional Latinized Greek terms for right-angled, obtuse-angled, and acute-angled triangles.
*   **Petitiones / Communes animi conceptiones:** The standard medieval terms for Postulates and Common Notions (Axioms).
*   **Scholium (Sciendum est...):** This paragraph is not part of Euclid’s original text but is a commentary (likely by Campanus) discussing the nature of infinity in continuous magnitudes versus discrete numbers.

...and it will be, through the second part [of Proposition] 20, that $a$ is to $c$ as $f$ is to $b$. And because $a$ and $c$ are prime <note>original: "pmi"; here meaning relatively prime, having no common divisor</note> and $e$ divides $c$, then by [Proposition] 24, $e$ itself will be prime to $a$. Therefore, by [Proposition] 23, $a$ and $c$ are the least in their proportion; it follows therefore by [Proposition] 21 that $c$ divides $b$. And because it was posited that it divides $e$, then $b$ and $c$ will not be prime to each other—which is contrary to the hypothesis.

**Proposition 26.**

[Diagram: four horizontal lines of varying lengths, labeled from top to bottom: a, b, c, d]

**I**f there are two numbers prime to each other, that which is produced from one of them multiplied by itself is prime to the remaining number.
¶ Let $a$ and $b$ be prime to each other, and from $a$ multiplied by itself let $c$ be produced. I say that $c$ is prime to $b$. For let $d$ be equal to $a$; then $d$ will be prime to $b$, and from $a$ multiplied by $d$ comes $c$. Therefore, through the premise, it is clear that $c$ is prime to $b$, which is what we proposed.

**Proposition 27.**

[Diagram: six horizontal lines, labeled from top to bottom: a, b, e, c, d, f]

**I**f, when two numbers are compared to two others, each [of the first two] is prime to each [of the second two], then the product of the first two will be prime to the product of the second two.
¶ Let $a$ and $b$ be the first numbers, and $c$ and $d$ the later ones. Let each of the two, $a$ and $b$, be prime to each of the two, $c$ and $d$. Let $e$ be produced from $a$ times $b$, and $f$ be produced from $c$ times $d$. I say that $e$ is prime to $f$. This is concluded evidently by assuming [Proposition] 25 three times: for since $e$ is made from $a$ times $b$, and each of those is prime to $c$ and to $d$, then by that same proposition $e$ is prime to $c$ and likewise prime to $d$. Because $f$ is likewise made from $c$ times $d$, and each of those is prime to $e$, it will again be—by that same proposition—that $f$ is prime to $e$, which is what was proposed.

**Proposition 28.**

[Diagram: six horizontal lines, labeled from top to bottom: f, e, d, c, b, a]

**I**f there are two numbers prime to each other, and each is multiplied by itself, the resulting products will be prime to each other. And likewise, if each product is multiplied by its original root <note>original: "principiū"; literally 'beginning' or 'principle', referring to the base number $a$ or $b$</note>, the resulting products will also be prime to each other.
¶ Let $a$ and $b$ be prime to each other. Let each be multiplied by itself: let $c$ come from $a$, and $d$ from $b$. Likewise, let $a$ be multiplied by $c$ to produce $e$, and $b$ by $d$ to produce $f$. I say that $c$ and $d$ are prime to each other, and likewise $e$ and $f$ are prime to each other. For by [Proposition] 26, $c$ is prime to $b$; therefore, by the same logic, $d$ will be prime to $a$ and to $c$. Thus it is established that the first pair, $c$ and $d$, are prime to each other. ¶ The remainder follows thus: since each of the two numbers $a$ and $c$ is prime to each of the two $b$ and $d$, then by [Proposition] 27, $e$ will be prime to $f$, which is the remainder. Not only will $c$ be prime to $f$, but also by [Proposition] 25 it is prime to $b$ and to $d$; and likewise $f$ to $a$ and $c$. Thus, if one were to multiply the product by its original root infinitely many times, all the products would be prime to each other—and not only that, but any number derived from $a$ would be prime to any number derived from $b$.

**Proposition 29.**

[Diagram: three horizontal lines, the top one labeled a and b, the bottom one labeled d]

**I**f there are two numbers prime to each other, the sum composed of both <note>original: "qui ex ambobus coaceruatur"; the 'heaping together' or sum of the two</note> will be prime to each of the original numbers. If, however, the sum of both is prime to each of them, the two numbers will also be prime to each other.
¶ Let $a$ and $b$ be prime to each other. I say that the sum composed of them, $a+b$, will be prime to each of them, and vice versa. For if $d$ divides the whole $a+b$, and it divides one of them, it will—by common knowledge <note>original: "p cōez sciāz"; referring to a 'common notion' or axiom in Euclidean geometry</note>—divide the other as well. Therefore they would not be prime to each other; but this had been posited [that they are prime]. Thus the first part is clear. The second is as follows: let $a+b$ be prime to each of its components, which are $a$ and $b$. I say that $a$ and $b$...

**VII**

<note>This text appears to be from Book VII of Euclid’s *Elements*, which focuses on the properties of whole numbers.</note>

...are prime to each other: for if it is assumed that <term>the number $d$ measures</term><note>In Greek and Latin mathematics, "measuring" a number means that it divides into that number exactly, without a remainder.</note> both of the two numbers $a$ and $b$, it follows by <term>common knowledge</term><note>original: "communis scientia"; this refers to mathematical axioms or "common notions" that are accepted as self-evident.</note> that it also measures the number $a+b$ composed of them. For this reason, $a+b$ would not be prime to either of the two numbers $a$ or $b$. But it was assumed that it was prime to both. Therefore, an impossibility occurs. In the same way, if the sum of two numbers is prime to one of them, it will also be prime to the other, and thus the sum and the individual numbers are prime to each other. For let the sum composed of $a$ and $b$ be prime to $a$; I say that it will also be prime to $b$. Otherwise, let the number $d$ measure them; by logical conception, $d$ will measure $a$ since it measures the whole <insert>the sum $a+b$</insert> as well as the part taken away <insert>$b$</insert>. However, this was inconsistent, for the sum of $a$ and $b$ was prime to $a$.

**¶ Proposition .30.**
**Every composite number is measured by some prime number.**
¶ Let $a$ be any composite number; I say that some prime number measures it. For because it is composite, it will be measured by some number, let it be $b$. If $b$ is prime, then what is said is true. But if $b$ is composite, let $c$ be the number that measures it; $c$ will also, by common knowledge, measure $a$. If $c$ itself is prime, then the statement is proven. But if it is composite, another number $d$ must necessarily measure it, which by common knowledge will also measure $a$. By reasoning in this same way, because whenever a composite number occurs it is necessary to take a smaller number that measures it, it follows that one must eventually arrive at some prime number. Otherwise, an impossibility would occur, and contrary to the principles of logic, the numbers would decrease into infinity. <note>The Greeks did not accept the idea of an infinite descent of whole numbers; they believed you must eventually hit a "unit" or a prime building block.</note>

**¶ Proposition .31.**
**Every number is either prime or is measured by a prime number.**
¶ Let $a$ be any number; I say that it is either prime or is measured by a prime. Because if it is not prime, it will be composite; and every such number is measured by some prime through the preceding proposition. Therefore $a$ is either prime or is measured by a prime, which is what was proposed.

**¶ Proposition .32.**
**Every prime number is prime to every number that it does not measure.**
¶ Let $a$ be a prime number not measuring $b$; I say that $a$ and $b$ are <term>prime to each other</term><note>original: "contra se primi"; this is what we now call "coprime." It means they share no common factors other than 1.</note>. For if $c$ measures both of them, it would not be true that $a$ is a prime number.

**¶ Proposition .33.**
**If a number produced from two others is measured by some prime number, it is necessary that the same prime measures one of those two.**
¶ Let $c$ be the product of $a$ times $b$, and let $d$ be a prime number which is assumed to measure $c$. I say that $d$ measures either $a$ or $b$. For let it measure $c$ according to the number $e$. If, therefore, it does not measure $a$, it will be prime to it by the preceding proposition; and therefore they will be the <term>least in their proportion</term><note>original: "minimi in sua proportione"; referring to a fraction in its simplest, reduced form.</note> by Proposition 23. And since $a$ is to $d$ as $e$ is to $b$...

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proofs from Book VII of a geometry treatise, likely Euclid's Elements. It focuses on finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers.</meta>

VII

¶ Let the given numbers be ***a*** and ***b***. Of these, if the smaller measures <note>original: "numerat"; in classical mathematics, one number "measures" another if it divides into it exactly, like a ruler measuring a length</note> the larger, then the larger is the number we seek <note>The goal here is to find the Least Common Multiple</note>. Otherwise, the larger of them would have to measure a number smaller than itself.

If, however, neither measures the other, and if they are <term>prime to each other</term> <note>meaning they share no common factors other than 1</note>, then the number which results from ***a*** multiplied by ***b***—let this be ***c***—will be the smallest of all numbers that ***a*** and ***b*** measure. 

For if they were to measure a smaller number than it, let that be ***d***, which they measure according to the factors ***e*** and ***f***. It will then follow, by the second part of Proposition 20, that ***a*** is to ***b*** as ***f*** is to ***e***. And because ***a*** and ***b*** are the <term>least of their proportion</term> <note>meaning the ratio is expressed in its lowest terms</note> by Proposition 23, ***a*** will measure ***f*** by Proposition 21. 

And because, by Proposition 18, ***c*** is to ***d*** as ***a*** is to ***f***—for the products of ***b*** multiplied by ***a*** and ***f*** result in ***c*** and ***d***—it follows that ***c*** measures ***d***. But ***d*** was stated to be smaller <note>It is logically impossible for a larger number to divide evenly into a smaller one, thus proving that no smaller common multiple than c can exist</note>.

<summary>This page provides a geometric proof for finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers that are prime to each other, demonstrating that their product is the smallest possible number they both divide into.</summary>
<keywords>Least Common Multiple, Arithmetic, Euclid, Prime to each other, Proportions, Divisibility, Mathematical Proof</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proofs from Book VII, likely of Jordanus de Nemore's Arithmetica, focusing on finding the least common multiple of denominators to identify a number that contains specific fractional parts.</meta>

# VII

Let **d** therefore be multiplied by **c**, and let **e** be the result; and let **e** be multiplied by **b**, and let **f** be the result; and let **f** also be multiplied by **a**, and let **g** be the result, which I say is the number we are seeking. For since **g** itself results from **a** multiplied by **f**, according to proposition 17 <note>The author refers to Proposition 17 of the current book of the Arithmetica, which deals with the relationships of products and their factors.</note>, **f** will be the part of **g** named by **a**. And since **f** results by the same reasoning from **b** multiplied by **e**, **e** will be the part of **f** named by **b**. But also because of this, **d** will be the part of **e** named by **c**. And because <term>unity</term> <note>original: "vnitas"; in medieval mathematics, "unity" refers to the number 1, which was often considered the source of numbers rather than a number itself.</note> is the part of **d** named by **d** itself, it is clear that **g** has the parts as proposed. 

If, therefore, **g** were not the smallest such number, let there be a smaller one **h**. And let **k** be its part named by **a**, and **l** be the part of **k** named by **b**, and **m** be the part of **l** named by **c**, and also let **n** be the part of **m** named by **d**. It will then follow through proposition 18 that **g** is to **f** as **h** is to **k**; and **f** is to **e** as **k** is to **l**; and **e** is to **d** as **l** is to **m**. Moreover, **d** is to unity as **m** is to **n**. Therefore, through proposition 15, in the <term>proportion of equality</term> <note>original: "proportione equalitatis"; this refers to a compounded ratio where the first term relates to the last in the same way across two series.</note>, **g** will be to unity as **h** is to **n**. Therefore, by permutation, **g** will be to **h** as unity is to **n**. Thus, since **h** is smaller than **g**, **n** must be smaller than unity. It follows, therefore, that this is impossible, for a part of a number cannot be smaller than unity. <note>In this system of arithmetic, "parts" or divisors must result in whole numbers; a "part" smaller than 1 would imply a fraction of the unit, which was excluded from this type of proof.</note> Therefore, **g** is the smallest number having the parts as proposed. Once this is found, if one cares to have the second smallest, or any number of them, they must be taken through multiples of the smallest, as was said before. This, however, is proposed in another way as proposition 39, in this manner:

| a | b | c | I | | g | f | e | d | | h | k | l | m | n |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | | | | | | | 1360 | 120 | 30 | | |

<note>Diagram 1: This table represents the relationship between denominators (a, b, c, I) and the resulting numbers and their parts (g, f, e, d and h, k, l, m, n). The numbers 1360, 120, and 30 are examples of quantities found through this multiplication.</note>

¶ Given any number of parts: to find the smallest number containing them.

¶ If the proposed parts are **a**, **b**, and **c**, and their <term>denominators</term> <note>original: "denominantes"; the numbers that name the parts, such as 3 naming the 'third part' (1/3).</note> are **d**, **e**, and **f**. Let the smallest number that **d**, **e**, and **f** measure <note>original: "numerant"; meaning they divide into it evenly.</note> be taken, and let it be **g**. I say this is what we seek: for the proposed parts will be in it according to proposition 37. If this were not the smallest number containing them, let it be **b**, which **d**, **e**, and **f** will measure according to proposition 38. Therefore, **g** would not be the smallest number measured by them, which is a contradiction, since it was assumed to be. 

However, I understand the parts **a**, **b**, and **c** to be placed indeterminately and not under a fixed quantity; for otherwise it would not be necessary that the smallest number measured by **d**, **e**, and **f** would be the smallest number containing the proposed parts. For it happens that one finds very many parts which a number measured by their denominators does not contain. For example: three numbers which are **120**, **90**, and **72** are parts of the same number. The first is indeed the third, the second the fourth, and the third the fifth. Yet the smallest number that measures their denominators, which is **60**, does not contain these parts. <note>This is a crucial distinction: the number 60 has a 3rd (20), a 4th (15), and a 5th (12), but it is too small to contain the specific values 120, 90, and 72.</note> One must therefore insist, if the parts are set under a certain quantity, upon the first consequence of this demonstration; for it does not follow, as argued through proposition 37, that if a <term>ternary</term> <note>The number three.</note> measures this number, then this number is placed as its third part; but rather it *has* a third part. On account of which, the proposition is the same in either mode, but according to the first mode, that which is intended to be proposed seems more convenient.

One must notice, however, that since every part has a quantity, it is possible to set any number and any kind of parts according to quantity, and to inquire which smallest number contains them and under what denominators. It is established that the smallest number containing them is the <term>least common multiple</term> <note>original: "minimu numeratu ab eis"; the smallest number measured by them.</note> of them. Those numbers by which it measures them are the ones that name those parts in that number. Conversely, it is possible to set any number and any kind of denominations, and to inquire in what smallest number these denominations are found and according to what quantities. It is also established that the smallest number is the least common multiple of those denominators; those numbers by which they measure it are the ones that determine the quantities. In both cases, the smallest is sought because there are infinite numbers that contain these parts on one hand, and in which these denominations are found on the other. 

Again, it is possible to set any number of parts and just as many denominations, or any number of denominations and just as many parts. But not just any with any; rather, certain parts with certain denominations. For if I set the parts three, four, and five, and their denominations as 6, 7, and 8, and I ask what number contains these parts under those denominations, I would be like a vain seeker asking for the impossible. <note>If you define a part's value as 3 and its denominator as 6, the whole must be 18. If you also say another part is 4 with denominator 7, the whole must be 28. Since 18 does not equal 28, the conditions are impossible.</note> It is therefore fitting to set certain parts with certain denominations, and not just by chance, and to inquire what number contains the set parts under the set denominations. It is not a matter of which smallest number, for there is only one; for whether one part and one denomination are proposed, or many and many, the result is unique.

[Diagram 1: A circle with center 'c' and a line 'c-d' extending outside. Another circle with center 'd' passes through 'e' and 'f'. Points 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f' are marked.]

...of the equilateral triangle <note>original: "equilateri"; refers to the triangle constructed in the first part of Proposition 2</note> which is opposite the given point, namely side **d.c.** I shall extend through the center of the described circle to its circumference; and let the whole line thus extended be **d.c.e.** According to its length, I will draw a circle with the center at **d**, which shall be circle **e.f.** And afterwards, I shall extend side **d.a.** to the circumference of this last circle, and let it meet its circumference at point **f.** I say, therefore, that **a.f.** is equal to **b.c.** For **b.c.** and **c.e.** are equal, because they go out from the center of circle **c** to its circumference. Similarly, **d.f.** and **d.e.** are equal because they go out from the center of circle **e.f.** to the circumference. But **d.a.** and **d.c.** are equal because they are sides of an equilateral triangle. Therefore, if **d.a.** and **d.c.** are taken away from **d.e.** and **d.f.**, which are equal, the remainders, which are **a.f.** and **c.e.**, will be equal. Since each of the two lines **a.f.** and **c.b.** is equal to **c.e.**, they are equal to each other. Therefore, from point **a**, we have drawn the line **a.f.** equal to **b.c.**, which was proposed.

**Proposition 3.**
**P**roposing two unequal lines, to cut off from the longer of them a part equal to the shorter.
Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.**, and let **a.b.** be the shorter. I wish to cut from **c.d.** a line that is equal to **a.b.** First, from point **c**, I draw one line equal to **a.b.** by what the preceding proposition taught; let this be **c.e.** Therefore, with the center placed at point **c**, I shall describe a circle according to the length of **c.e.**, which will cut the line **c.d.** Let it, therefore, cut it at point **f.** Line **c.f.** will be equal to line **c.e.** because both go out from the center of the same circle to the circumference; and since each of the two lines **a.b.** and **c.f.** is equal to **c.e.**, they are equal to each other; which was proposed.

[Diagram 2: Two triangles, a-b-c and d-e-f, which appear congruent. Points 'g' and 'h' are marked on lines between 'e' and 'f'.]

**Proposition 4.**
**O**f all cases of two triangles where two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other, and the two angles contained by those equal sides are equal to each other, the remaining sides corresponding to each other will also be equal; the remaining angles of the one will be equal to the remaining angles of the other, and the whole triangle will be equal to the whole triangle. <note>This is the "Side-Angle-Side" (SAS) theorem of triangle congruence.</note>
Let there be two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** Let side **a.b.** be equal to side **d.e.**, and side **a.c.** equal to side **d.f.**, and angle **a** equal to angle **d.** Then I say that base **b.c.** is equal to base **e.f.**, and angle **b** is equal to angle **e.** Also, angle **c** is equal to angle **f.** Which is proved: I shall place triangle **a.b.c.** upon triangle **d.e.f.** so that angle **a** falls upon angle **d**, and side **a.b.** upon side **d.e.**, and side **a.c.** upon side **d.f.** And it is clear through the penultimate common notion <note>original: "penultimam perceptionem"; referring to Euclid's Axiom/Common Notion 4: "Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another."</note> that neither the angles nor the sides will exceed each other, because angle **a** is equal to angle **d**, and the sides placed upon the others are equal to those they are placed upon by the hypothesis. Therefore, points **b** and **c** will fall upon points **e** and **f.** If, therefore, line **b.c.** falls upon line **e.f.**, the proposal is clear: because since line **b.c.** placed upon line **e.f.** does not exceed it, nor is it exceeded by it, it is equal to it by the conversion of the penultimate common notion. By the same reasoning, angle **b** will be equal to angle **e**, and angle **c** equal to angle **f.** If, however, line **b.c.** does not fall upon line **e.f.**, but falls inside the triangle like line **e.g.f.** or outside like line **e.h.f.**, then two straight lines would enclose a surface, which is against the last postulate. <note>original: "vltimā petitionē"; Euclid's postulate that two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>

[Diagram 3: An isosceles triangle a-b-c with its sides extended downwards to 'd' and 'e'. Lines are drawn from 'b' to 'e' and 'c' to 'd', intersecting at a point.]

**Proposition 5.**
**I**n every triangle with two equal sides <note>An isosceles triangle.</note>, it is necessary that the angles which are at the base be equal; and if the two equal sides are extended straight, the two angles under the base will also be equal to each other.
Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** whose side **a.b.** is equal to side **a.c.** I say that angle **a.b.c.** is equal to angle **a.c.b.**, and if **a.b.** and **a.c.** are extended as far as **d** and **e**...

Therefore, when proposing parts and their denominations <term>denominations: in medieval arithmetic, this refers to the number that names the part, such as '3' for a third or '4' for a fourth</term> in a whole, one should not ask which is the *least* number that contains these parts under those denominations, but rather which *single* number contains them. 

But if one proposes parts only, it happens that one asks which is the least number that contains them and by what [numbers] they are denominated in it. It is also suitable, when proposing only denominations, to ask which parts are named by them and in what least number they are found. However, it seems more convenient to inquire about parts through denominations than denominations through parts; for indeed, the diversity of proportions accompanies the diversity of denominations, not of parts.

### Proposition 11
**Given** a straight line and a point marked upon it, to draw a perpendicular line supported on both sides by two equal and right angles.

Let .a.b. be the given line in which there is a given point .c., from which it is necessary to draw a perpendicular. Therefore, by the third [proposition], I make the line .b.c. equal to the line .a.c., and upon the whole [line] .a.b. I construct an equilateral triangle .a.b.d., and I draw the line .c.d., and I say that this [line] is perpendicular to line .a.b. I consider the two triangles .a.c.d. and .b.c.d.; and because the two sides .a.c. and .c.d. of triangle .a.c.d. are equal to the two sides .c.b. and .c.d. of triangle .c.b.d., and the base .a.d. [is equal] to the base .b.d., then by the 8th [proposition], angle .a.c.d. will be equal to angle .b.c.d. Wherefore each of them will be a right [angle] by the definition of a right angle; and the line .c.d. is perpendicular to the line .a.b. by the definition of a perpendicular line: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 12
**From a point** marked outside, to lead a perpendicular to a given line of indefinite length.

Let .a. be the point marked outside line .b.c., from which it is necessary to lead a perpendicular to it. Therefore, let the line .b.c. be extended in either direction as much as is pleasing, and upon point .a. let a circle .b.c. be described so that it intersects the given line at points .b. and .c.; and let the lines .a.b. and .a.c. be drawn, and let the angle .b.a.c. be divided into equal [parts] by the line .a.d. according to the 9th [proposition]. I say that .a.d. is perpendicular to the line .b.c. I consider the two triangles .a.b.d. and .a.c.d.; and because the two sides .a.b. and .a.d. of triangle .a.b.d. are equal to the two sides .a.c. and .a.d. of triangle .a.c.d., and the one angle at .a. is equal to the other, then by the 4th [proposition] the base .b.d. will be equal to the base .d.c., and angle .a.d.b. equal to angle .a.d.c. Wherefore each of them is right, and the line .a.d. is perpendicular to the line .b.c. by the definition of a right angle and of a perpendicular line: which is what was proposed.

---

### Proposition 13
**Every** straight line standing upon a straight line makes two angles on either side [that] are either right or equal to two right angles.

Let it be that line .a.b. stands upon line .c.d. If it were perpendicular upon it, it would make two right angles by the prior [statement] of the definition. If, however, it were not perpendicular upon it, let .b.e. be drawn from point .b. perpendicular upon .c.d. by the eleventh [proposition]. And the two angles .e.b.c. and .e.b.d. will be right by the prior [statement] of the definition. Because, therefore, the two angles .d.b.a. and .a.b.e. are equal to the angle .d.b.e. itself, they, with angle .c.b.e., will be equal to two right angles. Wherefore the three angles which are .d.b.a. and .a.b.e. and .b.c. [sic, likely .e.b.c.] are equal to two right angles. But angle .c.b.a. is equal to the two angles .c.b.e. and .e.b.a. Therefore the two angles .c.b.a. and .a.b.d. are equal to two right angles: which is what was proposed. From which it is evident that the whole space which surrounds any point in any plane surface is equal to four right angles.

---

### Proposition 14
**If** two lines from a point of one line should go out into opposite directions and have made two angles about themselves [that are] right or equal to two right angles, those two lines are directly joined to each other and are one line.

Let it be that from point .b. of line .a.b., two lines .b.c. and .b.d. go out into opposite directions and make two angles which are .c.b.a. and .d.b.a. equal to two right angles. Then I say that the two lines .c.b. and .d.b. are directly joined to each other and are one line. And this is, as it were, the converse of the [previous] proposition. For if it were not one line, then let .c.b. be extended in a continuous and direct [line]. Because it is not one line with .d.b., it will pass above it as .b.e. or below it as .b.f. Because, therefore, the line .a.b. falls upon the straight line which is .c.b.e., the angles .c.b.a. and .e.b.a. will be equal to two right angles by the preceding [proposition]. And because all right angles are equal to one another by the 3rd petition [postulate], the angles .c.b.a. and .d.b.a. are also equal to two right angles by the hypothesis. Therefore the two angles .c.b.a. and .e.b.a. will be equal to the two angles .c.b.a. and .d.b.a. Therefore, the common angle .c.b.a. being taken away, angle .e.b.a. will be equal to angle .d.b.a., the part to the whole, which is impossible. Similarly, you will prove [by] line .c.b. being extended that angle .d.b.a. is equal to angle .f.b.a. if by chance an adversary should say that the line .c.b. extended falls below .b.d.

### Translator's Notes on Abbreviations and Readings:
*   **pūcto u / puncto n**: In Prop 11, the OCR reads "u", but the mathematical context and typical Ratdolt phrasing suggest "a puncto in ea signato" (from a point marked in it) or "puncto dato" (a given point).
*   **priusitionem**: This appears to be a contraction in the OCR or the source text for *praecognitionem* or a reference to a *prior* definition (*prius* + *diffinitionis*). In these editions, it refers back to the definitions at the start of Book I.
*   **z / &**: The Tironian note "z" is used throughout as a shorthand for *et* (and).
*   **depto / dempto**: In Prop 14, *depto* is a common medieval spelling/contraction for *dempto* (having been taken away/subtracted), a standard step in Euclidean proofs where a common angle is subtracted from both sides of an equation.
*   **piuersa / conuersa**: In Prop 14, the OCR "piuersa" is clearly *conversa* (the converse), as Prop 14 is the logical converse of Prop 13.
*   **q'libz / quibuslibet**: Used in the corollary of Prop 13 to mean "in any" or "whatever."
*   **petitiōem / petitionem**: This refers to the *Postulates* (Petitions) of Euclid.
*   **proper nouns**: Diagram markers (.a., .b., .c., etc.) have been kept exactly as they appear in the Latin text.

# VIII

...by the first part of Proposition 13, it is necessary that *c* measures <note>In ancient mathematics, one number "measures" another if it divides into it exactly, without a remainder.</note> *d*. It is therefore necessary that *b* measures it, even though it does not measure it; which is impossible. Moreover, just as it is necessary for the negative statements opposite to the affirmations demonstrated in Proposition 13 to be reversed, so too is it necessary for the negative statements opposed to those affirmations demonstrated in the preceding proposition to be reversed. Hence, if a cube does not measure a cube, neither will its **side** <note>original: "latus"; the "side" of a cube refers to its cube root.</note> measure the side of the other. Conversely, if the side of one does not measure the side of the other, then the cube itself will not measure the other cube. This is demonstrated by the preceding proposition through the **negation of the consequent** <term>destructione consequentis: a logical method where if the effect is proven false, the cause must also be false</term>, just as was proposed in Proposition 13. Therefore, the author <note>Referring to Euclid, the original author of the *Elements*.</note> did not explicitly state this, but intended for it to be understood through what had already been proposed.

### Proposition 24

**Of** <note>The large decorative 'N' begins 'Numerorum' (Of numbers).</note> similar plane numbers, the proportion of one to the other is as the proportion of a square to a square.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be <term>similar plane numbers</term> <note>Numbers representing two-dimensional areas whose sides are proportional, such as 6 (2x3) and 24 (4x6).</note>. I say that the proportion of one to the other is as a square to a square. For by the 16th proposition, there will be one mean number between them in continuous proportion, which is **c**. Taking, therefore, the three least numbers in their proportion—which are **d**, **e**, and **f**—by the second corollary, **d** and **f** will be squares. And since by equal proportionality **a** is to **b** as **d** is to **f**, it stands that what was proposed is true.

### Proposition 25

**Of** <note>The large decorative 'O' begins 'Omnium' (Of all).</note> all two similar solid numbers, the proportion of one to the other is as the proportion of some cube to another cube.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar solids: I say that the proportion of one of them to the other is as some cube to some other cube. Indeed, by the 18th proposition, there are two mean numbers between them according to continuous proportion, which are **c** and **d**. In their proportion, let there be the four least numbers: **e**, **f**, **g**, and **h**, of which **e** and **h** will be cubes by the second corollary. Since, therefore, by equal proportionality **a** is to **b** as **e** is to **h**, the proposition is clear.

**An** <note>The large decorative 'P' begins 'Par' (An [even number]).</note> <term>even number</term> is that which can be divided into two equal parts. ¶ An <term>odd number</term> is that which cannot be divided into two equal parts, and which exceeds an even number by one unit. ¶ <term>Evenly even</term> <note>Latin: 'Pariter par'. In modern terms, a power of 2 (2, 4, 8, 16...).</note> is that which all even numbers measuring it do so by even times. ¶ <term>Evenly odd</term> <note>Latin: 'Pariter impar'. An even number that, when divided by 2, yields an odd number (6, 10, 14...).</note> is that which all even numbers measuring it do so by odd times. ¶ <term>Evenly even and odd</term> <note>Latin: 'Pariter par et impariter'. Even numbers that have both even and odd divisors, typically those divisible by 4 but also containing an odd factor (12, 20, 24...).</note> is that which even numbers measuring it do so some by even times and some by odd times. ¶ <term>Oddly odd</term> <note>Latin: 'Impariter impar'. The product of two odd numbers.</note> is that which all odd numbers measuring it do so by odd times. ¶ A <term>perfect number</term> <note>A number equal to the sum of its proper divisors, like 6 (1+2+3) or 28.</note> is called that which is equal to all its parts by which it is measured. ¶ A number is called <term>abundant</term> if it is less than all its parts <note>The sum of its divisors is greater than the number itself.</note>. ¶ It is called <term>deficient</term> <note>Latin: 'Diminutus'.</note> if it is greater than its parts.

### Proposition 1

**If** <note>The large decorative 'S' begins 'Si' (If).</note> there be two similar plane numbers, that which is produced from the lead of one into the other will necessarily be a square number.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar plane numbers, from whose multiplication **c** is produced. I say that **c** is a square. For let **d** be made from **a** multiplied by itself. By the 18th proposition of the seventh book, **d** is to **c** as **a** is to **b**. And since between **a** and **b** there falls one mean according to continuous proportionality by the 17th proposition of the eighth book, it follows by the 8th proposition of the same that one mean also falls between **d** and **c**. Thus, since **d** is a square, by the 20th proposition of the same, **c** is also a square, which is what was proposed.

**d** ————    **c** ————

### Proposition 32.

**[O]**f every triangle, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior angles opposite to it; and it is necessary that all three of its angles together are equal to two <term>right angles</term><note>A right angle is 90 degrees; therefore, two right angles equal 180 degrees, the sum of a triangle's angles.</note>.

¶ Let there be triangle **a.b.c.** whose side **b.c.** is extended to **d.** I say that the exterior angle **c** <note>original: "angulus.c.extrinsecus"; the text refers to the angle formed outside the triangle at vertex C.</note> is equal to the two interior angles **a** and **b** opposite to it joined together; and that the three angles of triangle **a.b.c.** joined together are equal to two right angles.

From point **c**, I draw **c.f.** parallel to **a.b.** according to the teaching of the preceding [proposition]: angle **f.c.a.** will be equal to angle **a** because they are <term>alternate angles</term><note>When a line crosses two parallel lines, the angles on opposite sides of the crossing line are equal.</note> by the first part of [proposition] 29; and exterior angle **f.c.d.** is equal to interior angle **b** by the second part of the same. Therefore, the whole exterior [angle] **a.c.d.** is equal to the two interior angles **a** and **b** opposite to it; which is the first [part]. And because the two angles **a.c.b.** and **a.c.d.** are equal to two right angles by [proposition] 13, the three interior angles **a**, **b**, and **c** will be equal to two right angles; which is the second thing proposed.

¶ From this, however, it is clear that for any polygonal figure, all the angles taken together are equal to as many right angles as the number by which it is distant from the first [figure], doubled. For example, of polygonal figures, the triangle is the first; because if it were made of only two lines—since a figure must be an enclosure of lines—then two straight lines would include a surface, which is impossible by the <term>last postulate</term><note>Euclid's axioms state that two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>. Quadrilaterals are the second; pentagons the third. Likewise, any figure will be in that order according to the number of its sides or angles, once <term>two</term><note>original: "binario"</note> is subtracted from it.

I say therefore that for a triangle, which is the first, all angles are equal to two right angles. For a quadrilateral, which is the second, they will be equal to four right angles; and for a pentagon, which is the third, they will be equal to six right angles. This is manifest because any such figure can be resolved into as many triangles as its distance from the first, by drawing straight lines from any of its angles to all the opposite angles. Since all the angles of every triangle are equal to two right angles, all many-sided figures will have angles equal to twice as many right angles as its distance from the first; which is what was proposed. 

For example: let there be pentagon **a.b.c.d.e.** From its angle **a**, I draw lines to angles **c** and **d** opposite it. The whole pentagon will be resolved into triangles **a.b.c.**, **a.c.d.**, and **a.d.e.** Since the angles of each of these are equal to two right angles, the pentagon's angles will be equal to six right angles; which is double that number by which it is distant from the first [the triangle], or double the number of its angles or sides after subtracting two.

¶ We can also propose the same thing this way: saying that all the angles of any polygonal figure taken together are equal to as many right angles as double the number of its angles, with four subtracted. For by marking any point within the figure and drawing lines from it to each angle, the figure itself will be resolved into as many triangles as it has angles. Therefore, all the angles of all those triangles taken together will be equal to twice as many right angles as there are angles in the figure. Since all the angles of the triangles surrounding that middle point are equal to four right angles by [proposition] 13, the proposition is clearly established.

¶ Similarly, it is also clear that for any polygonal figure, all the <term>exterior angles</term> are equal to four right angles. For the interior and exterior angles together are equal to twice as many right angles as the figure has angles, by [proposition] 13. But the interior ones are equal to twice as many right angles as there are angles, minus four. Therefore, the exterior ones must be equal to four right angles; which is what was proposed.

For example: let the sides of the proposed pentagon be extended so that exterior angles are made. **a.b.** is extended to **f**, **b.c.** to **g**, **c.d.** to **h**, **d.e.** to **k**, and **e.a.** to **l**. By [proposition] 13, the two angles—interior **a** and exterior **a**—will be equal to two right angles; and by the same reasoning, the two angles—interior **b** and exterior **b**; and so on...

### **Proposition 33.**
**IF** two other lines connect the ends of two lines that are parallel and of equal length, those lines will also be equal and parallel.
Let there be two lines $ab$ and $cd$, equal and parallel, whose extremities I join with the lines $ac$ and $bd$. I say that these lines are also equal and parallel. I draw the line $ad$. Because lines $ab$ and $cd$ are parallel, angle $bad$ will be equal to angle $adc$ by the first part of Proposition 29 <note>original: "p p̄mā ptē.29."</note>. Therefore, the two sides $ab$ and $ad$ of triangle $abd$ will be equal to the two sides $dc$ and $da$ of triangle $dca$, and angle $a$ of the first triangle is equal to angle $d$ of the second. Therefore, by Proposition 4, the base $bd$ of the first is equal to the base $ac$ of the second, and angle $adb$ of the first is equal to angle $dac$ of the second. Furthermore, because these are alternate angles <note>original: "coalterni"</note>, the lines $bd$ and $ac$ will be parallel according to Proposition 27. And since it was previously proven that they are equal, both parts of the proposition are clear.

[Diagram: A parallelogram abdc with a diagonal ad.]

### **Proposition 34.**
**EVERY** surface bounded by parallel sides <note>A parallelogram.</note> has opposite sides and angles that are equal to one another, and the diameter <note>The diagonal.</note> divides the surface in half.
Let there be a surface $abcd$ of parallel sides, such that line $ab$ is parallel to $cd$, and $ac$ is parallel to $bd$. I say that the two lines $ab$ and $cd$, as well as the two lines $ac$ and $bd$, are equal. Similarly, I say that angle $a$ is equal to angle $d$, and angle $b$ to angle $c$. I draw the diameter $ad$, which also divides that surface through the middle. Since $ab$ and $cd$ are parallel, angles $bad$ and $cda$ (which are alternate) will be equal by Proposition 29. Also, since $ac$ and $db$ are parallel, angles $cad$ and $bda$ (which are alternate) will be equal by the same proposition. I consider the two triangles $adb$ and $dac$. Since the two angles $a$ and $d$ of triangle $adb$ are equal to the two angles $d$ and $a$ of triangle $dac$, and the side $ad$ upon which those angles lie is common to both triangles, then by Proposition 26, side $ab$ will be equal to side $cd$, side $ac$ to side $bd$, and angle $b$ to angle $c$. And because the whole angle $a$ is clearly equal to the whole angle $d$ by the second common notion <note>The "Common Notion" that if equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.</note>, the entire proposition with its corollary is evident.

[Diagram: A parallelogram abdc with a diagonal ad.]

Therefore, line $d.e.$ is parallel to line $a.c.$, which is a proposition that will be useful to you for the fifth [proposition] of the fourth [book].

<margin>Corollary</margin>

**S** ¶ If two equal triangles are established upon equal bases on one and the same line and on the same side, it is necessary that they be contained between two parallel lines.

¶ Let there be two equal triangles $a.b.c.$ and $d.e.f.$ established upon two bases, $b.c.$ and $e.f.$, and on the same side. I say they are between two parallel lines. This is the converse of Proposition 38, and it is proved by it just as the preceding was proved by Proposition 37. From point $a$, let a line be drawn parallel to line $b.f.$ If it passes through point $d$, the proposition is clear. If, however, it passes above, as line $a.g.$, let $e.d.$ be extended to it at point $g$, and let line $g.f.$ be drawn. Then, by Proposition 38, triangle $a.b.c.$ will be equal to triangle $g.e.f.$; therefore, triangle $d.e.f.$ would be equal to triangle $g.e.f.$—a part to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, it will not pass above. Let it then pass below, and let it cut line $d.e.$ at point $h$ <note>The transcription reads .b. but the logic and diagram imply a point like .h. or .k. to avoid confusion with the base.</note>, and let line $f.h.$ be drawn. Triangle $h.e.f.$ would then be equal to triangle $a.b.c.$, and thus to triangle $d.e.f.$—a part to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, because it cannot pass anywhere except through point $d$, the proposition is clear.

[Diagram 2: Two equal triangles abc and def on the same baseline.]

**S** ¶ If a parallelogram and a triangle are established on the same base and within the same parallel lines, the parallelogram will happen to be double the triangle.

¶ Let there be a parallelogram $a.b.c.d.$ and a triangle $e.b.d.$ on the base $b.d.$ and between lines $a.e.$ and $b.d.$ which are parallel. I say the parallelogram is double the triangle. I shall draw the diameter $a.d.$ in the parallelogram, and triangle $a.b.d.$ will be half of the parallelogram by the conclusion of Proposition 34. And because triangle $e.b.d.$ is equal to triangle $a.b.d.$ by Proposition 37, it is clear that triangle $e.b.d.$ is half of the parallelogram $a.b.c.d.$, which is what was proposed. Similarly, it can also be proved that if a parallelogram and a triangle are established on equal bases and between parallel lines, the parallelogram will be double the triangle. Euclid did not set this down separately because it is easily clear from this and the preceding corollary, and from Proposition 38, by dividing the parallelogram into two triangles by a diameter, or [by constructing them] on the base of the parallelogram between the same parallel lines.

### Proposition 42.
To describe a surface of equidistant sides [a parallelogram] whose angle is equal to an assigned angle, and the surface itself is equal to an assigned triangle.
Let the assigned angle be $A$, and the assigned triangle be $BCD$. I wish to describe a surface of equidistant sides equal to triangle $BCD$, of which each of the two angles positioned opposite one another is equal to $A$. I divide the base $CD$ in half at point $E$, and I draw line $BE$, and from point $B$ I lead $BF$ equidistant [parallel] to $CD$. Through [Proposition] 38, triangle $BED$ will be equal to triangle $BEC$; wherefore triangle $BED$ is half of the total triangle $BCD$. Therefore, upon point $E$ of line $DC$, I constitute angle $DEG$ equal to angle $A$, and I complete the parallelogram $GEFD$. Because through the preceding [proposition] it is also double to triangle $BED$, it will also be equal to triangle $BCD$ through this common notion: those things whose halves are equal are also equal themselves. For triangle $BED$ is the half of both; wherefore we have described the parallelogram $GEFD$ equal to triangle $BCD$, of which each of the two opposite angles $GED$ and $DFG$ is equal to angle $A$, which was proposed.

### Proposition 43.
In every parallelogram space, it is necessary that the complements of those parallelograms which are about the diameter [diagonal] are equal to one another.
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram in which I shall draw the diameter $BC$, and I shall draw $EF$ equidistant to each of the two sides $AB$ and $CD$, which cuts the diameter at point $K$. From [this point] I shall lead $KG$ equidistant to each of the two sides $AC$ and $BD$, and I shall produce it until it cuts each side $AB$ and $CD$. Let the whole [line] be $GKB$. It will be that the whole parallelogram $ABCD$ is divided into four parallelograms, of which two—namely $ECKB$ and $GKBF$—are said to consist about $CB$ because the diameter passes through their middle, and therefore they are about the diameter. The remaining two, namely $AEGK$ and $KHFD$, are called "complements." It is said that these two complements are equal. For there are two triangles, $ABC$ and $CDB$, equal through the conclusion of [Proposition] 34. Similarly, also, the two triangles $GKB$ and $FKB$ [Note: likely $GKB$ and $BFE$ in typical diagrams] are equal through the same conclusion of 34. And the two triangles $CEK$ and $KHC$ [are] similarly equal through the same corollary. Therefore, with the two triangles $BGK$ and $KCC$ [sic, $KEC$] taken away from the total triangle $ABC$, and the two remaining triangles $BFK$ and $KCH$ taken from the other total triangle $CDB$, the remainders—which are the two said complements—will be equal through a common notion; which is what was proposed.

[Image: Diagram for Proposition 43 showing a large parallelogram divided by a diameter and inner lines]

### Proposition 44.
A straight line being proposed, to describe upon it a surface of equidistant sides whose angle is equal to an assigned angle, and the surface itself equal to an assigned triangle.
To describe a surface of equidistant sides upon some line is to make that line one side of the surface itself. Therefore, let $AB$ be the given line, $C$ the given angle, and $DEF$ the given triangle. Upon line $AB$, I wish to describe one surface of equidistant sides so that line $AB$ is one of its sides, and each of its two opposite angles is equal to angle $C$, and the total surface itself is equal to triangle $DEF$. This [proposition] differs from 42 because here it gives the side of the one surface to be described, namely line $AB$, but there [it gave] none. When therefore I wish to do this, I join line $AG...$

...to line $AB$ in a straight line, which I set equal to line $CF$, the base of the given triangle, upon which I constitute one triangle equal and equilateral [congruent] to it. Which I do in this manner: I constitute angle $AGK$ equal to angle $C$, and angle $GAK$ equal to angle $F$ through [Proposition] 23. and since $GA$ had been placed equal to $CF$, triangle $GAK$ will be equal and equilateral to triangle $CFD$ through [Proposition] 26. I shall therefore divide $GA$ into equal parts at point $B$ [Note: $B$ is likely an error for a new point $H$ in the geometry], and I shall draw $KB$, and I shall lead from point $K$ a line $MKN$ equidistant to line $GB$. Through [Proposition] 38, triangle $ABK$ will be equal to triangle $GBK$. Then, upon point $A$ of line $GA$, I shall make angle $GAL$ through [Proposition] 23 equal to the given angle $C$; and I shall complete upon base $AB$ and between the equidistant lines $GB$ and $MN$ the surface of equidistant sides $MLBA$, which through [Proposition] 41 will be double to triangle $KBA$, wherefore it is equal to the total triangle $KGA$, and wherefore also to the given triangle $DEF$. I shall therefore draw $BN$ equidistant to $AL$, and I shall produce the diameter $NA$, which I shall draw out until it concurs with $MB$ at point $O$, and I shall complete the surface of equidistant sides $MONQ$. And because through [Proposition] 15, angle $LAB$ is equal to angle $BAP$, therefore angle $BAP$ is equal to angle $C$. Therefore, upon the given line $AB$, there has been described a surface of equidistant sides $ABPQ$ equal to the given triangle $DEF$, each of whose two opposite angles, which are $APQ$ [Note: likely $ABQ$ and $APQ$], is equal to the given angle $C$; which was proposed.

### Proposition 45.
To describe a square from a given line.
Let $AB$ be the given line, from which I wish to [describe a square]. From points $A$ and $B$ of line $AB$, I lead through [Proposition] 11 lines $AC$ and $BD$ perpendicular to line $AB$, which will be equidistant through the last part of [Proposition] 28. And I set each of them equal to the same $AB$ through the second [proposition], and I draw line $CD$. It will be equal and equidistant to line $AB$ through [Proposition] 33. And because each of the two angles $A$ and $B$ is a right angle, each of the two $C$ and $D$ will be a right angle through the last part of [Proposition] 29. Therefore, by definition, $ABCD$ is a square, which is what was proposed.
The same otherwise: let $AC$ be perpendicular upon line $AB$ through [Proposition] 11, and let it be equal to it as before. And from point $C$, through [Proposition] 31, let $CD$ be led equidistant to $AB$, and let it be set equal to it. And let line $DB$ be led, which through [Proposition] 33 will be equal and equidistant to $AC$. And all angles are right through the last part of [Proposition] 29; wherefore by definition we have the [result] proposed.

### Notes on the Latin and OCR:
1.  **Proposition Numbering:** This text follows the Campanus of Novara tradition. In modern editions of Euclid, Proposition 45 is usually 46 (the square), and 46 is 47 (the Pythagorean Theorem).
2.  **Abbreviation *conel'*:** This appears to be a shorthand for *conclusio* (conclusion) or *corollarium* (corollary). In this context, it refers to the results previously established in Proposition 34.
3.  **OCR Unclear Readings:**
    *   *adra...* in Prop 45: Clearly intended to be *quadratum describere*.
    *   *bas iz / basiz*: A typo for *basim* (base).
    *   *mioꝝ*: Expanded as *minorum* (smaller).
    *   *ypothemisas*: A medieval Latinization of the Greek for hypotenuses, often used for auxiliary lines in the Pythagorean construction.
    *   *fm*: Standard abbreviation for *secundum* (according to).

But triangle $B, F, C$ is equal to triangle $B, A, D$ by Proposition 4, because sides $F, B$ and $B, C$ of the first [triangle] are equal to sides $A, B$ and $B, D$ of the latter, and angle $B$ of the first is equal to angle $B$ of the latter, for each consists of a right angle and the common angle $A, B, C$. Therefore, the parallelogram $B, F, G, A$ is double the triangle $A, B, D$. 

But the parallelogram $B, D, L, M$ is also double the same triangle by Proposition 41, because they are established upon the same base, namely $B, D$, and between the parallel lines $B, D$ and $A, L$. Therefore, by <term>common notion</term><note>original: "cōmunē sciām" — referring to Euclid's Axioms or Common Notions, specifically "things equal to the same thing are equal to each other."</note> the square $A, B, F, G$ and the parallelogram $B, D, L, M$ are equal, because their halves—namely the aforementioned triangles—are equal. In the same way and through the same propositions, using triangles $K, B, C$ and $A, E, C$ as intermediaries, we shall prove that the square $A, C, B, K$ is equal to the parallelogram $C, E, L, M$. Therefore the proposition is evident.

### Proposition 47
<note>This is the converse of the Pythagorean Theorem, typically numbered as Proposition 48 in standard editions.</note>

**If the [square] produced from one side of a triangle multiplied by itself is equal to the two squares described from the two remaining sides, then the angle which that side opposes is a right angle.**

¶ To multiply a line by itself is to describe its square. ¶ Let there be a triangle $A, B, C$, and let the square of side $A, C$ be equal to the squares of the two sides $A, B$ and $B, C$ joined together. I say that angle $B$, which side $A, C$ opposes, is a right angle; and this is the <term>converse</term> of the previous [proposition]. 

¶ From point $B$, I draw line $B, D$ perpendicular to line $B, C$ by Proposition 11, which I set as equal to $A, B$, and I extend line $D, C$. By the preceding proposition <note>referring to the Pythagorean theorem just proven</note>, the square of $D, C$ will be equal to the two squares of the two lines $D, B$ and $B, C$. And because $B, D$ was placed as equal to $B, A$, it will be by common notion—which states that the squares of equal lines are equal—that the squares of the two lines $A, B$ and $B, D$ are equal. Wherefore, the square of $D, C$ will be equal to the square of $A, C$. Therefore, by another common notion which is the converse of the previous—namely, that lines whose squares are equal are themselves equal—$D, C$ will be equal to $A, C$. Wherefore, by Proposition 8, angle $B$ of triangle $A, B, C$ is a right angle, which is what was to be proposed.

### Proposition 48
<note>Typically Proposition 47 in some alternate arrangements or a specific construction lemma.</note>

**Given any two squares, to describe a <term>gnomon</term> equal to the other square.**
<note>A gnomon is the L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger one.</note>

¶ Let two squares be proposed, namely $A, B$ and $C, D$, and let it be proposed to produce a gnomon around $A, B$ equal to the square $C, D$. Therefore, let one side of square $A, B$ be extended in a continuous straight line to the equality of one side of square $C, D$, and let this be $F, E$, so that $F, E$ is equal to one of the sides of square $C, D$. And from $E$, I shall draw a straight line to $A$. Let there be, therefore, a <term>right-angled triangle</term><note>original: "triangul⁹ orthogoni⁹"</note> because $F$ is a right angle. 

Therefore, let it be argued according to the <term>penultimate [proposition] of the first [book]</term><note>original: "fm penultimā primi" — This is a common medieval way to refer to the Pythagorean theorem (Prop. 47), as Book I usually has 48 or 49 propositions.</note> thus: the square of $E, A$ is as much as the square of $E, F$ and the square of $F, A$ [combined]. But the square of $E, F$ is equal to square $C, D$, and the square of $F, A$ is equal to square $A, B$. Therefore, the square of $A, E$ is equal to squares $A, B$ and $C, D$ [together]. Likewise, $E, F, A$ is a triangle, therefore the sides $E, F$ and $F, A$ are longer...

Every **rectangular parallelogram** <term>rectangular parallelogram: essentially what we call a rectangle today; a four-sided shape with opposite sides parallel and all right angles</term> is said to be **contained** by the two lines that form the right angle.

¶ A **parallelogram** is a surface with sides that are equidistant <note>original: *equidistātū*; in modern terms, we say the sides are parallel</note> from each other.

¶ A **rectangular parallelogram** is one that has all right angles. It is produced by extending one of the two sides that form its angle into the other; for this reason, it is said to be "contained" by those two lines.

In every parallelogram-shaped area, those parallelograms that the **diameter** <note>original: *diameter*. In this historical context, the "diameter" of a square or rectangle refers to what we now call the diagonal.</note> cuts through the middle are said to **stand around** that same diameter.

Of those parallelograms that stand around the same diameter, any one of them taken together with the two **supplements** <note>the two remaining areas in the larger parallelogram that the diagonal does not pass through</note> is named a **gnomon** <term>gnomon: an L-shaped area remaining after a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from a corner of a larger one</term>.

¶ Which parallelograms are said to "stand around the diameter" and which are the "supplements" was explained above in the 43rd demonstration of the first book. ¶ For let there be a parallelogram **a.b.c.d.** whose diameter is **a.d.** Let two lines **e.f.** and **g.h.** be drawn parallel to the opposite sides of the said parallelogram, intersecting each other on the diameter **a.d.** at point **k**. The parallelogram itself will then be divided into four smaller parallelograms. Each of the two parallelograms which are **a.g.e.k.** and **k.f.h.d.**, which the diameter cuts through the middle, is said to "stand around the diameter." The remaining two, which the diameter does not cut, are called **supplements**. These two supplements, along with either of the aforementioned parallelograms standing around the diameter, compose a certain figure called a **gnomon**. This gnomon lacks only the one remaining parallelogram standing around the diameter to complete the entire parallelogram; if that were added above...

# Book II

## Proposition 2.
**S**i a line be divided into parts, the product <note>original: "ductu," literally a "leading" or "drawing" of one line along another to form an area</note> of the whole line multiplied by itself is equal to the products of the whole line multiplied by each of its parts.

¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into **a.c.**, **c.d.**, and **d.b.** I say that the product of the whole **a.b.** into itself—which is the area **a.c.b.f.**—is equal to the products of the whole line into each of the said parts, which will be clearly seen once **c.g.** and **d.h.** are drawn parallel to **a.c.** and **b.f.** ¶ Alternatively, let a line **k.** be taken equal to **a.b.** By the previous proposition, the product of **k.** into the whole **a.b.** is equal to the product of **k.** into all the parts of **a.b.** And because the product of **k.** into **a.b.** is as much as **a.b.** into itself, and **k.** into all the parts of **a.b.** is as much as **a.b.** into all its own parts (because **k.** and **a.b.** are equal), it is clear that the proposition is true.

## Proposition 3.
**S**i a line be divided into two parts, the product of the whole line multiplied by either of the parts is equal to the product of that part multiplied by itself plus the product of the two parts multiplied by each other.

¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into **a.c.** and **b.c.** I say that the product of the whole **a.b.** into its part **a.c.** is equal to the square of that same part **a.c.** and the product of that same part **a.c.** into **b.c.** Let the square of line **a.c.** be made, which is **a.c.d.f.**, and let the surface <note>The word "superficies" refers to the area or 2D shape.</note> **a.b.d.e.** be completed; the proposition will then be clear. ¶ Alternatively, let **g.** be equal to **a.c.** Since **b.a.** into **a.c.** is the same as **a.c.** into **a.b.** (and vice versa), and **a.c.** into **a.b.** is the same as **a.c.** into **c.b.** and into itself (just as **g.** into the same), and since by the first proposition of this book **g.** into the whole **a.b.** is the same as into **a.c.** and **c.b.**, the proposition is clear: namely, that **a.c.** into **a.b.** is the same as into itself and into **c.b.** Therefore, conversely, **a.b.** into **a.c.** is the same as **a.c.** into itself and into **c.b.**, which is what we wanted to demonstrate.

->[Diagram: A rectangle divided into two vertical sections. The top vertices are **d, f, e** and the bottom are **a, c, b**. A line **g** is to the left.]<-

## Proposition 4.
**S**i a line be divided into two parts, the square produced by the whole line multiplied by itself is equal to the squares of both parts and twice the product of one part multiplied by the other. ¶ From this it is manifest that in every square, the two surfaces through which the diameter <note>original: "diameter," referring to the diagonal line of the square.</note> cuts through the middle are both themselves squares.

¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into **a.c.** and **b.c.** I say that the square of the whole **a.b.** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **b.c.** and double that which is produced by the multiplication of one of them by the other. I shall describe the square of one of the parts; let it be **c.d.b.e.**, the square of line **c.b.** To this I shall join a <term>gnomon</term> <note>An L-shaped geometric figure formed by removing a smaller square from a corner of a larger one.</note> following the direct path of the other line, namely **a.c.**, which I shall do in this way: in the described square I shall draw the diagonal **b.d.**, and from point **a.** I shall draw a perpendicular line to line **a.b.**, which shall be **a.k.** I shall extend **a.k.** and the diagonal **b.d.** until they meet at point **f.** From point **f.** I shall produce **f.g.** parallel to line **a.b.**, and I shall extend **f.g.** and **b.e.** until they meet at point **g.** <note>The text likely means extending the lines to complete the outer square.</note> And I shall extend **c.d.** to **h.** and **e.d.** to **k.** And because the two sides **d.e.** and **e.b.** of triangle **d.e.b.** are equal, by the 5th proposition of the first book, the two angles **e.d.b.** and **e.b.d.** will be equal. And because angle **e.** is a right angle, by the 32nd proposition of the first book, each of them will be half of a right angle. By the same reasoning, each of the two angles **c.d.b.** and **c.b.d.** will be half of a right angle. Therefore, by the second part of the 29th proposition of the first book, each of the four angles **b.f.d.**, **b.d.f.**, **k.f.d.**, and **k.d.f.** will be half of a right angle. Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the first book, **f.g.** and **g.b.** are equal, and similarly **f.a.** and **a.b.** By like reasoning **f.h.** and **h.d.**, and also **f.k.** and **k.d.** Wherefore each of the two surfaces **a.b.g.f.** and **k.d.h.f.** is a square. And because the total square **a.b.f.g.**, which is the square of line **a.b.**, consists of two squares that stand around the diagonal (which are the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**) and of two <term>supplements</term> <note>The remaining rectangles in a divided square that are not the primary squares along the diagonal.</note>, each of which is produced from **a.c.** into **b.c.**, our proposition is clear. ¶ Alternatively, let line **a.b.** be divided as before into **a.c.** and **c.b.**

## Proposition 8

**SI** <note>Large decorative initial S</note> a line is divided into two parts, and a line equal to one of those parts is added to its length: the square created from the whole combined line multiplied by itself will be equal to four times the rectangle formed by the original line and the added part, plus the square of the other part.

¶ Let AB be divided at point C in whatever way it happens. To this, let BD be added, which is equal to CB. I say that the square of the whole line AD—which is ADEF—is equal to four times the product of AB and BD, plus the square of AC. This will be made clear by drawing the diagonal DE and the lines CG and BH parallel to the line DF, cutting the diagonal at points K and L. Through these points, let PQ, KR, and MN, LO be drawn parallel to AD. For by the fourth corollary of this book <note>Euclid II.4</note>, each of the surfaces <term>surfaces</term><note>In this context, "surfaces" refers to the geometric areas or rectangles formed within the larger square.</note> RG, NQ, and BM will be squares. And because CB was set as equal to BD, both surfaces CL and LP will be squares. There will be four equal squares dividing the square CP. And because the entire <term>gnomon</term><note>A gnomon is the L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller square is removed from a corner of a larger square.</note> surrounding the square RG is four times the size of the rectangle formed by AB and BD, and four times the surface AL, the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 12.

**I**n those triangles that have an obtuse angle: the side <note>The text uses "ea que... subtendit," referring to the side of the triangle opposite the angle.</note> that stretches opposite the obtuse angle is greater in its power than the squares of both the remaining sides containing the obtuse angle by as much as twice the rectangle contained under one of those sides and the line added to it in a straight line toward the obtuse angle, which is marked off by the perpendicular outside the triangle.

¶Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** having angle **a** as obtuse. From point **c**, let a perpendicular line be drawn to line **b.a.**, which will necessarily fall outside the triangle **a.b.c.**; otherwise, the obtuse angle would be a right angle or less than a right angle by the 16th proposition of the first book. Let **c.d.** therefore be the perpendicular upon line **a.b.** extended as far as **d**. I say that the square of side **b.c.**, which is stretched opposite the obtuse angle, is greater than the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.c.** surrounding the obtuse angle by as much as twice that which is formed from **b.a.** times **a.d.** Indeed, the "power" <note>The term "potentia" refers to the area of the square formed by a line. To "be able" (posse) means to have an area equal to a square.</note> of a line with respect to its square is such that any line is said to "be able" to do as much as the product of it being multiplied by itself. For by the 4th proposition of this book, the square of **b.d.** will be equal to the two squares of the two lines **b.a.** and **a.d.** and twice that which is formed from **b.a.** times **a.d.** And because the square of **b.c.** (by the second-to-last proposition of the first book <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Book I, Prop 47).</note>) is equal to the square of **b.d.** and the square of **d.c.**, it will be equal to the squares of the three lines **b.a.**, **a.d.**, and **d.c.**, and twice that which is formed from **b.a.** into **a.d.** But by the same rule, the square of **a.c.** is equal to the squares of **a.d.** and **d.c.** Therefore, the square of **b.c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **b.a.** and **c.a.** and twice that which is formed from **b.a.** times **a.d.** Wherefore **b.c.** is "able" to do more than the two lines **b.a.** and **a.c.** by twice that which is formed from **b.a.** times **a.d.** For we have already said that any line is said to be "able" as much as the product of it multiplied by itself, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .1.

**To find the center of a given circle.** Whence it is manifest that of two straight lines terminated at the circumference in the same circle, neither bisects the other orthogonally unless it passes through the center.

Let the proposed circle be $a.b.c.$, of which we wish to find the center. I draw in the circle itself a line $a.c.$ in whatever way it may happen, which I divide into equal [parts] at point $d.$ From this [point] I draw a perpendicular to line $a.c.$, which I join to the circumference on both sides, namely $e.d.b.$ This I again divide into equal [parts] at point $f$, which I say is the center of the circle. 

For if it is not, it will be either elsewhere, either on the line $e.b.$ or outside it. It is not on the line $e.b.$, for if it were in it, such as at point $g$, the line $e.f.$ would be greater than line $e.g.$, namely the part [being greater] than the whole, which is impossible. 

But if it were outside the line $e.b.$, as at point $h$ [OCR: $b$], let the lines $h.a, h.d, h.e$ be drawn. And because the sides $h.d$ and $d.a$ of triangle $h.d.a$ are equal to the sides $h.d$ and $d.e$ [sic, likely $d.c$] of triangle $h.d.e$, and the base $h.a$ [is equal] to base $h.e$, the angle $a.d.h$ will be equal to angle $e.d.h$ by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book]. Wherefore each is a right angle; and since the angle $a.d.b$ had also been a right angle, $a.d.h$ would be equal to $a.d.b$ by the 3rd postulate [OCR: *petitionem*] of the first [book], namely the [part] to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore the center of the given circle is not anywhere but at point $f$, which was proposed.
