### Proposition 13.

**To describe a circle within a given equilateral and equiangular pentagon.**

Let there be an assigned equilateral and equiangular pentagon—for this is not necessarily possible for other types <note>Only "regular" pentagons (those with equal sides and angles) allow for a perfectly centered inscribed circle.</note>—labeled **a, b, c, d**. I wish to inscribe a circle within it. This is essentially the converse of Proposition 11. I divide two of its adjacent angles, which are **a** and **e**, into equal halves by drawing lines **a, f** and **e, f** until they meet at point **f** inside the pentagon, which I say is the center of the circle. They will meet because half of the total angle **a** and similarly half of the total angle **e** is less than a right angle. <note>In a regular pentagon, the internal angles are 108 degrees; half of that is 54 degrees. Since 54 + 54 is less than 180, the lines must eventually intersect according to Euclid's parallel postulate.</note>

If they did not meet inside the pentagon, they would meet either outside the pentagon, or on a side of the pentagon, or at one of its angles opposite the two respective angles.

Suppose they first meet outside at point **f**. Let line **b, f** be drawn. Because the two sides **e, a** and **a, f** of triangle **e, a, f** are equal to the two sides **b, a** and **a, f** of triangle **b, a, f**, and angle **a** of one is equal to angle **a** of the other, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book], the base **e, f** will be equal to the base **f, b**. And because the partial angle **a** is equal to the partial angle **e** (on account of the total angle **a** being equal to the total angle **e**), it will follow by the 6th [proposition] of the first [book] that **f, a** is equal to **f, e**. Therefore, **f, a** is equal to **f, b**. Thus, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], the two angles—the total **b** and the partial **a**—are equal. This would mean that the partial angle **a** is equal to or greater than the total angle **a**, which is impossible.

Suppose, then, they meet at point **f** upon the side **b, c**. By arguing through the same premises and method, the partial angle **a** would be equal to the total angle **a**, which is impossible. If by chance they should meet at angle **c**, it would be by the same [reasons] and in the same way that **c, b** would be equal to **c, a**, and therefore yet again, as before, partial angle **a** would be equal to total angle **a**.

Since this cannot be, let the point of intersection, which is **f**, be within the pentagon. From this point, I draw 5 perpendicular lines to its 5 sides, which shall be **f, g**, **f, b**, **f, k**, **f, l**, and **f, m**. <note>The letter **b** in **f, b** may be a transcription error for **h**, following the alphabetical sequence of the other points.</note> And to its two adjacent angles on either side of the divided angles, which are **b** and **d**, I draw lines **f, b** and **f, d**. Because the two angles **a** and **m** of triangle **a, f, m** are equal to the two angles **a** and **g** of triangle **a, f, g**, and side **a, f** is common, then by the 26th [proposition] of the first [book], **f, m** is equal to **f, g**. By the same [reasoning], you will also prove **f, l** is equal to **f, m**, taking the two triangles **z, f, m** and **e, f, l**. Because again the two sides **a, f** and **a, b** of triangle **a, f, b** are equal to the two sides **a, f** and **a, e** of triangle **a, f, e**, and angle **a** of one is equal to angle **a** of the other, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book], the partial angle **b** is equal to the partial angle **e**. And because the total angle **b** is equal to the total angle **e**, and the total angle **e** has been divided into equal parts, then the total angle **b** is also divided into equal parts. In the same way, you will prove that the total angle **d** is divided into equal parts because of the equality of partial angle **d** and partial angle **a**, taking triangles **e, a, f** and **e, d, f**. Understand the same regarding the quindecagon (15 sides); through it, figures of 30 and 60 sides will be known, and all those whose sides are continuously doubled.

### Definition 1
[Decorative initial **P**] **A part** is a quantity of a larger quantity, the smaller of the larger, when the smaller measures the larger.

¶ **Part** is sometimes taken in the proper sense: and this is that which, when taken a certain number of times, constitutes its whole precisely, without decrease or increase; it is said to "measure" its whole by that number according to which it is taken to form the whole. He [Euclid] defines such a part here, which we call a <term>multiplicative part</term> <note>A "multiplicative part" is an exact divisor, like 2 is a part of 6. This is distinct from a "part" in the general sense, like 2 being a part of 5.</note>. ¶ It is sometimes taken in a common sense: and this is any smaller quantity which, however many times it is taken, results in less or more than its whole. This we call an <term>aggregative part</term>; it is so called because it constitutes its whole together with another different quantity, but by itself, however many times it is taken, it does not produce the whole.

### Definition 2
[Decorative initial **M**] **A multiple** is the larger of the smaller when the smaller measures it.

¶ **Part** is spoken of in relation to the **whole**: and their relationship to each other consists of these two extremes. Therefore, having defined the smaller extreme, he [Euclid] here defines the larger. He calls it a "multiple" because the smaller, taken a certain number of times, constitutes it. Therefore, they are terms said in relation to each other: "part" and "multiple." For every part is a <term>submultiple</term> <note>Latin: *submultiplex*. If 10 is a multiple of 2, then 2 is the submultiple of 10.</note>, as is clear from its definition.

### Definition 3
[Decorative initial **P**] **Ratio** <note>original: *proportio*. While the text uses the word "proportion," in modern mathematics, this relationship between two quantities is called a "ratio."</note> is a certain relation of one quantity to another, of two quantities of whatever size, provided they are of the same kind.

¶ **Ratio** is the relationship of two things of the same kind to each other, in that one of them is larger or smaller than the other, or equal to it. For ratio is not only found in quantities, but also in weights, powers, and sounds. Plato, in the *Timaeus*, wishes ratio to exist in weights and powers where he demonstrates the number of elements; that ratio exists in sounds is clear from music. For as Boethius says in his fourth book [of *De Institutione Musica*], if any string is divided into two unequal parts, there will be the same ratio between those parts and their sounds, in an inverse manner. But in whatever things ratio is found, they participate in the nature and property of quantity; for it is not found in any two things except in the sense that one of them is larger, smaller, or equal to the other. ¶ Moreover, it is a property of quantity that something is called "equal" or "unequal" according to it, as Aristotle intends in the *Categories* <note>original: *Praedicamentis*. This refers to Aristotle’s work on the classification of things.</note>. From this it is clear that ratio is primarily found in quantity, and through quantity in all other things. Nor is there a ratio in any things which does not have something similar in some quantities. For this reason, Euclid rightly said that ratio exists simply in quantity when he defined it through the relationship of two quantities of the same kind to each other. ¶ The understanding of this definition is: that ratio is the relationship of two quantities to each other, which is considered in that one of them is larger or smaller than the other, or equal to it. By this it is clear that they must be of the same kind: such as two numbers, or two lines, or two surfaces, or two bodies, or two places, or two times. For it cannot...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of mathematical proportions, likely following a general definition of quantity or magnitude. It transitions from general comparisons to the specific classification of rational and commensurable proportions.</meta>

**BOOK**

A line cannot be called greater or lesser than a surface or a body, nor can time be compared to place. Rather, a line is compared to a line, and a surface to a surface. For only **univocal** <note>Things of the same kind or category, sharing a single definition or nature.</note> things are comparable to one another.

When the text mentions a "certain relation," you should not understand this to mean "known" or "perceived," but rather "determined," so that the sense is: **Proportion** is the determined relation of two quantities—so determined, I say, that it is this specific relation and no other. It is not necessary for every relation between two quantities to be known by us, nor even by nature. 

¶ For one type of proportion concerns **discrete** <term>discrete quantities: things made of distinct, separate units, such as whole numbers</term> things, like numbers, while another concerns **continuous** <term>continuous quantities: things that are unbroken and infinitely divisible, such as lines, surfaces, or time</term> things. In the case of numbers, the lesser is either a part or multiple parts of the greater, as is demonstrated in the seventh <note>Likely a reference to Book VII of Euclid’s *Elements*, which focuses on the theory of numbers.</note> book; therefore, in all of these, the relation is certain and known. 

¶ However, among continuous things, proportion is defined more broadly. Among them, there are cases where the lesser quantity is a part or parts of the larger; for all such things, the proportion is known through the mediation of numbers, and this is called a **rational** proportion. All such quantities are also called **commensurable** <note>original: *communicantes*; literally "communicating" or sharing a common measure.</note> because one and the same unit of measure necessarily measures both of them.

<summary>This passage defines proportion as a determined relationship between two quantities of the same kind, distinguishing between discrete proportions (numbers) and continuous proportions (geometry). It introduces the concept of rational or commensurable proportions where two quantities share a common measuring unit.</summary>

### PAGE 61

...of [propor]tions, because there is no proportion between quantities of different genera: and this will be established in at least three terms. However, [proportionality] is discontinuous when there are four quantities, whether all are of the same genus, or the first two are of one and the last two of another: so that by whatever proportion the first precedes the second, in the same [proportion] the third precedes the fourth: as when we say as $a$ is to $b$, so $c$ is to $d$. And any one of them will be either only an antecedent or only a consequent: nor is it necessary that all four be of the same genus as was the case in continuous proportionality: because the consequent of the first proportion does not continue as the antecedent of the second: but it is possible that they be of the same genus, and it is possible that they be of different [genera]. For just as it happens that a line is found to be double or triple to a line, so a surface to a surface: and a body to a body: and time to time: and a number to a number. Having seen what continuous and discontinuous proportionality are, let us explain the preceding definition of continuously proportionals. He says: "Quantities are continuously proportional whose equimultiples are either equal to each other, or those which add to or subtract from each other without interruption." For example: Let there be three quantities of the same genus, $a, b, c$, for which $d, e, f$ are taken as equimultiples: so that just as $d$ is a multiple of $a$, so $e$ is a multiple of $b$, and $f$ of $c$. And they will all be in the same genus. For multiples and submultiples are in the same genus. Let $d, e, f$ either be equal to each other: or let them behave in adding or subtracting such that as $d$ adds over $e$ or subtracts from it, so $e$ adds over $f$ or subtracts from it. When these multiples, I say, behave thus, the three quantities $a, b, c$ will be continuously proportional. However, you should not understand "similarly [**siliter** for *similiter*] to behave in adding or subtracting" in terms of quantity, but in terms of proportion: otherwise the definition would be false. For the equimultiples of any quantities of the same genus exceeding each other by equal differences also exceed each other by equal differences: whence they behave similarly in adding and subtracting as to the quantity of excess. Yet the prior quantities are not continuously proportional; rather, the smaller proportion is always the larger. This happens because their multiples do not exceed each other similarly in terms of proportion, but only in terms of the quantity of excess: for there, in the smaller multiples, is a larger proportion. For example: let three numbers be taken exceeding each other by equal differences, namely arithmetic [progression]: as 2, 3, 4. All equimultiples of these three exceed each other equally: doubles by two, triples by three, and so on for the rest: yet 2, 3, 4 are not continuously proportional: indeed the smaller proportion is larger: for their [first] proportion is sesquialterate [3:2] and the larger is sesquitertian [4:3]. Because there is no likeness of proportions between them, there will be no proportionality between them, neither continuous nor discontinuous. It is clear, therefore, that this likeness of addition or subtraction is not to be understood in terms of the quantity of excess, but in terms of proportion. Thus, the sense of the preceding definition will be: "Continuously proportionals are those whose all equal multiples are continuously proportional." But he did not wish to propose the definition under this form because then he would define the same by the same; yet clearly the matter is convertible with his definition. However, it is necessary for the three quantities $a, b, c$ to be of the same genus so that their multiples may be equal to each other, or behave similarly in adding or subtracting. For if $a$ and $b$ were of different genera, then $d$ and $e$ (the multiples of $a$ and $b$) would also be of those same different genera: because multiples and submultiples are of the same genus: wherefore $d$ would not be equal to $e$, nor greater or less than it. For quantities of different genera are not comparable to each other.

**Definition:** Quantities which are said to be according to one proportion, the first to the second and the third to the fourth, are those whose equimultiples of the first and third, when compared to the equimultiples of the second and fourth, are alike either in addition, or diminution, or equality, when taken in the same order.

Having set down the definition of continuously proportional quantities above, he here sets down the definition of discontinuously proportionals: which is that for any four quantities, if equimultiples of the first and third are taken, and equimultiples of the second and fourth: and the multiple of the first relates to the multiple of the second as to addition, diminution, or equality, just as the multiple of the third relates to the multiple of the fourth: then the proportion of the first of them to the second will be as the third to the fourth. For example: Let there be four quantities $a, b, c, d$. Let equimultiples be taken for the first and third, $a$ and $c$, such as doubles, which let be $e$ and $f$. Likewise for the second and fourth, $b$ and $d$, let other equimultiples be taken, such as triples, which are $g$ and $h$. Let these four multiples thus taken be compared to each other according to the order of the first four quantities: namely, as $e$ is compared to $g$ and $f$ to $h$ (but not $e$ to $f$ or $g$ to $h$), let them be similar in addition, diminution, and equality: namely, if $e$ exceeds $g$, similarly $f$ exceeds $h$; or if $e$ is less than $g$, $f$ is similarly less than $h$; or if $e$ is equal to $g$, $f$ is similarly equal to $h$. Then the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$. Let the likeness in adding or subtracting be understood here as in the definition of continuous proportionals: namely, not as to the quantity of excess, but as to proportion. As for what he says, "taken in the same order," let it be understood as explained: namely, that the multiples are not referred to each other according to the order of those quantities for which equimultiples are assumed—so that the multiple of the first is not referred to the multiple of the third, or the multiple of the second to the multiple of the fourth—but let it be referred according to the first order of the four quantities themselves: namely, the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth. Thus, the sense of this definition will be: "Discontinuously proportionals are four quantities whose proportion of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, when, having taken equimultiples of the first and third and equimultiples of the second and fourth, the proportion of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second will be as the proportion of the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth." But he did not define it under this form for the reason mentioned before, though in fact it is the same. It is not necessary, however, that the four quantities $a, b, c, d$ be of the same genus: because $b$ is not continued in proportion with $c$, but the first two can be of one genus and the following two of another. This is clear because it is necessary to refer the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth... **Definition:** When there are equimultiples of the first and third, and likewise equimultiples of the second and fourth, and the multiple of the first adds over the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not add over the multiple of the fourth: the first shall be said to be of a greater proportion to the second than the third to the fourth.

Having defined proportional quantities, he defines improportional quantities. Those are improportional between which there is a [lack of] likeness of proportions, which happens in two ways: either because the proportion of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, or because it is less; and therefore there are two species of it. The first is when the proportion of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, and this is called "greater improportionality." The second is when the proportion of the first to the second is less than the third to the fourth, and this is called "lesser improportionality." He therefore defines those between which there is a greater proportion... but he does not set down the definition of those between which there is a lesser proportion, because it is clear from the other. Therefore, when there are four quantities for whose first and third equimultiples are taken, and for the second and fourth equimultiples, and the multiples of the first and second related to each other do not behave similarly to the multiples of the third and fourth related to each other in addition, diminution, and equality: then these four quantities will be improportional. If it should be that the multiple of the first is equal to the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third is less than the multiple of the fourth; or that the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third is equal or less than the multiple of the fourth; or that the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second and similarly the multiple of the third [is greater than] the multiple of the fourth, yet it exceeds more as to proportion (not as to quantity of excess)... in any of these four ways there will be a greater proportion of the first to the second than the third to the fourth. In the four opposite ways, there will be a lesser proportion... Examples of all these are evidently taken from numbers. That "addition" of the multiple of the first over the multiple of the second, but not the third over the fourth, of which the author speaks in the definition, has a breadth encompassing these four predicted modes... For the sense of this definition is: when multiples are taken as proposed, if there is a greater proportion of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second than the third to the fourth, there will be a greater proportion of the first to the second... Or we can say that the "addition" of the first multiple over the second multiple... is strictly accepted as the words of the definition sound... He did not put the other three modes of addition in the said definition because this one is clearer than all of them and sufficient for the said definition. Nowhere...

**Definition 9**
If, however, proportionality is established among at least three terms.
After the author defined proportion, proportionality, and proportional and improportional quantities, he shows what is the minimum number of terms in which proportionality can consist; but he does not set the maximum, because that cannot be taken: for any proportion can be continued in infinite terms, whether it be a rational or irrational proportion. For proportionality, at least two similar proportions are required, because proportionality is a likeness of proportions. Any proportion has an antecedent and a consequent; therefore any proportionality has at least two antecedents and two consequents: this is impossible to happen in fewer than three terms, in which the middle term becomes both antecedent and consequent: and therefore the proportionality will be continuous... Discontinuous, however, will not be in fewer than four, because in it every term is only an antecedent or only a consequent [**prns** for *consequens*]...

**Definition 10**
If there be three quantities continuously proportional, the proportion of the first to the third will be called the duplicate proportion of the first to the second.
He defines the proportion which is between the extreme terms of a continuous proportionality established in three terms... if the proportion of the first to the second is as the second to the third, the proportion of the first to the third will be as the first to the second "duplicated": that is, composed of two such [proportions]. Or, what is the same: it will be the proportion of the first to the second multiplied into itself. For example, in numbers: Let 3 numbers be continuously proportional, and let them be continuously doubles, as 2, 4, 8. The proportion of the first to the third will be as the proportion of the first to the second multiplied into itself: for the proportion of the first to the second is double; double multiplied into itself produces quadruple; hence the proportion of the extremes is quadruple: namely the double of double.

**Definition 11**
When there are four quantities continuously proportional, the proportion of the first to the fourth will be called the triplicate proportion of the first to the second.

### PAGE 65

...He defines the proportion which is between the extreme terms of a continuous proportionality established in four terms: and says that if there are four quantities continuously proportional, the proportion of the first to the fourth will be as the triplicate proportion of the first to the second; that is, composed of three such [proportions]... or what is the same: the proportion of the first to the second multiplied by itself and then by the product. For example, in numbers: there are four numbers continuously proportional, and let them be continuously triples: as 1, 3, 9, 27. The proportion of the first to the fourth will be as the proportion of the first to the second multiplied into itself and then the product multiplied [by the proportion]: the proportion of the first to the second is triple; triple multiplied into itself produces ninefold [**nouplam**], and triple into ninefold produces twenty-sevenfold [**vigincupla septupla**]. Therefore, the proportion of the extremes is twenty-sevenfold, which is the triple of triple... He did not define the proportion of extremes of continuous proportionality established among more than four terms because dimensions found in natural things do not exceed the number three. For the denomination of a proportion of two quantities between which no medium is placed has the nature of a line. But of those where one medium is interposed in continuous proportionality, it has the nature of a surface, because it is made from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two into itself. For everything produced from the multiplication of a line into a line has the nature of a surface: if into itself, a square; if into another, an oblong [**altera parte altera longioris**]. But the denomination of the proportion of those quantities between which two media are interposed in continuous proportion has the nature of a solid: because it comes from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two first into itself (from which multiplication a surface is produced) and then into the product (from which multiplication comes a solid or body): for everything produced from the multiplication of a line into a surface grows into a solid. It is therefore as if he said: a proportion of two quantities is a simple interval and has the nature of a simple dimension like a line; the proportionality of three is a double interval and has the nature of a double dimension like a surface; the proportionality of four is a triple interval and has the nature of a triple dimension like a solid. And because dimensions do not proceed further, therefore he did not define the proportion contained between the extremes of proportionality established in five or more terms; or he did not define it because their proportion is had from the predicted definitions. For if in three terms the proportion of extremes consists of the proportion of the first duplicated, and in four terms of the same triplicated: in five terms it consists of the same quadruplicated, and in six of the same quintuplicated...

---

### PAGE 66

**BOOK [V]**

...between the interposed extremes. And note that even in continuous proportionality, the proportion of the extremes is produced from all the intermediate proportions. From the aforesaid it appears that the proportion of the extremes of continuous proportionality in three terms is denominated from a square: in four terms it is denominated from a cube: whose side is the denomination of the proportion of the first to the second. For example, in numbers: Let there be four numbers continuously proportional which are continuously triples: 3, 9, 27, 81. The proportion of the first to the second is denominated by three [**ternario**], for it is triple: of the first to the third by nine [**nonario**] which is the square of three, for it is ninefold. But the proportion of the first to the fourth is denominated by 27, which is the cube of the denomination of the proportion of the first to the second, namely of three, for it is twenty-sevenfold. And the proportion of extremes of continuous improportionality in three terms is denominated by a non-square surface [**superficiali non quadrato**], whose sides are the denominations of the proportions themselves; and in four terms it is denominated by a non-cube solid, whose three sides are the denominations of the three proportions: which is also clear in numbers. Let there be four numbers continuously improportional: which are 2, 4, 12, 48. In these the proportion of the first to the second is double; of the second to the third triple; and therefore of the first to the third sixfold; of the third to the fourth quadruple; and therefore of the first to the fourth twenty-fourfold [**vigincupla quadrupla**]. Six [**senarius**], which is the denomination of the proportion of the first to the third, is a surface number whose sides are two and three, which are the denominations of the first two proportions. 24, which is the denomination of the proportion of the first to the fourth, is a solid whose sides are 2, 3, and 4...

**Definition 12**
Quantities which are in one proportion, antecedent to consequent and antecedent to consequent, shall be said *econtrario* [conversely] as consequent to antecedent, so consequent to antecedent. Likewise *permutatim* [permutedly], as antecedent to antecedent, so consequent to consequent.

He defines the species of proportionality which are six: namely *conversa*, *permutata*, *disiuncta*, *coniuncta*, *eversa*, and *equa*. These species are as certain modes of arguing: he defines first *conversa* and *permutata*, in which the antecedents and consequents remain the same in substance; which is not the case in *disiuncta*, *coniuncta*, or *eversa*; and in which nothing external is taken as in *equa*. He calls the first extreme of the proportion the "antecedent," and the second the "consequent." He intends by this definition that if the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, and from this I conclude: therefore $b$ to $a$ is as $d$ to $c$ (namely, so that I make consequents out of antecedents and antecedents out of consequents), this mode of arguing is called proportionality *e contrario* or *conversa*. But if I argue thus: $a$ to $b$ as $c$ to $d$, therefore $a$ to $c$ as $b$ to $d$ (namely, so that both extremes of the first proportion become antecedents, and both extremes of the second become consequents), he intends that this mode of arguing be called proportionality *permutata*...

---

### PAGE 67

**Proposition 13**
*Coniuncta* [joined] proportionality is said whenever as the antecedent with the consequent is to the consequent, so also the [other] antecedent with the [other] consequent is to the consequent.

He defines *coniuncta*, *disiuncta*, and *eversa*, in which nothing external is taken, but the terms do not remain the same in substance... if it be $a$ to $b$ as $c$ to $d$, and I conclude: therefore the whole $a+b$ is to $b$ as the whole $c+d$ is to $d$, this mode of arguing is called proportionality *coniuncta*.

**Proposition 14**
*Disiuncta* [disjoined] proportionality is called the equal comparison of the augments of the antecedents over the consequents.

He intends that if the proportion of the whole $a+b$ to $b$ is as the whole $c+d$ to $d$, and from this I conclude: therefore $a$ to $b$ as $c$ to $d$, this mode of arguing is called *disiuncta* proportionality.

**Proposition 15**
*Eversa* [averse/inverted] proportionality is called the likeness of proportions of any antecedents to their own augments over their consequents.

He intends that if it be $a$ to $b$ as $c$ to $d$, and from this I conclude: therefore $a$ to $a-b$ as $c$ to $c-d$, this mode of arguing is called *eversa* proportionality.

**Proposition 16**
*Equa* [equal] proportionality is said when, many quantities being proposed and others equal in number applied in one proportion, with an equal number of middle [terms] removed, there is a likeness of the proportions of both extremes.

He defines *equa* proportionality, which is taken from outside to prove the proposition. He intends that if any number of quantities are taken, as $a, b, c$, and likewise as many others (whether of the same genus or another) as $d, e, f$, and the second are in the proportion of the first, either in the same order (as if it be said $a$ to $b$ as $d$ to $e$, and $b$ to $c$ as $e$ to $f$) or in inverse order (as if it be said $a$ to $b$ as $e$ to $f$ and $b$ to $c$ as $d$ to $e$), and from this it is concluded: therefore $a$ to $c$ as $d$ to $f$... the author proves four of these six modes... *Permutata* in 16, *disiuncta* in 17, *coniuncta* in 18, *equa* in 22 and 23... But *conversa* or *eversa* he does not demonstrate because *conversa* is clear from the definition of discontinuously proportional quantities... Let us now demonstrate how *conversa* is manifest... Let the proportion $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$, I wish to demonstrate it will be $b$ to $a$ [as $d$ to $c$]...

---

### PAGE 68

**BOOK [V]**

...as $d$ to $c$. Let equimultiples $e$ to $a$ and $f$ to $c$ be taken; likewise $g$ to $b$ and $h$ to $d$ as equimultiples. It will be by the conversion of the definition... I understand then $b$ as first, $a$ second, $d$ third, $c$ fourth... it will be by the said definition the proportion of $b$ (first) to $a$ (second) as $c$ (third) to $d$ (fourth), which is the proposition. Thus the mode of arguing called *conversa* proportionality is established. The principles of this fifth book seem very difficult to many... for nothing seems to adhere more immediately to the intellect than that for any two equal quantities there is one proportion to a third; which, however, the seventh [proposition] of this fifth book demonstrates from the definition of discontinuous proportionality, which at first seems far removed from the intellect. For who would not more easily concede that the proportion of two equal quantities to a third is the same, than [the definition] that if multiples of the first and third... behave similarly in addition, diminution, and equality, the proportion of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth? But if we look subtly, it will clearly stand that the intellect cannot be united to the fact that the proportion of two equal quantities to a third is one, except through [knowing] what it is to be one proportion. For if one is ignorant of what it is to be one proportion... how will he know that two equal quantities have the same proportion to a third? Therefore, the intellect undoubtedly needs to have knowledge of this thing through its definition... Similarly, the first apprehension judges more immediately that for two unequal quantities, the proportion of the larger to another is greater than the smaller to the same (which the 8th demonstrates)... but neither can this be understood except through what it is to be a "greater proportion." Therefore, it was necessary to define those which are called proportional and those which are improportional... Proportional are those whose proportion is one; improportional those whose proportions are diverse. Thus he defined quantities whose proportion is one, and those in which the extremes are connected without the media being dissociated, which he called "continuously proportional"... and those in which an interruption happens in the middle, and these are "discontinuously proportional"...

---

### PAGE 69

**BOOK [V]**

...and he also defined quantities which are improportional, of which one proportion is greater than another. And if every proportion were known [**scita**] or rational, then it would be easy for the intellect to know which proportions were one and which diverse. For those which would have one denomination would be one; those with diverse, diverse. This facility is manifest from arithmetic, since the proportion of all numbers is fixed [**sata**] and rational. Whence **Jordanus** in the second [book] of his *Arithmetic*, thus defining which proportions are the same and which diverse, says those are the same which receive the same denomination; the greater which [receive] the larger [denomination], and the smaller which [receive] the smaller. But there are infinite irrational proportions whose denomination is not knowable; wherefore since **Euclid** considers proportionals commonly in this book (not restricting them to rational or irrational, since he considers proportion found in continuous things which is common to both), he could not define the identity of proportions through the identity of denominations like the arithmetician: because, as was said, the denominations of many proportions are simply unknown. But a definition ought to be made from better-known things; whence the "malice" of irrational proportions compelled Euclid to set down such definitions. Because he could not... define proportionality through identity of relationships [**habitudinum**] or denominations of the terms themselves... he was forced to take refuge in the multiples of the terms; so that from their relationships as to excess and equality... he might hunt for the proposed definition. For nothing is more the same in any kind of inequality than the multiples of terms... And because proportion is the relationship of two quantities of the same genus... identity of proportions is a similar equality... or similar majority... or similar minority. And this similar equality... exists among any four quantities when it is among all their equimultiples... What he says in the fifth definition... is as if he said: "I call all those quantities continuously proportional... whose equimultiples are similarly continuously equal, or similarly continuously greater, or similarly continuously less"... And what he says in the sixth definition... is as if he said: "I call all four quantities discontinuously proportional... whose equimultiples of the first and third relate to all equimultiples of the second and fourth similarly either in equaling, or adding, or subtracting"...

---

### PAGE 70

**BOOK [V]**

...first to the second as third to the fourth. And what he says in the 8th definition is as if he said: "I call a greater proportion of the first to the second than the third to the fourth that in which the first more exceeds the second than the third exceeds the fourth... where some multiple of the first adds over some multiple of the second, [while] some multiple of the third... does not add over some multiple of the fourth..." Some have attempted to demonstrate these definitions, among whom **Ametus filius Joseph** [Ahmad ibn Yusuf] attempted to demonstrate them in his epistle which he composed *On Proportion and Proportionality*; and he took three [principles] by way of position as if they were self-evident principles needing no proof. The first of which is that if there be four quantities such that the proportion of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then conversely the proportion of the second to the first will be as the fourth to the third; and this is the mode of arguing which Euclid called above *conversa* proportionality. And he erred, because he said a proposition was self-evident whose antecedent and consequent are unknown. For it is unknown what it is for the proportion of the first quantity to the second to be as the third to the fourth; therefore, this being posed as unknown, it is impossible to understand what follows from it... His second principle was: that if there be four quantities... if the first be greater than the second, the third will be greater than the fourth; if less, less; if equal, equal. The third was that... the first is to any multiple of the second as the third is to an equimultiple of the fourth... He failed in these... he also failed in the second, third, and fifth demonstrations, in each of which he argues from the 8th or 10th [propositions] of this [book] which are themselves proved from the definition of discontinuous proportionality... For when you wish to take a quantity which relates to $c$ in the proportion of $g$ to $d$, I will give [**vabo** for *dabo*] to you a greater or lesser or equal to $a, b$ indifferently as I wish; wherefore he does not demonstrate, or it happens to him [to use] a circle and for principles to be more unknown than the conclusions. Therefore, principles must be assumed with Euclid as known... and conclusions are to be demonstrated from them.

**Proposition 1**
If there be any number of quantities which are equimultiples of as many others, or each equal to each, it is necessary that just as one of those is to its fellow [**comparem**], the whole aggregate from these is similarly related to all those [others] taken together.

Let there be any number of quantities, which let be $a, b, c$, and as many others, which let be $d, e, f$, being equimultiples each to its fellow...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Euclid's Book V, shifting from the definition of continuous proportion to the formal definition of equal ratios (proportionality) for any four magnitudes, commonly known as the Eudoxean definition of proportion.</meta>

BOOK

**Quantities** which are said to be in the same ratio—the first to the second and the third to the fourth—are those where, when equal multiples are taken of the first and the third, and other equal multiples are taken of the second and the fourth, the multiples of the first and third respectively exceed, fall short of, or are equal to the multiples of the second and fourth, when compared in that same order.

Having previously set down the definition of quantities in continuous proportion <note>original: "continue proportionalium," referring to a series like A:B :: B:C</note>, he here sets down the definition of quantities in discontinuous proportion <note>original: "incontinue proportionalium," referring to a series like A:B :: C:D</note>. This definition states that for any four quantities, if equal multiples <term>equimultiples: results of multiplying different starting values by the same number</term> are taken of the first and third, and likewise equal multiples are taken of the second and fourth, and if the multiple of the first relates to the multiple of the second in terms of exceeding, falling short, or being equal exactly as the multiple of the third relates to the multiple of the fourth, then the ratio of the first to the second is the same as the third to the fourth. 

For example: Let there be four quantities **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d**. Let equal multiples be taken of the first and third (**a** and **c**), such as the double, which we shall call **e** and **f**. Then, let other equal multiples be taken of the second and fourth (**b** and **d**), such as the triple, which we shall call **g** and **h**. These four multiples must be compared to one another according to the order of the original four quantities: that is, **e** compared to **g**, and **f** compared to **h** (but not **e** to **f** or **g** to **h**). If they are similar in their exceeding, falling short, or equality—meaning that if **e** is greater than **g**, then **f** must also be greater than **h**; or if **e** is less than **g**, then **f** is less than **h**; or if **e** equals **g**, then **f** equals **h**—then the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as **c** to **d**. 

This similarity in exceeding or falling short should be understood here just as in the definition of continuous proportions: namely, not in the specific amount of the excess <note>original: "excessus," the numerical difference between two values</note>, but in the relationship of the proportion. 

Furthermore, when he says **taken in the same order**, it should be understood as explained: that the multiples are not compared to each other based on the order of the quantities from which they were multiplied. For instance, the multiple of the first is not compared to the multiple of the third, nor the second to the fourth. Instead, they are compared according to the original order of the four quantities: the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth. 

The meaning of this definition, therefore, is: Four quantities are in discontinuous proportion when the ratio of the first to the second is the same as the third to the fourth because, when equal multiples are taken of the first and third, and equal multiples of the second and fourth, the ratio of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second is as the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth. He did not define it in this exact phrasing for the reason mentioned before, though in reality the result is the same. 

It is not necessary, however, for the four quantities **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d** to be of the same kind <term>genus: a category of magnitude, such as lines, areas, or volumes</term>. This is because **b** is not linked in a continuous proportion with **c**. Rather, the first two can be of one kind (e.g., lines) and the following two of another (e.g., areas). This is evident because it is necessary to relate the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the third to the fourth. One does not relate the multiple of the first to the multiple of the third, which would require them to be the same kind. It was necessary to take equal multiples of the first and third, and equal multiples of the second and fourth, rather than equal multiples of the first and second, because unless the terms of the first ratio are linked to the terms of the second through the taking of multiples, there would be no way to determine if the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as **c** to **d**.

# Definition 7
**Quantities** whose ratio is the same are called proportional.

After defining quantities in continuous and discontinuous proportion, he defines proportional quantities simply; this is clear from the definition itself.

This definition is significant because it allows mathematicians to compare magnitudes even if they cannot be measured by a common unit (incommensurable magnitudes).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Euclid's Book V, moving from the definition of proportional magnitudes (magnitudes sharing the same ratio) to the definition of magnitudes with different ratios.</meta>

# Page V

[[image: decorative initial C]] **When** <term>equimultiples</term> <note>The same multiples—for example, doubling or tripling both numbers.</note> of the first and third are taken, and likewise equimultiples of the second and fourth are taken, if the multiple of the first exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth, then the first is said to have a **greater ratio** to the second than the third has to the fourth.

Having defined proportional quantities, he now defines <term>non-proportional</term> <note>original: "improportionales"</note> quantities. These are quantities between which there is no equality of ratios. This occurs in two ways: either because the ratio of the first to the second is greater than that of the third to the fourth, or because it is smaller. Therefore, there are two species of this. The first is when the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth; this is called **greater non-proportionality**. The second is when the ratio of the first to the second is smaller than the third to the fourth; this is called **lesser non-proportionality**. He defines those between which there is a greater ratio of the first to the second than the third to the fourth (which is greater non-proportionality), but he does not provide a definition for those with a lesser ratio because it is clear from the other.

Therefore, when there are four quantities, and equimultiples are taken for the first and third, and equimultiples for the second and fourth, if the multiples of the first and second related to each other do not behave similarly to the multiples of the third and fourth related to each other in terms of exceeding, falling short, or being equal, then these four quantities will be non-proportional. 

This can happen in four ways where the ratio of the first to the second is greater:
1. If the multiple of the first is equal to the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third is less than the multiple of the fourth.
2. If the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third is equal to or less than the multiple of the fourth.
3. If the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, and similarly the multiple of the third is greater than the multiple of the fourth, yet the first exceeds its counterpart more in terms of <term>proportion</term> <note>The relative relationship, rather than the simple subtraction of the numbers.</note> (not necessarily in the absolute quantity of the excess).
4. If the multiple of the first is less than the multiple of the second, and similarly the multiple of the third is less than the multiple of the fourth, yet the first falls short by less in terms of proportion than the third falls short of the fourth.

In any of these four ways, the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than the third to the fourth. Conversely, in the four opposite ways, the ratio of the first to the second will be less than the third to the fourth. Examples of all these can clearly be taken from numbers. 

The "exceeding" of the first multiple over the second, while the third does not exceed the fourth (which the author speaks of in the definition), has a "breadth" that covers these four modes. For the meaning of this definition is: when multiples are taken as proposed, if there is a greater ratio of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second than there is of the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth, then the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than the third to the fourth. He did not define it in this exact form for the same reason mentioned before. Or we can say that the "exceeding" of the first multiple over the second (and not the third over the fourth) spoken of in the definition of greater non-proportionality is taken literally as the words sound, and only extends to the second of the four modes mentioned. However, in reality, in any of those four modes, the first ratio is greater than the second. The sense of that definition is: if, when multiples are taken, it is not necessary for the multiple of the third to exceed the fourth just because the multiple of the first exceeds the second, then the first ratio is greater. He did not include the other three modes of exceeding in the definition because this one is the clearest of them all and sufficient for the definition. Never...

**greater non-proportionality** <note>original: "maior improportionalitas"; when the first ratio is larger than the second.</note>
**excess** <note>original: "excessus"; the amount by which one quantity is greater than another.</note>

The commentary breaks down the logic into four specific mathematical scenarios or "modes" where this inequality occurs.</summary>

--- Page 64 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of ratios and proportions, specifically addressing how to identify when one ratio is greater than another, and defining the minimum number of terms required for continuous and discrete proportions.</meta>

...Indeed, there is a **greater ratio** of the first of four quantities to the second than of the third to the fourth: whenever it happens that some equal multiples are found for the first and the third, which, when compared to equal multiples of the second and fourth, show that the multiple of the first exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. <note>original: "maior proportio... addere super." This is Euclid’s classic definition of a "greater ratio" using the method of equimultiples. If you can find a multiplier that makes the first term bigger than the second, but that same multiplier doesn't make the third term bigger than the fourth, the first ratio is larger.</note> It is never possible to find this situation without it being the case that the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, as we will demonstrate below in the tenth [proposition] of this [book]. These <term>unproportional quantities</term> <note>quantities that do not form an equal proportion</note> can be of different kinds, just as <term>discrete proportional</term> <note>quantities in a ratio like A:B = C:D, where the middle terms are different</note> quantities can be if there is a discrete lack of proportion between them: as if it were said that the ratio of *a* to *b* is greater than *c* to *d*. However, if there is a **continuous** lack of proportion, they will necessarily all be of the same kind, just as they are in a continuous proportion: as if it were said that the ratio of *a* to *b* is greater than the ratio of *b* to *c*.

# Definition 9
[[image: decorative initial E]] **If, however, a proportionality is established, it must be among at least three terms.**
After the author has defined <term>ratio</term> <note>the relationship between two quantities</note>, <term>proportionality</term> <note>the equality of two ratios</note>, and proportional and unproportional quantities, he now shows what the minimum number of terms is between which a proportionality can exist. He does not set a maximum number because one cannot be determined; any ratio can be continued through infinite terms, whether it is a <term>rational ratio</term> <note>a ratio expressible by whole numbers</note> or an <term>irrational ratio</term> <note>a ratio like the diagonal of a square to its side, which cannot be written as a simple fraction</note>. For a proportionality, at least two similar ratios are required, because proportionality is the "likeness of ratios." Since every ratio has an <term>antecedent</term> <note>the first term</note> and a <term>consequent</term> <note>the second term</note>, every proportionality must have at least two antecedents and two consequents. This is impossible to achieve in fewer than three terms, in which the middle term becomes both a consequent (to the first) and an antecedent (to the last). Therefore, the proportionality will be **continuous**. Thus, a continuous proportionality is established in at least three terms. A **discrete** <note>or "incontinuous"</note> proportion, however, cannot exist in fewer than four terms, because in that case every term is only an antecedent or only a consequent. Understand the same regarding the minimum number of terms for unproportionality: if it is continuous, it will be between at least three terms; if discrete, at least four.

# Definition 10
[[image: decorative initial S]] **If three quantities are in continuous proportion, the ratio of the first to the third is said to be the duplicate ratio of the first to the second.**
He defines the ratio that exists between the outer terms of a continuous proportionality consisting of three terms. He says that if the ratio of the first to the second is the same as the second to the third, the ratio of the first to the third is the **duplicate** of the ratio of the first to the second. That is, it is composed of two such ratios; or, which is the same thing, the ratio of the first to the third is the ratio of the first to the second multiplied by itself. <note>In modern terms, if a/b = b/c, then a/c = (a/b)².</note> For example, in numbers: Let there be 3 numbers in continuous proportion, and let them be continuously doubled: such as **2, 4, 8**. The ratio of the first (2) to the third (8) will be as the ratio of the first to the second (2 to 4) multiplied by itself. The ratio of the first to the second is **double**; but "double" multiplied by itself produces **quadruple**. Hence, the ratio of the outer terms is quadruple—namely, "the double of the double." Or, according to the first explanation, the ratio of the outer terms is like the first to the second "duplicated," because a quadruple consists of two doubles.

# Definition 11
[[image: decorative initial C]] **When four quantities are in continuous proportion, the ratio of the first to the fourth is called the triplicate ratio of the first to the second.**

[[image: diagram on the left. A line with points a, s, b, c and numbers 4, 2.]]

<note>Vocabulary: irrational (not expressible as a ratio of integers), rational (expressible as a ratio of integers), duplicate (squared ratio), triplicate (cubed ratio), quadruple (fourfold), terms (the individual numbers or magnitudes in a ratio).</note>

<summary>This page explains Euclid's definitions for comparing unequal ratios and establishes that a continuous proportion requires at least three terms, while a discrete one requires four. It also introduces "duplicate" and "triplicate" ratios, which we today understand as squaring or cubing a ratio.</summary>
<keywords>ratio, continuous proportion, discrete proportion, duplicate ratio, triplicate ratio, antecedents, consequents, Euclid's Elements</keywords>

--- Page 65 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of ratios and proportions, specifically moving into "triplicate" ratios (the ratio of the first to the fourth term in a sequence) and the geometric analogy of dimensions.</meta>

[[original page: V]]

He defines the proportion which exists between the extreme terms of a <term>continued proportionality</term> <note>A sequence where the ratio between successive terms is constant, such as 1:3 = 3:9 = 9:27.</note> established in 4 terms: and he says that if there are 4 quantities in continued proportion, the ratio of the first to the fourth will be as the ratio of the first to the second **triplicated**—that is, composed of three such ratios, since three such are found within it. Or, what is the same thing: the ratio of the first to the fourth will be as the first to the second triplicated—that is, multiplied by itself, and then multiplied again by that product. 

For example, in numbers: Suppose there are four numbers in continued proportion, and let them be continuous triples, such as 1, 3, 9, and 27. The ratio of the first to the fourth will be like the ratio of the first to the second multiplied by itself and then by the resulting product. Now, the ratio of the first to the second is triple; triple multiplied by itself produces ninefold, and triple multiplied by ninefold produces <note>original: "vigincupla septupla"</note> **twenty-seven-fold**. Therefore, the ratio of the extremes will be twenty-seven-fold, which is the "triple of the triple" <note>The author is describing the calculation of $3^3$ (3 x 3 x 3 = 27).</note>. Or, according to the earlier explanation, the ratio of the extremes is as the ratio of the first to the second triplicated, because twenty-seven-fold consists of three triples. 

He did not, however, define the proportion of extremes in a continued proportionality consisting of more than four terms; this is because the dimensions found in natural things do not exceed the number three. The <term>denomination</term> <note>The numerical value or name that identifies a specific ratio.</note> of a proportion of two quantities between which no middle term is placed has the nature of a **line**. But the denomination of those between which one middle term is placed in continued proportionality has the nature of a **surface**, because it results from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two by itself. 

Now, everything produced from the multiplication of a line by a line has the nature of a surface: if indeed it is multiplied by itself, it is a **square**; if by another, it is a rectangle <note>original: "alteram parte altera longioris" — literally "longer on one side than the other."</note>. But the denomination of the proportion of those quantities between which two middle terms are placed in continued proportion has the nature of a **solid**: because it comes from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two first by itself—from which multiplication a surface is produced—and then by that product, from which multiplication a solid or body results. For everything produced from the multiplication of a line by a surface grows into a solid. 

It is, therefore, as if he were saying: the proportion of two quantities is a simple interval, having the nature of a simple dimension like a **line**; the proportionality of three terms is a double interval, having the nature of a double dimension like a **surface**; and the proportionality of four terms is a triple interval, having the nature of a triple dimension like a **solid**. 

And because dimensions do not proceed further, he did not define the proportion contained between the extremes of a proportionality established in five or more terms. Or perhaps he did not define the proportion in these cases because their proportion can be understood from the preceding definitions. For if in three terms the ratio of the extremes consists of the ratio of the first terms **duplicated** <note>Squared.</note>, and in four terms it consists of the same **triplicated** <note>Cubed.</note>, then in 5 terms it consists of the same **quadruplicated**, and in six terms **quintuplicated**. 

Just as in three terms in continued proportion the ratio of the extremes contains the ratio of the first terms twice, and in 4 terms three times, so in 5 terms it will contain it four times, and in six terms five times, and so on. Thus, the ratio of the extremes in terms in continued proportion always contains the ratio of the first terms as many times as there are total terms minus one. 

Similarly, if the ratio of the extremes of a continued proportionality consisting of three terms is that which is produced from the ratio of the first terms multiplied by itself once, and in 4 terms multiplied by itself twice, then in five terms it is that produced from the ratio of the first terms multiplied by itself three times, and in 6 terms four times. Thus, there are always two more terms than there are multiplications, or the number of multiplications is equal to the middle terms.

<meta>This page continues a mathematical discussion on the properties of ratios and proportions, specifically focusing on how the total ratio across multiple terms is calculated through multiplication of intermediate values.</meta>

[[original page: BOOK]]

...with the extremes placed in between. And note that even in continuous proportionality <note>A sequence where the ratio between each successive term is the same, like 3, 9, 27...</note>, the ratio of the extremes is produced from all the intermediate ratios. From the aforesaid, it appears that the ratio of the extremes of a continuous proportionality consisting of three terms takes its value from a **square**; while in a sequence of four terms, it takes its value from a **cube**. The "side" of this square or cube is the value <term>denomination: the numerical value of a ratio, found by dividing the first term by the second</term> of the ratio of the first term to the second. 

For example, in numbers: Let there be four continuously proportional numbers which are continuously triple: **3, 9, 27, 81**. 
*   The ratio of the first to the second (3 to 9) is named from **3**, for it is triple. 
*   The ratio of the first to the third (3 to 27) is named from **9**, which is the **square** of 3, for it is ninefold. 
*   But the ratio of the first to the fourth (3 to 81) is named from **27**, which is the **cube** of the ratio value of the first to the second—namely, 3; for it is twenty-sevenfold. 

And the ratio of the extremes of continuous *disproportionality* <note>original: "improportionalitatis"; here referring to a sequence where the ratios between terms are not the same</note> consisting of three terms is named from a **surface** <note>Meaning a non-square area (like a rectangle) formed by multiplying two different numbers</note> that is not a square, whose sides are the values of the ratios themselves. In a sequence of four terms, it is named from a **solid** that is not a cube, whose three sides are the values of the three ratios. This is also clear in numbers. 

Let there be four continuously disproportionate numbers: **2, 4, 12, 48**. 
*   The ratio of the first to the second (2 to 4) is **double** (2). 
*   The second to the third (4 to 12) is **triple** (3), and therefore the first to the third (2 to 12) is **sixfold** (6). 
*   The third to the fourth (12 to 48) is **quadruple** (4), and therefore the first to the fourth (2 to 48) is **twenty-fourfold** (24). 

Thus **6**, which is the value of the ratio of the first to the third, is a "surface" whose sides are 2 and 3 (the values of the first two ratios). **24**, which is the value of the ratio of the first to the fourth, is a "solid" whose sides are **2, 3, and 4**, which are the values of the three ratios existing between those four terms.

# Definition 12
[[image: decorative initial Q]] Quantities that are in one ratio—<term>antecedent: the first term in a ratio</term> to <term>consequent: the second term in a ratio</term> and antecedent to consequent—will be spoken of **conversely** as: the consequent is to the antecedent, so the [second] consequent is to the [second] antecedent. Likewise, **permuted**: as the [first] antecedent is to the [second] antecedent, so also is the [first] consequent to the [second] consequent.

He defines the types of proportionality, of which there are six: namely **converted**, **permuted**, **disjoined**, **joined**, **everted**, and **equal**. These types are like certain modes of reasoning. He first defines **converted** and **permuted** proportionality, in which the antecedents and consequents remain the same in substance—which is not the case in disjoined, joined, or everted proportionality—and in which nothing extra is taken (as happens in "equal" proportionality). 

He calls the **antecedent** the first term of the ratio and the **consequent** the second. He intends by this definition that:
1.  **Converted (or Contrary) Proportionality:** If there is a ratio of *a* to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and from this I conclude: therefore *b* is to *a* as *d* is to *c*. In other words, I make consequents out of antecedents and vice-versa.
2.  **Permuted Proportionality:** If I argue thus: *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, therefore *a* is to *c* as *b* is to *d*. Here, both first terms of the ratios become antecedents and both second terms become consequents. In this mode of reasoning, the antecedent of the second ratio becomes the consequent, and the consequent of the first becomes the antecedent.

# Proposition .13.
[[image: decorative initial C]] **Joined proportionality** <note>original: *Coniuncta proportionalitas*; today we often call this "composition" of ratios.</note> is so called whenever, as the antecedent with the consequent is to the consequent, so also the [other] antecedent with [its] consequent is to [its] consequent.

He defines joined, disjoined, and averse proportionality, in which no external terms are taken, yet the terms do not remain as they were. They are the same in substance, and he means that if it were the case that **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, and I conclude from this that: therefore the whole **a** + **b** is to **b** as the whole **c** + **d** is to **d**, then this method of arguing is called joined proportionality.

# Proposition .14.
[[image: decorative initial D]] **Disjoined proportionality** <note>original: *Disiuncta proportionalitas*; also known as "division" of ratios.</note> is said to be the equal comparison of the excesses <term>excesses: the amount by which the first part of a ratio is larger than the second</term> of the antecedents over the consequents.

He means that if there were a proportion of the whole **a** + **b** to **b** as the whole **c** + **d** is to **d**, and from this I conclude that: therefore **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, then this method of arguing is called disjoined proportionality.

# Proposition .15.
[[image: decorative initial E]] **Averse proportionality** <note>original: *Aversa proportionalitas*; also known as *eversa* or "conversion" of ratios.</note> is said to be the similarity of proportions of any antecedents to their own excesses over their consequents.

He means that if **a** were to **b** as **c** is to **d**, and from this I conclude that: therefore **a** is to **a** minus **b** as **c** is to **c** minus **d**, then this method of arguing is called averse proportionality.

# Proposition .16.
[[image: decorative initial E]] **Equal proportionality** <note>original: *Equa proportionalitas*; often called the *ex aequali* property.</note> is said to be—when many quantities are proposed and others of the same number are applied in a single proportion—the similarity of the proportions of the extremes of both sets after an equal number of middle terms have been removed.

He defines equal proportionality, which is taken from outside the original terms to prove a proposition. He means that if any number of quantities are taken, such as **a**, **b**, **c**, and likewise just as many others (whether they are of the same kind as the first or another), such as **d**, **e**, **f**, and the second set are in the same proportion as the first—either in the same order, such as saying **a** is to **b** as **d** is to **e**, and **b** is to **c** as **e** is to **f**; or in a reversed order, such as saying **a** is to **b** as **e** is to **f**, and **b** is to **c** as **d** is to **e**—and from this it is concluded that: therefore **a** is to **c** as **d** is to **f**, then this method of arguing is called equal proportionality.

Of these <note>original: *Chorum*, likely a scribal error for *Horum* (of these).</note> six ways of arguing, which are called the species of proportionality, the author proves four in the text below in this fifth [book]. He proves **permuted** proportionality in the 16th [proposition] of this [book]; **disjoined** in the 17th; **joined** in the 18th; and **equal** proportionality he demonstrates in the 22nd and 23rd. However, in the 22nd, it is when the quantities are proportional in the same order; in the 23rd, it is when they are proportional in a reversed order. 

He does not demonstrate **converted** proportionality or **averse** proportionality because converted is clear from the definition of quantities that are proportionally discontinuous. Averse is clear from the mutual permutation in [proposition] 19, as we will say regarding that same 19th proposition. Let us now demonstrate how converted proportionality is manifest from the definition of proportionally discontinuous quantities. Let there be, therefore, the proportion of **a** to **b** as **c** is to **d**; I wish to demonstrate that it will be **b** to **a**... <note>The text cuts off here, leading into the mathematical proof.</note>

[[image: diagram on the right.

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Euclid’s Elements, specifically focusing on Book V and the formal definitions of proportionality.</meta>

# BOOK

Just as d is to c, let e be taken to a and f to c as equimultiples <note>original: "eque multiplicia"; quantities multiplied by the same factor</note>. Similarly, let g be taken to b and h to d as equimultiples. By the conversion of the definition of quantities in continued proportion <term>continue proportionalium</term> <note>A sequence where the middle term serves as both the consequent of the first ratio and the antecedent of the second, like a:b = b:c</note>, e, f, and g will behave the same way in addition, subtraction, and equality as f, a, and b. I understand then that b is the first, a is the second, d is the third, and c is the fourth. Let equimultiples b and h be taken for the first and third. Thus, e and f are equimultiples for the second and fourth. Because the multiples of the first and second, which are g and e, relate to each other in terms of subtraction and equality just as the multiples of the third and fourth, h and f, relate to each other: then, by the said definition, the proportion of the first, b, to the second, a, is as the third, c, to the fourth, d, which is what was proposed.

It is clear, therefore, that this method of arguing is called converted proportionality <term>conversa proportionalitas</term> <note>The rule of "inversion" in ratios: if a:b = c:d, then b:a = d:c</note>. However, the principles of this fifth book seem very difficult to many, and some of the conclusions he demonstrates from them seem even further removed from the understanding. Indeed, nothing seems to cling more immediately to the intellect than the idea that any two equal quantities have the same single proportion to a third; yet the seventh proposition of this fifth book demonstrates this from the definition of discontinuous proportionality <term>incontinue proportionalitatis</term> <note>Also known as discrete proportion, involving four distinct terms like a:b = c:d</note>, which at first seems very far removed from the mind. 

For who would not more easily grant that the proportion of two equal quantities to some third is the same, than grant that for four quantities, if equimultiples of the first and third compared to equimultiples of the second and fourth behave similarly in addition, subtraction, and equality, then the proportion of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth? But if we look closely, it will be clearly established that the mind cannot truly grasp that the proportion of two equal quantities to a third is one and the same, unless it understands what it *is* for a proportion to be "one." For if one is ignorant of what it means for one proportion to be the same as another, how can he know that two equal quantities have the same proportion to a third? 

Therefore, before the intellect can grasp that proposition which seemed so easily conceivable, it undoubtedly needs the knowledge of this thing which is provided through its definition. Afterward, it must consider whether that definition applies to two equal quantities compared to a third. If the definition is found to fit those quantities, the proposition is concluded; if not, then the opposite. Thus, the proposition is not "immediate," even though a superficial glance judged it to be so. 

Similarly, the first impression judges it more immediate to the intellect to believe that for two unequal quantities, the ratio of the greater to the third is larger than the ratio of the smaller to the same (which the 8th proposition here demonstrates), than to believe the definition of a "greater" proportion: that for four quantities, there is a greater proportion of the first to the second than of the third to the fourth when, with equimultiples taken of the first and third, and others of the second and fourth, the multiple of the first exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. The aforementioned proposition is demonstrated from this, but similarly, it cannot be understood except through what it means for a proportion to be "greater." 

Therefore, it was necessary to define those things which are called proportional quantities and those which are im-proportional. Proportional quantities are those whose proportion is one <note>i.e., the same</note>. Im-proportional are those whose proportions are different. Thus, he defined quantities whose proportion is one; and those in which the outer terms <note>the "extrema"</note> are connected without the middle terms being separated, he called continued proportionals <term>continue proportionales</term>, stating that this proportionality exists in at least three terms because one term must be taken twice as the middle. And those in which an interruption occurs in the middle, these are discontinuous proportionals <term>incontinue proportionales</term>, and this proportionality requires at least four terms because of the use of a different middle term.

<summary>This page explains the logical necessity of Euclid's rigorous definitions of proportionality in Book V, arguing that even "obvious" mathematical truths require formal definitions to be truly understood. It specifically distinguishes between continued proportions (three terms) and discontinuous/discrete proportions (four terms).</summary>
