--- Page 69 ---
[[original page: 5]]

And he <note>Likely referring to Euclid, the Greek mathematician.</note> also defined quantities that are incommensurable, where one ratio might be larger than another. If every ratio were "known"—that is, rational—then it would be easy for the mind to recognize which ratios were identical and which were different. This is because those that had the same "denomination" <note>The "denomination" of a ratio is its numerical value; for example, the denomination of a 4 to 2 ratio is 2.</note> would be the same, and those with different denominations would be different. This ease is obvious in arithmetic, since the ratio of all numbers is fixed and rational.

For this reason, *Jordanus* <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a prominent 13th-century mathematician.</note> in the second book of his *Arithmetic*, when defining which ratios are the same and which are different, says that those which receive the same denomination are the same. The greater ratio receives the greater denomination, and the smaller receives the smaller. 

But there are infinite "irrational" ratios <note>These are ratios that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of whole numbers, such as the relationship between the side of a square and its diagonal.</note> whose denomination is not knowable. Therefore, since Euclid in this book considers proportional things in a general sense—not restricting himself to rational or irrational ones, but considering proportion as found in "continuous magnitudes" <note>Physical quantities like lines or areas, rather than just whole numbers.</note> which applies to both—he could not define the identity of ratios through the identity of denominations as the arithmetician does. This is because, as stated, the denominations of many ratios are simply unknown. 

However, a definition must be made from things that are better known; thus the "malice" <note>The author uses the word "malicia" (malice) to describe the stubborn, difficult nature of irrational numbers that refuse to be easily measured.</note> of irrational ratios forced Euclid to establish such definitions. Because he could not define proportionality (the identity of ratios) through the identity of the relationships or denominations of the terms themselves—due to the irrationality of those relationships—he was forced to turn instead to the **multiples** of the terms. 

He did this so that he could hunt for a definition by considering the multiples of these terms in equal quantities, looking at their "excess" or "equality." By doing this, they are reduced to the nature of the irrationality being discussed. For in any kind of inequality, nothing is more identical to the terms than their multiples, nor are the relationships of terms more consistent than the relationships of their multiples. 

And because a proportion is a "habititude" <term>relationship</term> between two quantities of the same kind, considered in terms of whether they are equal or one is larger, the identity of proportions between four quantities—the first to the second and the third to the fourth—is a "similar equality" of the first to the second and the third to the fourth. It might also be a "similar majority" or a "similar minority." This similar equality, majority, or minority exists between any four quantities when it holds true for all their equally-taken multiples. 

Therefore, what he says in the **fifth definition**—"quantities which are said to have a continuous proportionality," and so on—is as if he were saying: I call all those quantities "continuously proportional" if they are similarly equal, similarly greater, or similarly smaller across all their equal multiples. That is, if their multiples are also continuously proportional; if this fails at any point among the multiples, I say they are not continuously proportional.

Furthermore, what he says in the **sixth definition**—"quantities which are said to be according to one ratio, the first to the second and the third to the fourth," and so on—is as if he were saying: I call all four quantities "discontinuously proportional" (meaning the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth) when the first and second, and the third and fourth, behave similarly in terms of being equal, adding, or subtracting. This occurs when all equal multiples of the first and third, compared to all equal multiples of the second and fourth, behave the same way—either being equal, greater, or smaller. This means the multiples of the first have the same ratio to the multiples of the second as the multiples of the third have to the multiples of the fourth. If this relationship fails anywhere among the multiples, I say there is no proportion.

It clarifies Euclid's 5th and 6th definitions from Book V of the Elements regarding how to identify equal ratios across different types of magnitudes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book V of Euclid’s Elements, specifically focusing on the definitions of ratios and the first proposition regarding multiples. It critiques the earlier work of the mathematician Ahmad ibn Yusuf.</meta>

->[[original page: BOOK]]<-

...the first to the second is as the third to the fourth. What he says in the 8th definition <note>referring to Euclid's definition of "greater ratio" in Book V</note> is as if he were saying: I call a "greater ratio" of four quantities—the first to the second [being greater than] the third to the fourth—when the first exceeds the second more than the third exceeds the fourth. Therefore, some <term>multiple</term> <note>a quantity that contains another a certain number of times without a remainder</note> of the first is greater than some multiple of the second; while some multiple of the third, taken according to the same numbering as the multiple of the first, does not exceed the multiple of the fourth taken according to the numbering of the multiple of the second. This constitutes a "greater ratio" of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second than that of the third to the fourth. 

Some have attempted to demonstrate these definitions. Among them, Ametus, son of Joseph, <note>Ahmad ibn Yusuf, a 9th-10th century Egyptian mathematician</note> tried to prove them in his letter which he composed regarding ratio and proportionality. He took three points as postulates, as if they were principles which he claimed were self-evident and required no proof. 

The first of these is: if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then conversely, the ratio of the second to the first will be as the fourth to the third. This is the mode of reasoning which Euclid called "inverse proportion" above. And he [Ametus] erred because he claimed a proposition was self-evident whose <term>antecedent</term> <note>the first term of a ratio</note> and <term>consequent</term> <note>the second term of a ratio</note> are unknown. For it is unknown what it means for the ratio of the first quantity to the second to be the same as the third to the fourth; therefore, with this being unknown, it is impossible to understand what follows from it. Likewise, because the consequent is unknown, it is impossible to understand what precedes it. 

His second principle was: if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, if the first is greater than the second, the third will be greater than the fourth; if less, less; and if equal, equal. 

The third was: if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then the first will be to any multiple of the second as the third is to the equally-sized multiple of the fourth. 

He fell into the same error in these two principles as he did in the first. For he accepted unknowns as knowns in all of them; therefore, he did not demonstrate anything. He also erred in his second, third, and fifth demonstrations, in each of which he argued from the 8th or 10th [proposition] of this book, which are themselves proven from the definition of continuous proportionality. For he argued thus: if the ratio of *a* to *b* is as *c* to *d*, and it is greater than the ratio of *g* to *d*, let there be a part *v. b.* of *a. b.* to *c* as *g* to *d*. By this, it appears he assumes that for two unequal quantities *a. b.* and *u. b.* related to *c*, the greater quantity holds a greater ratio to it and the lesser a lesser ratio—or that a quantity will have a smaller ratio to *c* if it is smaller than *a. b.* The first of these is demonstrated in the 8th [proposition] of this book, and the second in the 10th. For when you wish to take a quantity that relates to *c* in the same ratio as *g* to *d*, I can give you one that is greater, smaller, or equal to *a. b.* indifferently, just as I wish. Therefore, he does not demonstrate it, but rather falls into <term>circular reasoning</term> where the principles are more obscure than the conclusions. Thus, with Euclid, we must suppose the principles to be known, and not prove the principles from the conclusions, but the conclusions from the principles.

# Proposition .1.
[[image: decorative initial S]] If there are any number of quantities which are <term>equimultiples</term> <note>multiplied by the same number</note> of an equal number of other quantities, it is necessary that just as one of them is to its partner, so also the total <term>aggregate</term> of the first set will be to the total of the second set.

Let there be any number of quantities, which are *a*, *b*, and *c*, and an equal number of others, which are *d*, *e*, and *f*. Let each be the same multiple of its partner, or let them be individually equal to them, in this manner:

[[image: a diagram showing two rows of quantities.
Top line: a, 2, b, 3, c, 4.
Bottom line: d, 2, e, 3, f, 4.]]

<summary>This page discusses the logic of ratios, critiquing Ahmad ibn Yusuf for using circular reasoning to "prove" Euclid's definitions. It also introduces the first proposition of Book V, which states that the sum of multiples is the same multiple of the sum of the original parts.</summary>
<keywords>Ahmad ibn Yusuf, Euclid's Elements, Book V, ratio, proportion, circular reasoning, multiples, Proposition 1, magnitudes</keywords>

--- Page 71 ---
This text is a Latin translation and commentary on Book V of Euclid’s *Elements*, which concerns the theory of magnitudes and proportions. The style is characteristic of late medieval or Renaissance mathematical Latin (likely from an edition such as that of Campanus of Novara or a similar commentator).

### Translation

**[Page V]**

¶ Just as $a$ is a multiple of $d$, so $b$ is a multiple of $f$; it [the text] means if $a$ is equal to $d$, that likewise $b$ is equal to $f$. Then if each were equal to each, the proposition is clear through this common science [notion]: if equals be added to equals, the wholes will also be equal. If, however, they were all equimultiples of their counterparts, by dividing them according to the quantity of their submultiples: the sum from the first part of $a$ and the first of $b$ and the first of $c$ will be equal to the sum from $d, e, f$, on account of the aforementioned common science, with this helping: those things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other. ¶ Likewise also the sum from the second parts of the magnitudes $a, b, c$ will be equal to the sum from $d, e, f$, and so concerning the rest: and because this can be done as many times as $d$ is contained in $a$, it will be that the equal sum from $d, e, f$ is contained in the sum from $a, b, c$ as many times as $d$ is contained in $a$. Because as many times as $d$ numbers $a$, so many times the sum from $d, e, f$ numbers the sum from $a, b, c$; it is clear that just as $a$ is a multiple of $d$, so the sum of $a, b, c$ is [a multiple] of the sum of $d, e, f$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 2

**If there be six magnitudes, of which the first is the same multiple of the second as the third is of the fourth; and the fifth is the same multiple of the second as the sixth is of the fourth: it will be fitting that the whole of the first and fifth be the same multiple of the second, and the whole of the third and sixth be the same multiple of the fourth.**

¶ Let there be six magnitudes: $a$ the first, $b$ the second, $c$ the third, $d$ the fourth, $e$ the fifth, $f$ the sixth. And let $a$ and $c$ be equimultiples to $b$ and $d$, and likewise let $e$ and $f$ be equimultiples to the same. I say that just as the whole sum from $a$ and $e$ is a multiple of the magnitude $b$, so the whole sum from $c$ and $f$ is a multiple of the magnitude $d$. For because the number according to which $b$ is contained in $a$ is equal to the number according to which $d$ is contained in $c$; likewise also the number according to which $b$ is contained in $e$ is equal to the number according to which $d$ is contained in $f$; it will be through the common science which is: if equals be added to equals, etc., the number according to which $b$ is contained in the sum of $a$ and $e$ is equal to the number according to which $d$ is contained in the sum of $c$ and $f$. Wherefore, just as the sum of $a$ and $e$ is a multiple of $b$, so the sum of $c$ and $f$ is a multiple of $d$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 3

**If a first be the same multiple of a second and a third of a fourth, and if equal multiples be taken of the first and the third: the multiple of the first to the second and the multiple of the third to the fourth will be equimultiples.**

¶ Let there be six magnitudes: $a$ the first, $b$ the second, $c$ the third, $d$ the fourth, $e$ the fifth, $f$ the sixth. And let $a$ to $b$ and $c$ to $d$, and likewise $e$ to $a$ and $f$ to $c$ be equimultiples. I say that as $e$ is a multiple of $b$, so is $f$ of $d$. For let $e$ be divided according to the magnitude $a$ of its multiple, and $f$ according to the magnitude $c$; and on account of the equality of the parts of $e$ to $a$ and of the parts of $f$ to $c$, it will be that any of the parts of $e$ is just as multiple of $b$ as any of the parts of $f$ is of $d$. Since therefore just as the first part of $e$ is a multiple of $b$, so the first part of $f$ is a multiple of $d$; and likewise just as the second part of $e$ is a multiple of $b$, so the second of $f$ is of $d$; therefore it will be through the preceding [proposition] that the sum from the two first parts of $e$ is the same multiple of $b$ as the sum from the two first parts of $f$ is of $d$. And because again the third part of $e$, if there be any third part, is the same multiple of $b$ as the third [part] of $f$ is of $d$, it will be through the same that the whole sum from the three first parts of $e$ is the same multiple of $b$ as the whole sum from the three first parts of $f$ is of $d$. ¶ And so if there be more parts of $e$ and $f$, by always composing the following with the sum of the prior, you will conclude

**[Page LIBER]**

that $e$ is the same multiple of $b$ as $f$ is of $d$, through the preceding [proposition] taken as many times as there are parts in $e$ or in $f$ minus one; and thus the proposition is clear.

---

### Proposition 4

**If the ratio of the first to the second be as the third to the fourth: let equimultiples be assigned to the first and the third. And likewise let equal multiples be assigned to the second and the fourth; the assigned multiples will be proportional in the same order.**

¶ Let the ratio of $a$ the first to $b$ the second be as $c$ the third to $d$ the fourth. And let $e$ to $a$ and $f$ to $c$ be taken as equimultiples. Likewise $g$ to $b$ and $h$ to $d$ as equimultiples: I say that the ratio of $e$ to $g$ is as $f$ to $h$. I shall take $k$ to $e$ and $l$ to $f$ as equimultiples, likewise $m$ to $g$ and $n$ to $h$ as equimultiples: and because $e$ and $f$ are equimultiples to $a$ and $c$, and likewise $k$ and $l$ are equimultiples to $e$ and $f$, they will be through the preceding [proposition] $k$ and $l$ equimultiples to $a$ and $c$; through the same also $m$ and $n$ will be equimultiples to $b$ and $d$. Wherefore, through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality [discrete proportion]: $k$ to $m$ and $l$ to $n$ will behave similarly in adding, diminishing, and equating. Because therefore $k$ and $l$ are equimultiples to $e$ and $f$, and likewise $m$ and $n$ are equimultiples to $g$ and $h$, the ratio of $e$ to $g$ will be as $f$ to $h$ through the definition of non-continuous proportionality, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 5

**If there be two magnitudes of which one is a part of the other, and there be subtracted from each of them the same part [proportionally]: the remainder will be to the remainder just as the whole is the same multiple of the whole.**

¶ Or thus: if [a magnitude] be an aliquot part of another, it [the remainder] will be as great a part of the remainder as the whole is of the whole. Let magnitude $ab$ be as great a part of magnitude $cd$ as $eb$ is of $ab$. And let $ab$ be subtracted from magnitude $cd$, and let the residue be $fc$; and $fd$ will be equal to $ab$. Likewise also let $eb$ be subtracted from magnitude $ab$, and let the residue be $ea$. I say that whatever part magnitude $ab$ is of magnitude $cd$, so great a part is magnitude $ae$ of magnitude $cf$. For since $fd$ is equal to $ab$, $fd$ will be the same multiple of $eb$ as $cd$ is multiple of $ab$. I shall place therefore $dg$ as the same multiple of $ae$ as $fd$ is multiple of $eb$; and it will be from the first [proposition] of this [book] that magnitude $fg$ is the same multiple of $ab$ as $fd$ is multiple of $eb$. And because $cd$ was thus a multiple of $ab$ as $fd$ was a multiple of $eb$, wherefore through the common science $cd$ and $fg$ are equal to each other. Therefore, with magnitude $fd$ taken away from each of them, $cf$ will be equal to $dg$. And because $dg$ was the same multiple of $ae$ as $fd$ was of $eb$, and therefore as $ab$ of $eb$, wherefore also as $cd$ of $ab$, $cf$ will be the same multiple of $ae$ as the whole $cd$ of the whole $ab$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 6

**If there be two magnitudes equimultiples of two others, and two smaller magnitudes be subtracted from the two larger ones, each from its own multiple: the two remainders will be either equimultiples of those same parts, or equal to them.**

**[Page V]**

¶ Let magnitudes $ab$ to $c$ and $de$ to $f$ be equimultiples: and let $e$ be subtracted from $ab$ and $f$ from $de$, and let the residues be: from $ab$ indeed $ag$, and from $de$, $db$. And let $gb$ be equal to $c$, and $be$ be equal to $f$. I say that the two residues $ag$ and $db$ will be equal to the two magnitudes $c$ and $f$, or equimultiples to them. Let $ag$ first be equal to $c$. I say that $db$ is equal to $f$. For I shall take magnitude $ek$ equal to $f$; it will be through the preceding hypotheses that as many times as $f$ is in $bk$, so many times is $c$ in $ab$. Wherefore just as $ab$ is a multiple of $c$, so $bk$ is a multiple of $f$. But it was also thus that $de$ was a multiple of the same $f$. Therefore through the common science $bk$ will be equal to $de$. With their common magnitude $be$ subtracted, $db$ will be equal to $ek$, wherefore equal to $f$, which is the proposition. ¶ If however $ag$ be a multiple of $c$, I shall set $ek$ to be the same multiple of $f$; and it will be as before that as many times as $f$ is in $bk$, so many times is $c$ in $ab$. But it was also so many times in $de$; therefore it will be as before that $de$ is equal to $bk$, and $db$ to $ek$. Wherefore just as $ag$ is a multiple of $c$, so $db$ is a multiple of $f$, which is the proposition. Alternatively, since magnitude $ab$ contains magnitude $c$ according to the same number as magnitude $de$ contains magnitude $f$, and with one [unit] taken away from it, there remains the unit or the number according to which $ag$ contains $c$ and according to which $db$ contains $f$, it is clear that magnitudes $ag$ and $db$ are equal or equimultiples to magnitudes $c$ and $f$.

---

### Proposition 7

**If two equal magnitudes be compared to any other, there will be one [and the same] ratio of them to it; and likewise the ratio of that one to them is one.**

¶ Let there be two equal magnitudes $a$ and $b$, which are compared to any third, such as to $c$. I say that the ratio of $a$ to $c$ and $b$ to $c$ is the same; and likewise the same of $c$ to $a$ and $c$ to $b$. The first is proved thus: for since $c$ is the consequent to $a$ the first and to $b$ the third, it will be in the ratio of the second and fourth. Therefore I shall take $d$ to $a$ the first and $e$ to $b$ the third as equimultiples; and I shall take $f$ as any of the multiples of $c$ which is the second and fourth. And because $a$ and $b$, of which $d$ and $e$ are equimultiples, are set as equal, it will be that if $d$ is divided according to magnitude $a$ and $e$ according to magnitude $b$, the parts on both sides are equal in number and magnitude: in number indeed by the hypothesis on account of the equality of the multiplication on both sides; in magnitude however through this common science repeated as often as necessary: those which are equal to the same are equal to each other. Because therefore the first of the parts of $d$ is equal to the first of the parts of $e$, and the second to the second, and the rest to the rest; and there are as many parts in $d$ as there are in $e$, it will be through the first of this [book] that $d$ is equal to $e$. Wherefore through the common science: if two equal magnitudes are compared to another third: either both magnitudes $d$ and $e$ are similarly greater than $f$, or similarly smaller, or equal to it. Therefore from the definition of non-continuous proportionality: the ratio which is of $a$ the first to $c$ the second, the same is of $b$ the third to $c$ the fourth, which is the proposition. ¶ The second you will prove in the same way with the order reversed: so that $c$ is placed as the first and third, $a$ as the second, and $b$ as the fourth. Since indeed the magnitude $f$, which is the equimultiple of the first and third, is either similarly greater than magnitudes $d$ and $e$ (which are equimultiples of the second and fourth), or similarly smaller, or equal to them; it will be through the same definition that the ratio of $c$ the first to $a$ the second is as $c$ the third to $b$ the fourth, which is the second proposition.

**[Page LIBER]**

---

### Proposition 8

**If two unequal magnitudes be proportioned to one magnitude, the greater will have a greater ratio, the smaller a smaller. And of that [one magnitude] to them, the ratio to the smaller will be greater, and to the greater it will be smaller.**

¶ Let there be two unequal magnitudes $a$ and $bc$, and let $bc$ be the greater, and let them be proportioned to the same magnitude which is $d$. I say that the ratio of $bc$ to $d$ is greater than $a$ to $d$, and on the contrary the ratio of $d$ to $a$ is greater than $d$ to $bc$. The first is proved thus: I shall set $eb$ equal to $a$, and I shall multiply $ce$ as many times so that there results a magnitude greater than $d$, and let it be $fg$. And I shall take $kf$ as such a multiple of $be$, and similarly $h$ as such a multiple of $a$ as $fg$ is a multiple of $ce$. And it will be through the first of this [book] that $h$ is the same multiple of $a$ as $kg$ is a multiple of $bc$. $h$ will also be equal to $kf$, because their submultiples, which are $a$ and $be$, were set as equal. I shall also set that $h$ is not smaller than $d$, but equal or greater; for I shall multiply each of the three magnitudes $ec, be,$ and $a$ equally: so that $fg$, the multiple of $ec$, results greater than $d$, and that $h$, the multiple of $a$, does not result smaller than the same. Then I shall multiply $d$ so that there results a magnitude greater than $h$, and let $m$ be the first magnitude of the multiples of $d$ which is greater than $h$. Under which I shall take the greatest multiple of $d$, or one equal to it, if $m$ is first in the order of multiples of $d$, which let be $l$. And it will be that $l$ is not greater than $h$, and $m$ will consist of $d$ and $l$, because every multiple consists of the next preceding multiple and the simple [the magnitude itself]: as triple from double and simple: except the first multiple which consists of the simple twice. ¶ Because therefore $h$ is equal to $kf$, $kf$ will not be smaller than $l$. Therefore $kf$ and $d$ will not make less than $l$ and $d$, wherefore they will not make less than $m$. And because $fg$ is greater than $d$, $kg$ will be greater than $m$. ¶ I understand therefore the magnitude $bc$ as the first, $d$ as the second, $a$ as the third, $d$ as the fourth: and that for the first and third equimultiples have been taken, namely $kg$ and $h$. Likewise also for the second and fourth equimultiples, indeed the same in the ratio of two, which is $m$. And $kg$, the multiple of the first, exceeds $m$, the multiple of the second; but $h$, the multiple of the third, does not exceed $m$, the multiple of the fourth. It will be through the definition of greater proportionality that the ratio of $bc$ the first to $d$ the second is greater than $a$ the third to $d$ the fourth, which is the first [part]. ¶ The second you will prove through the same definition in the reverse order: let $d$ be the first and third, $a$ the second, and $bc$ the fourth. For $m$, the multiple of the first, exceeds $h$, the multiple of the second. But $m$, the multiple of the third, does not exceed $kg$, the multiple of the fourth: wherefore the ratio of $d$ to $a$ is greater than $d$ to $bc$, which is the second [part]. ¶ From the manner of this demonstration, the sufficiency of the definition of greater proportionality is clear, which the author placed at the beginning of this fifth [book]. For nowhere is there a greater ratio of the first of four magnitudes to the second than of the third to the fourth, unless it happens that some equimultiples to the first and third are found, which when they are related to some equimultiples of the second and fourth, the multiple of the first is found to exceed the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. We shall find these multiples thus, as we shall demonstrate below after the 12th [proposition] of this [book].

---

### Proposition 9

**[Page V]**

**If there be a ratio of any magnitudes to one magnitude, [and it be] one [the same], those magnitudes are equal. If indeed the ratio of one to them be one, it is necessary that those [magnitudes] be equal.**

¶ Let the ratio of two magnitudes $a$ and $b$ to $c$ be one. I say they are equal. And if conversely the ratio of $c$ to each of them be the same, I still say they are equal. This is the converse of [Prop.] 7. The first is clear thus: for if they are not equal, but one of them greater, say $a$, it will be through the first part of the preceding that the ratio of $a$ to $c$ is greater than $b$ to $c$, which is against the hypothesis. The second is also clear: that if $a$ is greater than $b$, it will be through the second part of the preceding that the ratio of $c$ to $b$ is greater than to $a$, which is also against the hypothesis.

---

### Proposition 10

**If there be a greater ratio of one to some magnitude, that magnitude [the first] is greater. If indeed there be a greater ratio of one to the same [magnitudes], it is necessary that [the second] be smaller.**

¶ But if the ratio of $a$ to $c$ be greater than $b$ to $c$, I say $a$ is greater than $b$. And if the ratio of $c$ to $b$ be greater than $c$ to $a$, I still say $a$ is greater than $b$. This is the converse of [Prop.] 8. The first is clear through the first part of [Prop.] 7 and through the first of [Prop.] 8; for through the first part of the seventh, $a$ will not be equal to $b$, nor even smaller through the first of the eighth. The second indeed is clear from the second parts of the same.

---

### Proposition 11

**If ratios of magnitudes be equal to any one [ratio], it is necessary that those ratios also be equal to each other.**

¶ This proportionality, which Euclid numbered among the common conceptions of the mind at the beginning of the first [book]—those which are equal to the same are equal to each other—as it is understood in the case of quantities, he demonstrates here as it is applied to ratios. Let therefore each of two ratios, which are $a$ to $b$ and $c$ to $d$, be equal to the ratio which is $e$ to $f$. I say the ratios $a$ to $b$ and $c$ to $d$ are equal to each other. For I shall take $g$ to $a$, and $h$ to $c$, and $k$ to $e$ as equimultiples. Likewise $l$ to $b$, and $m$ to $d$, and $n$ to $f$ as equimultiples: and because by the hypothesis the ratio of $e$ to $f$ is as $a$ to $b$, and similarly as $c$ to $d$, it will be through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality taken twice: if $k$ exceeds $n$, that $g$ exceeds $l$ and $h$ exceeds $m$. And if $k$ is less than $n$, that $g$ is less than $l$ and $h$ is less than $m$. And if $k$ is equal to $n$, that $g$ is equal to $l$ and $h$ is equal to $m$. Since therefore $g$ to $l$ and $h$ to $m$ behave similarly in adding, diminishing, and equating by means of $k$ and $n$, it will be through the definition of non-continuous proportionality that $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 12

**If the ratio of the first to the second be as the third to the fourth, but the ratio of the third to the fourth be greater than that of the fifth to the sixth: the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than that of the fifth to the sixth.**

¶ Just as in the preceding, what he demonstrates here is conceivable in proportionalities as it is in magnitudes: namely, that if two magnitudes were equal to each other, whatever one of them is greater than, the other will also be greater than. ¶ In ratios however this is demonstrated: so that if the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, but $c$ to $d$ is greater than $e$ to $f$, then $a$ to $b$ will also be greater than $e$ to $f$. For I shall take $g$ to $a$, and $h$ to $c$, and $k$ to $e$ as equimultiples. Likewise $l$ to $b$, and $m$ to $d$, and $n$ to $f$ as equimultiples: and because by the hypothesis the ratio of $c$ to $d$ is as $a$ to $b$, and as $c$ to $f$, it will be through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality that if $h$ exceeds $m$, then $g$ exceeds $l$; and through the conversion of the definition of greater proportionality that it is not necessary for $k$ to exceed $n$. Since therefore by means of $h$ and $m$, if $g$ exceeds $l$ it is not necessary for $k$ to exceed $n$, it will be through the definition of greater proportionality that the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is greater than $c$ to $f$, which is the proposition. ¶ In a similar way you will also prove that if $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, and $c$ to $d$ is smaller than $e$ to $f$, then $a$ to $b$ will be smaller than $e$ to $f$. For since $c$ to $d$ is smaller than $e$ to $f$, $e$ to $f$ will be greater than $c$ to $d$. Therefore through the conversion of the definition of greater proportionality, if $k$ exceeds $n$, it is not necessary that $h$ exceeds $m$. But if $h$ does not exceed $m$, $g$ does not exceed $l$. Therefore if $k$ exceeds $n$, it is not necessary that $g$ exceeds $n$. Therefore through the definition of greater proportionality, the ratio of $e$ to $f$ will be greater than $a$ to $b$. Therefore on the contrary: $a$ to $b$ will be smaller than $e$ to $f$, which is the proposition. ¶ From the manner of the demonstration of the eighth and this one, it will become manifest that if there were a greater ratio of the first of four magnitudes to the second than of the third to the fourth, it will happen that some equimultiples of the first and third can be found which, when compared to some equimultiples of the second and fourth, the multiple of the first is found to exceed the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. Which is clear thus: let there be a greater ratio of $a$ to $b$ than of $d$ to $e$. I shall set therefore the ratio of $a-f$ to $c$ to be as $d$ to $e$. And it will be through this 12th and through the 10th that $a-f$ is smaller than $ab$, and let it be smaller by the quantity $fb$, which I shall multiply so many times that there results a magnitude greater than $c$, which let be $gh$, with this condition: that $d$ multiplied as many times produces a magnitude not smaller than $e$, which let be $k$. Then I shall set $lg$ to be the same multiple of $af$ as $gh$ is a multiple of $fb$ or $k$ of $d$. And it will be through the first of this [book] that $lh$ is the same multiple of $ab$ as $kd$ is [of $d$]. Then I shall set $m$ to be the first magnitude multiple of $c$ which is greater than $k$, and I shall set $n$ as the same multiple of $e$ as $m$ is multiple of $c$. And it will be through the preceding hypotheses and the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality that magnitude $n$ is the first of the multiples of $c$ which will be greater than $lg$, nor will $lg$ be smaller than $c$. I shall take therefore under $n$ the greatest of the multiples of $c$, or one equal to it if by chance $n$ is the first of its multiples, which let be $o$. And $n$ will consist of $o$ and $c$. Because therefore $lg$ is not smaller than $o$, and $gh$ is greater than $c$, $lh$ will be greater than $n$. Wherefore since $k$ is smaller than $m$, the proposition is clear. ¶ We can also demonstrate the converse of this, namely that if it happens that some equimultiples of the first and third are found whose multiple of the first exceeds some multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth: the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than the third to the fourth. Which is proved thus: let there be four magnitudes $a$ the first, $b$ the second, $cd$ the third, $e$ the fourth. And let $f$ to $a$ and $g$ to $cd$ be equimultiples. Similarly $h$ to $b$ and $k$ to $e$ be equimultiples. And let $f$ exceed $h$, but $g$ not exceed $k$. I say that the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is greater than $cd$ to $e$. For if it were equal, through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality, $g$ would exceed $k$, which is against the hypothesis. If however it were smaller, let $cl$ to $e$ be as $a$ to $b$. And it will be through the 10th of this [book] that $cl$ is smaller than $cd$, and let it be smaller in quantity $ld$. I shall set therefore $mn$ to be the same multiple of $cl$ and $np$ multiple of $ld$ as $f$ is multiple of $a$.

**[Page V]**

And it will be through the first of this [book] that $mp$ is the same multiple of $cd$ as $f$ is a multiple of $a$. Each therefore of the two magnitudes $mp$ and $g$ is the equimultiple of magnitude $cd$. Therefore they are themselves equal. For this inference was demonstrated in the 7th of this [book]. And because $g$ is not greater than $k$, $mp$ will not be greater than $k$. But through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality, $mn$ is greater than $k$ because $f$ is greater than $h$. Therefore $mn$ is greater than $mp$, which is impossible. Wherefore the proposition remains.

---

### Proposition 13

**If there be a ratio of any number of magnitudes to as many others, [and it be] one, the ratio of all these taken together to all those taken together will be the same as the ratio of one to one.**

¶ What he first proposed concerning multiples, he proposes here concerning all ratios: whence this is a commonality [generalization] of that one, because every multiplicity is a ratio, but not conversely. Let there be therefore one ratio of $a$ to $b$, $c$ to $d$, and $e$ to $f$. I say that the ratio of the composite of $a, c, e$ to the composite of $b, d, f$ is the same as the ratio of $a$ to $b$. I shall take $g$ to $a$, $h$ to $c$, and $k$ to $e$ as equimultiples. Likewise $l$ to $b, m$ to $d$, and $n$ to $f$ as equimultiples. It will be through the first of this [book] that the composite of $g, h, k$ is the same multiple of the composite of $a, c, e$ as $g$ is multiple of $a$. Similarly through the same, the composite of $l, m, n$ will be the same multiple of the composite of $b, d, f$ as $l$ is multiple of $b$. And through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality taken twice, if $g$ exceeds $l$, $h$ exceeds $m$ and $k$ exceeds $n$. And if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. Therefore through the common science, if $g$ exceeds $l$, the composite of $g, h, k$ exceeds the composite of $l, m, n$. And if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. Therefore through the definition of non-continuous proportionality, the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is as the composite of $a, c, e$ to the composite of $b, d, f$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 14

**If four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be greater than the third, it is necessary that the second be greater than the fourth. If smaller, it is smaller. If indeed equal, it is also equal.**

¶ Let the ratio of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$. I say that if $a$ is greater than $c$, $b$ will be greater than $d$. And if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal. For if $a$ be greater than $c$, it will be through the first part of the 8th of this [book] that the ratio of $a$ to $d$ is greater than $c$ to $d$. Wherefore $a$ to $d$ will be greater than $a$ to $b$. Therefore through the second part of the 10th of this [book], $b$ will be greater than $d$, which is the proposition. If $a$ be smaller than $c$, it will be through the first part of the 8th that the ratio of $a$ to $d$ is smaller than $c$ to $d$. Wherefore $a$ to $b$ will be greater than $a$ to $d$. Therefore through the second part of the 10th, $b$ will be smaller than $d$. If however $a$ be equal to $c$, it will be through the first part of the 7th that $a$ to $d$ is as $c$ to $d$. Wherefore $a$ to $d$ is as to $b$. Thus through the second part of the 9th, $b$ will be equal to $d$, and thus the proposition is clear.

---

### Proposition 15

**If equimultiples be assigned to any magnitudes, there will be one ratio of those multiples and their submultiples [the original magnitudes].**

¶ Let $c$ to $a$ and $d$ to $b$ be equimultiples. I say that the ratio which is of $a$ to $b$, the same is of $c$ to $d$. Let $c$ be divided according to magnitude $a$, and $d$ according to magnitude $b$. And there are as many parts of $c$ as $d$. And because any part of $c$ to any part of $d$ behaves just as $a$ to $b$, it will be through the 13th of this [book] that $c$ to $d$ is as $a$ to $b$, which is the proposition.

**[Page LIBER]**

---

### Proposition 16

**If four magnitudes be proportional, they will also be proportional alternately [permutated].**

¶ Let the ratio of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$. I say that $a$ to $c$ will be as $b$ to $d$. And this is the mode of arguing which is called permutated proportionality. Its demonstration is clear thus: I shall take $e$ to $a$ and $f$ to $b$ as equimultiples; likewise $g$ to $c$ and $h$ to $d$ as equimultiples. It will be through the preceding [Prop. 15] that $e$ to $f$ is as $g$ to $h$. Wherefore through the 14th, if $e$ exceeds $a$ (?), $g$ [exceeds $c$?], and $f$ exceeds $b$ (?), and if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. Therefore through the definition of non-continuous proportionality $a$ to $c$ will be as $b$ to $d$, which is the proposition. It is necessary, however, that in permutated proportionality all four magnitudes be of the same genus.

---

### Proposition 17

**If magnitudes be proportional conjointly [by composition]: the same will also be proportional disjointly [by division].**

¶ Having demonstrated the mode of arguing which is called permutated proportionality, he demonstrates that which is called disjoint proportionality. Let therefore the ratio of $ab$ to $b$ be as $cd$ to $d$. I say that $a$ to $b$ will be as $c$ to $d$ (?). I shall take $gh$ to $a$ and $hk$ to $cb$, likewise $lm$ to $df$ and $mn$ to $fc$ as equimultiples. It will be through the first of this [book] that $gh$ is the same multiple of $ab$ as $gb$ is multiple of $a$. And $cln$ is the same multiple of $de$ as $lm$ is multiple of $df$. And therefore through the preceding hypotheses $gk$ is just as multiple of $ab$ as $lnd$ is of $e$. Again I shall set $kp$ to $cb$ and $nq$ to $fe$ as equimultiples; they will be through the second [proposition] $bp$ to $cb$ and $de$ equimultiples. Therefore through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality, if $gk$ exceeds $bp$, $ln$ exceeds $mq$. And if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. With the common parts $bk$ and $mn$ taken away, it will be through the common science that if $gb$ exceeds $kp$, $lm$ exceeds $nq$. And if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. Therefore through the definition of non-continuous proportionality the ratio of $a$ to $cb$ is as $df$ to $fe$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 18

**If magnitudes be proportional disjointly [by division], they will also be proportional conjointly [by composition].**

¶ He demonstrates the mode of arguing which is called conjoint proportionality, and it is the converse mode of the prior one. For the demonstration of which, let the disposition of the preceding be resumed. And let all its hypotheses remain, except that the ratio of $ac$ to $cb$ is set to be as $df$ to $fe$. I say that the ratio of $ab$ to $bc$ will be as $de$ to $fe$. For it follows from this hypothesis and the other hypotheses of the preceding concerning multiples taken equally, through the conversion of the definition of non-continuous proportionality: if $gb$ exceeds $kp$, $lm$ exceeds $nq$. And if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. Therefore, with the common parts $bk$ and $mn$ placed, it follows through the common science that if $gk$ exceeds $bp$, $gln$ exceeds $mq$. And if it diminishes, it diminishes; and if it equals, it equals. Wherefore through the definition of non-continuous proportionality, the ratio of $ab$ to $bc$ will be as $de$ to $cf$, which is the proposition. Alternatively, the same indirectly thus: since the ratio of $ac$ to $cb$ is as $df$ to $fe$, [suppose] $ab$ to $bc$ is not as $de$ to $cf$. Let therefore the ratio of $de$ to some other magnitude be as $ab$ to $bc$, which will be either greater than $ef$ or smaller. For if it were equal to it, the proposition would stand.

**[Page V]**

Let it first be greater, and let it be $eg$. And it will be through the preceding that $ac$ to $cb$ is as $dg$ to $g$. Wherefore $dg$ to $ge$ is as $df$ to $fe$. It follows therefore through the 14th that since $dg$ the first is smaller than $df$ the third, $ge$ the second will be smaller than $ef$ the fourth. But it was set that it was greater. Let therefore the ratio of $d$ to a smaller [than] $ef$, which let be $eh$, be as $ab$ to $bc$. And it will be through the preceding that $ac$ to $cb$ is as $db$ to $he$. Wherefore through the 11th, $db$ to $he$ is as $df$ to $fe$. And because $dh$ the first is greater than $df$ the third, $eh$ the second will be through the 14th greater than $ef$ the third. Which, because it is impossible, the proposition follows.

---

### Proposition 19

**If from two wholes two portions be cut off, and the whole be to the whole as the part cut off to the part cut off: the remainder will be to the remainder as the whole to the whole.**

¶ What the fifth [proposition] proposed concerning multiples, this one proposes universally concerning all ratios. Whence it is as much more common as ratio is than multiplicity. Let there be therefore two magnitudes $ab$ and $cd$, from which let two be cut off which are $be$ and $df$. And let the ratio of the whole $ab$ to the whole $cd$ be as $be$ cut off to $df$ cut off. I say that the ratio of $ae$ the residue to $cf$ the residue will be the same as the ratio of the whole $ab$ to the whole $cd$. For since $ab$ is to $cd$ as $be$ to $df$, it will be alternately $ab$ to $be$ as $cd$ to $df$. And disjointly [by division] $ae$ to $eb$ as $cf$ to $df$. And again alternately $ae$ to $cf$ as $eb$ to $fd$. And because it was thus that $ab$ was to $cd$, the proposition is clear. ¶ From this 19th and permutated proportionality, the mode of arguing which is called "everted" [converted] proportionality is demonstrated: as if $ab$ is to $bc$ as $cd$ to $df$. I say that $ba$ to $ae$ will be as $cd$ to $cf$. Because since $ab$ is to $bc$ as $cd$ to $df$, it will be alternately $ab$ to $cd$ as $bc$ to $df$. Wherefore through this 19th, $ba$ to $dc$ as $ae$ to $cf$. Therefore alternately $ba$ to $ae$ as $dc$ to $fc$, which is everted [proportion]. ¶ Also converse proportionality, which we demonstrated from the definition of non-continuous proportionality in explaining the principles of this fifth [book], can also be demonstrated here indirectly from permutated proportionality and the 7th and 9th of this [book]: as if the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, I say that $b$ will be to $a$ as $d$ to $c$. But if it were not $d$ to $c$ as $b$ to $a$, and since $a$ to $b-e$ as $c$ to $d$, it will be alternately $a$ to $c$ as $b$ to $d$. And because again $b$ to $a$ as $d$ to $e$, it will also be alternately $b$ to $d$ as $a$ to $e$. Wherefore $a$ to $e$ will be as $d$ to $c$. If therefore $e$ be not equal to $c$, the impossible and contrary of the second part of the 9th will happen. If however it be equal, $b$ will be to $a$ as $d$ to $c$, which is the proposition.

---

### Proposition 20

**If there be any number of magnitudes, and others according to their number, of which any two of the first [set] are according to the ratio of two of the latter [set]: it is necessary in the proportionality of equality [ex aequali] that if the first of the prior is greater than the last, the first of the posterior is also greater than the last. If smaller, smaller. If indeed equal, equal.**

¶ Euclid, being about to demonstrate the mode of arguing which is called equal proportionality [ex aequali], whether magnitudes of two orders are proportioned directly or crosswise [perturbed], premises two antecedents necessary for demonstrating the proposition: of which he first demonstrates equal proportionality when magnitudes of two orders are proportioned directly; and through the second when they are proportioned crosswise. Or he proposes these two antecedents concerning magnitudes of two orders equal in number, whatever they may be. For having taken magnitudes on both sides according to whatever number, they have truth. It is not

**[Page LIBER]**

necessary, however, that we demonstrate them except in three [magnitudes], for this is entirely sufficient for the proposition. Concerning any parts, it will be clear through equal proportionality once it has been demonstrated. ¶ Let there be therefore three magnitudes $a, b, c$, and let three others be taken which are $d, e, f$. And let the ratio of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$, and $b$ to $c$ as $d$ to $f$ (?). I say that if $a$ is greater than $c$, $f$ will be greater. And if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal. For if it is greater, it will be through the first part of the 8th a greater ratio of $a$ to $b$ than $c$ to $b$. Wherefore through the 12th, the ratio of $c$ to $d$ will be greater than $c$ to $b$. And because through converse proportionality $c$ to $b$ as $f$ to $d$, $c$ to $d$ will be greater than $f$ to $d$. Thus through the first part of the 10th, $c$ is greater than $f$, which is the proposition. If $a$ be smaller than $c$, it will be proved by the same and in the same way that $c$ is smaller than $f$. For there will be a smaller ratio of $a$ to $b$ than $c$ to $b$ through the first part of the 8th. And therefore through the 12th and through converse proportionality, $c$ to $d$ will be smaller than $f$ to $d$. Therefore through the first part of the 10th, $c$ will be smaller than $f$, which is the proposition. If however $a$ be equal to $c$, it will be through the first part of the 7th that the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $b$. And therefore through the second of the 11th and converse proportionality, $c$ to $d$ will be as $f$ to $d$. Wherefore through the first part of the 9th, $c$ is equal to $f$, which is the proposition. ¶ Some however demonstrated this conclusion through permutated proportionality in this way: the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, therefore alternately $a$ to $c$ as $b$ to $d$. And because again $b$ to $c$ as $d$ to $f$, it will be alternately $b$ to $d$ as $c$ to $f$. But $b$ to $d$ was as $a$ to $c$. Therefore through the 11th, $a$ to $c$ will be as $c$ to $f$. Thus through the 14th, if $a$ the first is greater than $c$ the third, $c$ the second will be greater than $f$ the fourth. And if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal, which is the proposition. These people, however, erred in their demonstration. Because if it were the intention of Euclid to demonstrate thus, it would not be necessary for him to premise this conclusion as an antecedent to equal proportionality. For if again one permutation of proportionality were made to which it was arrived, which is $a$ to $c$ as $c$ to $f$, it follows that $a$ is to $e$ (?) as $c$ to $f$, and this is equal proportionality. Furthermore, their conclusion does not follow unless all magnitudes of both orders were of one genus. For if $a, b, c$ are lines and $c, d, f$ surfaces, or bodies, or times: then there will not be a permutation of ratios. They sin, therefore, in demonstrating particularly that which is stated universally.

---

### Proposition 21

**If there be any number of magnitudes, and others according to their number, of which any two of the prior compared to any two of the posterior crosswise [perturbed] shall be according to their ratio: it is also necessary that if in the proportionality of equality the first of the prior is greater than the last, the first of the posterior is also greater than the last. If smaller, smaller. If indeed equal, equal.**

¶ The second antecedent: there are three magnitudes $a, b, c$, and let three others be taken which are $f, e, d$. And let the ratio of $a$ to $b$ be as $e$ to $d$, and $b$ to $c$ as $f$ to $e$. I say that if $a$ is greater than $c$, $f$ will be greater than $d$. And if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal. This however is proved through the same and in the same way as the preceding. For if $a$ be greater than $c$, the ratio of $a$ to $b$ will be greater than $c$ to $b$. Wherefore $e$ to $d$ will be greater than $c$ to $b$. And because $c$ to $b$ is as $e$ to $f$ through converse proportionality, $e$ to $d$ will be greater than $e$ to $f$. Therefore $f$ is greater than $d$ through the second part of the 10th, which is the proposition. If $a$ be smaller than $c$, then $c$ to $d$ will eventually be smaller than to $f$ (?). Wherefore through the same part of the same [Prop. 10], $f$ will be smaller than $d$. If however $a$ be equal to $c$, it follows that the ratio of $c$ to $d$ is as $c$ to $f$. Therefore through the second part of the 9th, $f$ will be equal to $d$, which is the proposition.

***

### Notes on Abbreviations and Readings
*   **ꝙ (quod):** Frequently used as a conjunction.
*   **ꝑ (per):** Through.
*   **ꝓ (pro):** For/instead of.
*   **ꝯ (con/com):** Used in words like *conjunctionem* or *componendo*.
*   **qꝫ (que):** Enclitic "and".
*   **ſm (secundum):** According to.
*   **sciam (scientiam):** "Science" or "knowledge," here referring to the *Common Notions* (Axioms) of Euclid.
*   **7 (et):** Standard Tironian note for "and."
*   **v⸀ (vult):** Means or signifies.
*   **vportheſes:** OCR error for *hypotheses*.
*   **incontinue proportionalitatis:** Discrete proportion (as opposed to continuous proportion).
*   **equa pproportionalitas:** *Ex aequali* proportionality.
*   **peruerſim:** Perturbed or crosswise proportion (Euclid V, Def. 18).
*   **submultiplicium:** Aliquot parts.

# **BOOK [V]**

...that just as **e** is a multiple of **b**, so **f** is a multiple of **d**, by the preceding [proposition] taken as many times as there are parts in **e** or in **f** minus one; and thus the proposition is clear.

**Proposition .4.**

**I**f the proportion <note>In this context, proportion refers to the relationship in size between two magnitudes.</note> of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth; and to the first and third equal multiples are assigned; and likewise to the second and fourth equal multiples are assigned: then the assigned multiples will be proportional in the same order.

Let the proportion of **a** (the first) to **b** (the second) be as **c** (the third) to **d** (the fourth). Let **e** be taken as a multiple of **a**, and **f** as an equal multiple of **c**. Likewise, let **g** be a multiple of **b**, and **h** an equal multiple of **d**. I say that the proportion of **e** to **g** is as **f** to **h**. I shall take **k** as a multiple of **e**, and **l** as an equal multiple of **f**. Likewise, **m** as a multiple of **g**, and **n** as an equal multiple of **h**. Because **e** and **f** are equal multiples of **a** and **c**, and **k** and **l** are equal multiples of **e** and **f**, they will be (by the preceding proposition) equal multiples of **a** and **c**. By the same reasoning, **m** and **n** will be equal multiples of **b** and **d**. Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of proportional magnitudes, **k** to **m** and **l** to **n** will behave similarly in adding, subtracting, and equating <note>original: "in addendo diminuendo et equando." This refers to the standard Euclidean test for proportionality involving multiples.</note>. Since, therefore, **k** and **l** are equal multiples of **e** and **f**, and **m** and **n** are equal multiples of **g** and **h**, the proportion of **e** to **g** will be as **f** to **h** by the definition of proportionality. This is what was to be shown.

**Proposition .5.**

**I**f there are two magnitudes of which one is a part of the other, and from each of them the same part is subtracted [respectively], the remainder will be the same multiple of the remainder as the whole is of the whole.

Or thus: if it be an aliquot <note>An "aliquot part" is a part that divides the whole exactly, like 2 is an aliquot part of 6.</note> part, the remainder will be the same part of the remainder as the whole is of the whole. Let the magnitude **a.b.** be the same part of magnitude **c.d.** as **e.b.** is of **a.b.** Let **a.b.** be subtracted from the magnitude **c.d.**, and let the remainder be **f.c.** <note>The letters refer to line segments in the diagram below.</note>. Thus **f.d.** will be equal to **a.b.** Similarly, let **e.b.** be subtracted from magnitude **a.b.**, and let the remainder be **e.a.** I say that whatever part the magnitude **a.b.** is of magnitude **c.d.**, the magnitude **a.e.** is the same part of magnitude **c.f.** For since **f.d.** is equal to **a.b.**, then **f.d.** will be the same multiple of **e.b.** as **c.d.** is a multiple of **a.b.** Therefore, I will set **d.g.** as the same multiple of **a.e.** as **f.d.** is a multiple of **e.b.** From the first [proposition] of this book, the magnitude **f.g.** will be the same multiple of **a.b.** as **f.d.** is a multiple of **e.b.** And because **c.d.** was the same multiple of **a.b.** as **f.d.** was a multiple of **e.b.**, each of the two magnitudes **c.d.** and **f.g.** is an equal multiple of magnitude **a.b.** Therefore, by common knowledge <note>original: "communem scientiam." This refers to a "Common Notion" or axiom in Euclidean geometry.</note>, **c.d.** and **f.g.** are equal to each other. Thus, by taking away magnitude **f.d.** from both, **c.f.** will be equal to **d.g.** And because **d.g.** was the same multiple of **a.e.** as **f.d.** of **e.b.**, and therefore as **a.b.** of **e.b.**, and also as **c.d.** of **a.b.**, it follows that **c.f.** will be the same multiple of **a.e.** as the whole **c.d.** is of the whole **a.b.** This is what was to be shown.

**Proposition .6.**

**I**f two magnitudes are equal multiples of two others, and two smaller magnitudes [which are equal multiples of the same others] are subtracted from the two larger ones, the two remainders will be either equal to those [original] magnitudes or equal multiples of them.

V

¶ Let the quantities **a b** and **d e** be equal multiples <note>original: "eque multiplices"</note> of **c** and **f**; and let **c** be subtracted from **a b**, and **f** from **d e**, and let the remainders be: from **a b**, indeed **a g**, and from **d e**, **d b**. It will then be that **g b** is equal to **c**, and **b e** is equal to **f**. I say that the two remainders **a g** and **d b** will be equal to the two quantities **c** and **f**, or be equal multiples of them. 

Suppose first that **a g** is equal to **c**. I say that **d b** is equal to **f**. For I shall take a quantity **e k** equal to **f**. It will then be, by the previous hypotheses, that as many times as **f** is in **b k**, so many times is **c** in **a b**. Therefore, just as **a b** is a multiple of **c**, so **b k** is a multiple of **f**. But **d e** was also such a multiple of the same **f**. Therefore, by <term>common knowledge<gloss>The Latin "communis scientia" refers to an axiom or common notion—a self-evident truth in geometry.</gloss></term>, **b k** is equal to **d e**. Thus, by taking away their common quantity **b e**, **d b** will be equal to **e k**, and therefore equal to **f**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ If, however, **a g** is a multiple of **c**, I shall set **e k** to be an equal multiple of **f**. It will then be as before: as many times as **f** is in **b k**, so many times is **c** in **a b**. But it was also in **d e** just as many times. Therefore, as before, **d e** is equal to **b k**, and **d b** to **e k**. Therefore, just as **a g** is a multiple of **c**, so **d b** is a multiple of **f**, which is what was proposed. 

Alternatively, since the quantity **a b** contains the quantity **c** according to the same number as the quantity **d e** contains the quantity **f**, and by subtracting one unit from it there remains the unit or number according to which **a g** contains **c** and according to which **d b** contains **f**, it is clear that the quantities **a g** and **d b** are equal or equal multiples of the quantities **c** and **f**.

### Proposition 7.

**[S]** If two equal quantities are compared to any other [quantity], their <term>ratio<gloss>The quantitative relation between two amounts showing the number of times one value contains or is contained within the other.</gloss></term> to it will be one and the same; likewise, the ratio of that [third] quantity to them is one.

¶ Let there be two equal quantities, **a** and **b**, which are compared to any third, such as **c**. I say that the ratio of **a** to **c** is the same as **b** to **c**, and likewise that of **c** to **a** and **c** to **b**. 

The first part is proved thus: since **c** is the <term>consequent<gloss>The second term in a ratio.</gloss></term> to **a** (the first) and to **b** (the third), it will stand in the relationship of the second and fourth terms. I shall take **d** as an equal multiple of **a** (the first) and **e** of **b** (the third); and I shall take **f** as any multiple of **c**, which is the second and fourth. Because **a** and **b** (of which **d** and **e** are equal multiples) are set as equal, it follows that if **d** is divided according to the quantity **a**, and **e** according to the quantity **b**, the parts in both will be equal in number and quantity. In number, indeed, by the hypothesis of equal multiplication; in quantity, however, by this common knowledge repeated as often as necessary: things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other. 

Since, therefore, the first of the parts of **d** is equal to the first of the parts of **e**, and the second to the second, and the others to the others, and there are as many parts in **d** as there are in **e**, then by the first [proposition] of this book, **d** is equal to **e**. Therefore, by common knowledge: if two equal quantities are compared to another third, either both quantities **d** and **e** are likewise greater than **f**, or likewise smaller, or equal to it. Therefore, from the definition of <term>discrete proportionality<gloss>The text uses "incontinue proportionalitatis," referring to the standard definition of proportional magnitudes where their multiples maintain the same greater-than, equal-to, or less-than relationship.</gloss></term>, the ratio of **a** (the first) to **c** (the second) is the same as **b** (the third) to **c** (the fourth), which is what was proposed. 

¶ You shall prove the second part in the same way by reversing the order: so that **c** is placed as the first and third, while **a** is the second and **b** the fourth. Since the quantity **f** (which is an equal multiple of the first and third) is either likewise greater than quantities **d** and **e** (which are equal multiples of the second and fourth), or likewise smaller, or equal to them, it will be by the same definition that the ratio of **c** (the first) to **a** (the second) is as **c** (the third) to **b** (the fourth), which is the second proposed point.

<note>Diagram description: A horizontal scale with points o, a, g, b, e. Labels indicate segments of 6 and 12, illustrating the equality of multiples d and e derived from equal quantities a and b.</note>

<meta>This page contains Proposition 8 from Book V of Euclid's Elements, focusing on the relationship between unequal magnitudes and their ratios to a third magnitude. This follows the general definitions of proportion established in the preceding pages.</meta>

**BOOK**

**Proposition 8.**

[Decorative initial S] If two unequal quantities are compared to one <note>original: "unā quantitatem"</note> quantity, the greater will possess a greater ratio, and the smaller a smaller ratio. Moreover, the ratio of that [single] quantity to those [two] will be greater toward the smaller quantity, and smaller toward the greater quantity.

¶ Let there be two unequal quantities, *a* and *bc* <note>The symbol "7" in the transcription is a shorthand for the Latin "et" (and).</note>, and let *bc* be the greater. Let them be compared to the same quantity, which is *d*. I say that the ratio of *bc* to *d* is greater than the ratio of *a* to *d*, and that conversely, the ratio of *d* to *a* is greater than the ratio of *d* to *bc*. 

The first part is proved thus: I will set *eb* equal to *a* <note>The segment *eb* is marked out on the larger line *bc* to represent the length of the smaller line *a*.</note>, and I will multiply the remainder *ec* <note>The difference between the greater and lesser quantities.</note> as many times as is necessary to produce a quantity greater than *d*; let this [multiple] be *fg*. Then I will take *kf* to be the same multiple of *be*, and similarly *h* to be the same multiple of *a*, as *fg* is a multiple of *ec*.

### Proposition 9

**[If]** several quantities have the same ratio to a single quantity, those quantities are equal to one another. If, however, a single quantity has the same ratio to several others, it is necessary that those others be equal.

¶ Let there be a single ratio of two quantities **a** and **b** to **c**. I say that **a** and **b** are equal. And if, conversely, there is the same ratio of **c** to both of them, I still say they are equal. This is the converse of Proposition 7 <note>The author is referring to the preceding proofs regarding the relationship between magnitudes and their ratios.</note>. 

The first part is clear as follows: for if they are not equal, but one of them is greater—for instance, **a**—then by the first part of the previous proposition, the ratio of **a** to **c** would be greater than the ratio of **b** to **c**. But this contradicts the hypothesis <note>original: "ypothe."</note>. 

The second part is also clear: for if **a** is greater than **b**, then by the second part of the previous proposition, the ratio of **c** to **b** will be greater than the ratio of **c** to **a**. This also contradicts the hypothesis.

### Proposition 10

**[If]** there is a ratio of one quantity to another that is greater than the ratio of a second to that same quantity, the first quantity is the greater. If, however, the ratio of one quantity to a second is greater than its ratio to a third, it is necessary for that third quantity to be the smaller.

¶ If there is a greater ratio of **a** to **c** than of **b** to **c**, I say that **a** is greater than **b**. And if there is a greater ratio of **c** to **b** than of **c** to **a**, I still say that **a** is greater than **b**. This is the converse of Proposition 8. 

The first part is clear through the first part of Proposition 7 and the first part of Proposition 8. For by the first part of Proposition 7, **a** will not be equal to **b**; nor will it be smaller, by the first part of Proposition 8. The second part is clear from the second parts of those same propositions.

### Proposition 11

**[If]** the ratios of certain quantities are equal to some one ratio, it is necessary that those ratios also be equal to each other.

¶ Euclid listed this proportion among the "common notions" <note>Euclid’s *Common Notions* are axioms—self-evident truths—found at the start of Book 1 of the *Elements*.</note> at the beginning of the first book: "things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other." While that is understood there regarding quantities, he demonstrates it here as it is applied to ratios. 

Therefore, let each of two ratios—**a** to **b** and **c** to **d**—be equal to the ratio **e** to **f**. I say that the ratios **a** to **b** and **c** to **d** are equal to each other. 

For I shall take **g**, **h**, and **k** as equimultiples <term>equimultiples: whole-number multiples of different quantities multiplied by the same factor (e.g., 2a, 2c, and 2e)</term> of **a**, **c**, and **e**. Likewise, let **l**, **m**, and **n** be equimultiples of **b**, **d**, and **f**. 

Because by the hypothesis the ratio **e** to **f** is as **a** to **b**, and similarly as **c** to **d**, it follows—by applying the definition of proportional magnitudes twice—that if **k** is greater than **n**, then **g** is greater than **l** and **h** is greater than **m**. If **k** is less than **n**, then **g** is less than **l** and **h** is less than **m**. And if **k** is equal to **n**, then **g** is equal to **l** and **h** is equal to **m**. 

Since, therefore, **g** to **l** and **h** to **m** behave in the same way regarding being greater, less, or equal by means of the intermediates **k** and **n**, it follows by the definition of proportionality <note>This refers to the formal definition of "same ratio" found in Euclid's Book V, Definition 5.</note> that **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, which is what was proposed.

## **Proposition 16.**

**If** there are four proportional quantities, they will also be proportional alternately.

Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** to **d**. I say that **a** will be to **c** as **b** is to **d**. This is the method of reasoning called <term>permuted proportionality</term> <note>In modern mathematics, this is the rule that if a/b = c/d, then a/c = b/d.</note>, the proof of which is demonstrated as follows:

Let **e** and **f** be <term>equal multiples</term> <note>meaning both are multiplied by the same number</note> of **a** and **b**, and likewise let **g** and **h** be equal multiples of **c** and **d**. 

By the preceding proposition <note>Proposition 15</note>, the ratio of **e** to **f** will be as **g** is to **h**. Therefore, by Proposition 14, if **e** is greater than **g**, then **f** is also greater than **h**; if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. 

Therefore, by the definition of <term>discrete proportionality</term> <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis." This refers to Euclid's rigorous definition of how four magnitudes relate when they are not part of a continuous scale.</note>, it follows that **a** is to **c** as **b** is to **d**, which is what was proposed. 

However, it is necessary that in permuted proportionality, all four quantities must be of the same <term>kind</term> <note>original: "eiusdem generis." This is a crucial constraint in Greek geometry: you can only compare lines to lines or areas to areas. You cannot have a ratio between a line and an area.</note>.

<summary>This page demonstrates Proposition 16 of Euclid's fifth book, proving that if four quantities are proportional, their positions can be swapped (alternated) while maintaining the same proportion. It highlights the requirement that all quantities must be of the same mathematical type for this to hold true.</summary>

### Proposition 19
**If two portions are cut away from two wholes, and the whole is to the whole as the portion cut away is to the portion cut away: then the remainder will be to the remainder as the whole is to the whole.**

While the fifth proposition <note>original: *Quā quinta pponit*</note> of this book addresses this in terms of multiples, this proposition speaks universally regarding all <term>proportions>the relationship between two quantities</term>. Thus, this one is more general than the one concerning multiples. Therefore, let there be two quantities, **a.b.** and **c.d.**, from which two portions are cut away, namely **b.e.** and **d.f.** Let the proportion of the whole **a.b.** to the whole **c.d.** be as the portion **b.e.** is to the portion **d.f.** I say that the ratio of the remainder **a.e.** to the remainder **c.f.** will be the same as that of the whole **a.b.** to the whole **c.d.** For since **a.b.** is to **c.d.** as **b.e.** is to **d.f.**, by <term>alternating>changing the order of the terms in a proportion (permutatim)</term> **a.b.** will be to **b.e.** as **c.d.** is to **d.f.**; and <term>by division>subtracting the bottom number of a ratio from the top (diiunctim)</term> **a.e.** is to **e.b.** as **c.f.** is to **f.d.**; and again, by alternating, **a.e.** is to **c.f.** as **e.b.** is to **f.d.**; and since it was already established that this is the ratio of **a.b.** to **c.d.**, the proposition is clear. 

From this 19th proposition and the rule of alternating proportionality, the method of reasoning called <term>everted proportionality>the ratio of a whole to its remainder (proportionalitas euersa)</term> is demonstrated. For example, if **a.b.** is to **b.e.** as **c.d.** is to **d.f.**, I say that **b.a.** will be to **a.e.** as **c.d.** is to **c.f.** Because since **a.b.** is to **b.e.** as **c.d.** is to **d.f.**, by alternating, **a.b.** will be to **c.d.** as **b.e.** is to **d.f.**; wherefore by this 19th proposition, **b.a.** is to **a.e.** as **a.e.** is to **c.f.**; therefore by alternating, **b.a.** is to **a.e.** as **c.d.** is to **c.f.**, which is what was proposed. 

<note>original: *Conuersa quoqz pportionali/ tas*</note> **Converted proportionality**—which we demonstrated from the definition of discontinuous proportionality when explaining the principles of this fifth book—can also be demonstrated here indirectly from alternating proportionality and the 9th proposition of this book. For if the proportion of **a.b.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, I say that **b.** will be to **a.** as **d.** is to **c.** If it were not so, let **d.** be to **c.** as **b.** is to **a.** Since **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, by alternating, **a.** will be to **c.** as **b.** is to **d.**; and because again **b.** is to **a.** as **d.** is to **e.**, by alternating, **b.** will be to **d.** as **a.** is to **e.** Wherefore **a.** will be to **e.** as **d.** is to **c.** If therefore **e.** is not equal to **c.**, an impossibility occurs, contradicting the second part of the 9th proposition. But if they are equal, then **b.** will be to **a.** as **d.** is to **c.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 20
**If there are any number of magnitudes, and others equal to them in number, which taken two and two have the same ratio: they will also be in the same ratio by equality. That is, if the first of the first set is greater than the last, the first of the second set will also be greater than its last. If it is smaller, it will be smaller. If equal, it will be equal.**

In order to demonstrate the method of reasoning called <term>equal proportionality>the "ex aequali" property, where ratios are compared across two different sequences (eq̄ pportionalitas)</term>—whether the quantities of the two orders are proportioned directly or crosswise—Euclid first presents two necessary preliminary points. Through the first of these, equal proportionality is demonstrated when quantities of two orders are proportioned directly; through the second, when they are proportioned crosswise. He proposes these two preliminaries concerning any equal number of quantities in two orders. For these truths hold even when any number of quantities are taken on both sides.

### BOOK FIVE

#### Proposition 22
**If there be any number of quantities, and others equal to them in number, any two of which are proportional in the same ratio to two of the first, they shall also be proportional in ordinate proportionality [<i>ex aequali</i>].**

Having demonstrated the antecedents to ordinate proportionality, [the author] here demonstrates it: first, when the quantities of the two orders are directly proportional. It is not necessary that he demonstrate this except when there are only three quantities in each of the two orders. For it follows evidently through this when there are four quantities in each order, and so on; and therefore it was also not necessary for its [proof] to be demonstrated previously except according to there being three quantities in each order.

¶ Let there be, therefore, three quantities $a, b, e$, and let three others be taken which are $c, d, f$; and let the proportion of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$, and $b$ to $e$ as $d$ to $f$. I say that $a$ will be to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$. For I shall take $g$ [as a multiple] of $a$ and $h$ of $c$ as equimultiples. Likewise, $k$ of $b$ and $l$ of $d$ as equimultiples; and again $m$ of $e$ and $n$ of $f$ as equimultiples. And by [Proposition] 4, $g$ will be to $k$ as $h$ is to $l$; and $k$ to $m$ as $l$ is to $n$. Wherefore, by [Proposition] 20, if $g$ is greater than $m$, $h$ [text reads $b$ in error] will be greater than $n$; and if less, less; and if equal, equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the proportion of $a$ to $e$ is as $c$ to $f$, which is what was proposed.

¶ This can also be demonstrated by [Proposition] 15 of this [book], having taken $g, k, m$ as equimultiples of $a, b, e$ and $h, l, n$ of $c, d, f$; for by [Proposition] 15, $g$ will be to $k$ as $h$ [text reads $b$] to $l$, and $k$ to $m$ as $l$ to $n$, with the rest carried out as before.

¶ But if there be more than three quantities in each order: for example, four; having added $p, r, q$ [note: the text adds $p$ and $q$ as the fourth terms], so that $e$ is to $p$ as $f$ is to $q$, it will again be $a$ to $p$ as $c$ is to $q$. For $a$ will be to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$, as has been demonstrated. Therefore, with $b$ and $d$ removed, there will be three quantities $a, e, p$ and another three $c, f, q$ as is proposed: wherefore $a$ is to $p$ as $c$ is to $q$. Thus it is demonstrated for 4 by means of 3, by removing one mean. In the same way, you shall demonstrate for 5 by means of 4, by removing two means; and for 6 by means of 5, by removing three; and so for the rest.

***

#### Proposition 23
**If there be any number of quantities, and others equal to them in number, any two of which are indirectly [perturbed] proportional according to the proportion of two of the prior ones, they shall also be proportional in ordinate proportionality.**

He demonstrates ordinate proportionality in quantities of two orders which are indirectly or cross-proportionally related. Nor is it necessary that he demonstrate this except when there are only three quantities in each of the two orders: for through this it follows evidently for whatever [number] may be placed in either order, just as was demonstrated in the preceding [proposition] concerning those directly proportional.

¶ Let there be, therefore, 3 quantities $a, b, e$, and let 3 others be taken which are $f, c, d$. And let the proportion of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$, and $b$ to $e$ as $f$ to $c$. I say that $a$ will be to $e$ as $f$ is to $d$. For I shall take $g$ of $a$, and $h$ of $c$, and $k$ of $f$ as equimultiples. Likewise $l$ of $b$, and $m$ of $c$, and $n$ of $d$ as equimultiples. And by the fourth [proposition], $g$ will be to $l$ as $b$ is to $n$ [unclear reading: likely error for $c$ to $d$ logic], and by [Proposition] 15, $l$ to $m$ as $k$ is to $h$. Wherefore by [Proposition] 21, if $g$ exceeds $m$, $k$ exceeds $n$; and if it is less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the proportion of $a$ to $e$ is as $f$ to $d$, which is what was proposed.

¶ This can also be demonstrated by [Proposition] 15 of this [book], having taken $g, l, m$ as equimultiples of $a, b, e$ and $k, h, n$ of $f, c, d$; for by [Proposition] 15, $g$ will be to $l$ as $b$ to $n$ [logic of perturbed proportion], and $l$ to $m$ as $k$ to $h$, with the rest carried out as before. Nevertheless, these and the preceding are more conveniently demonstrated according to the first mode.

¶ But if there be more than three quantities in each order: for example, four; having added $p, r, q$, so that $a$ is to $b$ as... [text continues on next page] ...$d$ is to $q$; and $b$ to $e$ as $c$ to $r$; and $e$ to $p$ as $f$ to $c$. It will again be $a$ to $p$ as $f$ is to $q$. For by the previously demonstrated things, $a$ will be to $e$ as $f$ is to $r$. Thus, with $b, r, d$ removed, there will be three quantities $a, e, p$ and another three $f, c, q$ as is proposed: wherefore $a$ is to $p$ as $f$ is to $q$. Thus, therefore, it is demonstrated for 4 by means of three, by removing one mean. In the same way, you shall demonstrate for 5 by means of four, by removing two means; and for 6 by means of 5, by removing three; and so for the rest.
