# IX [Proposition 12]

In numbers [starting] from unity in continuous proportion, any of the smaller [numbers] measures [divides] a larger one according to some [number] arranged within that same proportionality.

¶ Let there be [numbers] in continuous proportion from unity up to *.f.*. I say that none of them measures *.f.* except according to some other [number in the sequence]. For it is established that *.e.* measures *.f.* itself according to *.a.*, for it is established that *.e.* is to *.f.* as unity is to *.a.*. But *.d.* measures the same *.f.* according to *.b.*, for by equal proportionality *.d.* is to *.f.* as unity is to *.b.*. Concerning *.c.* also, it is clear in the same way that it measures it [*.f.*] according to itself. Conversely also, *.a.* measures it [*.f.*] according to *.e.*, because as unity is to *.e.*, so is *.a.* to *.f.*. *.b.* indeed measures it according to *.d.*, for as unity is to *.d.*, so is *.b.* to *.f.*. It is therefore true what is proposed. Indeed, whichever number is proposed to measure the last, it shall be below the last according to the whole [series] above unity; it is proven to measure it by equal proportionality and definition.

## Proposition 13

[Diagram of line segments f, e, d, c, b, a, and I]

If, in any number of numbers in continuous proportion from unity, the one which follows unity is a prime number, no one will measure the greatest of them except those numbers arranged in that proportionality.

¶ Let there be, as before, numbers in continuous proportion from unity up to *.d.*, and let *.a.* be a prime number. I say that no one will measure the last, nor simply any of them, unless it is one of those which precedes the last or that which is proposed to be measured. For let it be, if possible, that *.e.* is a [divisor] different from those which measure *.d.*. If it is prime, by [Proposition] 11 it will measure *.a.*; therefore *.a.* is not prime, which is [contrary to] the hypothesis. But if it is composite, it is necessary by the corollary to [Proposition] 30 of the Seventh [Book] that some prime number measures it, which will not be any but *.a.*. For if it is another [prime] besides *.a.*, such as *.f.*, since it is necessary that it measures *.d.*, it follows also that the same measures *.a.* by [Proposition] 11; thus also *.a.* would not be prime. Therefore *.a.* is the prime measuring *.e.*. Since *.e.* measures *.d.*, let it be according to *.g.*, and it will be by the second part of [Proposition] 20 of the Seventh, *.a.* is to *.e.* as *.g.* is to *.c.*. For let *.d.* be from *.a.* times *.c.*, and since *.a.* measures *.e.*, *.g.* will also measure *.c.*, and let it be according to *.b.*. Each [follows] as *.a.* would measure *.g.* just as it followed that it measured *.e.*. Otherwise, if *.g.* were indeed prime since it measures *.c.*, it follows by [Proposition] 11 that it measures *.a.*. But if it is composite, by the same it follows that a prime number measuring *.g.* measures *.a.*, which is inconvenient [inconsistent]. Therefore *.a.* measures it. It follows therefore by the second part of [Proposition] 20 of the Seventh that *.b.* also measures *.b.* [Note: likely a scribal error for another term], because as much is produced from *.a.* into *.b.* as from *.g.* into *.b.*. It is established that the product *.c.* measures *.b.*, therefore it is according to *.k.*. It is established, as first concerning *.g.*, that *.a.* measures *.b.*. For if not, *.a.* will [not] be prime; therefore by the second part of [Proposition] 20 of the Seventh, it follows that *.k.* measures *.a.*. For let it be as much from *.a.* into itself as from *.b.* into *.k.*. It is manifest, however, that *.k.* is not *.a.*, for none of the numbers *.g, b, k* is any of *.a, b, c, d*. For if *.g.* were any of those, since it measures *.d.* according to *.e.*, *.e.* would also be one of those by the premise. But it was not; thus neither is *.g.*. Similarly, since *.b.* measures *.c.* according to *.g.*, *.b.* will not be any of *.a, b, c.*. For it would be shown by the premise that *.g.* [is one], but it was shown that it is not; therefore neither is *.b.*. By the same reasoning, neither is *.k.*, for since it measures *.b.* according to *.b.*, if it were *.a.*, it would be proven by the premise that *.b.* also is *.a.*. But it was not; therefore *.k.* will not be *.a.*. But it measures it; therefore *.a.* is not prime, which is impossible.

¶ Otherwise the same: if *.e.*, different from *.a, b, c, d*, measures *.d.*, let it be according to *.f.* and *.g.*. [Since] the prime number *.a.* measures *.d.*, the product of *.c.* into *.f.* [Note: text here becomes compressed], it follows from [Proposition] 33 of the Seventh that it measures *.e.* or it measures *.f.*. Therefore, as *.d.* is from *.a.* into *.c.* as well as from *.e.* into *.f.*, it will be by the second part of [Proposition] 20 of the Seventh: *.a.* is to *.e.* as *.f.* is to *.c.*. ## Proposition 14

If a number is proposed which is the least that [certain] assigned prime numbers measure, no prime number will measure it except those assigned.

¶ Let *.a.* be the least number measured by the prime numbers which are *.b, c, d*. I say that no other prime besides these will measure *.a.*. If however there were *.e.*, a prime measuring it, since any of the numbers *.b, c, d* measures *.a.* (the product of *.e.* into *.f.*), and each of them is prime, it follows from [Proposition] 33 of the Seventh that each of them measures *.e.* or *.f.*. But no one measures *.e.* since it is prime; therefore each of them measures *.f.*. Since therefore *.f.* is less than *.a.*, inasmuch as it measures it according to *.e.*, *.a.* will not be the least [number] measured by them, which is inconvenient [a contradiction].

## Proposition 15

[Diagram with numerical examples of geometric progressions: 81, 108, 144, 192, 256, etc.]

If any number of numbers in continuous proportion are the least according to their proportion: whoever measures any of them will be commensurable to one of the terms of that proportion.

¶ Let *.a, b, c, d, e* be continuously proportional and the least according to the proportion of *.f.* to *.g.*, which [*.f* and *g*] are the least in their proportion. And let it be posited that *.h.* measures *.c.*. I say that *.h.* is commensurable to *.f.* or *.g.*. For let there be taken in the same proportion four least numbers which are *.k, l, m, n*. It is established from the second [proposition] of the Eighth that from *.f.* into *.m.* comes *.c.*; otherwise it would happen that there is something smaller than the minimum, which cannot be. Therefore by the corollary to [Proposition] 33 of the Seventh, *.h.* will be commensurable to *.f.* or *.m.*. If to *.f.*, the proposition is established. If however to *.m.*, let there be taken in the same proportion three least numbers which are *.p, q, r*, and it will be from the second of the Eighth that *.m.* is made from *.f.* into *.r.*, lest we be compelled to concede something smaller than the minimum. Wherefore by the aforesaid corollary, *.h.* is commensurable to *.f.* or *.r.*. But it was not *.f.*, for thus the proposition would stand; therefore it is commensurable to *.r.*. Since from the second of the Eighth, *.r.* is made from *.g.* into itself, it follows from the said corollary that *.h.* is commensurable to *.g.*, which is what was proposed.

# [BOOK X]

**Here ends the Ninth book. Here begins the Tenth book.**

[Decorative Initial Q]
Quantities for which there is one common quantity measuring them shall be called **communicating** [commensurable]. Those for which there is no one common quantity measuring them shall be called **incommensurable**. Lines communicating **in power** are those whose square surfaces one common surface measures. Lines incommensurable in power are those whose square surfaces one common surface does not measure. These things being so, it is manifest that to any given line many others are incommensurable, some in length only, some in length and in power. Let the line with which we reason be called **rational**. Lines communicating with it are called rational; those incommunicable to it are called **irrational** or **surds**. The square of the surface from which we reason by hypothesis is called rational. Surfaces communicating with it are called rational; those incommensurable to it are called irrational or surds. The sides which are able [to form] those squares are called rational. [Definition:] Any quantity can be so many times multiplied that it exceeds any given quantity of the same kind.

# IX

...to be prime to <term>c</term> <note>The letter 'c' refers to a specific number in the sequence being discussed.</note>, the sum of **b** and **c** to be prime to **a**, and likewise the sum of **a** and **c** to be prime to **b**. For it is clear from the **second proposition of the eighth book** that **a** is produced by **d** multiplied by itself, **b** is produced by **d** multiplied by **e**, and **c** is produced by **e** multiplied by itself. From the **22nd proposition of the seventh book**, it follows that **d** and **e** are <term>prime to one another</term> <note>Numbers that share no common divisor other than 1.</note>. Therefore, by the first part of the **29th proposition of the same book**, the whole sum of **d** and **e** will be prime to each of them. Since each of the two numbers **d** and the sum of **d** and **e** is prime to **e**, it follows by the **25th proposition of the same book** that the product of **d** and the sum of **d** and **e**—which is itself the sum of **a** and **b**—is prime to **e**. It follows then by the **26th proposition of the same book** that the sum of **a** and **b** is also prime to **c**, for **c** is the product of **e** multiplied by itself. 

¶ By a similar demonstration, you will prove that the sum of **b** and **c** is prime to **a**. But to show that the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b**, proceed as follows: since both **d** and **e** are prime to the whole sum of **d** and **e**, by the **25th proposition of the seventh book**, their product (which is **b**) will be prime to both **d** and **e**. Thus, by the **26th proposition of the same book**, the square of the sum of **d** and **e** (which is composed of **a**, **c**, and double **b**) will be prime to **b**. It follows therefore that the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b**. For it is necessary that when a sum of two numbers is prime to one of the numbers that compose it, it must also be prime to the remaining part; this was demonstrated above in the **29th proposition of the seventh book**. To strengthen this demonstration, one must establish that the sum of **a** and **b** is produced by multiplying **d** by the sum of **d** and **e**, assuming that **a** is **d** squared and **b** is **d** times **e**. Likewise, that the sum of **a**, **c**, and twice **b** is produced by the square of the sum of **d** and **e**, assuming as before that **c** is **e** squared. For the sake of this, we propose the following things to be demonstrated:

¶ **The product of one number multiplied by any number of other numbers is equal to the product of that same number multiplied by the sum of those numbers.** 

¶ The **first proposition of the second book** proposes the same regarding lines. <note>The author is connecting arithmetic to Euclid's geometric proofs where numbers are represented as line segments.</note> For let the products of **a** multiplied by **b**, **c**, and **d** be **e**, **f**, and **g**. I say that the product of **a** multiplied by the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** results in the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g**. For it follows from the inversion of the definition of multiplication that **b** is the same part of **e**, and **c** the same part of **f**, and also **d** the same part of **g**, as the unit is of **a**. Therefore, by the **fifth proposition of the seventh book**, the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** will be the same part of the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g** as the unit is of **a**. Therefore, by the definition [of multiplication], the product of **a** and the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** is the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g**, which is what was proposed.

¶ **The product of any number of numbers multiplied by one number is equal to the product of their sum multiplied by that same number.** 

¶ This is the converse of what was just demonstrated: as if **e**, **f**, and **g** are produced from **b**, **c**, and **d** multiplied by **a**, then the sum of those products will also be produced by the sum of the numbers multiplied by the same **a**. This is easily concluded from the **17th proposition of the seventh book** and the previous demonstration.

¶ **The product of any number of numbers multiplied by any number of other numbers is equal to the product of the sum of the first group multiplied by the sum of the second group.** 

¶ As if **a**, **b**, and **c** multiply **d**, **e**, and **f**, each multiplying each, and the products are added together. I say the total of the products is equal to the product of the sum of (**a**, **b**, **c**) multiplied by the sum of (**d**, **e**, **f**). For by the previous [proposition], the product of the sum of **a**, **b**, **c** multiplied by **d** is as much as each of them multiplied by that **d**; the same applies to **e** and **f**. Thus, by the proposition before that, the sum of those products equals the product of the sum multiplied by the sum, and so the proposition stands.

¶ **When a number is divided into any number of parts, the product of the whole multiplied by itself is equal to the products of the whole multiplied by all its parts.** 

¶ The **second proposition of the second book** proposes the same regarding lines. For instance, if **a** is divided into **b**, **c**, and **d**, I say that the product of **a** multiplied by itself is the same as **a** multiplied by all those parts: **b**, **c**, and **d**. For if **e** is set equal to **a**, it is clear from the first of these cases that the product of **e** multiplied by **a** is equal to its product with all the parts of **a**. But by definition, **e** times **a** is the same as **a** times itself, and **e** times the parts of **a** is the same as **a** times the same parts. ¶ It is therefore clear that what is said is true.

¶ **When a number is divided into two, the product of the whole multiplied by one of the parts is equal to the product of that part multiplied by itself and by the other part.** 

¶ The **third proposition of the second book** proposes the same regarding lines. Let **a** be divided into **b** and **c**. I say that the product of **a** times **c** is equal to **c** squared plus the product of **c** and **b**. For the product of **a** times **c** is equal to the product of **c** times **a** by the **17th proposition of the seventh book**. Taking **d** as equal to **c**, then **a** times **c** will be the same as **d** times **a**. But by the first of these [propositions], **d** times **a** is equal to its products with **b** and **c**. Therefore, because **d** times **a** and **b** and **c** is the same as **c** times **a** and **b** and itself (due to the equality of **c** and **d**), the proposition stands.

**BOOK**

b is to c; but a and b are the smallest in their ratio according to Proposition 23 of Book VII: it follows by Proposition 21 of the same book that a <term>measures</term><note>In ancient mathematics, "measures" means that one number divides another exactly without a remainder.</note> b, which since it also measures itself: a and b will not be <term>prime to each other</term><note>Also known as "coprime," meaning they share no common factor other than 1.</note>: which is the opposite of what was assumed.

[Diagram 1: Three horizontal line segments of varying lengths, labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' from left to right.]

**Proposition 18.**
If, in any number of continued proportionals, the two <term>extremes</term><note>The "extremes" are the first and last numbers in a sequence.</note> are prime to each other, then it is impossible for the last number to have the same ratio to another as the first has to the second.
<note>original: "Si quotlibet numerorum continue proportionalium duo extrema fuerint contra se primi..."</note>
¶ Let a, b, and c be in <term>continued proportion</term><note>A sequence where the ratio of each number to the next is constant, such as 2, 4, 8.</note>. And let a and c be prime to each other. I say that another number cannot be added to them in the same ratio. For if it can, let it be d. Therefore, because a is to b as c is to d, it will be true by permutation that a is to c as b is to d. But a and c are the smallest in their ratio by Proposition 23 of Book VII; therefore, by Proposition 21 of the same book, a measures b, wherefore it also measures c; for in numbers in continued proportion: if the first measures the second, it measures all of them, and simply any preceding number measures any following one. But because a also measures itself, a and c will not be prime to each other: which is an inconsistency.

[Diagram 2: Four horizontal line segments labeled 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'.]

**Proposition 19.**
Given two numbers, to investigate whether there is a third number in continued proportion with them.
¶ Let a and b be two given numbers: I wish to inquire whether a third can be added to them under continued proportion. Therefore, if they are prime to each other, it is impossible by Proposition 17. If, however, they are composite, let b be multiplied by itself and let c be produced. If a measures c, there will be [a third number]. If indeed it does not measure it, there will not be. For let it measure it according to d, which will be the one we seek, by the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII. Let us assume then that it does not measure it; yet let it be that a is to b as b is to d. Therefore, because from b multiplied by itself c is produced, it follows by the first part of Proposition 20 of Book VII that from a multiplied by d the same number results. Therefore, a measures c according to d. But it was assumed that it did not, whereby an impossibility follows.

[Diagram 3: Four horizontal line segments labeled 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'. Segment 'c' is notably longer than 'd'.]

**Proposition 20.**
Given three numbers in continued proportion, to inquire whether there is some fourth number in continued proportion with them.
¶ Let a, b, and c be in continued proportion. I wish to inquire whether another can be added to them under continued proportion. Therefore, if a and c are prime to each other, it is impossible by Proposition 18. If, however, they are composite: let d be the product of b multiplied by c. If a measures d, there will be [a fourth number]. If indeed it does not measure it, there will not be. For let it measure it according to e, which will be the one we seek, by the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII. Let us assume then that it does not measure it; yet let it be that a is to b as c is to e. Therefore, because from b multiplied by c comes d, it follows by the first part of Proposition 20 of Book VII that from a multiplied by e the same results. Therefore, a measures d according to e. But it was assumed that it did not. You can investigate the same thing for any number of continued proportionals proposed. For if the two extremes are prime to each other, the inquiry ends by Proposition 18. If, however, they are composite: when the second is multiplied by the last, if the first measures the product, then the number by which it measures it is what we seek, by the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII. If the first does not measure the product, there will be no fourth number: for if any were assumed, then by the first part of the same proposition, the first would measure the product according to that assumed number, which was [previously] assumed not to be measured.

IX

## Proposition 36.

[Decorative initial N] A number whose half is odd is "even-odd" <term>even-odd: A number that can be divided by 2, but the resulting quotient is an odd number (e.g., 6, 10, 14).</term>.
¶ Let *a* be a number whose half, let it be *b*, is odd. I say that *a* is even-odd. For let *c* be the number two; it is therefore manifest that *a* is produced from *c* multiplied by *b*. Now let *d* be any even number measuring <note>original: "numerans"; in this context, it means "dividing exactly" or "being a factor of"</note> *a*, which measures it according to *e*. By the second part of the 20th proposition of the seventh book, *e* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*. Therefore *e* measures *b*. Now, because *c* [the number two] measures *d*, it follows that *e* must be an odd number <note>If 2/d = e/b and d is even, then e must be odd for the proportion to hold when b is odd.</note>. Since *b* was also odd, it follows by definition that *a* is even-odd.

## Proposition 37.

[Decorative initial O] Every number that is not a power of two <note>original: "non duplus a duobus," literally "not doubled from two," referring to numbers that are not in the sequence 2, 4, 8, 16...</note> whose half is even, is both "even-even" and "even-odd" <term>even-even and even-odd: A number that has both even and odd factors, excluding the number 1.</term>.
¶ Let *a* be a number not doubled from two whose half, *b*, is set as even. I say that this number is both even-even and even-odd. For let *c* be the number two, from which it is manifest that it measures *a* according to *b*. Because *a* is truly not a power of two, it is necessary that if its half *b* is divided into two other halves, and the half of that half into two others, eventually a number will be encountered that prevents further division <note>meaning an odd factor</note>. This number, because it does not admit division, will be odd. Let the number where the division stops be *d*. It is necessary to stop at a number, for if the division proceeded all the way to unity <note>the number 1</note>, *a* would be one of the numbers doubled from two, which it is not. Regarding *d*, it is manifest that it measures *a* through this common principle: every number measuring another measures every number measured by that one. Let it therefore measure it according to *c*, and *e* will be even. Otherwise, since *d* is a greater odd number, it would follow by the 30th proposition of the 9th book that *e* is odd. Therefore, because the even number *b* measures *a* according to *c* (which is also even, being the number two), and the even number *c* measures the same according to *d* (which is odd), it stands by the definition that the number *a* is even-even and even-odd; which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 38.

[Decorative initial I] In the case of the second and the last of any numbers in continued proportion <term>continued proportion: A geometric progression where the ratio between successive terms is constant (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16).</term>, if an amount equal to the first is subtracted, it is necessarily proved that the remainder of the second is to the first as the remainder of the last is to the sum of all those preceding it.
¶ Let *a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h* be in continued proportion. From *c, d* let *c, k* be subtracted equal to *a, b*. And from *g, h* let *g, l* be subtracted [equal to *e, f*]. I say then that the proportion of *k, d* to *a, b* is the same as *l, h* to the sum of *e, f, c, d,* and *a, b*. Let an amount equal to *e, f* be taken from *g, h*, which shall be *g, m*, and an amount equal to *c, d* which shall be *g, n*. Then *l, n* will be equal to *k, d*. It is manifest by the 12th proposition of the seventh book that since *g, h* is to *g, m* as *g, b* is to *g, n*, the remainder *b, m* is to the remainder *m, n* as *g, b* is to *g, m*, and therefore as *e, f* is to *c, d*. In the same manner, *m, n* will be to *l, n* as *c, d* is to *a, b*. Permuting these, *b, m* to *e, f* and *m, n* to *c, d* will be as *l, n* to *a, b*. Thus, joined by the 13th proposition of the seventh book, the composite *l, h* (composed of *b, m, m, n,* and *l, n*) to the composite of *e, f, c, d,* and *a, b* will be as *l, n* is to *a, b*, and therefore as *k, d* is to *a, b*; which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 39.

[Decorative initial C] When numbers are set out in order from unity <note>the number 1</note> that are continually doubled until their sum makes a prime number, then the last of these multiplied by the sum produces a perfect number <term>perfect number: A number that equals the sum of its proper divisors (e.g., 6 = 1+2+3).</term>.
¶ Let *a, b, c, d* be continually doubled from unity. Let *e* be the sum of these and unity, and let *e* be a prime number. Let *d* be multiplied by *e*, and let the result be *f, g*. I say that *f, g* is a perfect number. Let *h, k, l* be taken as continually doubled from *e*, so that there are as many terms in *e, h, k, l* as there are in the doubled numbers starting from unity. By equal proportionality, *l* is to *e* as *d* is to *a*. Therefore, by the first part of the 20th proposition of the seventh book, the product of *a* and *l* is *f, g*. Since *f, g* comes from *d* multiplied by *e*, and because *a* is the number two, *f, g* is double *l*. Therefore *e, h, k, l* and *f, g*...

### Proposition 2.
**If** there be two unequal quantities, and the equal of the lesser is subtracted from the greater until a [remainder] less than it remains; and then the equal of that remainder is subtracted from the lesser until a [remainder] less than it is left; and again the equal of the second remainder is subtracted from the first until a [remainder] less than it is left: and if in this kind of continual subtraction no remainder is found that measures the one left before: it is necessary that those two quantities are incommensurable. 

[Note: The author] proposed something similar to this in the first [proposition] of the seventh [book] regarding numbers. Let there be two unequal quantities **a.** and **b.**, with **a.** being greater, from which if reciprocal subtraction is made as much as possible, and even if it is done infinitely, no quantity occurs which measures the one left before, I say they are incommensurable. For if there were a common measure **c.**, let **b.** be subtracted from **a.** as many times as possible, and let the residue be **d.**; let that residue be subtracted from **b.** as many times as possible and let the residue be **e.**. Let this subtraction be made until from either of the two quantities **a.** and **b.** there remains [a quantity] less than **c.**; for this must be possible by the preceding [proposition]. Let **e.** here be less than **c.**. Since therefore **c.** measures **b.** subtracted from **a.**, and also **a.**, it will measure by [common] conception the residue **d.**; and therefore since it measures **d.** subtracted from **b.** and also **b.** itself, it will measure the residue **e.**. But **e.** was less than **c.**; therefore a [greater] quantity measures a smaller, which is impossible.

### Proposition 3.
**P**roposing two unequal communicating [commensurable] quantities, to find the greatest quantity commonly measuring them. From this it is manifest: that which measures two quantities also measures the greatest quantity commonly measuring both. You cannot be ignorant of the demonstration of this if you are not ignorant of the second [proposition] of the seventh [book]; for the process is the same in both.

### Proposition 4.
**P**roposing three communicating quantities, to find the greatest quantity commonly measuring them. This is clear from the third [proposition] of the seventh [book], just as the previous was from the second of the seventh.

### Proposition 5.
**O**f any two communicating quantities, the proportion is as of a number to a number.
Let there be two communicating quantities **a.** and **b.**; I say that their proportion is as of some number to another number. For let **c.** be the greatest quantity commonly measuring **a.** and **b.**, found as the second [proposition] of this [book] teaches; which measures **a.** according to number **d.** and **b.** according to number **e.**. And **a.** will be to **c.** as **d.** is to unity: because as **a.** is a multiple of **c.**, so **d.** is a multiple of unity. And **c.** to **b.** as unity to **e.**, because as **c.** is a submultiple of **b.**, so unity is a submultiple of **e.**. Therefore by equal proportionality, **a.** is to **b.** as **d.** is to **e.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 6.
**If** there be two quantities whose proportion of one to the other is as a number to a number: it is necessary that those two are communicating. This is the converse of the prior; as if **a.** is to **b.** as number **c.** to number **d.**, the two quantities **a.** and **b.** will be communicating. For let **e.** measure **b.** as many times as there is unity in **d.**, and let **e.** measure **f.** as many times as there is unity in **c.** Since therefore **f.** is to **e.** as **c.** is to unity, and **e.** is to **b.** as unity is to **d.**, it will be by equal proportionality that **f.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**; wherefore also as **a.** is to **b.**. Therefore by the first part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **f.** is equal to **a.** Since therefore **e.** measures **f.**, by [common] conception it will measure **a.** Therefore **a.** and **b.** are communicating, for **e.** measured **b.**; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 7.
**O**f all two square surfaces whose sides communicate in length, the proportion of one to the other is as a square number to a square number. Therefore **a.** and **b.** are communicating, which is the second. 
The third indeed is from the first by destruction of the consequent. Similarly the fourth is clear from the second by destruction of the consequent.

### Proposition 8.
**If** there be two quantities communicating with one quantity: it is necessary that they are also commensurable to each other. Let each of the two quantities **a.** and **b.** communicate with quantity **c.**; I say **a.** and **b.** are commensurable. For by the 5th [proposition], **a.** is to **c.** as a number to a number; similarly also by the same, **c.** is to **b.** as a number to a number. Let therefore number **d.** be to number **e.** as **a.** to **c.**, and number **f.** to number **g.** as **c.** to **b.**. But the proportions which are **d.** to **e.** and **f.** to **g.** are contained in three terms which are **h., k., l.** [OCR has *b. k. l.*] as the 4th of the eighth teaches; and it will be by equal proportionality that **a.** is to **b.** as number **h.** to number **l.** [OCR has *b.* to *l.*]. By the 6th, therefore, **a.** and **b.** are communicating, which was proposed. 

From this also it follows that if there be two quantities mutually communicating: to whatever one of them communicates, the other also communicates; and to whatever one does not communicate, the other does not either. For let there be two communicating quantities **a.** and **b.**; and let any quantity **c.** be posited with which **a.** communicates; I say that **b.** will communicate with the same, which is clear from this eighth [proposition], since each of them communicates with **a.** by hypothesis. But if again **a.** and **b.** are communicating as before; let **c.** be any quantity with which **a.** does not communicate; I say that **b.** will not communicate with the same. For if **c.** communicated with **b.**, since by hypothesis **a.** communicates with the same **b.**, **a.** and **c.** would be communicating by this eighth [proposition]. But it was posited that they were not; wherefore what we said is established.

### Proposition 9.
**If** there be two communicating quantities: the whole produced from them will be communicating to each of them. If however the whole be commensurable to each, both will be commensurable. Let there be two commensurable quantities **a.** and **b.**; I say the whole composed of them, which is **c.**, is commensurable to each of them and vice versa. Furthermore, if the whole composed of them communicates with one of them, I say it will communicate with the other; and they similarly among themselves. The same also in the contrary: for if **a.** and **b.** are incommunicating, I say **c.** will be incommunicating to each of them and vice versa; and if **c.** is incommunicating to one of them, it will also be incommunicating to the other; and they also among themselves. 

Let therefore first **a.** and **b.** be communicating, and let their common measure be **d.**. Since it measures each of them, by a [common] conception similar to the antepenultimate, it will measure the whole **c.** Wherefore by definition **c.** will communicate with each of them, namely **a.** and **b.**. Conversely also if **c.** communicates with each of them, let **d.** be the common measure of all; it is established therefore by definition that **a.** and **b.** are communicating. 
But let **c.** communicate with one of them, which is **a.**; I say it will communicate with **b.**, and **a.** also and **b.** will communicate with each other. For let **d.** be commonly measuring **c.** and **a.**; because therefore **d.** measures the whole and the part taken away, by [common] conception it will measure the residue, namely **b.**; by definition therefore **c.** communicates with **b.**, and **a.** also communicates with **b.**. 
But if **a.** and **b.** are incommunicating, **c.** will be incommunicating to each of them: for if it communicated with each or even with one of them, they would also communicate with each other, which is against the hypothesis. Similarly also conversely, if **c.** is incommunicating to each of them or even to one of them, it will also be incommunicating to the remainder and they themselves to each other; which is plain from the pre-demonstrated [arguments] by destruction of the consequent.

### Proposition 10.
**O**f all four proportional quantities, if the first be communicating with the second: the third also will be communicating with the fourth. If however the first be incommensurable to the second: the third also will be incommensurable to the fourth. 

Let there be four proportional quantities **a., b., c., d.**; I say that if **a.** communicates with **b.**, **c.** also will communicate with **d.**; and if **a.** is incommensurable to **b.**, **c.** also will be incommensurable to **d.**; and if **a.** communicates with **b.** in power only, **c.** also will communicate with **d.** in power only. Yet the author does not propose that [last part], which is easily clear from the demonstration of the prior ones. For if **a.** communicates with **b.**, it will be by the 5th [proposition] **a.** to **b.** as a number to a number. Let it be therefore as **e.** to **f.**; but since by hypothesis **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, **c.** will be to **d.** as number **e.** to number **f.**. By the 6th, therefore, **c.** is communicating with **d.**, which is the first. 
The second is clear from the first by destruction of the consequent; for if **c.** were commensurable, since **c.** is to **d.** as **a.** to **b.** by hypothesis, it would be by the first part that **a.** is communicating with **b.**, but it was not; wherefore all that the author proposes is established. 
As to what we added, namely that if **a.** communicates with **b.** in power only, **c.** communicates with **d.** in power only: it is thus clear. Since **a.** does not communicate with **b.** in length, neither will **c.** from the second part of this [proposition] communicate with **d.** in length. But indeed, since the square of **a.** communicates with the square of **b.** by hypothesis, it will be by the 5th [proposition] the square of line **a.** to the square of line **b.** as a number to a number, which are **e.** and **f.**; and because the square of **c.** is to the square of **d.** as the square of **a.** is to the square of **b.**, the square of **c.** will also be to the square of **d.** as number **e.** to number **f.**. By the 6th, therefore, **c.** and **d.** communicate in power; and since they do not communicate in length, the proposition is established.

# BOOK

[Diagram: Three horizontal line segments labeled 'a', 'c', 'b'. To their right, two vertical segments labeled 'd', 'e'.]

**The ratio of any two commensurable <term>commensurable (quantities that can be measured by the same common unit)</term> quantities is as a number to a number.**

Let there be two commensurable quantities, *a* and *b*. I say that their ratio is as some number to another number. Let *c* be the greatest common quantity measuring both *a* and *b*, found as shown in the second proposition of this book <note>original: "scđā huius"; referring to Euclid's algorithm for finding a greatest common divisor</note>. Let *c* measure *a* according to the number *d*, and measure *b* according to the number *e*. Therefore, the ratio of *a* to *c* is as *d* is to unity <note>The number 1</note>, because just as *a* is a multiple of *c*, so is *d* a multiple of unity. And the ratio of *c* to *b* is as unity is to *e*, since just as *c* is a sub-multiple of *b*, so is unity a sub-multiple of *e*. Therefore, by equal proportionality, the ratio of *a* to *b* is as *d* to *e*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 6.

[Diagram: Four horizontal line segments labeled 'f', 'a', 'e', 'b'. To their right, two vertical segments labeled 'c', 'd'.]

**If there are two quantities whose ratio of one to the other is as a number to a number, those two must be commensurable.**

This is the converse of the previous proposition: if the ratio of *a* to *b* is as the number *c* is to the number *d*, then the two quantities *a* and *b* will be commensurable. For let *e* be a quantity measuring *b* as many times as unity is in *d*, and let *e* also measure *f* as many times as unity is in *c*. Since, therefore, the ratio of *f* to *e* is as *c* to unity, and the ratio of *e* to *b* is as unity to *d*, then by equal proportionality, the ratio of *f* to *b* is as *c* to *d*. Consequently, it is also as *a* to *b*. Therefore, by the first part of the 9th proposition of the fifth book, *f* is equal to *a*. Since, therefore, *e* measures *f*, by understanding <note>original: "per conceptionẽ"; by logical axiom</note> it must also measure *a*. Therefore, *a* and *b* are commensurable, for *e* was measuring *b* as well; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 7.

**For all two square surfaces whose sides are commensurable in length, the ratio of one to the other is as a square number to a square number. If, however, the ratio of a square surface to another square surface is as the ratio of a square number to a square number, their sides will be commensurable in length. But if the ratio of a square surface to another square surface is not as a square number to a square number, their sides will be incommensurable <term>incommensurable (quantities that have no common measure, like the side and diagonal of a square)</term> in length.**

[Diagram: Two squares. The smaller one on the left contains 'c' and has side 'a'. Below it are segments 'e' and 'g'. The larger one on the right contains 'd' and has side 'b'. Below it are segments 'f' and 'h'.]

Let *a* and *b* be two straight lines whose squares are *c* and *d*. I say that if *a* and *b* are commensurable in length, the ratio of *c* to *d* will be as a square number to a square number, and vice-versa. But if the ratio of *c* to *d* is not as a square number to a square number, *a* and *b* will be incommensurable in length, and vice-versa. However, this fourth point is not explicitly proposed <note>The author notes that the fourth part of the logical breakdown—the converse of the incommensurability—is often omitted from the initial statement</note>.

The first part is proven thus: if *a* and *b* are commensurable in length, they will (by Proposition 5) be in a ratio of two numbers, which let be *e* and *f*, whose squares are *g* and *h*. Because the ratio of *c* to *d* is the duplicate ratio of *a* to *b* (by the 18th proposition of the sixth book), it follows that the ratio of *c* to *d* is also as the duplicate ratio of *e* to *f*. But also (by the 11th proposition of the eighth book), the ratio of *g* to *h* is as the duplicate ratio of *e* to *f*. Therefore, the ratio of *c* to *d* is as *g* to *h*, which is the first point.

The second part: let the ratio of *c* to *d* be as the square number *g* to the square number *h*. I say that *a* and *b* will be commensurable in length. Since the ratio of *c* to *d* is the duplicate of *a* to *b*, and *g* to *h* is the duplicate of *e* to *f*, then the simple <note>The non-squared, or linear ratio</note> ratio of *a* to *b* is as the simple ratio of *e* to *f* (by Proposition 6). Therefore, *a* and *b* are commensurable, which is the second point.

The third point is clear from the first by "destruction of the consequent" <note>original: "a destructione cõsequentis"; a logical term for Modus Tollens, where denying the result denies the premise</note>. Similarly, the fourth point is clear from the second by the same logic.

From this third part, note that the diagonal <note>original: "diametꝝ"</note> is incommensurable with the side <note>original: "coste"</note>. For since the square of the diagonal is double the square of the side, and the ratio of "double" is...

...is not like that of square numbers: it follows that the diagonal is <term>incommensurable<note>From the Latin *incommensurabilis*. This means two lengths cannot be measured by the exact same unit, no matter how small; in modern terms, their ratio is an irrational number like the square root of 2.</note></term> to the side in length. 
Otherwise, since four is a square number, all <term>even-times-even<note>original: "pariter pares." In Euclidean mathematics, these are numbers formed by doubling (2, 4, 8, 16, etc.).</note></term> numbers would be squares, as would infinitely many others which are not squares. Furthermore, Aristotle <note>The text uses the abbreviation "Ar." referring to Aristotle, who famously used this "odd equals even" proof in his work on logic to demonstrate how a false premise leads to a contradiction.</note> leads to this absurdity if the diagonal is assumed to be commensurable to the side: that an odd number would be equal to an even number, which is shown thus. 

Let the diagonal **a.b.** be commensurable to the side **a.c.** By the 5th [proposition], **a.b.** will be to **a.c.** as one number is to another. Let these numbers be **e.** and **f.**, which are the smallest in their proportion; because of this, one of them must be odd. For if both were even, they would not be the smallest. Let their squares be **g.** and **h.** If, therefore, **e.** is odd, **g.** will also be odd by the 30th [proposition] of the ninth book. Let **k.** be double **h.**; then **k.** will be even by definition. Because, therefore, **a.b.** is to **a.c.** as **e.** is to **f.**, then by the 8th of the sixth and the 11th of the eighth, the square of **a.b.** is to the square of **a.c.** as **g.** is to **h.** Thus, **g.** is double **h.**—for such is the square of **a.b.** to the square of **a.c.** by the penultimate [proposition] of the first book <note>The "penultimate proposition of the first book" refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Euclid I.47).</note>—and because **k.** is also double **h.**, it follows by the 9th of the fifth book that the odd number **g.** is equal to the even number **k.**

But if **e.** is even and **f.** is odd: the proportion of **f.** to half of **e.** (let this half be **l.**) will be as **a.c.** is to half of **a.b.** (let this half be **a.d.**). Therefore, the proportion of the square of **a.c.** to the square of **a.d.** will be as the proportion of the number **h.** (which is odd by the 30th of the ninth book) to the square of the number **l.** (which we call **m.**). Let **k.** be set as double to **m.**; **k.** will then be even by definition. And since the square of **a.c.** is double the square of **a.d.** by the penultimate of the first book, **h.** will be double **m.** Since **k.** is also double **m.**, the odd number **h.** will be equal to the even number **k.** by the 9th of the fifth book, which is what was to be proven.

### ¶ Proposition .8.
**I**f there are two quantities <term>commensurable<note>original: "communicantes," literally "sharing" or "communicating." This refers to quantities that share a common measure.</note></term> with a single quantity, it is necessary that they are also commensurable with each other.

¶ Let each of the two quantities **a.** and **b.** be commensurable with the quantity **c.** I say that **a.** and **b.** are commensurable. For by the 5th [proposition], **a.** is to **c.** as a number is to a number; similarly, by the same [proposition], **c.** is to **b.** as a number is to a number. Therefore, let number **d.** be to number **e.** as **a.** is to **c.**, and number **f.** be to number **g.** as **c.** is to **b.** But the proportions **d.** to **e.** and **f.** to **g.** are contained in three terms **h. k. l.**, as the 4th of the eighth book teaches. By equal proportionality, **a.** will be to **b.** as the number **h.** is to the number **l.**; therefore, by the 6th [proposition], **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, which is what was to be proven.

¶ From this it also follows that if two quantities are commensurable with each other, whatever one of them is commensurable with, the other is also commensurable with; and whatever one is not commensurable with, neither is the other. For let two quantities **a.** and **b.** be commensurable, and let any quantity **c.** be one with which **a.** is commensurable. I say that **b.** will be commensurable with the same, which is clear from this eighth [proposition], since each of them is commensurable with **a.** by hypothesis. But if again **a.** and **b.** are commensurable as before, and let **c.** be any quantity with which **a.** is not commensurable, I say that **b.** will not be commensurable with it. For if **c.** were commensurable with **b.**, since **a.** is also commensurable with that same **b.** by hypothesis, then by this eighth proposition, **a.** and **c.** would be commensurable. But it was posited that they were not; therefore, what we have said is established.

**BOOK**

[Diagram on the left showing lines labeled a, b, c, d]

<note>original: "b. sint incomicantes"</note> If **b** and **a** are incommensurable <term>Incommensurable: Magnitudes that have no common measure, meaning they cannot both be expressed as whole numbers of the same unit.</term>, I say that **c** <note>In this context, **c** represents the sum or difference of the two lines.</note> will be incommensurable to each of them, and vice versa. Similarly, if **c** is incommensurable to one of them, it will also be incommensurable to the other, and they will also be incommensurable to each other.

First, let **a** and **b** be commensurable, and let their common measure be **d**. Since **d** measures <note>original: "numeret," literally "numbers," meaning it fits into the length an exact number of times.</note> both of them, by a concept similar to the one used two steps prior, it will also measure **c**. Therefore, by definition, **c** will be commensurable with each of them, namely **a** and **b**. Conversely, if **c** is commensurable with both, let **d** be the common measure of all; it is then clear by definition that **a** and **b** are commensurable. 

But if **c** is commensurable with only one of them, say **a**, I say that it will also be commensurable with **b**, and **a** and **b** will be commensurable with each other. For let **d** be the common measure of **c** and **a**. Because **d** measures the whole and the part taken away <note>A reference to the Euclidean algorithm where a smaller magnitude is subtracted from a larger one.</note>, it will, by this concept, measure the remainder, namely **b**. Therefore, by definition, **c** is commensurable with **b**, and **a** is also commensurable with **b**.

However, if **a** and **b** are incommensurable, then **c** will be incommensurable to each of them. For if it were commensurable with both, or even with one of them, then **a** and **b** would be commensurable with each other, which contradicts our hypothesis. Similarly, and conversely, if **c** is incommensurable to both of them, or even to one of them, it will also be incommensurable to the remaining one, and they will be incommensurable to each other. This is evident from what was demonstrated before by the "destruction of the consequent" <note>A logical proof method (modus tollens) where one proves a statement by showing that the denial of the conclusion leads to a contradiction of the premise.</note>.

**Proposition 10.**

[Diagram on the left showing lines labeled a, b, c, d, e, f]

**O**f any four proportional quantities, if the first is commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth. But if the first is incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth.

Let there be four proportional quantities, **a, b, c, d**. I say that if **a** is commensurable with **b**, then **c** will also be commensurable with **d**. If **a** is incommensurable with **b**, then **c** will also be incommensurable with **d**. And if **a** is commensurable with **b** in power <term>Commensurable in power: Lines whose squares can be measured by the same area, even if the lines themselves cannot be measured by the same unit length.</term> only, then **c** will also be commensurable with **d** in power only. 

Nevertheless, the author does not propose this last point explicitly because it is easily seen from the prior demonstration. For if **a** is commensurable with **b**, then by Proposition 5, the ratio of **a** to **b** is as a number is to a number. Let this be as **e** is to **f**. And because by hypothesis the ratio of **a** to **b** is as **c** is to **d**, then the ratio of **c** to **d** will be as number **e** is to number **f**, by Proposition 6. Therefore, **c** is commensurable with **d**, which is the first point. 

The second point is clear from the first by the "destruction of the consequent." For if **a** is incommensurable with **b**, it is necessary that **c** be incommensurable with **d**. For if it were commensurable, since **c** is to **d** as **a** is to **b** by hypothesis, then by the first part of this proof, **a** would be commensurable with **b**. But it was not; therefore, the whole of what the author proposes is established.

Furthermore, we added that if **a** is commensurable with **b** in power only, then **c** is commensurable with **d** in power only. This is shown thus: since **a** is not commensurable with **b** in length, then **c** will also not be commensurable with **d** in length, according to the second part of this proposition. But since the square of **a** is commensurable with the square of **b** by hypothesis, then by Proposition 5, the square of line **a** is to the square of line **b** as a number is to a number (let these be **e** and **f**). And because the square of **c** is to the square of **d** as the square of **a** is to the square of **b**, then the square of **c** will also be to the square of **d** as number **e** is to number **f**, by Proposition 6. Therefore, **c** and **d** are commensurable in power; and since they are not commensurable in length, the proposition is established.

...and the two lines **b, c** and **b, k** are incommensurable in length. For the same reason, any two of those four lines are incommensurable in length; thus, what we intended to show is clear.

### Proposition 18
**D**uas <note>original: "Duas lineas in potentia tantum rōnales cōicantes..."</note> lines that are rational in power only and commensurable, find two such that the square of the longer exceeds the square of the shorter by the square of a line that is incommensurable to the longer in length.

In this case also, let the same arrangement and the same hypotheses remain as in the previous proposition, with only this changed: that the ratio of the number **d, e** to neither of the two numbers **d, f** and **f, e** be as a square number to a square number. This will be easily done: let **d, e** be any square number divided into two non-square numbers—for example, if **d, e** is 9, **d, f** is 6, and **f, e** is 3. Reasoning as before, with this exception only: that **a, b** and **a, c** are incommensurable in length according to the last part of Proposition 7.

And it should be known that two lines of the kind that this and the previous proposition teach us to find, when added together, compose a <term>binomial</term> <note>literally "two-named"; a line formed by adding two incommensurable parts</note>; and when the smaller of them is subtracted from the larger, the remaining part is called a <term>residue</term> <note>also known as an apotome; the result of subtracting one incommensurable line from another</note>.

Note also that lines that are commensurable in <term>power only</term> <note>meaning their squares are related by a whole-number ratio, even if the lines themselves are not</note> can be one rational and the other irrational. For example, the <term>tetragonic sides</term> <note>square roots</note> of two surfaces where one is 25 feet and the other is 24 are rational in power only. For the side of the first surface is 5, but the side of the second cannot be expressed as a whole number. Or, both can be irrational, such as the sides of two surfaces where one is 24 feet and the other 23; the side of neither is a whole number, and they are incommensurable in length according to the last part of the seventh proposition.

If you wish to find more than two lines that are rational in power only, where one is more "powerful" than any of the others by the square of a line not commensurable with it in length: take a number that can be divided several times in such a way that the ratio of the whole to any of its parts, or of one part to another, is never like a square number to a square number. For example, 25 can be divided into 2 and 23; likewise into 5 and 20; and again into 7 and 18. And thus the process is the same as it was in the previous proposition.

### Proposition 19
**O**mnis <note>original: "Omnis superficies quā cōtinēt due linee potētialiter tātū rōnales..."</note> Every surface contained by two lines that are rational in power only and commensurable is irrational, and it is called a **medial surface**; and its <term>tetragonic side</term> <note>the side of a square equal in area to that surface</note> is also irrational and is called a **medial line**.

Let there be two lines **a, b** and **b, c** containing surface **a, c**, being rational in power only and commensurable (how these are found is clear from the previous and the one before that). I say that surface **a, c** is irrational. For let **c, d** be the square of **b, c**; it will be rational by hypothesis because line **b, c** is rational in power. And because (from the first proposition of Book VI) the ratio of **a, c** to **c, d** is as the ratio of **a, b** to **b, d**, and **a, b** is not commensurable with **b, d** (because by hypothesis it is not commensurable with its equal, **b, c**), it follows from the second part of Proposition 10 that **a, c** is also not commensurable with **c, d**. Therefore, by definition, surface **a, c** is irrational, and its square root is also irrational. This surface is called "medial" because it is a mean proportional between two rational surfaces—namely, between the squares of the two lines containing it—and the line that produces this area is called "medial" because it is also a mean proportional between two lines that are rational in power only, which are the sides of said surface. And this is what we wanted.

This is, as it were, the converse of the previous. Let **a** be a medial line. Let...

### Proposition 22.

**Every difference by which one medial area exceeds another medial area is proved to be irrational.**

Let each of two areas, $a, b$ and $a$, be medial: I say that the area $g$ [or $b$], which is the difference between them, is irrational. For let there be a line $c, d$ rational in length, to which is joined an area $d, e$ equal to area $a$, and an area $e, d, f$ equal to the total area $a, b$. How this may be done we have taught in the preceding [proposition]: because $d, f$ is equal to $a, b$ and $d, e$ equal to $a$, it will be, by conception, $g, f$ [the difference] is equal to $b$. If therefore area $b$ is not irrational but rational: then $f, g$, its equal, will be rational. But since line $e, g$ is rational in length just as its equal $c, d$, it will be by Proposition 16 that line $e, f$ is rational in length and commensurable to line $e, g$. However, by Proposition 20, each of the two lines $c, e$ and $c, f$ is rational only potentially [in square] and incommensurable to line $c, d$ in length: thus line $e, f$ is incommensurable to line $c, e$ in length. And because by the first [proposition] of the Sixth [Book], the square of line $e, f$ is to the area produced by $c, f$ and $c, e$ as $e, f$ is to $c, e$, it follows by the second part of Proposition 10 that the square of line $c, f$ is incommensurable to the area made from $e, f$ and $c, e$. Wherefore the square itself will be incommensurable to double the area of $e, f$ by $c, e$. Indeed, the square of $c, e$, since it is rational, is commensurable with the square of $e, f$; the whole composed of both will therefore be, by Proposition 9, commensurable with the square of $e, f$, and therefore incommensurable to double the area from $e, f$ in $c, e$. And because by the fourth [proposition] of the Second [Book] the square of line $c, f$ is equal to the two squares of the two lines $c, e$ and $c, f$ and to double the area from $c, e$ into $e, f$; and double the area $c, e$ into $e, f$ is incommensurable to the aggregate of the two squares of the two lines $c, e$ and $c, f$, it follows by those things added in Proposition 9 that the square of $c, f$ is incommensurable to the aggregate of the two squares of the two lines $c, e$ and $c, f$. But since the aggregate of these squares is rational, it follows that the square of line $c, f$ is not rational: and therefore line $c, f$ is not rational in square [power]: and for that reason the area $d, f$ will not be medial, nor $a, b$ which is equal to it; which is inconsistent as it is contrary to what was set forth: it remains, therefore, that area $b$ is irrational: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 23.

**Every area contained by two medial lines commensurable in square only is either rational or medial.**

Let there be two medial lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ commensurable only in square: I say that area $a, c$ contained by them is either rational or medial. For let $c, d$ be the square of line $b, c$ and $a, e$ the square of line $a, b$. These two squares will be, by hypothesis, commensurable, and by the first [proposition] of the Sixth [Book] the area $a, c$ will be medial, being the mean proportional between these squares. Let there be taken therefore line $f, g$ which is rational in length: to which is joined area $f, h$ equal to square $a, e$, and $b, k$ equal to area $a, c$, and $k, l$ equal to square $d, c$. These three areas $f, h, b, k$, and $k, l$ will be continuously proportional just as their equals

**[Page: BOOK]**

$a, e$, $a, c$, and $d, c$ are. Wherefore by the first [proposition] of the Sixth [Book], the three lines $g, h, h, m$, and $m, l$, which are their bases, will also be continuously proportional: and since the areas $f, h$ and $k, l$ are commensurable just as the two squares $a, e$ and $c, d$ are equal to them: it follows by the first of the Sixth and by Proposition 10 of this [Book] that line $g, h$ is commensurable with $m, l$. Each of them is rational in square by Proposition 20 of this [Book]: therefore the area of one of them into the other is rational: for every area contained by two lines rational in square [and] commensurable in length is necessarily rational, as is clear from the first of the Sixth and the first part of Proposition 10 of this [Book] and from the definition of rational areas. And because from the first part of Proposition 16 [of Book VI] the square of line $h, m$ is equal to the area of $g, h$ into $m, l$, the square of line $h, m$ will be rational. If therefore line $h, m$ is rational in length, or commensurable to line $k, m$ which is equal to line $f, g$, area $b, k$ will be rational by Proposition 15: and likewise its equal $a, c$. If however line $h, m$ be irrational in length, or incommensurable to line $k, m$ which is equal to line $f, g$, since it is rational at least in square—because its square is rational—it will be by Proposition 19 that area $b, k$ is medial: wherefore its equal $a, c$ is also [medial]. The proposition is therefore established. ¶ And note that if two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ were medial commensurable in length: area $a, c$ would only be medial: for area $a, c$ would be commensurable to each of the two squares $a, e$ and $c, d$ by the first of the Sixth and by the present hypothesis and by Proposition 10 of this [Book]: and therefore area $b, k$, being equal to $a, c$, would be commensurable to each area $f, h$ and $k, l$. Therefore by the first of the Sixth and Proposition 10 of this [Book], line $h, m$ would be commensurable to each of the two lines $g, h$ and $l, m$; and because both of these are rational only in square—not commensurable in length to line $f, g$—then $h, m$ would also be rational only in square: not commensurable in length to line $f, g$, and therefore not commensurable to line $h, d$ [or $h, m$]. Wherefore by Proposition 19, area $h, k$ will be only medial, and therefore $a, c$, which is equal to it, likewise. But if two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ were medial commensurable neither in length nor in square: area $a, c$ would be neither rational nor medial. For if it were so, namely that two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ were medial commensurable neither in length nor in square, the two squares $a, e$ and $c, d$ would be incommensurable. Thus the two areas $f, h$ and $k, l$ equal to them would also be incommensurable: wherefore the two lines $g, h$ and $m, l$ would be incommensurable by the first of the Sixth and by the second part of Proposition 10 of this [Book]. Since each of them is rational only in square by Proposition 20, the area of one of them into the other would be medial by Proposition 19. Therefore, since the square of line $h, m$ is equal to the said area produced by $g, h$ into $m, l$ by the first part of Proposition 16 of the Sixth, line $h, m$ would be a medial line by Proposition 19. Therefore, by Proposition 15, area $b, k$ would not be rational, nor by Proposition 20 would it be medial: wherefore neither would its equal $a, c$.

### Proposition 24.

**To find two medial lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational area, of which the longer is more powerful than the shorter by the square of a line commensurable to the longer in length.**

Since any two medial lines commensurable in square only contain either a rational or a medial area, as is clear from the preceding: it [the proposition] teaches how to find those two which contain a rational area and those which contain a medial area. Whence it is proposed to find two medial lines commensurable in square only: of which the longer can [do] more than the shorter by the square of some line commensurable to it in length, which contain a rational area. ¶ For this, according to the teaching of Proposition 17, I take two lines $a$ and $b$ rational only in square, commensurable [in square], of which the longer, which is $a$, can [do] more than the shorter, which is $b$, by the square of some line commensurable to it in length: and I set line $c$, according to the teaching of Proposition 9 of the Sixth [Book], as the mean proportional between $a$ and $b$. And I set it so that the ratio of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, as was said in the 10th of the Sixth. I say then that the two lines $c$ and $d$ are those which we seek. For it is clear from Proposition 19 that the area contained by the lines $a$ and $b$ is medial: and because by the first part of Proposition 16 of the Sixth, the square of line $c$ is equal to the said area, line $c$ will therefore be medial by Proposition 19. But since $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, and $b$ is commensurable with $a$ only in square by hypothesis—since both $a$ and $b$ are rational in square—it follows by Proposition 10 that $c$ also is commensurable with $d$ only in square. Thus by Proposition 21, since $c$ is a medial line, $d$ will also be medial: and by the first part of Proposition 12, line $c$ will be more powerful than line $d$ by the square of a line commensurable to it in length. If therefore the two lines $c$ and $d$ contain a rational area, they are such as we seek. That they contain a rational area, hold it thus: since $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, by permutation $a$ is to $c$ as $b$ is to $d$. But $a$ was to $c$ as $c$ was to $b$, therefore $c$ is to $b$ as $b$ is to $d$. Thus by the first part of Proposition 16 of the Sixth, the area contained by the two lines $c$ and $d$ is equal to the square of $b$. But the square of $b$ is rational by hypothesis, since it [the line] is rational in square: the area therefore contained by the two lines $c$ and $d$ is rational: wherefore the proposition is established.

### Proposition 25.

**To find two medial lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational area, of which the longer is more powerful than the shorter by the square of a line incommensurable to the longer in length.**

Having set two rational lines $a$ and $b$ commensurable only in square, of which the longer can [do] more than the shorter by the square of a line not commensurable with it in length—which are found according to the teaching of Proposition 18—and with other positions remaining just as argued in the preceding in a similar manner, it will be clear that the two lines $c$ and $d$ are such as we seek. And note that the two lines which this and the preceding [proposition] teach to find compose a **first bimedial**; and when the lesser of them is cut off from the greater, that which remains is called a **first medial residual**.

### Proposition 26.

**To find two medial lines commensurable in square only, containing a medial area, of which the longer can [do] as much more than the shorter as is the square of some line incommensurable to the longer in length.**

Since it has taught how to find two medial lines commensurable in square only containing a rational area... [The text here provides a summary of the construction of the **second bimedial**].

...And this was to be shown. ¶ The lines which this Proposition 29 [actually 26/29 transition] teaches to find compose a line powerful in two medials, and when the lesser is cut off from the greater, the remainder is called the line which, joined with a medial, makes the whole medial.

### Proposition 30.

**If two lines rational only in square, [and] commensurable [in square], are joined together in a straight line: the whole line composed of these will be irrational; and it is called a binomial.**

Let two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ be joined in a continuous straight line, rational only in square, [and] commensurable [in square]: which you will find by Propositions 17 and 18. I say the whole line $a, c$ composed of them is irrational, and it is called a **binomial** (*binominium*). For by the fourth [proposition] of the Second, the square of $a, c$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ and to double the area of one of them into the other. But the squares of both make a rational area by hypothesis; whereas double the area of one into the other makes a medial area by Proposition 19. Thus the squares of both taken together make an area incommensurable to double the area of one of them into the other. Therefore by Proposition 9, the square of $a, c$ will be incommensurable to the two squares of the two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ taken together; wherefore [it is] irrational by definition, since those two squares make a rational area. Therefore its square root [side], which is $a, c$, is also irrational by definition: thus the proposition stands.

### Proposition 31.

**If two medial lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational area are joined in a straight line: the whole line composed of these will be irrational and will be called a first bimedial.**

Let two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ be joined in a continuous straight line such as are proposed, which you will find through Propositions 24 and 25. I say that the whole line $a, c$ is irrational and it is called a **first bimedial** (*bimediale primum*). For double the area of $a, b$ into $b, c$ is rational by hypothesis. And the two squares of the two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$ taken together make a medial area, since each square is medial by hypothesis and one of them is commensurable with the other. Therefore double the area of one into the other is incommensurable to the two squares taken together. The whole aggregate from double the area and the two squares—and this is the square of the whole $a, c$ by the fourth of the Second—is incommensurable to double the area of one of them into the other by Proposition 9 of this [Book]. Since double the area is rational, the square of $a, c$ will be irrational, and therefore so is line $a, c$, which is what was proposed. ¶ The same otherwise: let line $d, e$ be rational in length, to which is joined area $d, f$ equal to the two squares of the two lines $a, b$ and $b, c$. This area $d, f$ will be medial since each square is medial by hypothesis and one of them is commensurable with the other. Wherefore by Proposition 20, line $d, g$ is rational in square only, not commensurable in length to line $d, e$. Again, to line $f, g$ which is equal to $d, e$, let area $f, b$ be joined equal to double the area $a, b$ into $b, c$. Area $f, b$ will be rational by hypothesis: wherefore by Proposition 16 line $g, b$ will be rational in length. Thus the two lines $d, g$ and $g, b$ are rational in square and commensurable only in square: therefore by Proposition 30 the whole line composed of them, which is $d, b$, is a binomial and irrational. Wherefore by Proposition 16, by the destruction of the consequent, area $e, b$ is irrational. And because by the fourth of the Second its square root is line $a, c$, it will be irrational by definition, which was the proposition to be demonstrated.

Let line $fg$ be <term>commensurable</term><note>Having a ratio that can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers.</note> in length with the given <term>rational</term><note>In this context, a line is "rational" if its square is commensurable with a standard unit square.</note> line $a$. I say, therefore, that the two lines $fg$ and $gh$ joined together in a straight line compose a **first binomial**. 

For line $fg$, which is the longer part, is <term>greater in power</term><note>Meaning the square of the first line is larger than the square of the second.</note> than line $gh$, which is the shorter part, by the square of line $fh$, according to the 30th [proposition] of the third [book] and the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book]<note>original: "per .30. tertij z penultimā pꝛimi". The "penultimate of the first" refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Book 1, Prop. 47).</note>. Moreover, line $fh$ is commensurable with line $fg$ in length by the second part of [Proposition] 7, since the ratio of their squares, $fg$ and $fh$, is as the square numbers $c$ and $d$. 

However, line $gh$ is proven to be rational in power only, and is not commensurable with line $fg$ in length; and therefore it is not commensurable with the given rational line $a$ either. For since the square of line $fg$ is to the square of line $fh$ as number $c$ is to number $d$, by inverse proportion the square of line $fg$ will be to the square of line $gh$ as number $c$ is to number $e$. Since, therefore, $c$ is a square number and $e$ is not a square, it follows by the last part of [Proposition] 7 that line $gh$ is incommensurable with line $fg$ in length. It remains, therefore, that $gh$ itself is rational in power only, and by addition, the lines $fg$ and $gh$ compose a **first binomial**; which was what was to be found.

->[Diagram: A semicircle is drawn with diameter $fh$. A point $g$ sits on the arc, and lines are drawn from $f$ to $g$ and $g$ to $h$, forming a right triangle $fgh$ within the semicircle. Below the semicircle are two reference lines labeled 'a' and 'b', accompanied by the numbers 4, 7, 9, and 16.]<-

## **To find the second binomial. Proposition 43.**

**S**it as before: let $a$ be the given rational line, $b$ a square number, and let $c$ be a non-square number divisible into $d$ (a non-square) and $e$ (a square), such that the ratio of the whole $c$ (which is non-square) to $d$ (which is also non-square) is as the ratio of square numbers. 

Such numbers are 12 and 48. For 12 is divisible into 9 (a square number) and 3 (a non-square); and the ratio of 12 to 3 is as 16 to 4, both of which are square numbers. In the same way, 48 is divisible into 36 and 12<note>original: "22". Given the mathematical context of the example (48 divided by 12 equals 4, a square), "22" is likely a transcription or printing error for "12".</note>. You will find such numbers in this way: Let $a$ be a square number, and let $b$ be one less [than a square number], the square of which is $c$. 

And let $d$ result from $b$ multiplied by $a$; then by the first [proposition] regarding the incidents of the ninth [book], $b$ will be the difference of $d$ to $c$. Let the same $a$ be multiplied by $c$ to produce $e$; and $e$ will be a square by the first part of the corollary to the second [proposition] of the ninth [book], because both numbers $a$ and $c$ are squares by hypothesis. Again, let $f$ be produced from $a$ multiplied by $d$, and $f$ will be what we seek. For by the last part of the aforementioned corollary, the number $f$ is not a square, because the number $d$ is not a square. For if the number $d$ were a square, there would also be...

...their squares are in proportion to the number of $c$ and $d$, whose proportion is as that of square numbers by hypothesis: the proposition is established. ¶ In another way also, the same is the line $g.h.$ commensurable [communicating] with the rational [line] positioned in length, which is easy to find; and let $c$ be a square number divisible into square $d$ and non-square $e$; and let the proportion of the square of line $g.h.$ to the square of line $f.g.$ be as number $c$ to number $c$ [likely an OCR error for $e$ or $d$]; and $f.g.$ will be incommensurable to line $g.h.$ in length through the last part of [Proposition] 7, and more powerful than it in the square of line $f.b.$ with which it is commensurable [communicates] in length: first through converse, then through everted proportionality: and through the second part of [Proposition] 7. #### Proposition 44.
**To investigate the third binomial.**
¶ The third binomial is also found thus: with line $a$ positioned as before, rational in length, let $b$ be a prime number, and $c$ a square number divisible into square $d$ and non-square $e$. Let all other things be as before: I say that the two lines $f.g.$ and $g.h.$ compose a third binomial: for neither of them is incommensurable [OCR error: should be commensurable] in length to the rational line $a$ positioned, but each is incommensurable: $f.g.$ indeed through the last part of [Proposition] 7; $h.g.$ truly through equal proportionality and the last part of 7. For it is through equal proportionality that the square of line $a$ is to the square of line $g.h.$ as number $b$ is to number $e$, with the square of line $f.g.$ and number $c$ mediating between them. However, numbers $b$ and $e$ are not in the proportion of any squares, since $b$ is a prime number. For if they were in the proportion of square numbers, it would be necessary by [Proposition] 16 of the eighth [book] and the eighth of the same that a third [number] should exist between them in continuous proportionality. Therefore, by [Proposition] 17 of the same, number $b$ would be a superficial [number], which is impossible since it is prime by hypothesis. Therefore, line $g.h.$ is incommensurable to line $a$, the rational line positioned, from the last part of [Proposition] 7. Because line $f.g.$ is more powerful than line $g.h.$ in the square of line $f.h.$ (from [Proposition] 30 of the third and the penultimate of the first), which is commensurable [communicates] with it in length from the second part of [Proposition] 7, from the definition of the third binomial, our intention is clear [patet].

#### Proposition 45.
**To scrutinize the fourth binomial.**
¶ In the finding of the fourth binomial, one must proceed in the same way as in the finding of the first, except that the square number $c$ is divided into two non-square numbers which are $d$ and $e$. All other things are to be managed here from the definition of the fourth binomial, just as there from the definition of the first binomial.

#### Proposition 46.
**To seek the fifth binomial.**
¶ The finding of this is just like the second binomial, except that the non-square number $c$ is divided into non-square $d$ and square $e$; so however that the proportion of $c$ to $d$ is not as a square number to a square number. All other things are to be searched for here from the definition of the fifth binomial just as they were sought there from the definition of the second binomial. Or, let it be that line $g.h.$ is commensurable [communicans] to line $a$, the rational line positioned, in length; and let square number $c$ be divided into two non-squares $d$ and $e$. Therefore, set the proportion of the square of line $g.h.$ to the square $f.g.$ as number $c$ to number $e$ [OCR reads $c$ again]; then affirm the proposition from the last part of [Proposition] 7 and the preceding hypotheses and converse and everted proportions, and again from the last part... from the definition of the fifth binomial.

#### Proposition 47.
**Finally, it is necessary to dwell upon the sixth binomial.**
The sixth binomial is to be scrutinized just like the third, and then here the square number [OCR error: should be non-square] $c$ will be divided into two non-squares $d$ and $e$. Other things as there, and from the definition of the 6th binomial, the lines which are proposed, $f.g.$ and $g.h.$, directly joined to one another, [compose] a sixth binomial; which was the thing proposed to be found.
