#### Proposition 48.
¶ **If a surface be contained by a first binomial and a rational line, the side which is powerful over it [its square root] must necessarily be a binomial.**
¶ Let surface $a.c.$ be contained by rational line $a.b.$ and a first binomial, which is $b.c.$ I say that the tetragonic side [square root] of surface $a.c.$ is a binomial. For let point $d$ be the common terminus of the two portions of the first binomial $b.c.$, whose greater portion is $b.d.$; it will be rational in length from the definition, and commensurable to line $a.b.$, the rational line positioned. Likewise, let the lesser portion, which is $d.c.$, be divided into equal parts at point $e$; and let line $d.b.$ be divided under that condition at point $f$, such that between its parts, which are $b.f.$ and $f.d.$, a mean proportional falls; how this is done was said in [Proposition] 13. Let lines $c.g., d.b., f.k.$ be drawn parallel to line $a.b.$ And because from the definition of the first binomial, line $d.b.$ is more powerful than line $d.c.$ in the square of a line commensurable to it in length, it follows from the second part of [Proposition] 13 that the two lines $b.f.$ and $f.d.$ are commensurable. Therefore, by [Proposition] 9, each of them is commensurable to the whole line $b.d.$; wherefore by definition both are rational in length. Therefore, by [Proposition] 15, each of the two surfaces $a.f.$ and $f.b.$ is rational. Let therefore the square $l.m.$ be described, whose side $l.r.$ is equal to surface $a.f.$, around which let a gnomon be placed, the diagonal $l.m.n.$ being protracted, to that quantity so that the square of the gnomon itself, which is $m.n.$, be equal to surface $f.b.$ And let its two supplements be $p.m.$ and $m.q.$, which must necessarily be equal to the two surfaces $d.g.$ and $g.c.$, which you may gather thus: for since line $d.c.$ is a mean proportional between lines $b.f.$ and $f.d.$, surface $d.g.$ will be (from the first [proposition] of the sixth [book]) a mean proportional between surfaces $a.f.$ and $f.b.$; wherefore also between the squares $l.n.$ [OCR error: $l.m.$] and $m.n.$ And because the supplement $p.m.$ is also a mean proportional between the said squares from the first of the sixth, it follows that $p.m.$ is equal to $d.g.$, and therefore $m.q.$ to $g.c.$ Therefore, line $l.p.$ is the tetragonic side [square root] of surface $a.c.$ This line I say is a binomial. For since both squares $l.m.$ and $m.n.$ are rational, the two lines $l.r.$ and $r.p.$ will be by definition rational in power. But through the first of the sixth, $a.f.$ is to $d.g.$ as $b.f.$ is to $d.c.$ But $b.f.$ is incommensurable to $d.e.$ [OCR error: $d.c.$?], because $b.f.$ is simply rational as was proved; $d.c.$ truly, because it commensurates in length with $d.e.$, will be rational in power only, through [Proposition] 18, which is manifest from the premises. Thus, through the second part of [Proposition] 10, surface $a.f.$ is incommensurable to surface $d.g.$ Therefore also square $l.m.$ to the supplement $p.m.$ Wherefore by the first of the sixth and the second part of [Proposition] 10, line $l.r.$ is incommensurable to line $r.p.$ From [Proposition] 30, therefore, it is established that line $l.p.$ is a binomial, which was to be shown.

#### Proposition 49.
¶ **If a surface be contained by a rational line and a second binomial, its tetragonic side will be a first bimedial.**
¶ Let the same figure and the same hypotheses as in the premise remain: and it will be from the definition of the second binomial that line $d.c.$ is rational in length: wherefore by [Proposition] 15, each of the two surfaces $d.g.$ and $g.c.$ [is rational], and therefore also the two supplements $p.m.$ and $m.q.$ will be rational. Line $b.d.$, however, will be rational in power only, and divided into two commensurable lines $f.d.$ and $b.f.$ from the definition of the second binomial and the premises and the second part of [Proposition] 13. By [Proposition] 19, therefore, each of the two surfaces $a.f.$ and $f.b.$, and therefore each of the two squares $l.m.$ and $m.n.$, will be medial. Therefore, both...

**[Page X]**

...lines $l.r.$ and $r.p.$ are medial, and commensurable in power also: for when line $b.f.$ commensurates with line $f.d.$, it follows that $a.f.$ commensurates with $f.b.$, wherefore square $l.m.$ with square $m.n.$, and therefore also line $l.r.$ with line $r.p.$ in power; in length, however, they do not commensurate: because one of them is to the other as $l.m.$ is to $m.p.$ Since therefore $l.m.$ does not commensurate with $m.p.$, because one is medial (namely $l.m.$) and the other rational (namely $m.p.$), it follows that $l.r.$ does not commensurate in length with $r.p.$ Because they contain a rational surface which is $m.p.$, it is established from [Proposition] 31 of this [book] that line $l.p.$ is a first bimedial.

#### Proposition 50.
¶ **If a surface be contained by a third binomial and a rational line, the line powerful over it will be a second bimedial.**
¶ Let the disposition and hypotheses remain as above: it will be from these hypotheses and the definition of the third binomial and [Proposition] 19 that each of the four surfaces into which surface $a.c.$ is divided is medial; wherefore each of the two squares $l.m., m.n.$ and each of the two supplements $p.m.$ and $m.q.$ will also be medial. Each, therefore, of the two lines $l.r.$ and $r.p.$ will be medial. And since the two surfaces $a.f.$ and $f.b.$ are commensurable because the two lines $b.f.$ and $f.d.$ are commensurable by the second part of [Proposition] 13, the two lines $l.r.$ and $r.p.$ will be commensurable in power, but in length not; because surface $l.m.$ does not commensurate with surface $m.p.$, because neither does $a.f.$ commensurate with $d.g.$ For line $b.f.$ does not commensurate with $d.e.$ Since therefore they contain a medial surface which is $p.m.$, it is established from [Proposition] 32 that line $l.p.$ is a second bimedial; which is the thing proposed.

#### Proposition 51.
¶ **If a surface be contained by a rational line and a fourth binomial: that which is powerful over that surface is a "major" line.**
¶ Remaining as in the premises, it will be from the hypothesis and the definition of the fourth binomial and [Proposition] 19 that each of the two surfaces $d.g.$ and $g.c.$ (and therefore each of the two $p.m.$ and $m.q.$) is medial; and the two squares $l.m.$ and $m.n.$ taken together are rational, because surface $a.d.$ is rational by the definition of the fourth binomial and [Proposition] 15. And because $d.b.$ is divided at point $f$ into two incommensurables by the second part of [Proposition] 14, surface $a.f.$ will be incommensurable to surface $f.b.$ Therefore also square $l.m.$ to square $m.n.$ Therefore, the two lines $l.r.$ and $r.p.$ are incommensurable in power, and since they contain a medial surface $p.m.$ and both their squares taken together are rational, it is established by [Proposition] 33 that line $l.p.$ is a major line, which was to be shown.

#### Proposition 52.
¶ **If there be a surface contained by a rational line and a fifth binomial, whatever line is powerful over it is convicted by necessity to be "powerful over a rational and a medial."**
¶ In this also, something from the previous disposition and positions of the lines must be changed: with these remaining, it will be from those things which are set in the definition of the fifth binomial and [Proposition] 15 that each of the two surfaces $d.g.$ and $g.c.$ (and therefore each of $p.m.$ and $m.q.$) is rational, and the whole $a.d.$ [is rational]; wherefore also the two squares $l.m.$ and $m.n.$ taken together are medial from [Proposition] 19. And since from the second part of [Proposition] 14, line $f.b.$ is incommensurable to line $f.d.$, and therefore surface $a.f.$ to surface $f.b.$, and square $l.m.$ to square $m.n.$, line $l.r.$ will be incommensurable in power to line $r.p.$ But because they contain a rational surface $p.m.$ and both their squares taken together are medial, conclude from [Proposition] 34 that line $l.p.$ is powerful over a rational and a medial; which was promised.

**[Page: LIBER (Book)]**

#### Proposition 53.
¶ **If a surface be contained by a sixth binomial and a rational line, the line which is powerful over it is proved to be "powerful over two medials."**
¶ This [Proposition] 53 still allows you to rest from drawing figures: for it is content with the premise's disposition and positions. Which being standing, it is necessary from the points themselves and the disposition—that is, the definition of the last binomial and [Proposition] 19—that any of the surfaces $a.d., d.g.,$ and $g.c.$ [be medial], on account of which both squares $l.m.$ and $m.n.$ taken together and $p.m.$ and $m.q.$ are medial. And since $b.f.$ and $f.d.$ (on account of which $a.f.$ and $f.b.$, and therefore $l.m.$ and $m.n.$) are incommensurable, the two lines $b.c.$ [error for $l.r.$] and $r.p.$ are incommensurable in power. But because they contain a medial surface $p.m.$, and both their squares taken together are medial, which is incommensurable to double the surface of one into the other: which is proved from the fact that surface $b.b.$ [error: $l.m.$?] is incommensurable to surface $b.c.$ [error: $d.c.$?] because line $d.b.$ is incommensurable to line $d.c.$, it follows from [Proposition] 35 that line $l.p.$ is that which is powerful over two medials.

#### Proposition 54.
¶ **If a rectangle equal to the square of a binomial be applied to a rational line, its [other] side will be found to be a first binomial.**
¶ These six following are the converses of the six preceding in order; of this, however, this is the intention. Let line $a.b.$ be a binomial divided at point $c$ into two lines $a.c.$ and $c.b.$ according to its definition. Let the square of its terms $a.b.$ be $b.d.$, and let line $e.f.$ be rational in length, to which is applied surface $c.g.$ equal to square $b.d.$ I say that the second side of this surface, which is line $f.g.$, is a first binomial. For let square $b.d.$ be divided into two squares $b.b.$ and $b.d.$ [error: $h.b.$ and $h.d.$?] which are the squares of the two portions of the binomial; and into two supplements $a.b.$ and $b.k.$ [error: $a.h.$ and $h.k.$?], each of which is contained under the two portions of the binomial; and it will be from the definition of the binomial which is had through [Proposition] 30 that each of those squares is rational. And through [Proposition] 19 each supplement is medial. From the surface $c.g.$, therefore, let there be cut off surface $e.l.$ equal to square $d.b.$, and $l.m.$ equal to square $b.b.$, and $l.n.$ through $p$ equal to one of the two supplements... it will be that the remainder $p.g.$ is equal to the other supplement: wherefore by the first of the sixth, line $n.q.$ is equal to line $q.g.$ From the premises it is manifest that each of the two surfaces $e.l.$ and $l.m.$, therefore the whole surface $e.n.$, is rational. And each of the two equals $n.p.$ and $p.g.$, and therefore the whole $m.g.$, is medial. Wherefore by [Proposition] 16, each of the two lines $f.l.$ and $l.n.$ and the whole line $f.n.$ is rational in length; and commensurable to line $e.f.$ positioned as rational. And by [Proposition] 20 each of the two $n.q.$ and $q.g.$ and the whole $n.g.$ is rational in power only, incommensurable to line $m.n.$, and therefore to line $e.f.$ and consequently to line $f.n.$ in length. If therefore line $f.n.$ [OCR: $f.a.$] which is greater than line $n.g....$ were more powerful than line $n.g.$ in the square of a line commensurable with itself in length, then from the definition of the first binomial it is manifest that line $f.g.$ is a first binomial. This, moreover, is so: for as between the two squares $d.b.$ and $b.b.$ surface $a.b.$ is a mean proportional by the first of the sixth, it is convinced from the earlier hypotheses that surface $m.q.$ is a mean proportional between surfaces $e.l.$ and $l.m.$ Wherefore by the first of the sixth, line $n.q.$ which is half of line $n.g.$ is a mean proportional between the two lines $f.l.$ and $l.n.$ That therefore which is made from $f.l.$ into...

**[Page X]**

...$l.n.$ is as much as that from $n.q.$ into itself by [Proposition] 16 of the sixth; and therefore by [Proposition] 4 of the second, as much as a fourth part of the square of line $n.g.$ Thus, by the first part of [Proposition] 13, since line $f.n.$ is divided by a surface applied to it equal to the fourth part of the square of the shorter line $n.g.$ such that to complete the whole line $f.n.$ a square surface is lacking [a common phrasing for the application of areas], into two commensurables at point $l$, $f.n.$ will be more powerful than $n.g.$ in the square of a line commensurable with itself in length: therefore the proposition is established.

#### Proposition 55.
¶ **If a surface equal to the square of a first bimedial be applied to a rational line, its remaining side must be a second binomial.**
¶ Let line $a.b.$ be a first bimedial divided at point $c$ according to its term. Let other things be as before: I say line $f.g.$ is a second binomial. For surface $m.g.$ will be rational because the bimedial parts of the first contain a rational surface, and the three surfaces $e.l., l.n.$ and the whole $e.n.$ are medial and commensurable, because the portions of the first bimedial are medial lines commensurable in power only from [Proposition] 31 and 18. Therefore line $n.g.$ will be rational in length, commensurable to line $e.f.$, the rational line positioned. And by [Proposition] 20, line $f.n.$ is rational in power only, which since it is greater than line $n.g....$ and being more powerful in the square of a line commensurable with it in length... from the definition line $f.g.$ will be a second binomial, which is the thing proposed.

#### Proposition 56.
¶ **When a rectangular surface equal to the square of a second bimedial has been applied to a line rational in length, its second side must necessarily be a third binomial.**
¶ If line $a.b.$ be a second bimedial divided through its term at point $c$, while all other things are as before: line $f.g.$ will be a third binomial. For it will be from [Proposition] 32 and our positions that each of the surfaces $e.n.$ and $m.g.$ is medial: wherefore by [Proposition] 20, each of the two lines $f.m.$ [error for $f.n.$] and $n.g.$ will be rational in power only. But because the parts of the second bimedial are commensurable in power only, surface $e.l.$ will be commensurable to surface $l.m.$, and therefore line $f.l.$ more powerful than line $l.n.$: therefore it is by the first part of [Proposition] 13 that $f.n.$ [is more powerful than] $n.g.$ in the square of a line commensurable to itself in length. And since surfaces $a.b.$ [meaning the product $a.c \times c.b$] and square $b.b.$ are incommensurable because lines $a.c.$ and $c.b.$ are incommensurable, and therefore also both squares taken together are incommensurable to both supplements taken together. Because the squares commensurate with each other by hypothesis, and the supplements also are equal to each other, it follows that surface $e.n.$ is incommensurable to surface $m.g.$ and therefore line $f.n.$ to line $n.g.$ By the definition, therefore, line $f.g.$ is a third binomial, which is proposed.

#### Proposition 57.
¶ **If a rectangle equal to the square of a "major" line be applied to a rational line, the other of the sides containing it will be a fourth binomial.**
¶ If this line $a.b.$ also be a major line divided according to its term at point $c$, and all other things are not otherwise than before: line $f.g.$ will be a fourth binomial. For since both squares of the portions of the major line taken together are rational, surface $e.n.$ will be rational; and therefore by [Proposition] 16, line $f.n.$ is rational in length, commensurable to line $e.f.$ the rational line positioned. Surface $m.g.$ truly will be medial because the portions of a major line contain a medial surface. Thus by [Proposition] 20, line $n.g.$ is rational in power only. And since also the portions of the aforesaid line $a.b.$ are incommensurable in power, surface $e.l.$ will be incommensurable to $l.m.$, and therefore line $f.l.$ to line $l.n.$ Therefore by the first part of [Proposition] 14, line $f.n.$ is more powerful than line $n.g.$ in the square...

**[Page: LIBER (Book)]**

...of a line incommensurable to itself. From the definition, therefore, line $f.g.$ is a fourth binomial; which was proposed.

#### Proposition 58.
¶ **If there be applied to a rational line a rectangular form equal to the square of a line powerful over a rational and a medial, its other side must necessarily be a fifth binomial.**
¶ With line $a.b.$ proposed as that which is powerful over a medial and a rational, divided according to its definition at point $c$, let nothing be changed of the rest. It follows that line $f.g.$ is a fifth binomial. For since the parts of this line $a.b.$ contain a rational surface, it is necessary that surface $g.m.$, and therefore by [Proposition] 16, line $n.g.$ be rational. And since both squares of the parts of this line taken together are medial, surface $e.n.$ will be medial and by [Proposition] 20, line $f.n.$ rational in power only. But because the portions of the predicted line are incommensurable in power, surface $e.l.$ will be incommensurable to surface $m.l.$, and therefore also line $f.l.$ to line $l.n.$ Therefore, by the first part of [Proposition] 14, line $f.n.$ is more powerful than line $n.g.$ in the square of a line incommensurable to itself. By the definition, therefore, of the fifth binomial, conclude the proposition.

#### Proposition 59.
¶ **Whenever a rectangular surface equal to the square of a line powerful over two medials has been applied to a rational line, the second side of that same surface is convicted of being a sixth binomial.**
¶ In this [Proposition] 59, let line $a.b.$ be the line powerful over two medials: those things which are besides this, let them remain as above, and line $f.g.$ will then be a sixth binomial, which you will not be able to be ignorant of if you are not unmindful of each of the premises... and so our intention is clear in this.

#### Proposition 60.
¶ **Every line commensurable to any of the binomials is proved to be a binomial under the same species.**
¶ Let line $a$ be a binomial of any species; and let line $b$ be commensurable to it in length: I say line $b$ is a binomial of the same species as $a$. For let the binomial portions be $a.c.$ and $d$, and both will be rational in power only, commensurable by [Proposition] 30. Let line $b$ truly be divided through [Proposition] 12 of the sixth according to the proportion of $c$ to $d$ into $e$ and $f$. And it will be through conjoined and everted and permuted proportionality that $c$ is to $d$ as $e$ is to $f$, as $a$ is to $b$. Since therefore $a$ and $b$ are commensurable, they will also be (by the first part of [Proposition] 10) $c$ and $e$, and likewise $d$ and $f$, commensurable. If therefore $a$ [error: $c$] was commensurable in power only, $e$ will be also; if however in length, $e$ also. And in the same way if $d$ is rational in power only or even in length, so also will be $f$. Similarly from [Proposition] 12, if $c$ is more powerful than $d$ in the square of a line commensurable with itself in length, or if by chance incommensurable, $e$ will be more powerful than $f$ in the square of a line commensurable to itself or even incommensurable. It is necessary from the definitions of the six species of binomials that $a$ and $b$ be of the same species of binomial. But if line $b$ commensurates with binomial $a$ in power only, line $b$ will also be so. But it is not necessary that it be a binomial of the same species; indeed it is impossible that both together fall under the first species of binomials or under the second, fourth, or fifth. But it is necessary that both fall under the first three or both under the last three: for it is impossible for one of them to be in any of the first three species and the other in any of the last three. For since $a$ commensurates with $b$ in power only, $c$ also with $e$ and $d$ with $f$ will commensurate then in power only, from [Proposition] 10. If therefore either of the two lines $c$ and $d$ were rational in length, its partner from lines $e$ and $f$ will not be rational in length. It is not therefore possible that $a$ and $b$ fall together under any of those species of binomials in which one of the two...

**[Page X]**

...portions of the binomial is rational in length. These species, however, are: first and second, fourth and fifth. But truly because through [Proposition] 12, the two lines $c$ and $e$ together are more powerful than the two lines $d$ and $f$ in the squares of two lines commensurable or incommensurable to them in length: it is necessary that both binomials $a$ and $b$ fall together under the first three species of binomials or together under the last three from the definition of the species themselves. But why do you doubt line $b$ is a binomial? Since $c$ and $e$ are commensurable in power only, and likewise also $d$ and $f$ are, and $c$ and $d$ are rational in power: it is convicted that $c$ and $f$ [error: $e$ and $f$] are rational in power only; which, because they do not commensurate in length just as $c$ and $d$ proportional to them do not, they compose a binomial without doubt through [Proposition] 30 of this [book].

#### Proposition 61.
¶ **Every line commensurable to either of the bimedials is convicted by necessity of being a bimedial under the same species.**
¶ What is said has truth, whether it commensurates in length or even in power only, any line with either of the bimedials. For let two lines be commensurable, $a$ and $b$, in whichever of the two predicted ways. And let $a$ be a first or second bimedial: I say that $b$ is also a first or second bimedial as $a$ was. For $a$, the bimedial, being divided into its bimedial portions from which it is composed through [Proposition] 31 and 32, which are $c$ and $d$, $b$ is also divided into $e$ and $f$ by the proportion of $c$ to $d$ as is taught in [Proposition] 12 of the sixth. Surface $g$ being positioned as contained under $c$ and $d$, and $k$ under $e$ and $f$. And square $b$ [error: $h$?] being positioned for $d$, and $l$ for $f$, it will be through conjoined and everted and permuted proportionality just as in the premise that $c$ is to $e$ and $d$ is to $f$ as $a$ is to $b$. Just as therefore from the position of $a$ and $b$ they are commensurable, whether this be in length or in power, so $c$ and $e$, likewise $d$ and $f$, will be commensurable. But because $c$ and $d$ are medial, commensurable in power only: it follows from [Proposition] 21 that $e$ and $f$ are also medial through [Proposition] 10, commensurable in power only, since they are proportional to $c$ and $d$ by hypothesis. And since by the first of the sixth $g$ is to $h$ as $c$ is to $d$, and $k$ is to $l$ as $e$ is to $f$, $g$ will be to $h$ as $k$ is to $l$, and permuted $g$ to $k$ as $h$ to $l$. Because therefore $h$ is commensurable with $l$, because their two sides which are $d$ and $f$ commensurate in length or in power according as $a$ and $b$ commensurate in one of them, it follows from [Proposition] 10 that $g$ and $k$ also commensurate with each other. Therefore $k$ is rational or medial just as $g$ was, from the definition of a rational surface or [Proposition] 21. In this indeed the first bimedial differs from the second bimedial: that the portions of the first bimedial into which it is divided according to its term contain a rational surface; of the second bimedial, however, a medial. If therefore $a$ was a first bimedial, surface $g$ will be rational, wherefore also $k$, and therefore $b$ a first bimedial through [Proposition] 31. But if $a$ was a second bimedial, surface $g$ will be medial, on account of this also $k$, and $b$ therefore by [Proposition] 32 will be a second bimedial; because of which the proposition is established. The same in another way: for rational line $c.d.$ positioned, with $a$ as either of the bimedials and $b$ commensurable to it in length or power: let surface $c.e.$ be applied equal to square $a$, and $f.g.$ equal to square $b$; and surfaces $c.e.$ and $f.g.$ will be commensurable because the squares equal to them, which are the squares of lines $a$ and $b$, are commensurable by hypothesis: from the first of the sixth and [Proposition] 10 of this [book] it is necessary that the two lines $d.e.$ and $e.g.$ be commensurable. And because if $a$ was a first bimedial, line $d.e.$ will be a second binomial through [Proposition] 55, therefore $e.g.$ also a second binomial through the premise, wherefore the tetragonic side [square root] of surface $f.g.$, and that is $b$, is a first bimedial through [Proposition] 49. But truly if $a$ was a second bimedial, line $d.e.$ will be a third binomial through [Proposition] 56, therefore $e.g.$ is a third binomial through the premise, wherefore also the tetragonic side of surface $f.g.$, that is $b$, is a second bimedial through [Proposition] 50. It is manifest therefore that what is proposed is true.

#### Proposition 62.
¶ **Every line commensurable to a "major" line is a major line.**
¶ This also has truth, if in either way a line is commensurable to a major line. For let $a$ be a major line, and $b$ commensurable to it in any way: $b$ will be a major line. For $a$ being divided into those portions from which it consists through [Proposition] 33, which are $c$ and $d$, and $b$ according to their proportion into $e$ and $f$, and $g$ being positioned as the surface contained under $c$ and $d$, and $k$ under $e$ and $f$; and $m$ and $h$ being the squares of $c$ and $d$, and $n$ and $l$ of $e$ and $f$, $m$ will be to $h$ [error: $b$?] as $n$ to $l$ through the second part of [Proposition] 18 of the sixth, and conjoined $m$ and $h$ to $h$ as $n$ and $l$ to $l$, and permuted $m$ and $h$ to $n$ and $l$ as $h$ to $l$. Since therefore $h$ commensurates with $l$, because $d$ commensurates with $f$ either in length or in power, according as $a$ commensurates with $b$, it follows that both squares $m$ and $h$ taken together commensurate with both squares $n$ and $l$ taken together. Since therefore the first two taken together are rational through [Proposition] 33, the last two will also be rational by definition. But because it is necessary that surface $k$ be medial just as $g$ is from [Proposition] 21, and lines $e$ and $f$ be incommensurable in power just as $c$ and $d$ from [Proposition] 10, it is concluded through [Proposition] 33 that line $b$ is the line which is called major, which is the thing proposed. ¶ The same in another way: since $a$ is a major line to which $b$ commensurates whether in length or in power: a rational line $c.d.$ being taken, let surface $c.i.c.e.$ [error: $c.e.$] be applied equal to the square of line $a$, then $f.g.$ equal to the square of line $b$; since therefore the squares of the two lines $a$ and $b$ are commensurable by hypothesis, surface $e.e.$ [error: $c.e.$] will be commensurable to surface $f.g.$, therefore by the first of the sixth and [Proposition] 10, line $d.e.$ [is commensurable] to line $e.g.$ in length. But because from [Proposition] 57 line $d.e.$ is a fourth binomial, $e.g.$ will also be a fourth binomial through [Proposition] 60: therefore from [Proposition] 51 line $b$, powerful over surface $f.g.$, is a major line.

#### Proposition 63.
¶ **If any line commensurates with a line "powerful over a rational and a medial," it is proved to be itself powerful over a rational and a medial.**
¶ It is also true that in whatever way any line is commensurable to a line powerful over a rational and a medial, whether in length or in power only, it is itself also powerful over a rational and a medial: which just as before is proved in a double way: it is necessary before... that as the two lines $c$ and $d$ are incommensurable in power, so also are $e$ and $f$ through [Proposition] 10. And just as $g$ is a rational surface (for such do the portions of a line powerful over a rational and a medial contain), so also through the definition let $k$ be rational, and just as the two squares $m$ and $h$ taken together are medial: so also through [Proposition] 21 the two squares $n$ and $l$ taken together will be medial: therefore from [Proposition] 34, $b$ is powerful over a rational and a medial. As for the second way, it is necessary from [Proposition] 58 that line $d.e.$ be a fifth binomial, therefore also $e.g.$ through [Proposition] 60 line $e.g.$ is a fifth binomial: wherefore through [Proposition] 52 the tetragonic side of surface $f.g.$, which is $b$, will be a line powerful over a rational and a medial; which is proposed.

#### Proposition 64.
¶ **Every line commensurable to a line powerful over two medials: is itself also powerful over two medials.**
¶ This also, with the same disposition and positions remaining, in that double way as the premises: will be proved to be true whether line $b$ commensurates with line $a$ (powerful over two medials) in length or in power. For as to the first mode of argumentation, surface $g$ will be medial through [Proposition] 35, therefore $k$ through [Proposition] 21 since it commensurates with it; both squares $m$ and $h$ taken together will be from the same [Proposition] 35 medial: therefore the two $n$ and $l$ taken together through [Proposition] 21. But because the two squares $m$ and $h$ taken together from the predicted [Proposition] 35 are incommensurable to double the surface $g$... as both $l$ and $n$ taken together are incommensurable...

**[Page X]**

...to double the surface $k$. Since therefore $e$ and $f$ are incommensurable in power just as $c$ and $d$, it will be from [Proposition] 35 that line $b$ is powerful over two medials. As for the second mode of solid argumentation, $d.e.$ will be a sixth binomial through [Proposition] 59, therefore also through [Proposition] 60 line $e.g.$ will be a sixth binomial, wherefore through [Proposition] 53 the tetragonic side of surface $f.g.$, which is $b$, will be powerful over two medials, which is the thing proposed.

#### Proposition 65.
¶ **If two surfaces, of which one is rational and the other medial, be joined: the line powerful over the whole surface composed therefrom will be some one of the four irrational lines, namely: either a binomial, or a first bimedial, or a major line, or powerful over a rational and a medial.**
¶ As if $a$ be a rational surface and $b$ medial, the line powerful over the whole $a.b.$ will be some one of the four premised. For let line $c.d.$ be rational, to which let $e.c.$ be applied equal to $a$, and $f.g.$ equal to $b$; and from [Proposition] 16, line $d.e.$ will be rational in length, commensurable to line $c.d.$ positioned as rational; and from [Proposition] 20 line $e.g.$ rational in power only; and from [Proposition] 30 line $d.g.$ is a binomial. Since one of the binomial portions, which is $d.e.$, is rational in length commensurable to the rational line positioned, which is $c.d.$, it will be from the definition of the species of binomial either a first binomial, or second, or fourth, or fifth: but it will not be the third or sixth from the definition. Therefore from [Proposition] 48, 49, 51, and 52, the line powerful over the whole $c.g.$, which is equal to the two $a$ and $b$ together, will be either a binomial or a first bimedial, or a major line, or powerful over a rational and a medial: which is the thing proposed. But it will not be a second bimedial or powerful over two medials: because if it were a second bimedial, line $d.g.$ would be a third binomial from [Proposition] 56; and if it were powerful over two medials, line $d.g.$ would be a sixth binomial from [Proposition] 59. But it was neither: whence our intention is clear.

#### Proposition 66.
¶ **When two incommensurable medial surfaces have been joined together, the line powerful over the whole surface is either one of the two irrational lines, namely: either a second bimedial or powerful over two medials.**
¶ As if $a$ and $b$ be two incommensurable medial surfaces. For if they were commensurable, the surface composed from them would be medial from [Proposition] 9 and 21; wherefore also the line powerful over it would be medial from [Proposition] 19. I say that the line powerful over the composition of both will be either a second bimedial or powerful over two medials. Let line $c.d.$ be rational: and the surface applied to it $c.e.$ equal to $a$, and surface $f.g.$ equal to $b$. And it will be from [Proposition] 20 that line $d.e.$, and likewise line $e.g.$, is rational in power only. And since surfaces $c.e.$ and $f.g.$ are incommensurable just as $a$ and $b$ equal to them, therefore lines $d.e.$ and $e.g.$ from the first of the sixth and [Proposition] 10 of this [book]: from [Proposition] 30 line $d.g.$ will be a binomial. Since each of the binomial portions, which are $d.e.$ and $e.g.$, is incommensurable to the rational line positioned, which is $c.d.$, it will be from the definition a third or sixth binomial. Therefore, the line powerful over the whole $c.g.$, equal to the proposed $a$ and $b$, will be from [Proposition] 50 and 53 either a second bimedial or powerful over two medials; which is the thing proposed.

#### Proposition 67.
¶ **When a binomial line has been positioned, and the other irrational lines following it: none of them will be under the term of another.**
¶ It means that if any line such as $a$ were any of the six previously proved irrational lines, which are the binomial and its five companions, it will not be any of the others. For if a surface equal to its square be applied to rational line $b.c.$, which is $b.d.$: if indeed $a$ were a binomial: $c.d.$ will be from [Proposition] 54 a first binomial. Which if it were a first bimedial: $c.d.$ will be from [Proposition] 55 a second binomial. If however a second bimedial: $c.d.$ will be from [Proposition] 56 a third binomial. And if a major line, $c.d.$ will be from [Proposition] 57 a fourth binomial. But if powerful over a rational and a medial, or if powerful over two medials: $c.d.$ will be from [Proposition] 58 a fifth binomial, or from [Proposition] 59 a sixth binomial. And because it is impossible for $c.d.$ to be at once under different species of binomials (which is impossible by definition), it is impossible for $a$ to be at once under different species of the six previously described irrational lines. Regarding the medial line, it is established that it too is none of the six following, namely neither a binomial nor any of its companions. For when a surface equal to the square of a medial line is applied to a rational line: its second side is rational in power [only] from [Proposition] 20. When, however, a surface is equal to the square of a binomial or any of its companions: its second side is irrational both in length... and so for the rest through [Proposition] 54 and 5, and 6 following, wherefore it is itself irrational both in length and in power through [Proposition] 30. Since therefore it is impossible for the same line to be rational in power and irrational both in length and in power: it is undoubtedly impossible for a medial line to be a bimedial or any of its five companions.

#### Proposition 68.
¶ **If a line be cut off from a line, and both were rational in power only and commensurable: the remaining line will be irrational and will be called a "residue" [apotome].**
¶ Let line $b.c.$ be cut off from $a.b.$, and let both be rational in power only, commensurable, such as [Euclid] taught to find in [Propositions] 17 and 18. And these are the ones which compose a binomial. I say that the remainder $a.c.$ is irrational and is itself called a residue. For it is established from [Proposition] 7 of the second [book] that the squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ taken together (which compose a rational surface by hypothesis and the definition of a rational surface and [Proposition] 9 of this [book]) are as much as double the surface $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ with the square $a.c.$ And since from [Proposition] 19 surface $a.b \times b.c.$ is medial, therefore also its double is medial through [Proposition] 21, and therefore irrational through [Proposition] 19. It follows that both squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ taken together are incommensurable to double the surface of one of them into the other. Wherefore by [Proposition] 9 also to the square of line $a.c.$ From the definition, therefore, the square of line $a.c.$ is irrational, since it is incommensurable to a rational [quantity], namely both squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ taken together. Thus also from the definition, line $a.c.$ is irrational, which is the thing proposed. Exemplarily in the figure, let surface $e.g.$ be equal to both squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ taken together: and it will be rational. Likewise, let surface $d.f.$ be equal to double the surface of one into the other: and it will be from [Proposition] 19 medial, and it will be from [Proposition] 7 of the second surface $f.g.$ equal to the square of line $a.c.$ And since surface $e.g.$ is incommensurable to surface $d.f.$, the same will be from [Proposition] 9 incommensurable to $f.g.$ Wherefore $f.g.$ is irrational and its tetragonic side [square root] is $a.c.$

#### Proposition 69.
¶ **If a line has been cut off from a line, and both were medial commensurable in power only and containing a rational surface: the remaining line will be irrational and called a "first medial residue."**
¶ Let line $b.c.$ be cut off from line $a.b.$; and let both be as proposed, which you will find from [Propositions] 24 and 25; and these are the ones which join a first bimedial. I say that the remaining line $a.c.$ will be irrational and itself called a first medial residue. For both of their squares taken together will be medial: truly double the surface of one into the other rational. Thus, both squares taken together are incommensurable to double the surface of one into the other. Because therefore both squares taken together are composed from double the surface of one into the other and the square of line $a.c.$, it follows through [Proposition] 9 that the square of line $a.c.$ is incommensurable...

### Notes on Abbreviations and OCR:
1.  **ꝝ → rum**: Standard Latin contraction (e.g., *numerorum*).
2.  **ꝓ → pro**: (e.g., *proportio*).
3.  **7 → et**: Tironian note for "and".
4.  **ꝑ → per**: (e.g., *per hypothesim*).
5.  **ꝙ → quod / quoque / quae**: Context-dependent; in "vtraqꝙ", it is *utraque*.
6.  **ū → um**: Macron indicating an "m" or "n" (e.g., *binomium*).
7.  **rōnali → rationali**: Common scientific abbreviation.
8.  **ꝯ → con- / com-**: (e.g., *communicans*, *concluserit*).
9.  **ł / lineaqꝙ**: The "ł" with a stroke usually stands for *linea*.
10. **pꝝ → patet**: "It is clear/evident."
11. **Geometric Terms**:
    *   *Binomium*: Binomial ($a + b$).
    *   *Bimediale*: Bimedial ($\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$).
    *   *Rationale/Mediale*: Rational and Medial lines/areas.
    *   *Residuum*: Residue or Apotome ($a - b$).
    *   *Potens*: "Powerful over," used to describe the side of a square equal to a certain area.
    *   *Latus tetragonicum*: The side of a square (square root).
12. **OCR Errors**:
    *   "nnmer⁹" should be *numerus*.
    *   "pꝓpoutionalitatē" should be *proportionalitatem*.
    *   In Proposition 44, "nnmer⁹ pꝛimus" is *numerus primus* (prime number).
    *   "cōicātes" is *communicantes* (commensurable).

**Proposition 48.**

[Large initial S] **I**f an area is contained by a **first binomial** <note>A line composed of two rational parts that are commensurable only in square, where the square of the greater term is larger than the square of the lesser by the square of a line commensurable with the greater.</note> and a **rational line**, then the side which is powerful over it <note>The "side" refers to the square root; a line whose square equals the given area.</note> must necessarily be a **binomial**.

Let the area *a.c.* be contained by the rational line *a.b.* and the first binomial, which is *b.c.* I say that the <term>square side</term><note>original: "latus tetragonicum"</note> of area *a.c.* is a binomial. For let point *d* be the common boundary of the two portions of the first binomial in *b.c.*, of which the greater portion is *b.d.* This portion will be rational in length by definition and commensurable with the line *a.b.*, which was set as rational. Likewise, let the smaller portion, which is *d.c.*, be divided into two equal parts at point *e*. Let line *d.b.* be divided at point *f* under the condition that a <term>mean proportional</term><note>A value that mediates between two others in a geometric ratio (a:x = x:b).</note> falls between its parts, which are *b.f.* and *f.d.*—how this is done was stated in Proposition 13. Now let lines *c.g.*, *d.h.*, and *f.k.* be drawn parallel to line *a.b.* Because, by the definition of the first binomial, line *d.b.* is more powerful than line *d.c.* by the square of a line that communicates <note>is commensurable</note> with it in length, it follows from the second part of Proposition 13 that the two lines *b.f.* and *f.d.* are communicating. Therefore, by Proposition 9, each of them is communicating with the whole line *b.d.*, and thus by definition both are rational in length.

Because of this, by Proposition 15, each of the two areas *a.f.* and *f.b.* is rational. Therefore, let a square *l.m.* be described, whose side *l.r.* is equal to the area *a.f.* Around this, let a <term>gnomon</term><note>The L-shaped part of a square remaining after a smaller square is removed from one corner.</note> be placed by extending the diagonal *l.m.n.* to such a quantity that the square of the gnomon itself, which is *m.n.*, is equal to area *f.b.* Let its two supplements be *p.m.* and *m.q.*, which must be equal to the two areas *d.g.* and *g.c.* You may gather this as follows: since line *d.e.* is the mean proportional between lines *b.f.* and *f.d.*, the area *d.g.* will be (by the first part of Book 6) the mean proportional between areas *a.f.* and *f.b.*, and therefore between the squares *l.m.* and *m.n.* And because the supplement *p.m.* is also the mean proportional between the said squares (from the first part of Book 6), it follows that *p.m.* is equal to *d.g.*, and therefore *m.q.* is equal to *g.c.* Thus, line *l.p.* is the square side of area *a.c.*

I say that this line is a binomial. Since both squares *l.m.* and *m.n.* are rational, the two lines *l.r.* and *r.p.* will be <term>rational in power</term><note>Meaning their squares are rational, though the lines themselves may be irrational.</note> by definition. Furthermore, by the first part of Book 6, *a.f.* is to *d.g.* as *b.f.* is to *d.e.* But *b.f.* is incommensurable with *d.e.*, because *b.f.* is rational simply (as proved), whereas *d.e.*, because it communicates in length with *d.c.*, which is rational only in power, will itself be rational only in power by Proposition 18. This is manifest from the preceding hypotheses. Thus, by the second part of Proposition 10, area *a.f.* is incommensurable with area *d.g.*, and therefore square *l.m.* is incommensurable with supplement *p.m.* Wherefore, by the first part of Book 6 and the second part of Proposition 10, line *l.r.* is incommensurable with line *r.p.* From Proposition 30, it is therefore established that line *l.p.* is a binomial, which was to be shown.

Therefore, by Proposition 15, both areas *d.g.* and *g.c.*, and consequently the two supplements *p.m.* and *m.q.*, will be rational. However, line *b.d.* will be rational in power only. Lines **l, r** and **r, p** are <term>medial<note>A "medial" line is the side of a square equal in area to a rectangle formed by two rational lines that are commensurable only in square.</note></term> lines and are also <term>commensurable in square<note>Two lines are "commensurable in square" if the squares built upon them have a ratio to one another that a square number has to a square number.</note></term>. For since line **b, f** is <term>commensurable<note>Commensurable means having a common measure; being in a ratio of whole numbers.</note></term> to line **f, d**, it follows that **a, f** is commensurable to **f, b**. Therefore, square **l, m** is commensurable to square **m, n**, and thus line **l, r** is also commensurable to line **r, p** in square. However, they are not commensurable in length, because the ratio of one to the other is as **l, m** is to **m, p**. Since, therefore, **l, m** is not commensurable with **m, p**—because one is medial (namely **l, m**) and the other is rational (namely **m, p**)—it follows that **l, r** is not commensurable in length with **r, p**. Because they contain a <term>rational<note>A "rational" area is one that is commensurable with the square on the assigned "standard" rational line.</note></term> surface, which is **m, p**, it is established by the 31st proposition of this book that line **l, p** is a **first bimedial** line.

# BOOK

## Proposition 53.

-> **If a surface is bounded by a sixth binomial and a rational line, then the line that is powerful in that surface is proven to be powerful in two medials.** <-

<note>original: "I binomio sexto linea qz rōnali superficies contineatur linea que in eam potest: in duo in medialia potens esse probatur." This proposition identifies the square root of a specific area. In modern terms, if you have an area defined by a "sixth binomial" (a specific complex irrational number), its square root belongs to a class of lines called "the side of the sum of two medial areas."</term>

**Theorem 53** still allows you to rest from drawing diagrams <note>original: "ociari a pingendo figuras"</note>; for it is satisfied with the arrangements and positions set out previously. ### Proposition 55
**[Decorative Initial S]** If a surface equal to the square of a **first bimedial** <term>first bimedial: an irrational line formed by the sum of two medial lines that are commensurable in power only and contain a rational rectangle</term> is joined to a rational line, its remaining side must be a **second binomial**.

¶ Let the line **a.b.** be a first bimedial divided at point **c.** according to its boundary. Let the other parts be as before: I say that the line **f.g.** is a second binomial. For the surface **m.g.** will be rational because the parts of the first bimedial contain a rational surface, and the three surfaces **e.l.**, **l.m.**, and the whole **e.n.** are medial and commensurable <note>original: "cōicātes"; meaning they share a common measure</note> because the portions of the first bimedial are medial lines commensurable in power only by the 31st [proposition] and by the 18th. Therefore, the line **n.g.** will be rational in length and commensurable to the given rational line **e.f.**; and by the 20th, the line **f.n.** is rational in power only. Since it is greater than the line **n.g.** according to the first of the two preceding demonstrations of the 35th [proposition] joined to the first part of the 6th, that which has a greater power than the square of a line commensurable with itself in length, by the first part of the 13th [proposition], it will be by definition the line **f.g.**, a second binomial, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 56
**[Decorative Initial C]** When a rectangular surface equal to the square of a **second bimedial** <term>second bimedial: an irrational line whose parts are commensurable in power only and contain a medial rectangle</term> is joined to a line rational in length, it is necessary that its side be a **third binomial**.

¶ If the line **a.b.** is a second bimedial divided by its boundary at point **c.**, and all other things are as before: the line **f.g.** will be a third binomial. For from the 32nd [proposition] and our assumptions, both surfaces **e.n.** and **m.g.** will be medial: wherefore by the 20th, both of the two lines **f.n.** and **n.g.** will be rational in power only <term>rational in power only: lines whose squares are rational, but whose lengths are not</term>. **Every line commensurable with a major line is itself a major line.**
<note>original: "Omnis linea cōicans linee maiori: est linea maior." A "major line" is a specific type of irrational line formed by the sum of two lines that are incommensurable in square, where the sum of their squares is rational and the area they contain is medial.</note>

And this also holds true: if in any way a line is commensurable <note>original: "cōicans" (communicans). **The same by another way.** Since **a** is a major line with which **b** is commensurable, whether in length or in power: taking a rational line which is **c d**, let a surface **c e** be applied to it equal to the square of line **a**; then **f g** equal to the square of line **b**. ### Proposition 63.

**If any line is commensurable with a line that is "powerful" in a rational and a medial area, it is proved that it is itself powerful in a rational and a medial area.**

### Proposition .70.

**If a line be cut from a line, and both be medial, commensurable only in power, and containing a medial [area]: the remaining line shall be irrational, called a second medial residue.**

Let there be here also a line **a.b.** [from which] **b.c.** is cut off [Note: text says *abscisa ex linea a.b.*, but logic dictates from a longer line, perhaps *a.c.* or *a.b.* is the whole]. I say that the remaining line, which is **a.c.**, is irrational, and it is called a second medial residue. For by the hypothesis of [Proposition] 21, both squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together are medial. Likewise, also, twice the area of the one in the other is medial. Since, therefore, from [Proposition] 22, a medial does not differ from a medial except in an irrational [Note: *differentia*], the square of line **a.c.**—in which, by [Proposition] 7 of the Second [Book], the two squares **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together exceed twice the area of one in the other—will be irrational; wherefore also line **a.c.** is irrational.

By a figured example, this can also be made clear as before. Since this is the difference of one medial area **e.g.** to the medial area **d.f.**, it is irrational by [Proposition] 22, and its tetragonic side **a.c.** is also irrational.

The same [is shown] otherwise: Let line **d.e.** be rational, to which is joined the area **d.f.** equal to twice the area of the one in the other, and **e.g.** equal to both squares taken together. By [Proposition] 7 of the Second [Book], **f.g.** will be equal to the square of **a.c.** Because **e.g.** is medial, the line **d.g.** will be rational only in power by [Proposition] 20. Likewise, since **e.b.** is medial, the line **d.b.** will be rational by the same [proposition], and similarly only in power. Here also **a.b.** and **b.c.** are as proposed, which are found through [Proposition] 29, and they are those which compose a line potential in two medials. And the remaining line **a.c.** will be irrational, called that which, joined with a medial, produces a medial whole. You may easily conclude this by a double argumentation through the preceding ones, if you attend diligently to the process of [Proposition] 70. And it is necessary to premise here a [lemma] for the demonstrations of the following things, which is the [proposed thing].

If there be four quantities, the difference of the first to the second being as the third to the fourth: the difference of the first to the third will be, by permutation, as the second to the fourth. This must be understood regarding quantities related in the same way: as when the first is greater than the second, so also the third is greater than the fourth; and when lesser, then lesser. For example, let the difference [*oria*] of **a.** to **b.** be as **c.** to **d.** I say that **a.** to **c.** will be as **b.** to **d.** For by this common notion [*common pceptione*], the difference of the extremes is composed of the differences of those same to the means. The difference of **a.** to **d.** is composed of that which is **a.** to **b.** and that which is **b.** to **d.** But that which is **b.** to **d.** is proposed by the same notion from that which is **b.** to **c.** and that which is **c.** to **d.** And because by hypothesis the difference of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, and that which is **b.** to **c.** is common, it follows by common knowledge [*common fciam/scientiam*] that **a.** to **c.** is as **b.** to **d.**, which is the thing proposed.

### Proposition .74.

**To a residue, no line except one only can be joined so that both are under the same term as those which were before separation.**

Let line **a.c.** be a residue, and let the remaining [part] cut off be **b.c.** from **a.b.** Then **a.b.** and **b.c.** are rational, communicating only in power from [Proposition] 68. I say that **a.c.** itself can be joined to no other line [other than] **b.c.** under this definition, neither greater than **b.c.** nor lesser than **b.c.** If however it can, let it be composed with **c.d.**, either greater or lesser than **c.d.** [Note: likely should be **b.c.**]. Because of this, both lines **a.d.** and **d.c.** will be rational, communicating only in power. Therefore, from [Proposition] 7 of the Second [Book], the squares of both lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together exceed twice the area of the one of them in the other by the square of **a.c.** Likewise, also, the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.** taken together exceed twice the area of the one of them in the other by the square of the same **a.c.** It follows from the preceding antecedent that the difference of the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together to the two squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.** taken together is as the difference of twice the area of **a.b.** in **b.c.** to twice the area of **a.d.** in **d.c.** Since, however, the two squares of each section taken together are rational by hypothesis, but twice the area of one part in the other of each section is medial by hypothesis [Proposition] 19, there will be one and the same difference of two rational areas and two medial areas. But this is impossible: for rational areas do not differ except in a rational area, as is clear through the definition of a rational area and by [Proposition] 9; whereas medial [unclear: *ends mid-sentence*].

### Scholarly Notes & Abbreviations:

*   **oria / oriã:** Abbreviation for *differentia* (difference). This is a common medieval mathematical shorthand where "ria" with a macron represents the suffix.
*   **ronalis / irronalis:** *Rationalis* and *Irrationalis*.
*   **potentia tm̃ / tū:** *Potentia tantum* (commensurable in power only, i.e., their squares are commensurable but the lines are not).
*   **tetragonicum latus:** Literally "tetragonal side," the standard term for a square root or the side of a square area.
*   **7. sedi:** *Septima secundi* (The 7th proposition of the 2nd Book of Euclid).
*   **ꝑ / p̄:** *Per* (through/by).
*   **ꝯ / Con:** Likely *Consectarium* (Corollary) or a marker for the start of the proof.
*   **pntis:** Likely *presentis* or *positis*. In the context of "a destructione," it refers to a *reductio ad absurdum* (proof by contradiction).
*   **fciām / fciã:** *Scientiam*. "Communis scientia" is the standard translation for Euclid's "Common Notions" (Axioms).
*   **Proposition Numbering:** The text contains two propositions numbered 73. In the standard Heiberg numbering of Euclid, these correspond to the different types of irrational residues (minor, the side of a rational plus a medial area, etc.) found in Book X. The text also includes a Lemma between 73 and 74 regarding proportional differences.

**Proposition .82.**
**To investigate the third residual.**
¶ The third residual is obtained in this way: let line **a** be a rational <term>rational: a line whose length can be expressed as a number or whose square is commensurable with a standard unit</term> number, and let square number **e** be divided into non-square **f** and square **g**. Let a first number **b** be taken so that the square of line **a** is to the square of line **bc** as **b** is to **e**. Furthermore, let the square of line **bc** be to the square of line **cd** as **e** is to **f**. It will follow from the definition—and if you have any doubt, consult the section on the third binomial—that line **db** is a third residual.

**Proposition .83.**
**To find the fourth residual.**
¶ Here, just as in the discovery of the first residual, let line **bc** be commensurable <term>commensurable: having a common measure; being in a whole-number ratio to one another</term> with the given rational line **a**. Let the square number **e** be divided into **f** and **g**, both of which are non-squares. Let the square of line **bc** be to the square of line **dc** as **e** is to **f**. You will know from the definition that line **db** is a fourth residual, provided you have not forgotten what you learned in the discovery of the fourth binomial.

**Proposition .84.**
**To demonstrate the fifth residual.**
¶ When you wish to find the fifth residual, let line **cd** be commensurable in length <note>original: "in longitudine"</note> with the given rational line **a**, just as it was in the inquiry of the second residual. Let the square number **e** be divided into **f** and **g**, neither of which is a square, as in the preceding proposition. Let the square of line **cd** be to the square of line **bc** as **f** is to **e**. From these conditions and the definition, one may conclude—having sufficient knowledge of the fifth binomial—that line **db** is the fifth residual.

**Proposition .85.**
**To find the sixth residual at last.**
¶ The sixth residual is found thus: as before, let line **a** be the given rational, and let square number **e** be divided into non-squares **f** and **g**. Let **b** be the first number, and let the square of line **a** be to the square of line **cb** as **b** is to **e**. Moreover, let the square of **bc** be to the square of **cd** as **e** is to **f**. From the definition, line **db** will be the sixth residual. If your mind does not fully grasp this, it is proper for you to practice the discovery of the sixth binomial.

### Proposition 92

**If an area equal to the square of a residue** <term>residue: *residuum*; a type of irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another that is commensurable with it only in square</term> **is applied to a rational line, the other side must be a first residue.**

These six following propositions are the converses of the six preceding ones in order. The intent of this first one [Proposition 92] is as follows: if there is a surface *a.c.* joined to the rational line *a.b.*, and it is equal to the square of a residue *d.e.*, then its second side *b.c.* must necessarily be a **first residue**.

For let there be added to line *d.e.* (which is proposed to be the residue) the line by whose subtraction it became a residue; let this added line be *e.f.* According to Proposition 68, both lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* are rational in power <term>rational in power: *rationalis in potentia*; lines whose squares are commensurable with a given rational area, even if the lines themselves are length-incommensurable</term>, and one of them is incommensurable with the other in length. 

Therefore, let the square of line *f.e.* be described, which is *e.g.*, and the square of *d.e.* (which was set as the residue), which is *e.b.*, and let the complements *d.k.* and *f.l.* be added. <note>These "complements" or "supplements" refer to the rectangles needed to complete a larger square or gnomon in the geometric figure.</note> The square *g.b.* will then be the same as the square of line *d.f.*, and square *e.b.* will be like the surface *a.c.* Both squares *g.b.* and *g.e.* will also be rational. 

Therefore, let the surface *a.m.*, joined to the line *a.b.*, be equal to the square *g.b.*. Because of this, it will be rational; wherefore, by Proposition 16 <note>Referring to Book X of Euclid's Elements</note>, the line *m.n.* <note>The OCR likely misreads the diagram labels here; in geometric logic, this would refer to the segment of the base *b.m.*</note> is rational in length. Let the surface *p.n.* be equal to the square *e.g.*, which will also be rational for the same reason, and by Proposition 16, line *m.n.* is rational in length. 

Thus, the whole line *b.n.* is rational according to Proposition 9. Now, let *c.n.* be divided into equal parts at *m.q.* <note>original: "per equalia .m.q."</note> and let *q.r.* be drawn parallel to *a.b.*. It follows from the first proposition of the sixth book that *c.r.* is equal to *r.n.*

**Proposition .94.**

...they propose that it is true for the companions <note>original: "comittibus," likely a shorthand or OCR error for "commensurabilibus" (commensurables)</note>: those who have followed the usual pattern up to this point will not be able to ignore these things. Furthermore, whatever was said in those cases regarding commensurability in length and in power <note>The "power" of a line refers to the area of the square built upon it.</note> alone, the same must be understood in these cases as well. For every line commensurable with a residue, whether in length or in power only, is itself also a residue. However, if it is commensurable in length, it is not only a residue itself, but also a residue of the same species. 

For example: a line commensurable in length with a **first residue** is a **first residue**; and one commensurable with a **second** is a **second**. The same follows for the rest. However, if a line is commensurable with a residue in power only, it is also necessarily a residue, but not of the same species. Indeed, it is impossible for a line commensurable in power only with a first, second, third, fourth, or fifth residue to fall under that same species with it. Instead, it is necessary that both fall together under the first three species, or both together under the last three. 

Let there be, for example, line **a**, a residue to which line **b** is commensurable in length. I say that **b** will be a residue of the same species as **a**. For let line **c** be joined to line **a**, which is the line by whose subtraction **a** was made a residue; and let another line **d** be joined to **b**, such that **b** relates to **d** as **a** relates to **c**. Let **e** be composed of **a** and **c**, and let **f** be composed of **b** and **d**. 

By permuted proportionality, **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**; and by the 13th proposition of the fifth book, **c** is to **f** as **a** is to **b**, or as **c** is to **d**. Since, therefore, **a** is commensurable with **b**, it follows by the 10th proposition that **c** is commensurable with **d**, and **e** is also commensurable with **f**. And because it is also necessarily true by permuted proportionality that **e** is to **c** as **f** is to **d**, it follows by the 12th proposition that if **e** is more powerful than **c** by the square of a line commensurable with it in length (or if perhaps it is incommensurable), then similarly **f** is more powerful than **d**. And since every line commensurable in length to a <term>rational line</term> <note>A line whose length can be expressed as a whole number or a fraction relative to a given standard.</note> is similarly rational to it—I say similarly because both will be rational in length or both in power only—it follows from the definitions of residues that **b** is a residue of the same species as **a**.

### Translator’s Notes & Abbreviations:

*   **[1] potens / potens in:** Literally "capable of" or "being powerful over." In Euclidean Latin, this refers to the line which, when squared, produces the area in question (i.e., the square root or side of the area).
*   **[2] residuum:** Traditionally translated as "apotome" in modern editions of Euclid.
*   **[3] per 16:** Reference to Proposition 16 of Book X. Note that numbering in Renaissance editions often differs by a few digits from modern Heiberg-based editions.
*   **[4] latus tetragonicum:** Literally "the tetragonal side," meaning the square root or the side of a square.
*   **[5] f.g / c.g:** The text likely contains a minor scribal error or compression here; it refers to the ratio of the areas being the same as the ratio of the lines.

**Abbreviations and Readings:**
*   `cōicabunt` $\rightarrow$ *communicabunt* (will communicate / are commensurable)
*   `rōnalis` / `rōna` $\rightarrow$ *rationalis* / *rationa*
*   `tṁ` / `tātū` $\rightarrow$ *tantum* (only)
*   `ꝑ` $\rightarrow$ *per* (through/by)
*   `ꝙ` $\rightarrow$ *quod* (which/that)
*   `r` $\rightarrow$ This character is frequently used in this specific edition as a shorthand for *et* (and) or to separate logical steps in the proof.
*   `inediales` $\rightarrow$ Clearly a typo for *mediales*.
*   `reſiduū / reſidūū` $\rightarrow$ *residuum* (residual/apotome).
*   `incōmenſu` $\rightarrow$ *incommensurabilis*.
*   `ꝓpoſitum` $\rightarrow$ *propositum* (the thing proposed).

# THE BOOK

The irrational lines following it differ in species and <term>definition<note>original: "dione," an abbreviation for "definitione"</note></term> from one another, and no single line can fall under two or more species of these six irrational lines, which are the **residue** <note>Also known as an apotome; a line formed by subtracting one rational magnitude from another.</note> and its **five companions**. Furthermore, all species of the residue differ from all species of the **binomial**, and it is not possible for one line to be simultaneously a residue and a binomial of any species. The first part is shown thus: because the surfaces equal to the squares of the residue and its five companions, when <term>applied<note>A geometric method of "application of areas" used to find unknown lengths.</note></term> to a rational line, necessarily have their **second sides** <note>The width of a rectangle when the area and the other side are known.</note> different from each other, according to Proposition 92 and the five following it. These second sides are the first, second, and so on up to the sixth residue. The second part is shown in this way: if the same line could be both a residue and a binomial at once, let it be **a**. Let its square be applied to the rational line **b c**, and let it be **b d**. It would then follow from Proposition 54 that line **c d** is a first binomial, and from Proposition 92 that it is a first residue. Insofar as it is a first binomial, let it be divided into its binomial portions at point **e**, where the greater portion **c e** was <term>rational in length<note>A line whose length can be expressed as a whole number or fraction relative to a standard unit.</note></term> by definition. However, insofar as it is a first residue, let **d g** be added to it, which was a residue by its subtraction; then, by definition, **c g** would also be rational in length. Since both lines **c g** and **c e** are rational in length, line **e g** will also be rational in length by Proposition 9. But because line **d e** is <term>rational in power only<note>A line whose square is rational, but whose length is an irrational square root.</note></term>, since it is the smaller portion of a first binomial, line **d g** would be a residue by Proposition 68. And because it was rational in power only, such that through its subtraction line **c d** became a residue, an impossibility follows by Proposition 68. To make this clearer: let surface **b d** be applied to the rational line **b c**, equal to the square of line **d g**. Since line **d g** is rational in power, line **c d** will be rational in length by Proposition 16. But since line **d g** is also a residue, line **c d** will be a first residue by Proposition 92—which cannot be, since a line called a residue is irrational by Proposition 68.

### Proposition 107.

**L**inea <note>Large ornate initial L</note> which is called a **residue**, or any of the irrational lines that follow it, cannot be classified as a binomial or follow the order of any of the other irrational lines that follow the binomial. Although it is possible for the series of irrational lines to be produced to infinity, it is not possible for any of them to coincide in definition and order with those that preceded them.

Through this final proposition of the tenth book, he intends to show that the 13 irrational lines demonstrated herein—which are the **medial**, the **binomial** and its five companions, and the **residue** and its five companions—are each different from one another in species. No single line can belong to two or more of these species at once. Furthermore, the species of irrational lines can be extended to infinity, and none of them will coincide in definition and order. Remember that it has been demonstrated above that these 13 lines (namely the medial, the binomial and its 5 companions, and the residue and its 5 companions) are irrational: the medial from Proposition 19; the binomial and its five companions from Proposition 30 and the five following; and the residue and its five companions from Proposition 68 and the five following. You may conclude that none of these 13 irrational lines can coincide in species with any of the others in this way: Suppose that surfaces equal to the squares of these 13 irrational lines are applied to one and the same line that is rational in length, following their sequence. By Proposition 20, the second side of the first of these 13 surfaces (and the five following it) will be rational in power only. The second sides of the second of these 13 surfaces (and the five following) will be all the species of binomials in order—namely, the first binomial, the second, and so on to the sixth, as you will remember was demonstrated in Proposition 54 and the five following. Truly, the second sides of the eighth surface and the five following it are the species of residues in order—namely, the first residue and the residue...

**Proposition .1.**

[Decorative initial L] It is impossible for one part of a straight line to be in a plane and another part to be in space. <note>original: "in sublimi," literally "in the high" or "elevated."</note>
¶ Let there be a straight line *a-b*. I say that it is not possible for part of it to be in a plane and part of it raised upward. For if it were possible, let the part *a-c* be located in the plane and the part *c-b* be positioned in space, and let the line *a-c* be extended directly in the plane in which it is located as far as *d*. Thus, for one and the same line *a-c*, there would be two entirely different lines, *c-b* and *c-d*, added onto the same side in a straight line, which is impossible: from Proposition 13 of the first book.

**Proposition .2.**

[Decorative initial O] Any two lines that intersect one another are situated in one plane, and every triangle consists entirely in one plane.
¶ Let there be two straight lines *a-b* and *c-d* intersecting each other at point *e*. I say that they are in one plane, and I say that every triangle is entirely in one plane. For let point *f* be marked on line *c-d* and point *g* on line *a-b*, and let line *f-g* be drawn. Since it is impossible for part of the triangle *e-f-g* to be in a plane and part in space, because a part of one or more of its boundary lines would similarly be in a plane and part in space—and since this is impossible for lines by the previous proposition—it will also be impossible for the triangle. Therefore, the entire triangle *e-f-g* is in one plane. From this second part and the previous proposition, the first part of this second proposition is established.

**Proposition .3.**

[Decorative initial O] The common section of any two intersecting planes is a straight line.
¶ Understand this to be about flat surfaces <note>original: "planis superficiebus"</note> and what is said will be true. Let there be two flat surfaces *a-b* and *c-d* intersecting each other; I say that their common section will be a straight line. For let there be two points *e* and *f* at the ends of their common section, which are joined by a straight line *e-f*. If the line *e-f* is in both surfaces *a-b* and *c-d*, the proposition is proven. But if it is in neither, or not in one of them: since both points *e* and *f* are in both surfaces *a-b* and *c-d*, let a straight line *e-b-f* be drawn in that surface where the line itself was not. There would then be two straight lines *e-f* and *e-b-f* having the same two common endpoints, which is impossible. In this way, two straight lines would enclose a surface, which is against the final petition <note>The "final petition" refers to the 5th Postulate/Axiom of Book 1, which implies two lines cannot enclose a space.</note> of the first book.

### Proposition 5

Wherefore angle a-b-f is a right angle; and since angle a-b-d is also a right angle by hypothesis, there follows an impossibility, namely that a part would be equal to its whole <note>a fundamental axiom in Euclidean geometry: the whole is greater than the part</note>.

**Proposition 7.**
If a straight line is drawn from one point to another marked on two parallel lines: it is necessarily proved that the line is located in the same plane in which those two lines are situated.
¶ Let there be two parallel lines, **a.b.** and **c.d.**, which are established by definition to be in a single plane: let two points, **e.** and **f.**, be marked on them, and let the straight line **e.f.** be extended. I say, therefore, that line **e.f.** is located in the plane of lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** If **e.f.** were in another plane, such as hanging <note>original: "in sublimi," meaning extending into the third dimension</note> above it, that plane (if extended) would necessarily cut the plane in which the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** are situated. By the 3rd proposition of this book, their common section would be a straight line terminated by those same points, which is impossible; for in that case, two straight lines would enclose a surface. <note>This refers to a fundamental axiom of geometry: two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>

**Proposition 8.**
If two straight lines are erected parallel to each other from the same plane, and one of them stands <term>perpendicularly</term><note>A line is perpendicular to a plane if it makes right angles with all lines in that plane that it intersects.</note>, it follows that the other will also be perpendicular to the same plane.
¶ This is, as it were, the converse of the sixth proposition. Let there be two parallel lines, **a.b.** and **c.d.**, and let one of them, **c.d.**, be erected perpendicularly above any plane: I say that the other, **a.b.**, is also perpendicular to that same plane. Let exactly the same arrangement be made as in the sixth proposition: just as there, each of the two angles **f.d.b.** and **f.b.e.** will be a right angle. The first is a right angle by the initial setup; the second, however, by the 8th proposition of the first book. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of this book, line **f.b.** is erected perpendicularly above the plane in which the two lines **b.d.** and **b.e.** are located. And since, by the previous proposition, the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** are in the same plane as the two lines **b.d.** and **b.e.**, it follows that line **f.b.** is erected perpendicularly above the plane in which line **b.a.** is located. From the definition, therefore, angle **f.b.a.** will be a right angle; and since angle **d.b.a.** is also a right angle (by the last part of the 29th proposition of the first book), it follows by the 4th proposition of this book that line **a.b.** is perpendicular to the plane in which the two lines **b.d.** and **b.f.** are situated. Thus the proposition stands proven.

**Proposition 9.**
If two lines are parallel to the same line but are not in the same plane, it is necessary that they are also parallel to each other.
¶ Let each of the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** be parallel to line **e.f.**, and let them not all be in one plane: I say that these lines are also parallel to each other. Regarding those that are all in one plane, this was proven by the 30th proposition of the first book. But for those which are not in one plane, as is the case here with **e.f.** (which is understood to be raised up <note>original: "sursum erecta in sublimi," referring to a line standing in 3D space</note>), this remains to be proven. Therefore, let point **g.** be marked on it, from which two perpendiculars are drawn to the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.**, which shall be **g.b.** and **g.k.** By the 4th proposition of this book, line **e.f.** will be perpendicular to the plane in which the two lines **g.b.** and **g.k.** are situated. Thus, by applying the previous proposition twice, each of those two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** is perpendicular to the same plane (the one in which the lines **g.b.** and **g.k.** are situated). By the 6th proposition of this book, therefore, they are parallel to each other, which is the proposition to be shown.
