### Proposition 10
If two lines meeting each other at an angle are parallel to two other lines meeting each other [and] opposite to them, and are not in the same plane, it is proved that the two angles formed by them are equal to each other.

Let there be two lines $a.b.$ and $a.c.$ meeting at an angle at point $a$, parallel to two other lines which are $d.e.$ and $d.f.$, likewise meeting at an angle at point $d$, nor are they in one plane with them. I say that angle $a$ is equal to angle $d$. For let line $d.e.$ be equal to line $a.b.$, to which it was placed as being parallel, and [let] $d.f.$ be equal to $a.c.$, to which it is also placed to be parallel; and let lines $d.a.$, $e.b.$, and $f.c.$ be drawn. From [Proposition] 33 of the First [Book], taken twice, each of the two lines $b.e.$ and $e.f.$ [Note: likely $c.f.$] will be equal and parallel to line $a.d.$ Therefore, by the [common] conception and the [proposition] mentioned before, these same are equal and parallel to each other. And so, by [Proposition] 33 of the First [Book] repeated again, the two lines $b.c.$ and $e.f.$ are also equal and parallel; therefore, by [Proposition] 8 of the First [Book], the proposition is established.

### Proposition 11
From a given point in the air, to draw a perpendicular line to a given plane.

Let there be a point $a$ high in the air, from which we wish to draw a perpendicular to the underlying plane. Therefore, let line $b.c.$ be drawn in that plane, wherever it may happen, to which a perpendicular $a.d.$ is drawn from point $a$ itself, according to the teaching of [Proposition] 12 of the First [Book]. And again, from point $d$ in that plane to which the perpendicular is to be drawn from point $a$, let line $d.e.$ be extended, which is perpendicular to line $b.c.$, as [Proposition] 11 of the First [Book] teaches. To this line $d.e.$ let another perpendicular line be drawn from point $a$, which is $a.f.$ This I say is that which we intend. For let line $f.g.$ be parallel to line $b.c.$ And because each of the two angles $b.d.a.$ and $b.d.f.$ is a right angle, line $b.d.$ will be perpendicular to the plane in which triangle $a.d.f.$ is [located] by the fourth [proposition] of this [book]. And therefore, also by the eighth of this [book], line $g.f.$ will be perpendicular to the same plane. Therefore, by definition, angle $g.f.a.$ will be a right angle. And since angle $d.f.a.$ is also a right angle, it follows from the fourth [proposition] of this [book] that line $a.f.$ is perpendicular to the plane in which the two lines $d.f.$ and $f.g.$ are [located], which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 12
From a proposed plane and a point assigned in it, to erect a line perpendicularly to the given plane from that point.

When it is desired to lead out a perpendicular from any point assigned in the proposed plane: from any point high in the air, placed at will, let down a perpendicular to the same plane, as the preceding [proposition] taught. If it falls upon the assigned point, that is the one you seek. If not, however, draw [a line] from the assigned point parallel to the perpendicular [let down]. You will prove that this is the one you seek by the eighth [proposition] of this [book].

### Proposition 13
It is impossible for two lines to stand perpendicularly to a single plane from a single point.

For if it is possible that two lines should stand perpendicularly to one and the same plane from a single point: let it be understood that the plane in which the perpendiculars themselves are located is extended until it cuts the plane upon which the said lines stand perpendicularly. By the third [proposition] of this [book], their common section will be a straight line. And because, by definition, each of those two perpendiculars contains a right angle with the common section, it follows that a right angle would be a part of a right angle, which is impossible. Just as it has been demonstrated that it is impossible [for this to happen] from one and the same point outside the plane...

[Page break / Transition]

...[it is impossible for] two lines from one point to be perpendicular to the same plane. So we shall also demonstrate it is impossible for two lines drawn from one and the same point assigned outside the plane to be perpendicular to the same plane. For if this were so, they themselves would be parallel by the sixth [proposition] of this [book], which is impossible by the definition of parallel lines. It is established, therefore, from this that if some flat plane cuts another flat plane perpendicularly, and a perpendicular is drawn from some point of the cutting plane to the cut plane, it is necessary that it fall on their common section. Otherwise, from the same point of the cutting plane, let a perpendicular be drawn to their common section as [Proposition] 12 of the First [Book] teaches, and from the point where it falls with the common section, let another perpendicular be led out to the same common section in the cut plane as [Proposition] 11 of the First [Book] teaches. By the definition of a plane erected perpendicularly upon another plane, the angle which these two perpendicular lines contain will be a right angle. Therefore, by the fourth [proposition] of this [book], the first of these two perpendiculars is also perpendicular to the cut plane. Therefore, from one point, two lines have been drawn perpendicular to the same plane, which is impossible. Thus, our proposition remains.

### Proposition 14
[If] one line stands perpendicularly upon two assigned planes, those two planes, even if extended infinitely in any direction, will never meet.
[Note: The text here mentions "converso quoque" (conversely also)]:
Conversely also: namely, if a straight line falls upon two parallel planes which is perpendicular to one of them, it will also be perpendicular to the other.

### Proposition 16
If one plane cuts two parallel planes, their common sections will be parallel.

### Proposition 17
If three or more parallel planes cut two straight lines meeting each other or being parallel, the portions of those lines are proved to be proportional.

### Proposition 18
If a line stands perpendicularly in an assigned plane, every plane drawn from that line in any direction will be perpendicularly erected to the same assigned plane.

### Proposition 19
If two intersecting planes are both perpendicular to a single plane, their common section will be perpendicular to the same plane.

### Proposition 20
If three plane angles contain a solid angle, any two of those three angles taken together are greater than the remaining one.

### Scholarly Notes & Abbreviations

*   **Piter (Prop. 20):** An abbreviation for *pariter* ("equally" or "together").
*   **Ois (Prop. 18):** An abbreviation for *omnis* ("every").
*   **Impossibilee (Prop. 13):** A likely OCR error or printer's typo for *impossibile*.
*   **33. primi / 12. primi:** Refers to the numbered propositions in Euclid’s *Book I*.
*   **Conceptionem (Prop. 10):** Refers to the "Common Notions" (*communes animi conceptiones*) of Euclid.
*   **Superficiam (Prop. 11):** A late Latin/medieval variant or typo for *superficiem*.
*   **Geometric Labels:** The lowercase letters (a, b, c, etc.) correspond to the diagrams provided in the original text, which are standard for Euclidean geometry.

...that two lines upon one point can be perpendicular to the same surface.
We will also demonstrate in this way that it is impossible for two lines drawn from one and the same point marked outside a surface to both be perpendicular to that same surface. For if this were the case, the lines would be parallel to each other by the 6th proposition of this book, which is impossible by the definition of parallel lines <note>Parallel lines, by definition, never meet, yet these lines are stated to originate from the "one and same point."</note>. Thus, two perpendicular lines would be drawn from a single point to the same surface, which is impossible. Therefore, our proposition remains proven.

->**Proposition 14.**<-

[Decorative initial S] IF a single line stands <term>orthogonally</term> <note>perpendicularly</note> upon two assigned surfaces: those two surfaces, even if extended infinitely in any direction, will never meet.
     ¶ For, having established that one line stands perpendicularly to two surfaces, if it were possible for those surfaces to meet, they would meet at their common section, which by the 3rd proposition of this book will be a straight line. Let any point be marked [on that intersection], from which two lines are drawn within those two surfaces to the line that stands perpendicular to them. A triangle will then be formed by these two lines and the perpendicular. In this triangle, each of the two angles that meet the perpendicular line is a right angle, as is clear from the definition of a line standing perpendicularly to a surface. However, this is impossible by the 32nd proposition of the first book <note>Proposition 1.32 states that the sum of all internal angles in a triangle must equal two right angles (180 degrees); a triangle cannot have two right angles because the third angle would have to be zero.</note>.
     ¶ Conversely, if a straight line falls upon two parallel surfaces, and it is perpendicular to one of them, it will also be perpendicular to the other. ¶ For, having established two parallel surfaces, let a straight line be understood to penetrate both, standing perpendicularly to one of them. I say that the same line stands perpendicularly to the other surface. For let there be a surface intersecting the designated parallel surfaces along the line penetrating them. The common section of this intersecting surface and the first of the intersected surfaces (namely, the one the penetrating line stands perpendicular to) will contain a right angle with the penetrating line, by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface. If, therefore, the other common section of the same intersecting surface and the second of the two intersected surfaces does not contain a right angle with the same penetrating line, it would follow from the <term>final postulate of the first book</term> <note>The "Parallel Postulate," which suggests that lines that do not meet at right angles will eventually converge.</note> that those two common sections, if extended in one direction, must necessarily meet; therefore, the surfaces which were stated to be parallel would also necessarily meet. And since this is impossible, that angle must be a right angle. The same logic applies to any other surface intersecting these same parallel surfaces along the same line. Therefore, from the 4th proposition of this book and this 14th proposition, it is established that what we have said is true.

->**Proposition 15.**<-

[Decorative initial S] IF there are two lines meeting at an angle that are <term>equidistant</term> <note>parallel</note> to two other lines meeting at an angle, but not in the same surface: the two surfaces contained by those lines cannot meet in any part, no matter how far they are produced.

# XI

A solid angle is completed at point **a**. I say that any two of the <term>plane angles</term> <note>The flat angles on the surface of a three-dimensional shape that meet at a single vertex.</note> which form the <term>solid angle</term> <note>A 3D corner, like the tip of a pyramid.</note> at point **a**, when taken together, are greater than the third angle. 

For if these three plane angles are equal to one another, or if two are equal while the third is smaller than either of the two equal ones, it is clear by common knowledge that the statement is true. But if one of them is larger than either of the remaining two—whether those two are equal or unequal—it is still certain that this larger angle, when combined with either of the others, will be greater than the third. However, to prove that those two smaller angles, when taken together, are greater than this third angle which was set as the largest: consider it in this way. 

Let the angle **c.a.d.** be the largest of the three proposed plane angles, larger than either of the other two. From this angle, I will cut off an angle **c.a.e.** equal to angle **b.a.d.** <note>original: "c.a.d. equalem angulo. b.a.d." - The text appears to use 'e' as the internal point for the cut angle.</note> by drawing the line **a.e.** I will take a segment **a.g.** from this line **a.e.**, and from line **a.b.** a segment **a.f.**, which are set as equal. I will then draw a line from point **g**, however it may happen to fall on the surface of the two lines **a.c.** and **a.d.**, until it cuts **a.c.** at point **b** <note>The text likely means 'c' or a point on the line; standard proofs use a transversal line through g.</note> and **a.d.** at point **k**, and let this line be **b.g.k.** I will then draw the lines **f.b.** and **f.k.** 

Since, therefore, **a.f.** is equal to **a.g.** and **a.k.** is common to both, then by the <note>original: "per quartaꝛ pꝛimi"</note> fourth proposition of the first book, **f.k.** is equal to **k.g.** And because, from the <note>original: "ex.20.pꝛime"</note> 20th proposition of the first book, two sides of a triangle **b.f.** and **f.k.** are together greater than the side **b.k.**, it follows by common axiom that **b.f.** is greater than **b.g.** Therefore, by the <note>original: "per 25.pꝛimi"</note> 25th proposition of the first book, since line **a.f.** is equal to line **a.g.**, the angle **f.a.b.** is greater than angle **b.a.g.** Thus, by common axiom, it is established that the two angles **b.a.f.** and **f.a.k.** taken together are greater than the angle **b.a.k.**, which was to be demonstrated.

### Proposition 21

### Every solid angle is proved to be less than four right angles.

The magnitude of a **solid angle** is determined by the magnitude of the **plane angles** that contain that solid; therefore, this 21st proposition likewise proposes that any plane angles containing any solid angle, when taken together, are less than four right angles <note>In modern terms, the sum of the face angles at a vertex is always less than 360 degrees.</note>. 

For let there be a triangular pyramid **a.b.c.d.**, whose highest angle (since it could be any of its angles) we shall here call **a**. Regarding this, I say that the three plane angles containing **a** are less than four right angles. It is established from the <note>original: "ex.32.pꝛimi"</note> 32nd proposition of the first book that the nine angles of the three triangles surrounding this pyramid—which are **a.b.c.**, **a.c.d.**, and **a.d.b.**—are equal to six right angles. 

Regarding the three angles of its base, which is the triangle **b.c.d.**, it is also established that they are equal to two right angles. Since the six angles of the three aforementioned triangles surrounding our pyramid (the ones whose peak angle we are discussing), together with the three angles of the base, contain the other three solid angles of the pyramid, they are (by the previously assumed proposition) <note>Referring to Proposition 20.</note> greater than the three angles of the base. It follows that those six angles are greater than two right angles. Therefore, from the angles of the three triangles surrounding the pyramid, twice six angles <note>This likely refers to the total sum of angles in the triangles minus the base angles.</note> being removed, it remains by common knowledge that the remaining three which constitute the solid angle **a** are less than 4 right angles. 

If, however, the peak angle **a** in the assumed pyramid is contained by more than three plane angles (which will depend on the number of angles in its base), then since all angles of all triangles surrounding the pyramid, when taken together, are equal to as many right angles as twice the number of angles of its base (because there must be as many triangles surrounding the pyramid as there are angles of its base), and since all the angles of its base are equal to as many right angles as twice the number of its angles, minus four (as was demonstrated in the 32nd proposition of the first book)... <note>The text cuts off mid-argument, continuing the proof for polygons with more than three sides.</note>

### Proposition 25.
**I**F a certain surface cuts a parallelogrammic solid <note>a parallelepiped, or a 3D box where opposite faces are parallel</note> parallel to two of the solid's opposite surfaces, the two partial bodies that are joined at that cutting surface—as at a common boundary—are proportional to their bases.

Let the body **a.b.** be a parallelogrammic solid and let the surface **c.d.** cut it parallel to two of its opposite surfaces, which are **a.e.** and **f.b.** Let the surface **g.b.** be the base of the solid **a.b.** It is established by the previous proposition that this base has parallel sides. Let the common section of the two surfaces **c.d.** and **g.b.** be the line **b.d.**, which is established to be a straight line by the third proposition of this book, and by the 16th proposition it is parallel to **g.e.** Therefore, the two surfaces **g.d.** and **b.b.** <note>likely h.b. in the diagram</note> have parallel sides, and these are the bases of the two partial bodies into which the surface **c.d.** divides the solid **a.b.**

I say, therefore, that the ratio of solid **a.d.** to solid **b.c.** is as the base **g.d.** is to the base **b.b.** For let four lines be extended on both sides as much as one pleases, passing through the surface **c.d.** at its corners; these are **a.f.** and **e.b.** with the two others parallel to them. Let portions be taken from all of them on the side of point **b.** as many as one pleases, each placed equal to line **b.d.**, and on the side of point **e.** let others likewise be taken as many as one pleases, placed equal to line **e.d.** Upon these, parallelogrammic solids are established on both sides according to the requirements of their lengths. Let the solids on the side of point **b.** be **f.k.** and **l.m.**, and on the side of point **e.** the solids **a.n.** and **q.a.** <note>original: "q.a."</note>. From the <term>definition</term> <note>original: "dione," an abbreviation for "definitione"</note> of equal and similar bodies, each of the solids **f.k.** and **l.m.** will be equal to solid **e.b.**, and each of **a.n.** and **p.q.** is equal to **a.d.**

Therefore, let the argument be made just as in the first proposition of the sixth book: for as the solid **e.m.** is a multiple of solid **b.c.**, so the base **b.m.** is a multiple of base **b.b.**; and as the solid **q.c.** is a multiple of solid **a.d.**, so the base **q.b.** is a multiple of base **g.d.** And if base **b.m.** is equal to base **q.b.**, the solid **e.m.** is equal to solid **q.c.** from the definition of equal and similar bodies. And if the base is less than the base, the solid is less than the solid; and if greater, it is greater. This is clear from the definition, since if the larger base is cut down to the equality of the smaller and a parallelogrammic solid is described upon it, then by the definition of continuous proportionality, the ratio of solid **a.d.** to solid **c.b.** is as base **g.d.** to base **b.b.**, which is what was proposed.

In the same way, if any surface cuts a <term>prism</term> <note>original: "seratule," literally "little saw," a medieval term for a triangular prism</note> parallel to its two opposite triangular surfaces, the two partial bodies joined at that cutting surface as a common boundary will be proportional to their bases.

For let **a.f.** be the body of a prism whose two triangular surfaces are **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** It is established from the definition of a prism <note>original: "seratilis"</note> that each of the three surfaces **a.b.d.e.**, **b.c.e.f.**, and **a.c.d.f.** is a parallelogram. Therefore, let the surface **g.h.k.** cut this prism parallel to its two opposite surfaces **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** I say that the ratio of the prism **a.k.** to the prism **g.f.** is as the base **a.k.** is to the base **g.f.** This is proven just as with the parallelogrammic solids; for with the lines **a.d.**, **b.e.**, and **c.f.** extended in both directions, and having made prisms equal to prism **g.f.** on the side of point **e.**, and others equal to prism **a.k.** on the side of point **b.**, in any number on both sides, it follows from the definition of continuous proportionality. If you examine all these things with a watchful mind, it will not be difficult for you to conclude what we have said.

### [Book] XI

[If] two bases are reciprocal to their altitudes, it is necessary that the solids themselves be equal to one another.
¶ Whenever two solids of equidistant surfaces [parallelepipeds] are equal, it is necessary that their bases and altitudes be reciprocal, and conversely; just as he [Euclid] proposed in the 13th [proposition] of the Sixth [Book] concerning equiangular surfaces of equidistant sides [parallelograms]. However, in this 34th [proposition], this is proposed to be demonstrated concerning those parallelogram solids in which the lines of the altitudes stand orthogonally [at right angles] upon their parallelogram bases. But that which follows proposes the same concerning the rest...

### Proposition 35.
**I**f two solids of equidistant boundaries [parallelepipeds] are equal, their bases will be reciprocal to their altitudes. If, however, their bases are reciprocal to their altitudes, any two bodies of equidistant surfaces are proved to be equal.

---

### Proposition 36.
**I**f two solids of equidistant surfaces are similar, the ratio of each to the other will be as the triplicate ratio [i.e., the ratio of the cubes] of any of its sides to the relative side of the other.

---

### Proposition 31.
**S**olids of equidistant surfaces established upon equal bases, if they are of equal height and their angular lines stand orthogonally above the bases, shall be equal.

---

### Proposition 32.
**I**f solids of equidistant surfaces established upon equal bases are of equal height, but the angular lines do not stand orthogonally above the bases: it is necessary that they be equal.

### Proposition 33.
**A**ll solids of equidistant surfaces of equal height are proportional to their bases.

### Proposition 34.
**I**f two solids of equidistant surfaces, with the lines of the altitudes erected orthogonally upon the bases, are equal, their bases are reciprocal to their altitudes.

---

### Proposition 39.
**I**f there are any number of proportional lines, their solids—of equidistant and similar surfaces of each creation—will also be proportional.

---

### Proposition 40.
**I**f the sides of two opposite surfaces of a cube are cut, each into two middle [parts]: and from the points of the sections two surfaces go out, mutually cutting each other through the cube, their common section bisects the diameter of the cube into equal [parts]...

---

### Proposition 37.
**I**f there are two plane angles equal, upon which two hypothemises [altitudes of the faces/slant heights] are placed in the air, containing with the sides of the underlying angles individual angles equal to each other, and if two points are marked on those hypothemises, from which two perpendiculars are dropped to the surfaces of the proposed angles...

---

### Proposition 38.
**A** solid contained by three proportional lines will be equal to the solid which is contained by equal sides of the mean line.

---

### [Book] XII

### Proposition 41.
**I**f there are two serratile bodies [prisms], one of which has a triangular base and the other has a base of equidistant sides [a parallelogram] double to that triangular base, [and] they are of equal height, it is necessary that those two bodies be equal.

## Here begins the Twelfth Book.

### Proposition 1.
**O**f all two similar multiangular surfaces [polygons] described [inscribed] between two circles, the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of the squares produced from the diameters of the circles circumscribing them.

---

### Proposition 2.
**O**f all two circles, the ratio [of their areas] is as the ratio of the square of its diameter to the square of the diameter of the other.

### Translator’s Notes on Abbreviations and Terminology:

*   **Solida equidistantium superficierum:** Literally "solids of equidistant surfaces," the standard Renaissance term for **parallelepipeds**.
*   **Mutue / Mutuekeſas:** Refers to **reciprocal proportion**. In this context, it means the bases are inversely proportional to the heights ($B_1:B_2 = h_2:h_1$).
*   **Serratilia:** From *serrare* (to saw), referring to "sawable" solids or **prisms**.
*   **Ypothemiſe:** A Latinization of a Greek geometric term (hypothemis), here referring to the **slant heights** or lines forming a solid angle.
*   **Triplicata:** Triplicate ratio, which in modern terms means the ratio of the volumes is the ratio of the sides **cubed** ($s_1^3 : s_2^3$).
*   **Multiangularum:** Polygons.
*   **OCR Note:** In Proposition 35, the word **coꝝpa** is an abbreviation for *corpora* (bodies/solids). In Proposition 40, **eax** is likely a transcription error for *earum* (of them/their).

### Book XI

Therefore, solid **A.B.** is equal to solid **A.C.**, and so the proposition is established. 

¶ You can also prove the converses of this and the previous proposition, if you wish, by leading to an impossibility <note>original: "ducendo ad impossibile," a logical method known as *reductio ad absurdum* where a statement is proven by showing that its denial leads to a contradiction.</note>. For you would suppose any two solid parallelograms <term>solid parallelepipeds | three-dimensional figures where every face is a parallelogram, like a slanted box</term> to be equal and situated upon the same parallel base, and you will demonstrate them to be of the same height. 

This proposition and the previous one will serve as the middle steps of your demonstration. However, the impossibility to which you will be led is this: that a part is equal to its whole. This will be clearly evident if—from that solid which an opponent falsely claims to be taller, even though both are assumed equal and set on the same base—you cut off a solid parallelogram of the same height as the shorter one. You will then prove, using this proposition and the one before it, that this cut-off portion is equal to the shorter solid, and therefore it would be equal to the whole solid from which it was cut, according to common knowledge <note>original: "ex communi scientia," referring to the fundamental axioms or "Common Notions" of geometry, specifically that the whole is greater than the part.</note>.

**BOOK [XI]**

**Proposition 32.**
**S**i <note>A large decorative initial 'S' begins this section.</note> **parallelepipeds** <term>solida equidistantiū superficierū; literally 'solids of parallel surfaces'</term> established on equal bases are of equal height, even if their edges <note>the 'angular lines'</note> do not stand perpendicularly above their bases, it is necessary that they are equal to one another.
¶ When two bodies are constructed as proposed—namely, that they are of parallel boundaries and equal height, and on equal bases, but not standing upright <note>orthogonal</note> upon their bases, but rather both inclined upon them. If perpendicular lines are drawn from the four corners of their top surfaces to their bases, these will be individually parallel (from Proposition 6) and also (by hypothesis) individually equal to each other, for they define the height of the proposed solids. And if parallelepipeds are completed between them, it follows from the previous proposition that these two newly constructed solids are equal to one another. Since the two original solids and the two later ones share the same bases (namely, their top surfaces), it is clear from Proposition 29 or 30 and this **common notion**—that whatever things are equal to the same thing are equal to each other—that the proposition is true. From this, you can indirectly demonstrate the converse of this and the previous proposition by the same means if you wish, by leading to an absurdity <note>original: *ad id icōueniēs*; a proof by contradiction</note> just as in the converses of the two preceding ones: for you would assume two parallelepipeds to be equal and on equal bases, and prove them to be equally high; or you would assume them to be equally high and equal, and prove them to be on equal bases.

**Proposition 33.**
**O**mnia <note>A large decorative initial 'O' begins this section.</note> all **parallelepipeds** of equal height are proportional to their bases. ¶ Let there be two parallelepipeds of equal height established upon two bases, **a.b.** and **c.d.** I say that the proportion of these two solids, one to the other, is as the proportion of their bases, which are **a.b.** and **c.d.**, one to the other. Indeed, it is established from Proposition 24 that each of the two bases consists of parallel sides. Therefore, let two opposite and parallel sides in surface **a.b.** be extended, and between them let a surface of parallel sides be made, which is **f.e.**, equal to **c.d.** Then, above surface **f.e.**, let a parallelepiped be completed of the same height as the one established on base **a.b.**, and let the common boundary of both be that surface which rises above line **b.f.** Let these solids and their bases be called by the same names. Since base **f.e.** is equal to base **c.d.**, it follows from Proposition 31 or 32 that solid **f.e.** is equal to solid **c.d.** But because the vertical surface rising above line **b.f.** cuts the whole solid **a.e.** parallel to two opposite sides, it follows from Proposition 25 that the proportion of solid **f.e.** to solid **a.b.** is as base **f.e.** is to base **a.b.** And since **c.d.** and **f.e.** are equal as both bases and solids—the bases by hypothesis, and the solids by Proposition 31 or 32—it follows from the 7th proposition of the Fifth Book (applied twice, once for the bases and once for the solids) that the solids **a.b.** and **c.d.** and the bases **a.b.** and **c.d.** have one and the same proportion. This is what we wished to demonstrate. Its converse can also be demonstrated by the same means...

from the following: from these it is established that solid <term>parallelepipeds</term> <note>Latin: *solida parallelogramma*; solids whose six faces are all parallelograms</note> are equal to double the <term>prisms</term> <note>Latin: *serratilia*, literally "saw-like" solids; in this context, triangular prisms</note> themselves. For according to Proposition 28, they are half of the solid parallelepipeds of their own height; and there is one proportion between the solid parallelepipeds of their height and their bases according to Proposition 33. Therefore, since the proportion of the solid parallelepipeds is the same as that of the prisms—because as the single is to the single, so the double is to the double, according to Proposition 15 of the Fifth Book—the proportion of the bases of the solid parallelepipeds is the same as the proportion of the bases of the prisms. For either the bases of the prisms and the solid parallelepipeds will be the same—and this indeed will be the case when the bases of the prisms are quadrilateral, for then the solid parallelepipeds are to be completed from the prisms upon those same bases—or the bases of the prisms will be half <note>Latin: *subduple*</note> of the bases of the solid parallelepipeds. And this indeed will be the case when the bases of the prisms are commonly triangular; for then the solid parallelepipeds are to be completed from the prisms by adding triangular surfaces to the bases of the prisms so that the bases of the prisms, with the triangular surfaces added, become surfaces of equidistant sides <note>parallelograms</note>. Consequently, the proportion of the prisms is as the proportion of their bases. In the same way, if the prisms are equal and are commonly upon triangular bases or commonly upon quadrilateral bases, their bases will be <term>reciprocal</term> <note>Latin: *mutue*; inversely proportional</note> to their heights. But if their bases are reciprocal to their heights, the prisms themselves will be equal, just as Propositions 34 and 35 propose regarding solid parallelepipeds; this is easily evident from what was said in Proposition 35. If, however, the prisms are similar to one another, the proportion of one to the other will be as the <term>triplicate proportion</term> <note>The ratio of the volumes is the cube of the ratio of the sides</note> of the proportion of one side to the corresponding side of the other, just as Proposition 36 proposes regarding solid parallelepipeds; this will be easily clear to you from that same Proposition 36. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of the Sixth Book, the ratio of diameter $a.c$ to diameter $d.f$ is as side $a.b$ to side $d.e$ in duplicate ratio <term>duplicate ratio: the ratio of the squares of the lengths</term>. Since, therefore, from the second part of the 18th proposition of the Sixth Book, the ratio of two pentagons is as the ratio of side $a.b$ to side $d.e$ in duplicate ratio, and by the same reasoning, the ratio of the square of diameter $a.c$ to the square of diameter $d.f$ is as the duplicate ratio of diameter $a.c$ to diameter $d.f$. By this common notion—that things whose halves are equal are equal to each other—it is manifest what was proposed.

->**Proposition .2.**<-

**O**f all two circles, the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of the square of its diameter to the square of the diameter of the other. ¶Let there be two circles, $a.b$ and $c.d$, whose diameters are also called $a.b$ and $c.d$. I say, therefore, that the ratio of circle $a.b$ to circle $c.d$ is as the square of diameter $a.b$ to the square of diameter $c.d$. For it is manifest from this common science <note>referring to a mathematical axiom or "common notion"</note> that whatever the magnitude of any first thing is to a second, so must be any third thing to a fourth. Because the ratio of the square of diameter $a.b$ to the square of diameter $c.d$ is as circle $a.b$ to some surface which we shall call $e$, of whatever figure or form it may be placed. However, it is impossible for this surface to be either greater or smaller than circle $c.d$. For if it were possible for it to be smaller than circle $c.d$, let it then be smaller by the amount of surface $f$. Thus, circle $c.d$ would be equal to the two surfaces $e$ and $f$ taken together. It is established, therefore, from the 1st proposition of the Tenth Book, that because more than half can be repeatedly subtracted from circle $c.d$ and its remainders until a quantity remains that is smaller than $f$, let there be inscribed in it (as the 6th proposition of the Fourth Book teaches) a square $c.d.g.h$. It is established that this square is greater than half of the circle; for the square which is double to it is the square circumscribed around the circle, as is evident from the penultimate proposition of the First Book and the 7th of the Fourth. If, therefore, the portions <note>the segments of the circle</note> of the circle existing above the sides of the square, taken together, were less than surface $f$, that would suffice. But if not, let the four arcs existing above the said sides be divided into equal parts, and let the points dividing those arcs be joined to the extremities of the sides by straight lines. For example, let arc $c.g$ be divided into equal parts at point $k$, and let lines $k.c$ and $k.g$ be drawn, and so for the others. Each of the triangles described upon the sides of the square will be greater than half of the circular segment in which it exists, because every isosceles triangle is half of the parallelogram of its base, by the 41st proposition of the First Book. Let it be, then, that the portions existing upon the sides of the inscribed octagon, taken together, are less than surface $f$. For if this were not yet the case, I would not cease dividing the arcs (the sides of which are the chords of the figures just described) into equal parts, and inscribing an equilateral figure with twice as many sides as the first, always subtracting from those portions of the circle more than half until, by the 1st proposition of the Tenth Book, the portions existing upon the sides of some such figure inscribed in the circle, taken together, are less than surface $f$. Let them be as now described; and by this conception, the octagon $c.d$ will be greater than surface $e$. Therefore, in circle $a.b$, by the same method, let a similar octagon be inscribed, which shall be called $a.b$. From the previous premise, the ratio of octagon $a.b$ to the octagon...

### Translation

**[Conclusion of Proposition 2]**

...[of the circle] **c. d.**, just as the squares of the diameters **a. b.** [are] to the square of the diameter **c. d.** Therefore, by the 11th [proposition] of the fifth [book], just as the proportion of the circle **a. b.** is to the surface **e.**, so also by permutation is the polygon **a. b.** to the circle **a. b.**, as the polygon **c. d.** is to the surface **e.** And if the polygon **c. d.** be greater than the surface **e.**, the polygon **a. b.** will be greater than the circle **a. b.** But this is indeed impossible; therefore, surface **e.** is [not] smaller than circle **c. d.** [Note: *text suggests "c" for "e" here due to OCR/printing*].

But neither is it greater. For let it be so, if it were possible: since, therefore, the proportion of the square of diameter **a. b.** to the square of diameter **c. d.** is as the circle **a. b.** to the surface **e.**, so conversely the square of diameter **c. d.** to the square of diameter **a. b.** will be as the surface **e.** to the circle **a. b.** And it stands from the Common Notion [*communi scientia*] placed at the beginning of this demonstration that it is the same [ratio] of circle **c. d.** to some surface which may be **f.** And by the 14th [proposition] of the fifth [book], surface **f.** will be smaller than circle **a. b.** And so the proportion of the square of diameter **c. d.** to the square of diameter **a. b.** will be as circle **c. d.** to surface **f.**, which is smaller than circle **a. b.** 

But from this we demonstrated a little before that an impossibility follows: namely, that a polygon inscribed in a circle would be greater than the circle. Therefore, just as surface **e.** cannot be smaller than circle **c. d.**, so neither can it be greater; therefore, it is necessarily equal. Wherefore, by the second part of the 2nd [proposition] of the fifth [book], that which was proposed is clear.

#### Proposition 3

Every pyramid whose base is a triangle can be divided into two equal pyramids similar to each other and to the whole pyramid, and into two *seratilia* [prisms], both of which taken together are necessarily greater than half of the whole pyramid. 

Let there be a pyramid **a. b. c. d.** upon a triangular base **b. c. d.**, and let its vertex be the solid angle **a.**, from which three edges [*hypothenuse*] **a. b.**, **a. c.**, and **a. d.** descend to the three angles of the base. And let all the sides of the base be divided equally at three points **e. f. g.**, and likewise the three edges [divided] equally at three points **h. k. l.** [OCR reads *b. k. l.*]. And let two lines **e. f.** and **e. g.** be drawn in the base. Its base will be divided into three surfaces, of which two are the two triangles **b. e. f.** and **e. g. d.**, which, from the second part of the [proposition] of the sixth [book] and the division of similar surfaces, it is established are similar to each other and to the whole base, and equal to each other. 

From the 8th [common notion] of the first [book], it is known to be a tetragon [quadrilateral]: the parallelogram itself **e. c. f. g.**, which it is established is double to the triangle **e. g. d.** [OCR reads *c. g. d.*] by the 40th and 41st of the first. Let there be dropped again from point **h.** [OCR reads *b.*] two edges **h. e.** and **h. f.**, and from point **k.** the edge **k. g.**, and let the lines **h. k.**, **k. l.**, and **l. h.** be drawn. 

The whole pyramid **a. b. c. d.** is thus divided into two pyramids, which are **h. b. e. f.** and **a. h. k. l.**, and two *seratilia* [prisms], of which one is **c. f. g. k. e.** [labels slightly unclear in OCR] and is upon the quadrangular base **e. f. g. c.**, and the other is **e. g. d. h. k. l.** and is upon the triangular base **e. g. d.** 

Regarding the two pyramids **h. b. e. f.** and **a. h. k. l.**, that they are equal to each other and similar to themselves and the whole pyramid **a. b. c. d.**, this is established from the division... [citations to Book VI and XI]. Regarding the two *seratilia* [prisms], that they are equal, this is established from the last [proposition] of the 11th book. That indeed both *seratilia* taken together are greater than half of the total pyramid is manifest from this: that each of them is divisible into two pyramids, of which one is triangular and equal to one of the two into which the *seratilia* of the whole pyramid are divided, and the other is quadrangular and is double the other. Wherefore, both *seratilia* taken together are three-quarters of the total divided pyramid. If you desire to know this proportion, consult the 6th [proposition] of this 12th book. But it suffices for you to know, as far as the [current] proposition is concerned, that those two *seratilia* taken together exceed [the pyramids] by whatever quantity.

#### Proposition 4

If two pyramids of equal height, whose bases are triangles, are each divided into two equal pyramids similar to each other and to the whole, and into two equal *seratilia* [prisms], the proportion of the base of one to the base of the other will be as the proportion of its two *seratilia* to the two *seratilia* of the other. And it will be clear [concerning] all the *seratilia* which were in either of them...

### Scholarly Notes & Abbreviations

1.  **Seratilia**: This is a medieval Latin term (from *serare*, to saw/cut) used in Euclidean translations to describe the two prisms formed when a tetrahedron is bisected according to Euclid's method. Modern translations usually call these "prisms."
2.  **Hypothenuse**: In this context, it does not mean the side opposite a right angle, but refers to the lateral edges or "slant heights" of the pyramid.
3.  **Cõi ſcia (*communi scientia*)**: Literally "common knowledge," this is the standard medieval translation for Euclid's **Common Notions** (Axioms).
4.  **iraqȝ (*itaque*)**: The "qȝ" is a standard abbreviation for the suffix "-que."
5.  **z (*et*)**: The Tironian note "et" (looking like a 'z' or '7') is used throughout for the word "and."
6.  **oſtat (*constat*)**: The OCR often renders the "c" and "n" in *constat* poorly; it translates to "it is established" or "it consists of."
7.  **Geometric Labels**: There are minor discrepancies between the text and the diagram (e.g., the letter **h** being read as **b** by the OCR), which is common in early modern printing where type could be blurred. I have corrected the most obvious ones in the translation for logical consistency.

Let there be subtracted from it two <term>prisms</term> <note>original: "serratilia," literally 'saw-like' bodies, the term used here for triangular prisms</note> which, from what was previously stated, are more than half of the pyramid itself. Likewise, from each of the two remaining partial pyramids, let two prisms be removed in the aforementioned manner. Let this be done repeatedly until, regarding pyramid B, the opponent is forced by the first proposition of Book 10 <note>This refers to Euclid’s "Method of Exhaustion," which allows one to prove the equality of shapes by showing the difference between them can be made smaller than any assigned value.</note> to admit that what remains is less than the solid D. From common knowledge, the subtracted prisms will together be greater than C.

Therefore, let a similar subtraction of prisms be made from pyramid A. Let us understand that as many prisms have been subtracted from pyramid A as we subtracted from pyramid B. It follows from the corollary of the previous premise that as base A is to base B, so are the prisms subtracted from pyramid A to the prisms subtracted from pyramid B. But pyramid A was to solid C [in that same ratio]; therefore, the prisms of pyramid A are to the prisms of pyramid B as pyramid A is to solid C. By <term>alternating</term> <note>permutatim: a logical step in proportions where the middle terms are swapped</note>, the prisms of pyramid A are to pyramid A as the prisms of pyramid B are to solid C. And since the prisms of pyramid B are greater than solid C, the prisms of pyramid A would be greater than pyramid A. Since this is impossible <note>A part cannot be greater than the whole.</note>, solid C will not be less than pyramid B.

Nor can it be greater; for if this were posed—since the ratio of base A to base B is as pyramid A is to solid C—then conversely, base B would be to base A as solid C is to pyramid A. By the same common knowledge, it would be as pyramid B is to some solid, let it be D. It follows from Proposition 14 of Book 5 that solid D would be less than pyramid A, because pyramid B is assumed to be less than solid C. It would therefore be that base B is to base A as pyramid B is to a solid less than pyramid A. However, it has been demonstrated that this leads to an impossibility—namely, that the prisms subtracted from a pyramid would be greater than the pyramid from which they are subtracted. Therefore, it remains that solid C is equal to pyramid B, since it can be neither less nor greater. Thus, the ratio of pyramid A to pyramid B is as base A to base B; and this was what was to be demonstrated.

->**Proposition 6**<-
**Every <term>prism</term> <note>serratille</note> is divisible into three equal pyramids having triangular bases.**

Let there be a prism **a.b.c.d.e.f.** I say that it is divisible into three equal triangular pyramids. For in each of its three parallelogram faces, let a diagonal line be drawn so that one of those diagonals is connected to the other two—as if you were to draw lines **b.d.**, **b.f.**, and **f.a.** (which I have refrained from drawing to avoid confusion). The whole prism will then be divided into three triangular pyramids, which are easily proven to be equal from the twice-assumed previous premise.

However, since Euclid proposes nothing to be demonstrated concerning pyramids with many sides <note>lateral pyramids</note> except those solids whose bases are triangles—so that we might sufficiently derive knowledge of all things from the elements he provides—we believe it is not useless to add certain things to the demonstrations placed here. For Euclid, content with the elements alone, omitted many things which, although they follow from them, are nevertheless not clearly evident to students without difficulty. The first of these is this:

**If there are two solids, one of which is a prism and the other a pyramid whose base is triangular, and they are established on the same base or on equal triangles (or if the prism is on a quadrilateral base and the pyramid on a triangle that is half of the prism's quadrilateral base) and they are of equal height, the prism must be triple the pyramid.**

If, however, the prism is on a quadrilateral base, then let a triangle be added to the base of the pyramid, from which (and the base of the pyramid) a surface of parallel sides <note>a parallelogram</note> is formed...

## ¶ Proposition 7.

**[S]** **If two pyramids with triangular bases are equal, their bases will be reciprocally proportional to their heights. If, however, the bases and heights are reciprocally proportional, it is necessary that those same pyramids be equal to each other.**

¶ What the thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth propositions of the eleventh book proposed concerning solid parallelepipeds <note>Solid figures with six faces, each of which is a parallelogram.</note>—and what we demonstrated in the 36th of the same regarding prisms <note>original: *serratilibus*, literally "saw-like" solids; a common medieval term for prisms.</note>—this seventh proposition of the 12th book proposes concerning pyramids having triangular bases. For let two equal pyramids be understood upon two triangles <note>original: *trigonos*</note> **a** and **b**, which are themselves called **a** and **b**. I say, therefore, that the ratio of base **a** to base **b** is as the ratio of the height of pyramid **b** to the height of pyramid **a**. And if this should be the case, I say that pyramids **a** and **b** are equal. Let two other triangles, **c** and **d**, be added to the two triangles **a** and **b**, so that both surfaces **ac** and **bd** become parallelograms <note>literally: surfaces of equidistant sides</note>. And from these pyramids, let solid parallelepipeds of equal height to the proposed pyramids be completed upon bases **a** and **c** and **b** and **d**, which may similarly be called **ac** and **bd**. It is therefore manifest from the sixth proposition of this 12th book that pyramid **a** is the sixth part of solid **ac**, and pyramid **b** is the sixth of solid **bd**. Thus, from the 35th of the eleventh book, argue the proposition: the first part from the first, and the second from the second.

¶ **But if any two pyramids with multiple sides <note>Polygonal pyramids</note> are equal, their bases will be reciprocally proportional to their heights. If, however, their bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights, it is necessary for those same pyramids to be equal.**

¶ If the bases of both are triangular, it has been demonstrated that what we said is true. If only one is: let it be **a**, and let the base of the other pyramid be **b**. Let a triangle **c** be taken equal to the polygon **b**, and let a pyramid be made upon **c** of equal height to the pyramid which is upon **b**. Let **a**, **b**, and **c** be the names used for both the pyramids and the bases <note>original: *equivoca nomina*; the author uses one letter to refer to both the 3D solid and its 2D base.</note>. Since, therefore, by hypothesis the two pyramids **a** and **b** are equal, and from the last proposition placed between the previous ones and the sixth of this book, the two pyramids **b** and **c** are equal, then by common knowledge <note>An axiom or "common notion" in Euclidean geometry.</note> the two pyramids **a** and **c** are equal. Therefore, their bases are reciprocal to their heights from the first part of this 7th proposition. And since bases **b** and **c** are equal, the heights of pyramids **b** and **c** will also be equal. From the first and second parts of the 7th of the fifth book, bases **a** and **b** are reciprocal to the heights of pyramids **a** and **b**. The second part is proved in reverse; for if the ratio of base **a** to base **b** is as the height of pyramid **b** to the height of pyramid **a**, it will be from the 2nd and 1st parts of the 7th of the fifth book that the ratio of base **a** to base **c** is as the height of pyramid **b** to the height of pyramid **a**. Thus, from the second part of this 7th proposition, the two pyramids **a** and **c** are equal, wherefore by common knowledge the two pyramids **a** and **b** are also equal. If, however, neither of the proposed pyramids is triangular but both are polygonal—for example, one pentagonal and the other hexagonal—which may still be called **a** and **b**: let a triangle **c** similarly be taken equal to the hexagon **b**, upon which let a pyramid be made of equal height to pyramid **b**. The two pyramids **b** and **c** will be equal, and therefore the two that are **a** and **c** are also equal by conception <note>axiom</note>. Wherefore base **a** is to base **c** as the height of pyramid **c** is to the height of pyramid **a**, for this was just demonstrated. Therefore, from the seventh of the fifth book, base **a** is to base **b** as the height of pyramid **b** is to the height of pyramid **a**. The converse is clear in a reverse manner: for if base **a** is to base **b** was as the height of pyramid **b** to the height of pyramid **a**...

### Proposition 8.

**Of any two similar pyramids whose bases are triangular, the ratio of one to the other is as the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.** <note>In historical geometry, a "triplicate ratio" refers to the ratio of the volumes, which is the cube of the ratio of the linear sides (e.g., if the sides are 1:2, the volumes are 1:8).</note>

When two similar pyramids having triangular bases are proposed, complete two <term>parallelepiped solids</term> <note>A three-dimensional figure where every face is a parallelogram.</note> from them, just as was described in the demonstration of the previous proposition. These two parallelepiped solids will be similar because the pyramids themselves are assumed to be similar to each other. For the two solid angles which are common to both the pyramids and the parallelepiped solids are contained by surface angles equal in number and in size. Furthermore, the sides containing those surface angles are proportional. 

Therefore, according to Proposition 34 of the first book, the three surfaces of the parallelepiped solids that form the common solid angles are equiangular and have proportional sides. Thus, they are similar by the definition of similar surfaces. Wherefore, from Propositions 24, 7, and 13 of the fifth book, all six surfaces of these two parallelepiped solids are similar to one another. Therefore, by the definition of similar bodies, the solids themselves will be similar. 

Because the ratio of these solids and the pyramids is the same according to Proposition 15 of the fifth book—for the solids are six times the size of the pyramids <note>A parallelepiped can be divided into six pyramids of equal volume.</note> according to the sixth proposition of this book—and since the ratio of the solids is as the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides according to Proposition 36 of the eleventh book, and since the sides of the solids are the same as the sides of the pyramids: it will also follow, from Proposition 11 of the fifth book, that the ratio of the proposed pyramids is as the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides. This is what was to be shown.

**BOOK [XII]**

And since the prisms are completed by taking all the pyramids together, it is established that this proposition of ours is true.

¶ If any two <term>prisms</term><note>original: "columne laterate," literally "sided columns." In this period, prisms were often described as columns with many sides.</note> are equal in volume, their bases will be inversely proportional to their heights. If, however, their bases and heights are inversely proportional, it is necessary that those prisms be equal.

¶ For if the prisms are equal, their <term>pyramids</term><note>A pyramid sharing the same base and height as the prism.</note> will be equal, because every prism is triple its pyramid. If the pyramids are equal, then their bases will be inversely proportional to their heights, just as was demonstrated in the seventh proposition of this book. Since, therefore, the bases and heights of the prisms and their pyramids are the same, the first part of the proposition is established. Let the bases and heights of the proposed prisms then be inversely proportional; I say that the prisms will be equal. Since the bases and heights are the same for both the prisms and their pyramids, the bases and heights of the pyramids of the proposed prisms will be inversely proportional. If this is true as proposed regarding the prisms, then the pyramids will be equal as demonstrated in the seventh proposition of this book; therefore, the prisms are also equal since they are triple their pyramids, which makes the second part of the proposition clear.

¶ For any two similar prisms, the ratio of one to the other is the <term>triplicate ratio</term><note>The triplicate ratio of two lengths is equivalent to the ratio of their cubes (e.g., if the sides are in a ratio of 2:1, the volumes are in a ratio of 8:1).</note> of the ratio of a side to its corresponding side.

¶ If the prisms are similar, then by the definition of similar solids, their bases and the other surfaces surrounding them will be similar. Therefore, let their bases be divided into similar triangles equal in number, just as the 18th proposition of the sixth book proposes to be possible; and let the prisms themselves be divided into <term>triangular prisms</term><note>original: "seratilia," literally "saw-cut pieces." These are the smaller triangular prisms created when the base of a larger prism is subdivided into triangles.</note> existing upon these triangles. Take care, therefore, to prove that the triangular prisms of one are similar to the corresponding triangular prisms of the other; which you will easily prove from the hypothesis and the sixth, fourth, and fifth propositions of the sixth book, and the definition of similar surfaces and similar solids. Having proven this, then from the 36th proposition of the eleventh book, the ratio of each triangular prism of one to its corresponding triangular prism of the other is as the triplicate ratio of its side to the side of the other. And because the ratio of all the sides is the same, since all the triangular prisms of one are similar to their corresponding parts in the other, it follows from the 11th proposition of the fifth book that there is one ratio for all the triangular prisms of one to their corresponding parts in the other. Therefore, by the 13th proposition of the fifth book, the ratio of one triangular prism to its corresponding prism is the same as the ratio of all of them taken together to all the others taken together. And because on both sides all the triangular prisms taken together compose the prisms, and the corresponding sides of the triangular prisms are the corresponding sides of the main prisms, it is necessary by the 11th proposition of the fifth book that the ratio of the prisms be as the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides, which is what was proposed.

XII

If a certain body is removed from cylinder A, its remainder will be triple the size of pyramid A. <note>original: "columna" (column) for cylinder and "piramis" (pyramid) for the conical shape. The author is demonstrating that a cylinder is three times the volume of a cone with the same base and height.</note> Therefore, let a square be inscribed within circle A, upon which two prisms <term>prisms: here referring to "seratilia," or three-dimensional shapes created by "sawing" a solid, effectively triangular prisms</term> are to be erected to the same height as cylinder A. Regarding these two prisms taken together, it is clear that they constitute more than half of cylinder A, just as the square itself is known to be more than half of circle A. <note>The area of a square inscribed in a circle is $2r^2$, while the circle is $\pi r^2$; since 2 is more than half of 3.14, the square covers more than half the circle.</note> For if, from these prisms, there were completed solid parallelepipeds <term>parallelepipeds: six-faced solid figures where every face is a parallelogram, like a box</term> of which the prisms are halves, cylinder A would be a part of those two solids taken together.

Next, upon the sides of the inscribed square, construct four triangles with two equal sides <note>original: "duum equalium laterum," meaning isosceles triangles</note> within the segments of the circle. The sides of the square serve as chords to these segments, and the arcs of those segments are divided equally. Let these triangles be C, D, E, and F. Upon these triangles, also erect prisms to the height of cylinder A. It is then manifest that these prisms are greater than half of the segments of the cylinder that stand upon the segments of the circle.
