### **BOOK XII (Continued)**

...the body .c. can be neither less nor greater than the round pyramid .b.; it will necessarily be equal to it. Therefore, from the second part of [Proposition] 7 of the fifth [book], the proposition is established. However, let it not escape us that the process of this demonstration is restricted only to those columns and round pyramids whose axes stand perpendicularly upon their bases: for such were defined at the beginning of the eleventh [book]. Nevertheless, the property demonstrated here commonly applies to all similar round columns and similar round pyramids, whether their axes were erected orthogonally upon their bases or were inclined upon them. Let those round columns and pyramids whose axes stand orthogonally upon their bases be called "erect" for the sake of distinction; let the others indeed be called "inclined." And because in the beginning of the 11th, round columns or pyramids are not defined except only those which we call erect—the former indeed by the motion of a rectangle parallelogram, the latter truly by the motion of a right-angled triangle—we therefore judge it appropriate to define round columns and pyramids by definitions that apply commonly and univocally to both erect and inclined round columns and pyramids. 

Therefore, when a point is marked outside the surface of some described circle, which is joined to the circumference of that circle by a straight line, if that line—the marked point remaining fixed—is rotated around the described circle until it returns to the place from which it began to move: the body which is contained by the curved surface which this line describes by its motion and by the circle itself around which it is rotated, I call a **round pyramid** [cone]. And the circle around which this line is rotated, I call the **base** of that pyramid. Moreover, the fixed point marked outside the surface of the circle, I call the **cone** [apex] of the pyramid; and the straight line joining the center of the base with the cone of the pyramid, I call the **axis** or the **sagitta** [arrow] of the pyramid. And when this sagitta is perpendicular to the base, I say the pyramid is **erect**; when indeed it is inclined, I also call the pyramid **inclined**. 

Furthermore, when two equal circles are described in parallel surfaces, which a single plane surface passing through their centers intersects, and two relative sections of the two circumferences of those circles are joined by a straight line: if this line is rotated in the circumferences of those circles, remaining parallel to the position from which it began to move until it returns to its original place: the body which is contained by the curved surface which this line describes by its motion and by the two proposed circles, I call a **round column** [cylinder]. Its axis or sagitta is the straight line joining the centers of the two circles. And when this sagitta is perpendicular to the surface of each of the two circles, I say the column is **erect**. When indeed it is inclined upon the base, I call the column **inclined**. 

And when there are two round pyramids or columns from whose axes two surfaces emerge orthogonally erected upon their bases, and the angles which the axes and the common sections of these surfaces and the bases contain are equal to one another; and the proportion of the axis of one to the axis of the other is as the semi-diameter of the base of one to the semi-diameter of the base of the other: then I say those two pyramids to one another, or those two columns to one another, are **similar**. These definitions having been set forth, it must be demonstrated that of any two similar round pyramids or similar round columns, whether they be erect or inclined, the proportion of one to the other is as the triplicate proportion [the cube] of the diameter of the base of one to the diameter of the base of the other, which was demonstrated for the erect ones alone; however, for this purpose, we premise a necessary antecedent.

**If there are two round pyramids similar to one another, each of which two plane surfaces intersect through the axis, and if one of these two surfaces in each pyramid is orthogonally erected upon its base and the arcs of the bases contained between those two surfaces are similar: the angles which the axes and the two common sections of the bases and those surfaces (which are not placed orthogonally upon the bases) contain will be equal to one another.**

Let there be two round pyramids .a.b. and .c.d. whose bases are circles .e.f.g. and .h.k.l. and the axes are the two lines .a.b. and .c.d. and the diameters of the bases .e.g. and .h.l.; the centers of the bases are the two points .b. and .d.; the cones of the pyramids .a. and .c. are similar to each other. From their cones to the surface of the bases let two perpendiculars be drawn, as the 11th [book] teaches, which are .a.m. and .c.n. Let points .m. and .n. be joined with the centers of the bases by drawing lines .b.m. and .d.n. From the 18th [proposition] of the eleventh [book], surface .a.b.m., which emerges from axis .a.b., will be orthogonally erect upon the base of pyramid .a.b. In the same way, surface .c.d.n., which emerges from axis .c.d., will be orthogonally erect upon the base of pyramid .c.d. Therefore, let the two arcs .f.g. and .k.l. be similar; and let two surfaces .a.b.f. and .c.d.k. be understood to emerge from the axes and intersect the similar pyramids .a.b. and .c.d. I say, therefore, that the two angles .a.b.f. and .c.d.k. are equal to each other. 

For let two lines .f.m. and .k.n. be drawn. Therefore, since the two pyramids .a.b. and .c.d. are similar, and the two surfaces .a.b.m. and .c.d.n. standing orthogonally upon the bases emerge from their axes: by the definition of similar pyramids, angle .a.b.m. will be equal to angle .c.d.n. And because, by the definition of a line erected perpendicularly upon a surface, each of the two angles .a.m.b. and .c.n.d. is a right angle, from the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], the two first triangles .a.b.m. and .c.d.n. will have proportional sides, such that the proportion of line .a.b. to line .c.d. is as .b.m. to .d.n. and as .a.m. to .c.n. And because, from the definition of similar pyramids, the proportion of axis .a.b. to axis .c.d. is as semi-diameter .b.f. to semi-diameter .d.k., it will be from the 11th of the fifth: the proportion of .b.f. to .d.k. as .b.m. to .d.n. And since the two angles .f.b.m. and .k.d.n. are equal because the two arcs .f.g. and .k.l. are similar by hypothesis: from the sixth and fourth of the sixth, the proportion of .f.m. to .k.n. will be as .b.m. to .d.n.; and therefore as .a.m. to .c.n. And because again, from the definition of a line erected perpendicularly upon a surface, each of the two angles .a.m.f. and .c.n.k. is a right angle: from the sixth and fourth of the sixth, the proportion of .a.f. to .c.k. will be as .a.m. to .c.n., and therefore by the 11th of the fifth as .a.b. to .c.d. and as .b.f. to .d.k. Therefore, from the fifth of the sixth, the two angles .a.b.f. and .c.d.k. are equal to each other, which is what was proposed.

You will easily prove the same concerning similar round columns. This having been demonstrated, I say that of all two similar round pyramids, whatever they may be, whether erect or inclined, the proportion of one of them to the other is as the triplicate proportion [the cube] of the diameter of its base to the diameter of the other base. For let there be, as before, two round pyramids .a. and .b. whose bases are circles .a. and .b., and let the diameters of these circles also be .a. and .b. Let the proportion of pyramid .a. to body .c. be as the triplicate proportion of diameter .a. to diameter .b. Therefore, body .c. will be neither less nor greater than round pyramid .b. 

For let it first be possible that it is less by the quantity of body .d., so that the two bodies .c. and .d. taken together are equal to round pyramid .b. From the axis of pyramid .b., therefore, let a surface proceed which is orthogonally erect upon circle .b. Let the common section of this surface and circle .b. be line .e.f. passing through center .b., which will be the diameter of circle .b. And let another diameter be drawn in circle .b. intersecting this one orthogonally, which shall be .g.h. Thus, let square .e.g.f.h. be inscribed in circle .b., and in round pyramid .b. let there be understood a side-faced [polygonal] pyramid whose base is the square inscribed in circle .b.; which, as was proved above, will be greater than half of the round pyramid. And from its remainder let there be subtracted pyramids of the same height standing upon the triangles of the portions of circle .b.; and let this be done so many times until the remainder of the round pyramid .b. is less than body .d., according to the first [proposition] of the tenth [book]. And from the conception, the subtracted side-faced pyramid, which the partial subtracted side-faced pyramids compose, will be greater than body .c. 

Then, therefore, let another surface proceed from the axis of pyramid .a. which is orthogonally erect upon circle .a.; and let the common section of this surface and circle .a. be line .k.l., which for this reason will be the diameter of circle .a. Moreover, let another diameter be drawn in circle .a. intersecting this one orthogonally, which shall be .m.n. Thus, let square .k.m.l.n. be inscribed in circle .a.; and by dividing the arcs of the portions of circle .a. equally, let there be completed in circle .a. a polygon similar to that which is inscribed in circle .b. And to each angle of this polygon let straight lines be dropped from the cone of pyramid .a., completing upon that polygon a side-faced pyramid equal in height to pyramid .a. 

Moreover, you will prove this side-faced pyramid to be similar to the side-faced pyramid subtracted from round pyramid .b., which you will do in this manner: you will extend the axes in thought or in act in each of the pyramids .a. and .b., and from the centers of the bases you will draw straight lines to all the angles of the inscribed polygons. And from the pre-stated antecedent, all the angles which the axis of pyramid .a. contains with each of the lines drawn from the center of circle .a. to the angles of the polygon inscribed in it will be equal to their relative angles which the axis of pyramid .b. contains with each of the lines drawn from the center of circle .b. to the angles of the polygon inscribed in it. And because, from the definition of similar round pyramids, the proportion of the axis of pyramid .a. to the axis of pyramid .b. is as the semi-diameter of circle .a. to the semi-diameter of circle .b., it follows from the sixth and fourth of the sixth and the definitions of similar surfaces and similar bodies that the two side-faced pyramids .a. and .b. are similar. Proceed with the argument as before in the tenth. It is established, therefore, for all similar round pyramids that their proportion is as the triplicate proportion of the diameters of their bases. And because every round column is triple its pyramid—for this is sufficiently demonstrated whether the columns and pyramids be erect or inclined—it follows from the 15th of the fifth that also of any similar round columns the proportion is as the triplicate of their diameters.

### **Proposition 11**

**It is necessary that all two round pyramids or columns of equal height be proportional to their bases.**

Upon two circles .a. and .b., let there be placed, as before, two round pyramids of equal height, which are similarly called .a. and .b., and two round columns of equal height assigned the same letters .a. and .b. I say, therefore, that the proportion of the two pyramids .a. and .b. and the two columns .a. and .b. is as the two circles .a. and .b. This will be manifest regarding the columns if it is first demonstrated regarding the pyramids, for every round column is triple its pyramid. 

Regarding the pyramids, however, it will be established by indirect demonstration in this manner. For, from common knowledge, the proportion of round pyramid .a. to some body is as circle .a. to circle .b. Let that body be .c. I say, therefore, that body .c. can be neither greater nor less than round pyramid .b. For let it first be less by the quantity of body .d. Therefore, let a square be inscribed in circle .b. and let there be subtracted from round pyramid .b. a side-faced pyramid whose base is the square inscribed in circle .b., and from the portions of the pyramids let there be subtracted pyramids standing upon the triangles of the portions of the circle; and let this be done so many times until the remainder from pyramid .b. is less than body .d. The subtracted side-faced pyramid, which the partial subtracted pyramids compose, will be greater than body .c. 

Therefore, let there be inscribed in circle .a. a polygon similar to that polygon which is the base of the side-faced pyramid .b., and let a side-faced pyramid be completed upon it by lines drawn from the vertex of side-faced pyramid .a. to the angles of the inscribed polygon. And the two side-faced pyramids .a. and .b. will be of equal height. For this is proposed concerning the round ones; wherefore the proportion of side-faced pyramid .a. to side-faced pyramid .b. is as its base to the other's base, namely as polygon .a. to polygon .b. For this was demonstrated in the sixth [proposition] of this [book]. 

But truly, polygon .a. to polygon .b. is as circle .a. to circle .b., which is manifest from the first and second of this [book]. Thus, side-faced pyramid .a. to side-faced pyramid .b. is as round pyramid .a. to body .c. Wherefore, by permutation, side-faced pyramid .a. to round pyramid .a. is as side-faced pyramid .b. to body .c. And since side-faced pyramid .b. is greater than body .c., it follows that side-faced pyramid .a. is greater than round pyramid .a. But this is impossible, for it is a part of it. Therefore, body .c. will not be less than round pyramid .b. 

If, however, an adversary should posit that it is greater, we shall demonstrate the same impossibility to follow. For by inverse proportionality, the proportion of body .c. to round pyramid .a. will be as circle .b. to circle .a. Let there also be the same [proportion] of round pyramid .b. to some body which is .d. Since, therefore, body .c. is greater than round pyramid .b. by hypothesis, from the 14th of the fifth, round pyramid .a. will be greater than body .d. Thus, the proportion of circle .b. to circle .a. will be as round pyramid .b. to a certain body less than round pyramid .a. But this was previously demonstrated to be impossible, for it thus follows that a part would be greater than its whole. Therefore, body .c. is neither less nor greater than round pyramid .b., but only equal. Thus, from the second part of the seventh of the fifth, conclude the proposition. But so that what follows might be demonstrated more easily and firmly, a useful antecedent is to be premised, which is:

**If a certain surface intersects a round column parallel to its base, the two partial bodies which are terminated at that intersecting surface will be proportional to the portions of the axis of the column.**

This is similar to what was proposed in the 25th [proposition] of the eleventh book concerning solid parallelograms. And this is true not only of round columns, but simply of all columns, whether they be side-faced or round. He who firmly holds the argumentation of the first of the sixth or the 25th of the eleventh will be able to demonstrate this easily; for here, no differently than there, the proposition must be argued from the definition of continuous proportionality which was placed in the proem of the fifth book. 

One ought to observe, however, that whatever surface intersects a column parallel to its base also intersects it parallel to the surface of its opposite base. For whatever surfaces are parallel to one surface are also parallel to each other, as you have learned from what was said in the sixteenth [proposition] of the eleventh book. Wherefore it is manifest that all round columns whose bases are equal are proportional to their heights. The same also for side-faced ones; the same also for round pyramids, and even for side-faced ones, which will be established for pyramids if it is first proved for columns. For every column is triple its pyramid: the round one indeed from the ninth [proposition] of this [book], the side-faced one truly from those things which were demonstrated above in the eighth.

### **Proposition 12**

**If two round pyramids or columns are equal, their bases and heights will be reciprocal. If indeed their bases and heights are reciprocal, it is necessary that the pyramids or columns themselves be equal.**

The lines descending perpendicularly from the cones to the bases determine the height of the pyramids; however, those of the columns [descend] from their topmost surfaces to the bases. Therefore, let there be two equal round pyramids .a.b. and .c.d. and likewise two equal round columns .a.b. and .c.d. And let the common bases of both the pyramids and the columns be two circles .a. and .c. Let the common heights of both the pyramids and the columns also be determined by the lines .a.b. and .c.d. I say that the proportion of circle .c. to circle .a. is as height .a.b. to height .c.d. and vice versa. 

If this is proved for columns, it will be certain for pyramids, since every round column is triple its pyramid. If, therefore, the two heights .a.b. and .c.d. are equal, the proposition is established from the premised [proposition]. If, however, they are unequal, let .a.b. be greater and let .a.e. be taken equal to .c.d. And let column .a.b. be intersected by surface .e. parallel to its base .a. And from the premised antecedent, column .a.b. will be to column .a.e. as height .a.b. to height .a.e. And therefore, from the nearest part of [Proposition] 7 of the fifth, column .c.d. is to column .a.e. as height .a.b. to height .a.e. Wherefore, by the second part of [Proposition] 7 of the fifth, as height .a.b. to height .c.d. Moreover, from the premised [proposition], column .c.d. is to column .a.e. as circle .c. to circle .a. Thus, by the 11th of the fifth, height .a.b. is to height .c.d. as base .c. to base .a. Therefore the first part is established.

The second [part] will be established in the inverse way, the same disposition remaining. For let base .c. be to base .a. as height .a.b. to height .c.d. I say that the two columns .a.b. and .c.d. are equal. For, from the second part of [Proposition] 7 of the fifth, height .a.b. will be to height .a.e. as base .c. to base .a. And because, from the premised [proposition], column .c.d. to column .a.e. is as base .c. to base .a., and from the premised antecedent, column .a.b. to column .a.e. is as height .a.b. to height .a.e., it follows from the 11th of the fifth that column .c.d. to column .a.e. is as column .a.b. to the same .a.e. Therefore, from the first part of [Proposition] 9 of the fifth, the two columns .a.b. and .c.d. are equal. Wherefore the second part is also established.

### **Proposition 13**

**When two circles described from one center are proposed, to describe within the larger circle a multi-angled [polygonal] equilateral surface not touching the smaller circle.**

Let there be two circles .a.b.c.d. and .e.f. described from one common center, which is .g. I say that within the larger one, which is .a.b.c.d., it is possible for one polygon which is equilateral to be described, touching the smaller circle .e.f. with none of its sides. 

For let these two circles be divided into quadrants by two diameters intersecting each other orthogonally upon their center, which shall be .a.c. and .b.d. And let .e.f. be the diameter of the smaller, part of the diameter .a.c. which is of the larger diameter. And thus, therefore, from point .e. let a line be drawn on both sides to the circumference of the larger, orthogonally upon the diameter .e.f., which shall meet the circumference of the larger on this side indeed at point .b. and on that side at point .k. From the corollary of [Proposition] 15 of the third [book], line .h.e.k. [OCR: labels mismatch diagram letters] will be tangent to the smaller circle. 

Afterward, truly, divide the quadrant .a.b. of the larger circle into equal parts at point .l. according to the teaching of [Proposition] 29 of the third; then again, arc .a.l. equally at point .m. And since you do this several times, you will necessarily at last arrive at an arc which will be less than arc .a.b. [sic - likely means arc .a.k.]. Let this be .a.m. 

This is necessary because when there are two unequal quantities, if from the larger of them its half is taken, and again from the remainder its half, it is possible for this to be done so many times until at last a quantity less than the smaller of them is left, as was demonstrated in the first of the tenth. Since, therefore, by so dividing, one has arrived at an arc, however small, less than .a.b., such as is this arc .a.m.: let arc .a.n. be taken equal to arc .a.m., and let two lines .a.m. and .n.m. be drawn. 

Because, therefore, arc .a.k. is equal to arc .a.b.—which is manifest from the second part of the third of the third and the fourth of the first and the 28th of the third—and because arc .a.n. is equal to arc .a.m., it will be from common knowledge that arc .n.k. is equal to arc .m.b. Therefore, the two lines .m.n. and .k.b. are parallel. Therefore, line .m.n. cannot touch circle .e.f.; wherefore, much more strongly, neither can line .a.m. touch it. 

Since, therefore, it is established that circle .a.b.c.d. is divisible by arcs equal to arc .a.m., and therefore by the 28th of the third it is similarly established that within the circle itself equal chords to chord .a.m. can be continuously fitted, chording the circle itself polygonally: it is manifest that within the larger circle one equilateral polygon can be inscribed, one side of which is line .a.m. And because line .a.m. does not touch the smaller circle, it follows from the first part of the 13th of the third and the definition of lines equally distant from the center of a circle that the inscribed polygon touches the smaller circle with none of its sides, which is what was proposed. 

But why do you doubt that the two lines .m.n. and .k.b. are equidistant [parallel] when the two arcs .n.k. and .m.b. are equal? For this has obtained the unshakable truth: that two lines in one circle, not however intersecting each other—if from the circumference equal arcs are contained between the lines themselves—will be parallel. Draw indeed from center .g. line .g.p. perpendicular to line .m.n., which shall intersect line .b.k. at point .q., and extend lines .g.m., .g.n., .g.k., .g.b. And by the two arcs .n.k. and .m.b., subtend two chords which are also called .n.k. and .m.b. From the 28th of the third, these chords .n.k. and .m.b. will be equal because the arcs are equal. 

And by the second part of the third of the same third, line .n.p. will be equal to line .m.p. Since, therefore, each of the two angles which are .a.d.p. [sic] is a right angle by the definition of a perpendicular, from the fourth of the first, angle .n.p.g. will be equal to angle .p.g.m. But truly, by the eighth of the first, angle .k.g.n. is equal to angle .b.g.m. Thus, by the common science which is "if you add equals to equals, the wholes will be equal," angle .k.g.q. will be equal to angle .q.g.b. Therefore, by the fourth of the first, line .k.q. will be equal to line .q.b. Wherefore, by the first part of the third of the third, line .g.q. will be perpendicular to line .k.b. 

Therefore, from the first part of the 28th of the first, the two lines .n.m. and .k.b. are parallel, and this is what you were inclined to doubt. For it is possible to demonstrate this same thing otherwise: for let line .n.b. be drawn, and from the last [proposition] of the sixth, angle .b.m.n. will be equal to angle .n.b.k. because arc .b.m. is equal to arc .n.k. Therefore, from the 27th of the first, line .m.n. will be parallel to line .b.k. You will also prove the converse, if you please, in the inverse way. For if line .m.n. is parallel to line .b.k., arc .n.k. will be equal to arc .m.b. For from the first part of the 29th of the first, the two angles .b.m.n. and .n.b.k. will be equal; and therefore, from the last of the sixth, the two arcs .n.k. and .m.b. will also be equal.

### **Proposition 14**

**Given two spheres having one center, to figuratively constitute within the larger of them a solid of many bases [a polyhedron] not touching the surface of the smaller sphere. This being constituted, if in the smaller sphere or in any other sphere a similar body is intelligibly constituted, the proportion of the body of many bases constituted within the larger sphere to the body of many bases constituted within the smaller or another sphere will be as the triplicate proportion [the cube] of the diameter of the larger sphere to the diameter of the smaller or the other sphere.**

Let there be proposed two spheres .a.b.c.d. and .e.f. having one and the same center, which is .g. Let the larger of them be sphere .a.b.c.d. and the smaller truly sphere .e.f. We wish to constitute within the larger of them one body of many bases; concerning which we do not intend that the bases themselves be equal or similar, but that none of them should touch the surface of the smaller sphere. 

When, therefore, we wish to do this, we shall cut both proposed spheres together by one plane surface passing through their common center. From the definition of a sphere and the definition of a circle, the common sections of this intersecting surface and the surfaces of the proposed spheres will be lines containing circles. Therefore, let there be two circles .a.b.c.d. and .e.f. whose center is the center of the sphere, which center is .g. We shall therefore divide these two circles into quadrants by two diameters intersecting each other orthogonally upon the common center, which shall be .a.c. and .d.b. 

Afterward, in the larger circle, following the precept of the premised [proposition], we shall inscribe a polygon whose sides touch the smaller circle not at all. And let it suffice for the sake of example to have inscribed an equilateral dodecagon, so that in its quadrant of the larger circle, which is .c.d., there are three sides of this dodecagon, which are chords .d.h., .h.k., and .k.c. Since these are equal, by the first part of the 27th of the third, their arcs will also be equal. 

Then, from the two points .h. and .k., which are the extremities of the middle chord, we shall produce two diameters which are .h.m. and .k.l. And upon the center .g., we shall erect line .g.n. perpendicular to the surface of circle .a.b.c.d., which we shall produce until it meets the surface of the larger sphere at point .n. 

Then let us understand four surfaces intersecting the proposed spheres, each of which intersects them upon line .g.n. But let the first of them be upon line .g.n. and diameter .d.b.; the second upon line .g.n. and diameter .h.m.; the third truly upon line .g.n. and diameter .k.l.; the fourth however upon line .g.n. and diameter .c.a. From the definitions of a sphere and a circle, the common sections of these surfaces and the surface of the larger sphere will be lines containing circles. And the inscribed portions will be between point .n. and the four points which are .d., .h., .k., .c., quadrants of these circles, which quadrants are .d.n., .h.n., .k.n., and .c.n. 

This happens because all the angles which line .g.n. contains with each of the diameters drawn in the surface of circle .a.b.c.d. are right angles, by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface; right angles indeed in the center subtend a quarter of the circumference, which appears evidently from the last [proposition] of the sixth. 

Moreover, from the definition of equal circles, it is manifest that each of these four circles is equal to circle .a.b.c.d. For the diameter of all of them is the diameter of the larger sphere. Therefore, by [Proposition] 15 of the fifth, their quadrants are equal; wherefore the five arcs which are .d.n., .h.n., .k.n., .c.n., and .d.c. are equal. 

In each, therefore, of the four quadrants of the erected circles, let there be fitted hypotenusal chords, any of which is equal to the chord of the prostrate circle which are sides of the polygon inscribed in it; and one of these is chord .d.h. And let them be in the first indeed .d.q., .q.r., .r.n.; in the second truly .h.s., .s.t., .t.n.; in the third however .k.u., .u.x., .x.n.; and in the fourth let them be .c.o., .o.p., and .p.n. 

And let the **corausta** [connecting lines] joining the ends of the hypotenusal chords be drawn, which are .q.s., .s.u., .u.o., .r.t., .t.x., .x.p. You see, therefore, that in the fourth part of the upper hemisphere of the larger sphere—which fourth part is indeed .d.n.c.—a body of 9 bases is inscribed, of which three that meet at point .n. are triangular; the others however are quadrangular. And the hypotenusal sides of these quadrangular surfaces are equal, but not parallel. The **corausti** [connecting lines] intercepted between any two circles are parallel to each other and to the chords of the prostrate circle, but they are not equal to each other. This you will know if you drop perpendiculars from the extremities of the corausti to the surface of the lying circle. From which it is clear that they fall upon the diameters of the circles which the corausti connect, which you will easily perceive from those things demonstrated in [Proposition] 13 of the eleventh. 

For example: let two perpendiculars .q.y. and .s.z. be dropped from the two terms of the coraustus .q.s., falling on diameters .d.b. and .h.m.; and let lines .q.g. and .y.z. be drawn. From the fourth of the sixth, the two triangles .q.y.d. and .s.z.h. [OCR: labels unclear] will be similar; wherefore the proportion of the two perpendiculars .q.y. and .s.z. will be as that of the two chords .q.d. and .s.h. Since the chords are equal, the perpendiculars will also be equal. But they are parallel from the sixth of the eleventh. Therefore, from the 33rd of the first, coraustus .q.s. is equal and parallel to line .y.z. And because from the second part of the second of the sixth, line .y.z. is parallel to chord .d.h., and therefore smaller than it [OCR: garbled "e. a."], it follows from the 9th of the eleventh that coraustus .q.s. is also parallel to chord .d.h. and smaller than it from the conception. 

Since, therefore, the chords which are sides of the inscribed polygon in the lying circle are all equal to chord .d.h. and do not touch the smaller sphere: it is necessary that no side of these bases of the inscribed body—whether they be quadrangular or triangular—touches the same smaller sphere, since all these sides are equal to or smaller than those chords. Simply, however, I say that no one of these bases can touch the smaller sphere at any of its points, because every straight line drawn over any point of any of them parallel to the coraustus is necessarily smaller than the chord of the prostrate circle. 

If, therefore, the convexities of the other quadrants of the larger sphere—both of the upper hemisphere and the lower—are covered in its likeness with quadrangular and triangular surfaces: there will be inscribed in the larger sphere a body of 72 bases [a polyhedron] touching the surface of the smaller sphere not at all, as was proposed to be inscribed. 

I say, moreover, that if in any other sphere a similar body is placed, the proportion of one to the other will be as the triplicate proportion [the cube] of the diameter of one sphere to the diameter of the other. For there will be from the 72 bases of each body as many side-faced pyramids whose vertices will be in the centers of those spheres. You will complete these pyramids if you draw lines from each angle of the inscribed bodies—which are the extremities of the corausti—and the corausti themselves to the centers of the spheres. Study, therefore, to prove from the definition of similar bodies that all the pyramids of one are similar to their relative pyramids of the other. This being proved, from the 8th of this [book], the proportion of each one of them of one to its relative of the other will be as the triplicate proportion of the semi-diameters of the spheres themselves. For the semi-diameters of the spheres are the sides of all the pyramids. And because semi-diameters and diameters have one proportion from the 15th of the fifth, from the 13th of the same, you will easily conclude the proposition.

### **Proposition 15**

**Of all two spheres, the proportion of one to the other is as the triplicate proportion [the cube] of its diameter to the diameter of the other.**

Let there be two spheres .a.b. and .c.d. whose diameters are .a.b. and .c.d. I say that their proportion is as the triplicate proportion of their diameters. The demonstration of this is that the proportion of sphere .a.b. is neither to a smaller sphere than sphere .c.d., nor to a larger one, as the triplicate proportion of diameter .a.b. to diameter .c.d. 

Indeed, let the proportion of sphere .a.b. to sphere .e.f. be as the triplicate proportion of diameter .a.b. of sphere .a.b. to diameter .c.d. I shall demonstrate, therefore, that sphere .e.f. cannot be smaller nor larger than sphere .c.d. 

For if an adversary asserts it to be smaller, I shall imagine it to be included by sphere .c.d. and circumscribed from the same center; and I shall inscribe in sphere .a.b. that which is also called .a.b. by the name of its sphere. It is clear, therefore, from the second part of the premised [proposition] and the 11th of the fifth, that the proportion of sphere .a.b. to sphere .e.f. is as the body of many bases which is .a.b. to the body of many bases which is .c.d. [sic - likely means an inscribed body in sphere .c.d.]. For each is as the triplicate proportion of diameter .a.b. to diameter .c.d.; the former indeed from the hypothesis, the latter truly from the second part of the premised [proposition]. 

Wherefore, by permutation, the proportion of sphere .a.b. to the body of many bases .a.b. is as sphere .e.f. to the body of many bases .c.d. Since sphere .a.b. is larger than the body of many bases .a.b., sphere .e.f. will also be larger than the body of many bases .c.d. But this is impossible, for it is a part of it. Therefore sphere .e.f. is not smaller than sphere .c.d. 

If, however, the adversary should say it is larger, we shall refute him in this way: for by inverse proportionality, sphere .e.f. to sphere .a.b. will be as the triplicate proportion of diameter .c.d. to diameter .a.b. Let the same [proportion] be that of sphere .c.d. to sphere .g.b. And from the 14th of the fifth, sphere .g.b. will be smaller than sphere .a.b. because sphere .c.d. is posited as smaller than sphere .e.f. Wherefore the proportion of sphere .c.d. to some sphere smaller than sphere .a.b. is as the triplicate proportion of diameter .c.d. to diameter .a.b. But this is impossible, for from this it follows that a part is larger than its whole, as was demonstrated before. 

Thus sphere .e.f. is neither larger nor smaller than sphere .c.d. Therefore, from the 7th of the fifth, conclude the proposed conclusion, which puts an end to the twelfth book.

**The Twelfth Book Ends. The Thirteenth Book Begins.**

### **Proposition 1**

**When a line has been divided according to the proportion having a medium and two extremes [the Golden Ratio]: if a line equal to half of the proportionally divided line itself is added in length to the larger segment, it is necessary that the square of the line composed of those two be fivefold the square of the half of the same divided line.**

Let line .a.b. be divided at point .c. as [Proposition] 29 of the sixth teaches. And let its larger portion be line .b.c., to which .b.c. let line .b.d. be directly joined, which shall be equal to half of the whole .a.b. I say that the square of line .c.d. will be fivefold the square of line .b.d. 

For I shall square line .b.d., and let its square be .d.e.; and I shall place around this square a gnomon according to the quantity of line .b.c., with diameter .f.b.g. extended. And let the circumposed gnomon be .e.g.d. [labels in OCR/diagram may vary]. The surface composed therefrom, which is .b.k., will be as the square of line .c.d. 

I say, therefore, that the square .b.k. is fivefold the square .d.e. Let .e.l. be the square of the circumposed gnomon itself, to which let another gnomon be circumposed to the quantity of line .a.c., with diameter .f.b. extended to .m. Let this gnomon be .c.m.l. And let lines .c.n. and .p.l. be drawn parallel to the opposite sides, intersecting each other upon the diameter .f.m. at point .g. 

Moreover, it is manifest from the 22nd of the sixth that the [figure] composed of this second gnomon and the square .c.l.—and let the square itself be .a.q.—is the square of line .a.b., which from the fourth of the second must be fourfold the square .d.e. because line .b.d. is half of line .a.b. 

And since from the first part of the 16th of the sixth, surface .a.n.—and therefore by [Proposition] 43 of the first, surface .m.l.—is equal to square .c.l. (for .a.n. and therefore .m.l. comes from .b.a. times .a.c., and .c.l. comes from .c.b. times itself); and since from the first of the sixth .a.l. is double .l.d., and therefore equal to .l.d. and .c.e. taken together: it will be from this common knowledge (if you add equals to equals, the wholes become equal) that the square .a.q. is equal to the gnomon .e.g.d. 

Therefore, this gnomon is fourfold the square .d.e., just as the square .a.q. was. Thus the whole square .b.k., since it consists of a single and a fourfold [part], will be fivefold the same by common knowledge, which is what was proposed. 

The same is established otherwise from the fourth of the second: that the square of line .c.b. is fourfold the square of line .b.d. But by the second of the same, that which is formed from .a.b. into .b.c. and .a.c. is equal to the square of .a.b. But that which is formed from .a.b. into .b.c. is equal to that which is formed from .b.d. twice into .b.c., which is manifest from the first of the second, since .a.b. is double .b.d. But truly, that which is from .a.b. into .a.c. is, from the first part of the 16th of the sixth, equal to the square of .b.c. Thus, by common knowledge, that which is formed from .b.d. twice into .b.c. and from .b.c. into itself is equal to the square of .a.b., and therefore is fourfold the square .b.d. Wherefore, with the square of .b.d. added on, the whole aggregate will be fivefold, namely that which is formed from .b.d. twice into .b.c. with the square of .b.c. and the square of .b.d. And because from the fourth of the second this whole is equal to the square of .c.d., it is established that what we said is true.

### **Proposition 2**

**If to any bipartite line whose square is fivefold the square of either of its portions, a line is added in length until for that same portion the remaining proportion with the added [line] becomes double: that same double line will be divided according to the proportion having a medium and two extremes, and its larger portion will be the middle line.**

This is the converse of the premised [proposition]. It will also be demonstrated in a twofold way, just as that one was, by a retrograde path, the disposition remaining entirely the same. 

For example: let square .b.k. be fivefold the square .d.e., and line .a.b. double line .b.d. I say that line .a.b. is divided at point .c. according to the proportion having a medium and two extremes, and its larger portion is the middle line, as .b.c. 

It is established from the 4th of the second that square .a.q. is fourfold the square .d.e. Thus the gnomon .g.d.e. is equal to square .a.q. Wherefore the two supplements .l.d. and .c.e. taken together are as much as the gnomon .c.m.l. And the same supplements taken together are, from the first of the sixth, as much as .a.l. and therefore as much as .c.q. It follows that .c.q. is equal to the gnomon .c.m.l. 

Therefore, with surface .l.n. removed from both, the square .c.l. will be equal to surface .a.n. Since surface .a.n. is formed from .a.b. into .a.c., and square .c.l. is the square of line .c.b., from the second part of the 16th of the sixth, the proportion of .a.b. to .b.c. will be as .b.c. to .c.a. Therefore, from the definition of a line divided according to the proportion having a medium and two extremes placed in the beginning of the sixth book, conclude the proposition. 

Also otherwise: since the square of .c.d. is by hypothesis fivefold the square of .b.d., the square .a.b. indeed is from the fourth of the second fourfold the same. But the square of .c.d. is from the same [proposition] equal to the square of .c.b. and the square of .b.d. and to that which is formed from .b.d. twice into .c.b. It follows that that which is formed from .b.d. twice into .c.b. with the square of .c.b. is equal to the square of .a.b. 

But from .b.d. twice into .c.b. is as much as that which is from .a.b. into .b.c., because .a.b. is double .b.d. Therefore, what is formed from .a.b. into .b.c. with the square of .b.c. is equal to the square of .a.b. And because from the second of the second, what is formed from .a.b. into .b.c. and into .a.c. [sic - likely .a.b. into .a.c.] is equal to the square of .a.b., it follows from common knowledge that the square of line .b.c. is equal to that which is formed from .a.b. into .a.c. Therefore, from the second part of the 16th of the sixth and the definition, the proposition is established.

### **Proposition 3**

# **BOOK**

If two plane surfaces cut through the axis, and if one of these two surfaces in each pyramid is erected perpendicularly <note>original: orthogonaliter</note> upon its base, while the arcs of the bases contained between those two surfaces are similar: then the angles formed by the axes and the two common sections of the bases and those surfaces (the ones not erected perpendicularly) will be equal to each other.

### XII

Let a **lateral pyramid** <term>lateral pyramid: A pyramid with a polygonal base and flat triangular faces, as opposed to a cone.</term> be subtracted, the base of which is a square inscribed within circle **b**. As was proved above, this will be greater than half of the **round pyramid** <term>round pyramid: A term used historically to describe a cone.</term>. 

From the remainder of the cone, let further pyramids of the same height be subtracted, standing upon the triangles formed by the segments of circle **b**. This process should be repeated until the remainder of the round pyramid **b** is less than the solid body **d**, following the first proposition of the tenth book <note>original: "ex prima decimi". This refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book X, Proposition 1, which provides the mathematical foundation for the "Method of Exhaustion"—a way to find the area or volume of a curved shape by inscribing it with polygons of increasing sides.</note>. It will then follow from this principle that the total subtracted lateral pyramid (which is composed of those smaller partial pyramids) is greater than the solid body **c**.

Then, therefore, let another plane surface extend from the axis of pyramid **a**, standing perpendicularly upon circle **a**. Let the intersection where this surface meets circle **a** be the line **k-l**, which will therefore be the diameter of circle **a**. Then, let another diameter be drawn in circle **a** intersecting the first at right angles, which shall be **m-n**. In this way, the square **k-m-l-n** is inscribed in circle **a**. By dividing the arcs of the segments of circle **a** into equal parts, let a polygon be completed in circle **a** that is similar to the one inscribed in the [other] circle <note>The author is replicating the geometric construction from the first circle into a second circle to demonstrate that their properties remain proportional.</note>.

**D**iven two spheres having one center, to geometrically construct within the larger of them a solid of many bases <note>A polyhedron.</note> whose surface does not touch the smaller sphere.

### XII

¶ Suppose we are presented with two spheres, **a. b. c. d.** and **e. f.**, which share one and the same center, designated as **g.** Let the larger of these be sphere **a. b. c. d.** and the smaller be sphere **e. f.** Our objective is to construct within the larger sphere a "body of many bases" <term>polyhedron: a solid figure with many flat faces, such as a multi-sided gemstone</term>. # XIII

Let the sphere be called **a.b.** It is therefore evident, from the second part of the preceding premise and the eleventh proposition of the Fifth Book <note>original: *2.11.quiti*. This refers to Euclid's *Elements*, Book V, Proposition 11, which states that ratios which are the same as the same ratio are also the same as each other.</note>, that the ratio of sphere **a.b.** to sphere **e.f.** is the same as the ratio of the <term>polyhedron</term> <note>original: *corpis multaz basiu*, literally "a body of many bases." In this context, it refers to a multi-faceted solid shape inscribed within the sphere to approximate its volume.</note> within **a.b.** to the polyhedron within **c.d.** 

For each of these ratios is as the diameter of **a.b.** to the diameter of **c.d.** <term>triplicated</term> <note>original: *triplicata*. In Euclidean geometry, a "triplicate ratio" is the ratio of the cubes of the sides. Because these are three-dimensional spheres, their volume ratio is the cube of the ratio of their diameters.</note>. The first ratio is established by our hypothesis, while the second is established by the second part of the preceding theorem. Therefore, by <term>permutation</term> <note>An algebraic-like rearrangement of a proportion: if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d.</note>, the ratio of sphere **a.b.** to its inscribed polyhedron **a.b.** is the same as the ratio of sphere **e.f.** to the polyhedron **c.d.** 

Since sphere **a.b.** is greater than its inscribed polyhedron **a.b.**, it follows that sphere **e.f.** must also be greater than the polyhedron **c.d.** <note>If the first term of a ratio is larger than the second, the third term must be larger than the fourth for the proportion to hold.</note> However, this is impossible, for the polyhedron is merely a part of the sphere <note>A part cannot be greater than the whole.</note>. Therefore, sphere **e.f.** is not smaller than sphere **c.d.**

If, however, an opponent should claim that it is larger, we shall refute him in this way: for by <term>converse proportionality</term>, sphere **e.f.** will be to sphere **a.b.** as the diameter **c.d.** is to the diameter **a.b.**

### Proposition 4
**If any line be divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes [the extreme and mean ratio], and a line equal to the greater segment is added to it directly in length: the whole line composed therefrom will be divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes, and its greater segment will be the first line.**

Let line $ab$ be divided by the aforementioned ratio at point $c$, and let its greater segment be $cb$. Let there be added directly to the whole line $ab$ the line $bd$, which is equal to $cb$. I say that the whole line $ad$ is divided by the same ratio at point $b$, and its greater segment is line $ab$, which is the first line. For, by definition, $ab$ is to $bc$ as $bc$ is to $ca$. And since, by the seventh [proposition] of the fifth [book], $ab$ is to $bd$ as it is to $bc$; therefore, by the eleventh of the same, $ab$ is to $bd$ as $bc$ is to $ca$. Wherefore, by inverse proportionality, $bd$ is to $ab$ as $ac$ is to $cb$; and by composition [line] $da$ is to $ab$ as $ab$ is to $bc$. And since, by the seventh of the fifth, $ab$ is to $bc$ as it is to $bd$, it will be by the eleventh of the same: $da$ is to $ab$ as $ab$ is to $bd$. Therefore, by definition, line $ad$ is divided at point $b$ according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, and its greater segment is line $ab$, which is what was proposed. 

In the same way also, if from the greater segment of any line divided according to the aforesaid ratio there be subtracted a segment equal to the smaller segment: that greater segment itself will be divided according to the same ratio, and its greater segment will be the line subtracted. For example: Let line $ab$ be divided as proposed at point $c$, and let the greater segment be $ac$, from which $cd$ is subtracted equal to $cb$. I say that $ac$ is divided according to the same ratio at point $d$, and that its greater segment is line $dc$. For since, by definition, $ba$ is to $ac$ as $ac$ is to $cb$; and by the seventh of the fifth, $ac$ is to $cb$ as it is to $cd$; it will be by the eleventh of the same, $ba$ is to $ac$ as $ac$ is to $cd$. Therefore, by the 19th of the fifth: as $cb$ (the remainder) is to $da$ (the remainder). But by the seventh of the same, $cb$ is to $da$ as $cd$ is to $da$; thus $ac$ is to $cd$ as $cd$ is to $da$. By definition, therefore, what we have said is established. Thus, neither the addition which the author [Euclid] opposes, nor the subtraction which we propose from the opposite, however far it may be extended in length, departs from the property of the division of the original line.

### Proposition 5
**If any line be divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, the square of the whole line and the square of the smaller segment, both taken together, are triple the square which is described from the greater segment.**

Let line $ab$ be divided by the often-mentioned ratio at point $c$, and let its greater segment be line $cb$. I say that the squares of the two lines $ab$ and $ca$ taken together are triple the square of line $cb$. For these two squares taken together are, by the seventh [proposition] of the second [book], equal to the square of $cb$ and double that which is produced from $ab$ by $ac$. Likewise, because that which is produced from $ab$ by $ac$ is equal to the square of $cb$ by the definition and the first part of the 16th of the sixth [book]: the proposition is manifest.

### Proposition 6
**It is necessary that both segments of every rational line divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes be an apotome [residuum].**

Let line $ab$ be divided according to the said ratio at point $c$, [let $ab$ be] a rational [line]. I say that each segment of it is an apotome. For let its greater segment be $ac$, to which $ad$ is added directly, equal to half of the whole $ab$. Then $da$ will also be rational by the 6th [proposition] of the tenth book and the definition. It is established from the first [proposition] of this [book] that the square of line $dc$ is five times the square of line $da$. Therefore line $dc$ is commensurable to line $da$ in power [square] by definition, but not in length by the last part of the 7th of the tenth. Wherefore, by the 73rd [OCR says 68] of the tenth, line $ac$ is an apotome, since the two lines $cd$ and $da$ are both rational, being commensurable in power only. 

And because again, if to the rational line $ab$ a surface is applied equal to the square of line $ac$ (which is an apotome), its side will be the line $cb$ by the first part of the 16th of the sixth, it is necessary by the 97th [OCR says 92] of the tenth that line $cb$ be a first apotome; wherefore the proposition is established. Furthermore, if the greater segment of a line so divided as proposed be rational, the smaller will be an apotome. For example, let $ab$ be divided as before at $c$ according to the said ratio, and let its greater segment, which is $ac$, be rational, and let it be divided equally at $d$. It will be from the third [proposition] of this [book] that the square of $db$ is five times the square of $dc$. But since $dc$ is rational (of which $ac$ itself is the half), it follows that the two lines $db$ and $dc$ are rational, being commensurable in power only; wherefore, as before, line $cb$ is an apotome. 

But if a line rational in power only be divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, it is still necessary that both segments of it be an apotome. For let $ab$, rational in power only, be divided as proposed at point $c$, and let some line rational in length be taken, which is $de$, which is also divided at $f$ according to the aforesaid ratio. It is manifest therefore from the second [proposition] of the 14th book—which is strengthened by an unshakable demonstration without the support of any of those things which follow—that the ratio of $ab$ to $de$ is as $ac$ to $df$, and as $cb$ to $fe$. Since therefore $ab$ is commensurable with $de$ in power, it follows from the first part of the 10th [proposition] of the tenth [book] that $ac$ is commensurable with $df$, and $cb$ with $fe$, in power. And because each segment of line $de$ is an apotome, as appears from the aforesaid, it follows from the 103rd [OCR says 98] of the tenth that each segment of line $ab$ is an apotome, but not of the same species, as is demonstrated there. Wherefore it is established that of every line rational in length or in power only, divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, both segments are apotomes. 

And note that the first part of the prior demonstration, by which it is demonstrated that the greater segment of a line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes is an apotome if the whole line be rational, proceeds sufficiently whether the whole line is posited as rational in length or in power only. But the second part, by which this is demonstrated concerning the smaller segment—that it also is an apotome if the whole line is rational—does not proceed sufficiently unless the whole line be rational in length. The third part, however, by which it is proved that the smaller segment is an apotome, proceeds sufficiently whether the greater segment be rational in length or in power only. Therefore, to conclude concerning the greater segment of a line divided in the aforesaid manner that it is an apotome, it suffices to posit that the whole divided line is rational in power only; but to conclude this also of the smaller segment by means of the greater, it suffices to posit the greater segment to be rational in power only. But to conclude this of the smaller segment [directly], it is necessary to posit the whole line to be rational in length, or the second [proposition] of the 14th book must be used, as was said.

### Proposition 7
**If any pentagon having three equal angles be equilateral, the same pentagon is proved to be equiangular also.**

Let the pentagon $abcde$ be equilateral. And let any three of its angles, whether taken continuously or non-continuously, be taken as equal to one another; and let them first be taken non-continuously. Let angles $a$, $c$, and $d$ be those three which are posited as equal to one another; I say the whole pentagon is equiangular. And since by the fifth of the first, angle $bcd$ [OCR $bcd$] is equal to angle $bdc$ [OCR $bdc$] because the two sides $bc$ and $bd$ are equal, it will be from common knowledge that the total angle $e$ is equal to the total angle $d$. 

Similarly, you will prove the total angle $b$ to be equal to the total angle $c$; for by the fourth of the first, base $be$ is equal to base $ce$, and angle $abe$ is equal to angle $dce$. By the fifth of the same (namely, of the first), angle $cbe$ is equal to angle $ecb$; therefore from common knowledge, total angle $b$ is equal to total angle $c$. Let, then, the three angles $b, c, d$ taken continuously be equal, and thus also the pentagon will be equiangular. For by the 4th of the first, base $bd$ will be equal to base $ce$, and angle $cdb$ to angle $dce$; and since the two sides $be$ [sic] and $bd$ are equal... [text breaks off].

### Translator’s Notes on Abbreviations and Readings:
1.  **ꝓportio / ꝓpositio**: Standard abbreviations for *proportio* (ratio) and *propositio* (proposition).
2.  **⁊**: The Tironian *et*, translated as "and."
3.  **fm**: Abbreviation for *secundum* ("according to").
4.  **ꝙ**: Abbreviation for *quod* ("that" or "which").
5.  **Lunqz**: An OCR error for *Cumque* ("And since").
6.  **rōnalis**: *Rationalis* ("rational").
7.  **residuum**: In the context of Euclid's Book XIII, this refers specifically to the *apotome*, a type of irrational line defined in Book X. 
8.  **potentialiter tmaz**: *potentialiter tantum* ("in power only"), referring to lines that are commensurable only when squared.
9.  **cōicans**: *communicans* ("commensurable").
10. **Book Citations**: The text refers to "septima quinti" (V.7), "undecima eiusdem" (V.11), "16 sexti" (VI.16), etc. The OCR numbering for Book X propositions (e.g., 68, 92, 98) often differs by a few digits from modern Heiberg numbering due to different manuscript traditions used in the Renaissance (likely following the Campanus tradition). For example, "92 decimi" in the text refers to the property of the first apotome.
11. **p 2 / p 3**: These are signature marks or catchwords for the printer at the bottom of the pages.

### **Proposition 5.**

**If any line has been divided according to the <term>proportion having a mean and two extremes</term> <note>This is the classical name for the Golden Ratio. It occurs when the ratio of the whole line to the larger part is the same as the ratio of the larger part to the smaller part.</note>, the squares produced from the whole line and from the smaller portion, when both are taken together, are triple the square described from the greater portion.**

¶ Let line *a.b.* be divided by the often-mentioned proportion at point *c.*, and let its greater portion be line *c.b.* I say that the squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *c.a.*, when taken together, are triple the square of line *c.b.* For these two squares taken together are (from the seventh of the second book) equal to the square of *c.b.* plus twice the rectangle formed by *a.b.* and *a.c.* Likewise, because the rectangle formed by *a.b.* and *a.c.* is equal to the square of *c.b.* (from the definition and the first part of the 16th of the sixth book), the proposition is manifest.

### **Proposition 6.**

**For every <term>rational</term> <note>In Greek and Medieval geometry, a "rational" line is one whose length is known or commensurable with a given standard unit.</note> line divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, it is necessary that each portion be an <term>apotome</term> <note>The text uses "residuum." In the context of Euclid's Book X, this refers to an "apotome," a specific type of irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another that is only commensurable with it in square (in power).</note>.**

¶ Let there be a rational line *a.b.* divided at point *c.* according to the stated proportion. I say that each of its portions is an apotome. For let its greater portion be *a.c.*, to which is directly added *a.d.*, equal to half of the whole line *a.b.* Then *d.a.* will also be rational from the 6th of the tenth book and the definition. It is established from the first proposition of this book that the square of line *d.c.* is five times the square of line *d.a.* Therefore, line *d.c.* is commensurable with line *d.a.* in <term>power</term> <note>Commensurable "in power" means their squares have a ratio of a square number to a square number. Here, it means the square of one is five times the square of the other, making the lengths themselves incommensurable (involving the square root of 5).</note> by the definition, but not in length (from the last part of the 7th of the tenth book). Wherefore, by the 68th of the tenth book, line *a.c.* is an apotome, since the two lines *c.d.* and *d.a.* are both rational and commensurable only in power. And because, again, if to the rational line *a.b.* an area is applied equal to the square of line *a.c.* (which is an apotome), its other side will be line *c.b.* (from the first part of the 16th of the sixth book). It is necessary from the 92nd of the tenth book that line *c.b.* be a first apotome; wherefore the proposition is established. Furthermore, if the greater portion of a line so divided as proposed were rational, the smaller would be an apotome. For example: let *a.b.* be divided at *c.* as before by the said proportion, and let its greater portion *a.c.* be rational. Let it be divided equally at *d.* From the third proposition of this book, the square of *d.b.* will be five times the square of *d.c.* Since *d.c.* is rational (as it is half of *a.c.*), it follows that the two lines *d.b.* and *d.c.* are rational and commensurable only in power; wherefore, as before, line *c.b.* is an apotome. But truly, if a line rational only in power [is divided] according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes...

But indeed, the square *a.e.* is four times the square *b.e.* by the fourth [proposition] of the second book, since the line *a.e.* [the diameter] is double *b.e.* [the radius]. Therefore, by subtracting the square *b.f.* from both sides, it will be by common knowledge that the remaining square *f.d.* is equal to the remaining square *f.e.* Wherefore, also line *f.d.* is equal to line *f.e.*, by this common knowledge that those lines whose squares are equal are themselves equal. From this it is manifest that a perpendicular line drawn from the center of a circle to the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle is equal to half of the line drawn from the center of the same circle to its circumference.

I say that line **b.e.** is the side of a hexagon: for let two lines, **e.d.** and **b.d.**, be drawn to the center.
The angle **e.** will be equal to angle **b.d.c.** from Book 1, Proposition 5 <note>This refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, which states that in isosceles triangles, the angles at the base are equal.</note> because line **e.b.** is equal to line **b.d.** from the conclusion of Book 4, Proposition 15. Angle **d.b.c.** is also equal to angle **c.** from Book 1, Proposition 5. Therefore, from Book 1, Proposition 32, angle **a.d.b.** will be double angle **d.b.c.**; and since by the same reasoning angle **d.b.c.** is double angle **e.**, it follows that angle **a.d.b.** is four times angle **e.** This is from the common notion that whatever is the double of a double is fourfold. Since the same angle **a.d.b.** is four times angle **b.d.c.** from the last proposition of Book 6—because the arc **a.b.** is four times the arc **b.c.**—it is necessary by common knowledge that angle **e.** be equal to angle **b.d.c.** 

If, therefore, two triangles are understood—the whole triangle **d.e.c.** and the partial triangle **b.d.c.**—since the total angle **e.** is equal to the partial angle **b.d.c.** and angle **c.** is common to both, it is necessary from Book 1, Proposition 32, that they be equiangular. Therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 4, the proportion of the two sides **e.c.** and **c.d.** containing angle **c.** in the total triangle is as the two sides **d.c.** and **c.b.** containing the same angle in the partial triangle. Because the proportion of **e.c.** to **c.d.** is as **c.d.** to **c.b.** from the second part of Book 5, Proposition 7, and **d.c.** to **c.b.** is as **e.b.** to the same from the first part of the same, it follows from Book 5, Proposition 11, that the proportion of **e.c.** to **e.b.** is as **e.b.** to **b.c.** 

Therefore, by definition, conclude the proposition: that line **e.c.** is divided according to the <term>extreme and mean ratio</term> <note>Now commonly known as the Golden Ratio. In this proportion, the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller one.</note> and its greater segment is the side of the hexagon, which is what we needed to demonstrate. It is also fitting to demonstrate the converse, which is easily done by the reverse path; indeed, Ptolemy assumes this in Chapter 9 of the first book of the *Almagest* <note>Ptolemy’s *Almagest* (2nd century AD) was the most influential astronomical text of the Middle Ages; Chapter 9 specifically explains how to calculate the lengths of chords in a circle.</note> to demonstrate the quantity of the chords of the arcs of a circle. 

I say, therefore, that if any line is divided according to the extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is the side of a hexagon of some circle, its lesser segment will be the side of a decagon <note>A ten-sided polygon.</note> of the same circle. Conversely, that whose lesser segment is the side of the decagon, its greater segment will be the side of the hexagon of the same circle. For let the previous arrangement remain, with line **e.c.** divided at point **b.** according to the aforesaid proportion, and let its greater segment be **e.b.** I say that for whatever circle line **e.b.** is the side of the hexagon, line **b.c.** is the side of the decagon; and for whatever circle line **b.c.** is the side of the decagon, line **e.b.** is the side of the hexagon. 

I understand this to apply to equilateral hexagons and decagons. For if **e.b.** is the side of the hexagon inscribed in circle **a.b.c.**, it will be (by Book 4, Proposition 15) that **e.b.** is equal to **d.c.** And because the proportion of **e.c.** to **e.b.** is as **e.b.** to **b.c.** by hypothesis, it will be (from Book 5, Proposition 7) that **e.c.** is to **d.c.** as **d.c.** is to **c.b.** Therefore, from Book 6, Proposition 6, the two triangles **e.d.c.** and **d.c.b.** are equiangular; thus angle **e.** is equal to angle **b.d.c.**, for the proportional sides correspond to them. And since angle **a.d.b.** is four times angle **e.** (from Book 1, Proposition 32, applied twice, and Book 1, Proposition 5, applied twice), it follows that the same angle **a.d.b.** is four times angle **b.d.c.** Therefore, from the last proposition of Book 6, arc **a.b.** is four times arc **b.c.** Line **b.c.** is therefore the side of the decagon inscribed in **a.b.c.** 

But if line **b.c.** were the side of the decagon of circle **a.b.c.**, then **e.b.** would be the side of the hexagon of the same. Let it be understood, then, that equilateral decagons are inscribed in the two circles **a.b.c.** and **f.**, all of whose sides will be equal to line **b.c.** And because every equilateral figure inscribed in a circle is equiangular (as proven in Book 4, Proposition 15), it follows that both decagons are equiangular. # XIII

By the first part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book <note>original: "16.sexti"; referring to Euclid's Elements, Book VI, Proposition 16</note>, the rectangle produced by line **a.b.** and line **b.l.** is equal to the square of **d.b.** But indeed, it was proven previously that the area produced by **a.b.** and **l.a.** is equal to the square of **a.b.** <note>The OCR repeats "a.b." here, but geometrically this usually refers to the relationship between the sides of the pentagon, hexagon, and decagon.</note> Thus, the area produced by **a.b.** and **a.l.** together with that produced by **a.b.** and **l.b.** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.d.** And because, according to the second proposition of the second book <note>original: "scda secundi"; Euclid’s Elements, Book II, Prop. 2, which deals with dividing a line segment</note>, the area produced by **a.b.** multiplied by **l.a.** and **l.b.** is equal to the square of line **a.b.**; and since line **a.b.** is the side <term>side<gloss>Latin: "latus"; the length of one edge of a polygon</gloss></term> of an equilateral pentagon inscribed in the proposed circle; and line **a.b.** <note>This likely refers to segment **a.l.** or **b.l.** in the original diagram</note> is the side of an equilateral decagon; and line **b.d.** is, by the corollary of the 15th proposition of the fourth book, equal to the side of an equilateral hexagon inscribed in the proposed circle; then by this unshakable demonstration, that which was stated is established.

Therefore, line $b.c$ is commensurable in power with line $e.f$; and because line $e.f$ is a minor line, it follows from the 100th [proposition] of the tenth [book] that $b.c$ is also a minor line, which was proposed. Thus, whether the diameter of any circle is rational in length or in power only, it is necessary that the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in it be a minor line.

### Translation Notes and Abbreviations
*   **Abbreviations:** Standard scribal abbreviations have been expanded: *ꝙ* (quod), *ꝓ* (pro), *ꝑ* (per), *ē* (est/em), *ꝛ* (et), *bꝫ* (bus), *mō* (modo), *scʒ* (scilicet), *tm* (tantum), *sm/fm* (secundum).
*   **Potentialiter:** Translated as "in power" or "potentially," a technical term meaning that the squares of the lines are in the stated ratio (e.g., *potentialiter triplicem* means the square of one is triple the square of the other).
*   **Proper Nouns:** Aristeus, Apollonius.
*   **Unclear Readings:** The term *corhaustis/corhausti* appears to be a specialized or perhaps corrupted term for connecting edges; *ypothemisæ* refers to slant heights or hypotenuses.

...is to be described, [the thing] proposed. The **Corollary** is thus: Since $AB$ is triple to $BC$, by inverse proportionality $AB$ will be sesquialter [1.5:1] to $AC$. Therefore, from the second part of the conclusion of the 8th [proposition] of the Sixth [Book] and the corollary of the 17th of the same, the square of line $AB$ will also be sesquialter to the square of line $AD$; and the square of line $AD$ is equal to the side of the constructed pyramid. But truly $AB$ is the diameter of the sphere; it is established that this is what is said through the corollary. 

However, lest any doubt should arise concerning the anciently proposed truth, we wish to confirm it by demonstration in this manner. Let there be, therefore, upon line $AB$ a perpendicular line $CD$, which is placed as a mean proportional between the parts of line $AB$, which are $AC$ and $CB$, so that the proportion of $AC$ to $CD$ is as $CD$ to $CB$. And let a semicircle $ACB$ be described upon line $AB$. I say that the circumference of this semicircle will pass through point $D$, which is the extremity of the perpendicular. If it does not, it will either cut line $CD$ or pass above it entirely, passing beyond and including it without touching it. First, let it cut it at point $E$, and let lines $EB$ and $EA$ be drawn: from the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the Third [Book], the total angle $AEB$ will be a right angle. Thus, from the first part of the conclusion of the 8th of the Sixth, the proportion is $AC$ to $CE$ as $CE$ to $CB$. But truly, from the second part of the 8th of the Fifth, the proportion $AC$ to $CE$ is greater than $AC$ to $CD$, because $CE$ is smaller than $CD$. Since therefore $AC$ is to $CB$ as $AC$ to $CE$, and $CD$ to $CB$ as $AC$ to $CD$, it will be by the 12th of the Fifth that $AC$ to $CB$ is greater than $AC$ to $CB$; and therefore by the first part of the 10th of the Fifth, $AC$ is greater than $ADC$ [sic - possibly $AD$], namely that its part is greater than its whole, which is impossible. Therefore the circumference of the semicircle will not cut line $CD$. 

**Consequently**, let it pass beyond and let $CD$ be produced as far as the circumference; and let the whole be $CE$, and let lines $EB$ and $EA$ be drawn. It follows as before that line $CD$ is greater than line $CE$, which is also impossible. Therefore the proposition is established. Similarly, we say that if there be any right angle subtended by a base upon which a semicircle is drawn, it is necessary for the circumference to pass through that right angle. The first part of the 30th of the Third proposes the converse of this. What we say is established thus: **Consequently**, let angle $ABC$ be a right angle subtended by base $AC$, and let a semicircle be drawn upon it. I say that its circumference will pass through point $B$ in which the lines containing the right angle meet. The demonstration of this is that it will pass neither above nor below. If it should pass below, let it be $ABC$, and from angle $B$ let line $BD$ be produced perpendicular to the base $AC$, which cuts the circumference of the semicircle at point $E$, and let lines $EA$ and $EC$ be drawn. Angle $AEC$ will be a right angle from the first part of the 30th of the Third. But it is greater than angle $ABC$ by the 21st of the First; however, this is impossible by the third petition [postulate], since both are right: this one from the hypothesis, that one from the first part of the 30th of the Third. Therefore the circumference of the semicircle will not pass below angle $B$. Let it pass therefore above, and let it be $AFC$; let the perpendicular $DB$ be produced until it meets the circumference of the semicircle $AFE$ at point $F$, and let lines $FA$ and $FC$ be drawn. From the first part of the 30th of the Third, angle $AFC$ will be a right angle. Since also by hypothesis angle $ABC$ was a right angle, an impossibility follows by the 21st of the First as in the beginning. It remains, therefore, what we said. This is necessary for the knowledge of those things which follow.

### Proposition 14.
**To construct a cube circumscribable by an assigned sphere; and it will be manifest that the diameter of the same sphere is potentially triple to the side of the cube itself.**

Let the diameter of the assigned sphere be $AB$, upon which let semicircle $ADB$ be drawn; and let the diameter be divided at point $C$ according to the condition of the preceding, namely that line $AC$ be double to line $CB$. Let $CD$ be produced perpendicular to $AB$, and let $DB$ and $DA$ be drawn. Afterwards, let one square be made whose sides are all equal to line $BD$, and let it be $EFGH$, upon whose four angles let four perpendicular lines be erected as taught in the 12th of the Eleventh, perpendicular to the surface of the square itself, each of which is also equal to line $BD$. Let them be $CK, FL, GM, BN$ [Note: letters vary slightly from the diagram]. These four perpendiculars will be individually parallel to one another from the 6th of the Eleventh; and the angles they contain with the sides of the square are right from the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface. Then let the extremities of these perpendiculars be joined by drawn lines $KL, LM, MN, NK$. The cube will be completed, contained by six square surfaces. It is established from the 34th of the First that the four surfaces surrounding it are squares, since their opposite sides are the four perpendiculars; concerning the base, this was given. Truly, concerning the upper surface $KLMN$, that it is also square is established from the 34th of the First and the 10th of the Eleventh. Therefore from the 4th of the Eleventh it is manifest that the individual sides of the same cube stand orthogonally upon its two opposite surfaces. 

Now let us demonstrate that this cube is circumscribable by the assigned sphere. In one of its surfaces, let a diagonal be drawn—for example, in its base, let it be $EG$—and from the other extremity of this diagonal, let the diameter of the cube $EM$ be drawn. From the penultimate [proposition] of the First [Pythagorean Theorem], the square of $EG$ is double the square of $FG$; and therefore also to the square of $GM$, because $GM$ is equal to $FG$, for all sides of a cube are equal to each other. Again, from the penultimate of the First, the square of $EM$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $EG$ and $GM$, because angle $EGM$ is a right angle from the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface. The square of $EM$ will be triple to the square of $MG$, for it consists of the double and the simple. And since from the second part of the conclusion of the 8th of the Sixth, the square of $AB$ is also triple to the square of $BD$ (because line $AB$ is triple to line $BC$), and $BD$ is equal to $GM$, it follows that $EM$, which is the diameter of the cube, is equal to $AB$, which is the diameter of the sphere. Thus, if a semicircle is drawn upon $EM$ and rotated until it returns to the place from which it began, the sphere described will be equal to the assigned sphere. But truly this semicircle will make its passage through point $G$, because angle $EGM$ is a right angle, and for the same reason through the other individual right angles of the cube, which is manifest from the immediate preceding. It is established that the constructed cube is circumscribed by the assigned sphere, which was to be demonstrated. The demonstration of the corollary was made clear in the process of this demonstration.
