### Proposition 15.
**To compose a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases [octahedron] circumscribable by a proposed sphere; and it will be plain that the diameter of the same sphere is potentially double to the side of the body itself.**

**Consequently**, let the diameter of the proposed sphere be $AB$, which is divided into equal parts at point $C$. Let semicircle $ADB$ be drawn upon it, and let perpendicular $CD$ be produced to $AB$, and join point $D$ with $A$ and with $B$. Let one square be described whose individual sides are equal to line $BD$; let this square be $EFGH$, in which the two diameters $EG$ and $FB$ are drawn, intersecting each other at point $K$. It is established from the 4th of the First that each of these diameters is equal to line $AB$, which is the diameter of the sphere, since angle $D$ is right from the first part of the 30th of the Third and the individual angles of $EFGH$ are right from the definition of a square. It is established again that the same two diameters $EG$ and $FB$ divide each other into equal parts at point $K$. This is easily elicited from the 5th and 32nd of the First and the 6th of the same. Therefore, let line $KL$ be erected upon point $K$ perpendicular to the surface of the square, which is equal to half of the diameter $EG$ or $FB$, and let the hypotenuses $LE, LF, LG, LB$ be dropped. From those things which were given and by repeating the penultimate of the First, each of these hypotenuses will be equal to each other and equal to the sides of the square. You have therefore a pyramid of four equilateral and triangular bases constituted upon a square. 

**[PAGE XIII v.]**

Hence, therefore, under the square itself, place a similar pyramid in this manner: produce line $LK$ through the square as far as $M$, so that $KM$ existing below the square is equal to $LK$ existing above; and join point $M$ with the individual angles of the square by producing four other hypotenuses which are $ME, MF, MG, MB$. Concerning these, it is manifest from the penultimate of the First (just as with the others in the upper part) that they are equal to each other and to the sides of the square. We have therefore completed a body of 8 triangular and equilateral bases. That this is circumscribable by the assigned sphere, take as follows: it is established that line $LM$ is equal to the diameter of the assigned sphere, for each of them is equal to the diameter of the square. Therefore if a semicircle is drawn upon $LM$ and rotated until it returns to its place, the sphere which it describes by its motion will be equal to the assigned sphere. Truly, this semicircle will pass through the four angles of the square and simply all points of the circumference of the circle circumscribing the square, because the semi-diameter of the square (as line $FK$) and the portions of line $LM$ (which are $LK$ and $KM$) are equal to each other. By the definition of a figure being inscribed in another, the fabricated body is inscribable in the sphere described by the motion of this semicircle. And so also for the assigned sphere, since they are equal to each other by definition. The **Corollary** is manifest: for the two lines $DB$ and $DA$ are equal from the 4th of the First; therefore the square of $AB$ is double the square of $BD$ from the penultimate of the First. But the side of the fabricated body is equal to line $BD$; therefore the corollary is true.

It is established that line $BD$ is rational in power, since its square is one-fifth of the square of $AB$... therefore the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in this circle is a "minor" line.

### Proposition 17.
**To constitute a body of twelve equilateral and equiangular pentagonal bases [dodecahedron] circumscribable by an assigned sphere; and it will be plain that the side of the same body is irrational, which is called the "residue" [apotome].**

**Consequently**, [let there be] a cube according to what the 14th [proposition] teaches, circumscribable by the assigned sphere... [The text describes constructing the dodecahedron by building pentagons upon the edges of the cube]. 

...[Conclusion of Prop 17]... It is established that all lines drawn from point $O$ to the individual angles of the dodecahedron are equal to each other and to the semi-diameter of the sphere... Therefore it is circumscribable by the assigned sphere. I say again that the side of this figure is an irrational line, namely that which is called the "residue" [apotome]... 

There have been fabricated, therefore, through the 13th and the four following it, five equilateral and equiangular bodies, each of which is circumscribable by an assigned sphere. These solids are: First, of four triangular bases, called the **Tetrahedron**. Second is of six square bases, called the **Cube** or **Hexahedron**. Third, of eight triangular bases, called the **Octahedron**. Fourth is the **Icosahedron**, of twenty triangular bases. The Fifth consists of twelve pentagonal bases, called the **Dodecahedron**. These five are called the "regular solids" because they are equiangular and equilateral and circumscribable by a sphere and by one another. It is impossible for there to be more than these five... [The text provides the classic proof that only three, four, or five equilateral triangles, three squares, or three pentagons can meet at a vertex].

### Proposition 18.
**To find the sides of the five preceding bodies circumscribable by the same sphere, when only the diameter of the sphere is proposed to us.**

**Consequently**, let $AB$ be the diameter of some sphere proposed to us... let it be divided at $C$ so that $AC$ is double $CB$, and at $D$ into equal parts... [The construction identifies each side length on a single diagram]. 

$AE$ is the side of the 4-based pyramid. $EB$ is the side of the cube. $FB$ is the side of the 8-based figure. $NB$ is the side of the icosahedron. Line $PB$ is the side of the dodecahedron. 

Which of these sides are greater than others is held thus: $AE$ is the side of the pyramid, greater than the sides of the other bodies. After it follows $FB$, the side of the octahedron. In the third order follows $EB$, the side of the cube. In the fourth place is $NB$, the side of the icosahedron. The last of all is $PB$, the side of the dodecahedron. 

**Thus ends the Thirteenth Book.**

# Here begins the Fourteenth Book.
### Proposition 1.
**Every perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to the side of a pentagon inscribed within the same circle is proved equal to half the side of the decagon and half the side of the hexagon inscribed within the same circle, both halves being joined in a straight line.**

As the twelfth proposition of the eleventh book <note>original: "12. vndecimi"; this refers to Book XI of Euclid’s *Elements*, which transitions from plane geometry to solid (3D) geometry</note> teaches, four lines are drawn <term>perpendicular|Lines that meet at a 90-degree angle</term> to the <term>surface|the flat plane</term> of the square itself. Let each of these lines be set equal to line **b-d**, and let them be named **e-k**, **f-l**, **g-m**, and **h-n**. These four perpendiculars will be parallel to one another, according to the sixth proposition of the eleventh book. Regarding the chords <note>original: "coraustis," likely referring to the edges or lines connecting the vertices</note>, it has already been shown that they are equal to the sides of the pentagon. Thus, all the sides of these ten triangles are either sides of an equilateral pentagon inscribed for a second time in the circle, or they are equal to them; they are, therefore, equilateral triangles.

Furthermore, above the center of the circle, which is point **l**, erect another perpendicular equal to the previous ones, which shall be **l.m.** Join its upper extremity, which is point **m**, with each of the extremities of the previous five chords. From the 6th proposition of the eleventh book, this central perpendicular will be parallel to each of the angular perpendiculars. Therefore, from the 33rd proposition of the first book, these five chords will be equal to the radius <term>semidiameter: the radius of a circle</term> of the circle, and from the corollary of the 15th proposition of the fourth book, each of them is like the side of a hexagon. 

To the central perpendicular, therefore, let one line equal to the side of the decagon be added to each end: above, let **m.n.** be added to it; below, under the circle, let **l.p.** be added to it from the center of the circle. Afterward, let 5 hypotenuses be dropped from point **n** to the 5 upper angles of the ten triangles that are in the circuit; and from point **p**, let another 5 be dropped to the other five lower angles. These ten hypotenuses will be equal to each other and to the sides of the inscribed pentagon, according to the penultimate proposition of the first book and the 10th of this book, just as was demonstrated before regarding the other ten. 

You have, therefore, a body of 20 triangular and equilateral bases <note>An icosahedron</note> whose sides are all equal to the sides of the pentagon. Its diameter is the line **n.p.** Of these 20 triangles, ten stand in a circuit around the circle; five rise upward, meeting at point **n**; while the remaining five emerge downward, joining at point **p**. 

That this icosahedral body is circumscribable by a given sphere will be made manifest thus: since the line **l.m.** is equal to the side of a hexagon and **m.n.** to the side of an equilateral decagon which the circle **e.f.g.** circumscribes, the whole line **l.n.** will be divided, according to the ninth proposition of the present book, in extreme and mean ratio at point **m**, and its greater part will be the line **l.m.** <note>This refers to the Golden Ratio, often used in the construction of pentagons and icosahedra.</note> 

Let **l.m.** therefore be divided into two equal parts at point **q**. It follows from common knowledge that **p.q.** is equal to **q.n.**, for **p.l.** was placed equal to the side of the decagon just as **m.n.** was. Therefore **q.n.** is half of **n.p.**, just as **q.m.** is half of **m.l.** Since, therefore, the square of **n.q.** is five times the square of **q.m.** (from the 3rd proposition of this book), it follows from the 15th proposition of the fifth book that the square of **p.n.** is also five times the square of **l.m.** For, from the fourth proposition of the second book, the square of **p.n.** is four times the square of **q.n.**, and the square of **l.m.** is four times the square of **q.m.** by the same logic. Four times is to four times as simple is to simple <note>Meaning the ratio 4:4 is the same as 1:1</note>, as witnessed by the 15th proposition of the fifth book. 

But truly, the square of **a.b.** is five times the square of **b.d.** from the second part of the corollary of the 6th proposition of the sixth book; and from the corollary of the 17th proposition of the same book, **a.b.** is also five times **b.c.** because **a.c.** was four times the same. Because, therefore, **l.m.** is by hypothesis equal to **b.d.**, it follows from common knowledge that **a.b.** is equal to **n.p.** Therefore, if a semicircle is described upon line **n.p.**, and is rotated through the first position until it returns, the sphere described by its motion will be equal to the proposed sphere, by the definition of equal spheres. And since line **l.m.** is a mean proportional between **l.n.** and **n.m.**, and therefore between **l.n.** and **p.l.**, any radius of the circle will also be a mean proportional between **l.n.** and **l.p.** 

And since **l.m.** is equal to the radius of the circle, the semicircle described over **p.n.** will pass through all the points of the circumference of circle **e.f.g.**, and therefore through each of the angles of the solid constructed in that circumference. And because, by the same reasoning, each of the chords connecting the extremities of the angular perpendiculars with the extremity of the central one are mean proportionals between **p.m.** and **m.n.** (since each of them is equal to **l.m.**), it follows that the same semicircle passes also through the remaining angles of the established icosahedral figure. Therefore, this body is inscribable in a sphere.

# XIII

I say again <note>original: "dico iterum"</note> that the side of this figure is an irrational line, namely that which is called a **residue** <note>The "residue" or "apotome" is a specific type of irrational line in Euclidean geometry, formed by subtracting a rational line from another rational line that is commensurable only in power.</note>, if the diameter of the sphere circumscribing it is rational in length or in power. For since the diameter of the sphere is—according to the 14th proposition of this book—triple in power to the side of the cube, the side of the cube will be rational in power if the diameter of the sphere is rational in length or in power.

Furthermore, it is established from the 11th proposition that the line *r.p.* divides the line *a.d.* (which is the side of the cube) according to the <term>proportion having a mean and two extremes</term> <note>This is the classical definition of the Golden Ratio.</note>, and that its greater portion is equal to the side of the pentagon. And since its greater portion is a "residue" according to the sixth proposition of this book, it is manifest that the side of the dodecahedron figure is a residue, which is what we wished to demonstrate. 

Therefore, through the 13th proposition and the four following it, five equilateral and equiangular bodies have been constructed <note>These are the five Platonic Solids.</note>, each of which is circumscribable by the assigned sphere. These solids are:
*   First, indeed, one of four triangular bases, which is called the **tetrahedron**.
*   The second is of six square bases, which is called the **cube** or **hexahedron**.
*   The third is of eight triangular bases, which is called the **octahedron**.
*   The fourth is the solid **icosahedron**, which is of twenty triangular bases.
*   The fifth, truly, consists of twelve pentagonal bases and is called the **dodecahedron**.

These five are called the "regular solids" because they are equiangular and equilateral, and are circumscribable by a sphere and by one another. Indeed, it is impossible for there to be more than these five equilateral and equiangular solids.

For the constitution of any solid angle, it is necessary for at least three surface angles to meet. For a solid angle cannot be completed from only two surface angles. Since, therefore, three angles of any equilateral and equiangular hexagon are equal to four right angles <note>In a flat hexagon, each internal angle is 120 degrees. Three such angles equal 360 degrees, or four 90-degree right angles. A solid angle must sum to less than 360 degrees to "fold" into 3D space.</note>. But indeed, the three angles of a heptagon <note>seven-sided figure</note> or of any equilateral and equiangular figure with more sides are greater than four right angles, as is evidently shown from the 32nd proposition of the first book. Moreover, every solid angle must be less than four right angles, according to the witness of the 21st proposition of the eleventh book. It is therefore impossible for three angles of a hexagon or a heptagon—or simply any many-sided figure, even if equilateral and equiangular—to constitute a solid angle. 

Therefore, no equilateral and equiangular solid figure can be constituted from hexagonal surfaces or those of more sides. For if three angles of an equilateral and equiangular hexagon exceed four right angles, then four or more angles exceed it much more strongly. However, it is manifest that three angles of an equilateral and equiangular pentagon are less than four right angles, while four such angles are greater. Wherefore, it is possible for a solid angle to be constituted from three angles of an equilateral and equiangular pentagon, but from four or more it is impossible. 

And therefore, only one solid is constituted from equilateral and equiangular pentagons, namely that which is called the **dodecahedron**, in which the angles of the pentagons, taken three by three, complete the solid angles. From the fourth [proposition] of the first [book] and the twenty-seventh of the third [book], let this be the perpendicular line **c.d.** cutting **a.b.** at point **c** and its arc at point **d**. Therefore, as we said, line **a.c.** is equal to line **e.b.** and arc **a.d.** is equal to arc **d.b.** Let line **d.b.** be drawn, which it is established is the side of an equilateral <term>decagon</term> <note>A ten-sided polygon.</note> inscribed in the proposed circle, since it subtends half of a fifth of the whole circumference. I say, therefore, that line **c.e.** is equal to half of line **c.d.** and half of line **d.b.** joined together in a straight line. Let the diameter **d.c.** be completed, and let it be **d.c.g.**, and let **e.f.** be equal to **c.d.** and let **b.f.** be drawn. Then, from the fourth [proposition] of the first [book], **b.f.** will be equal to **b.d.**, and therefore by the fifth of the first [book], angle **b.d.f.** will be equal to angle **b.f.d.** It is established from the last [proposition] of the sixth [book] that angle **g.c.b.** is four times angle **b.c.d.** because arc **g.b.** is four times arc **b.d.** But indeed, by the thirty-second [proposition] of the first [book], angle **g.c.b.** is double angle **b.d.c.**, for it is external to the two [angles] which are **b.d.c.** and **d.b.c.**, and these are equal by the fifth of the first [book]. Therefore, angle **b.d.c.** is double angle **b.c.d.**; wherefore angle **b.f.d.** is also double angle **b.c.f.** But angle **b.f.d.** is equal to the two interior angles which are **b.c.f.** and **c.b.f.** by the thirty-second of the first [book]. Thus the two angles **b.c.f.** and **c.b.f.** are equal; and so by the sixth of the first [book], **c.f.** is equal to **b.f.**, and thus also **c.f.** is equal to **b.d.**, for **b.d.** and **b.f.** are equal to each other. Wherefore half of **c.d.** with half of **c.b.** is as much as half of **c.d.** with half of **c.f.** But indeed, half of **c.d.** with half of **c.f.** is as much as half of **c.f.** twice with half of **f.d.** Half of **c.f.** twice is as much as **c.f.** and half of **f.d.** is as much as **e.f.** Thus **c.e.** is as much as half of **c.d.** with half of **c.b.** and **d.b.**, which is what was proposed. The conclusion, however, is established thus: for it is manifest from the eighth [proposition] of the thirteenth book that a perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to the side of a <term>triangle</term> <note>Specifically, an equilateral triangle.</note> inscribed in it is equal to half of the line drawn from the center to the circumference. This was demonstrated there and concluded as a result. Since, therefore, from this first [proposition] of this fourteenth book it is clear that the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle to the side of a <term>pentagon</term> <note>A five-sided polygon.</note> is equal to half the line drawn from the center to the circumference and half the side of a decagon: it follows that the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle to the side of a pentagon is equal to the perpendicular drawn from the center to the side of the triangle, plus half the side of the decagon described within the same circle; and this is what is proposed in the conclusion.

Now, therefore, we must explain what **Aristeus** <note>Aristeus the Elder (c. 370–300 BCE), a mathematician known for work on "solid loci."</note> says in the book entitled *Exposition of the Knowledge of the Five Bodies*, and also **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BCE), famous for his work on Conics.</note> in his second "Gift" regarding the proportionality of a figure of 12 bases to a figure of 20 bases, saying: that the ratio of the surfaces of a figure having 12 bases to the surfaces of a figure having 20 bases is as the ratio of the volumes of the [figure of] 12 bases to the body of 20 bases. For indeed, the line drawn from the center of the circle of the pentagon of the figure of 12 bases, the <term>dodecahedron</term>, to its circumference is like the aforementioned line from the center of the circle of the triangle of the figure of 20 bases, the <term>icosahedron</term>, to its circumference. These are the words of the great Apollonius himself. They are to be understood, however, regarding a figure of 12 and a figure of 20 bases circumscribable by one and the same sphere. For the ratio of the body of a dodecahedron to the body of an icosahedron, when both are circumscribed by one and the same sphere, is as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together, just as Apollonius commemorates in the first part of the aforementioned words; which is also established by solid demonstration in the tenth [proposition] of this fourteenth book. And the circle circumscribing the pentagon of the dodecahedron is equal to the circle circumscribing the triangle of the icosahedron when the dodecahedron and icosahedron are circumscribed by the same sphere, just as Apollonius himself commemorates in the second part of the aforementioned words; which is also confirmed in the fifth demonstration of this book. Therefore, the antecedents to the eloquence of such great men must be set forth to be corroborated with unshaken truth.

Proposition .2.

<summary>This page provides a geometric proof relating the perpendiculars of inscribed polygons and cites the historical work of Aristeus and Apollonius regarding the ratio of surfaces and volumes for dodecahedrons and icosahedrons inscribed in the same sphere.</summary>

This text represents a portion of the medieval/Renaissance version of **Book XIV of the Elements** (traditionally attributed to **Hypsicles**), which concerns the comparison of the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron inscribed in the same sphere.

### XIIII [Book 14]

Whatever happens to one line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes [the Golden Ratio], is proved to happen to every line similarly divided, etc.

**[Demonstration]** Let there be two lines, $a.b.$ and $d.e.$, divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes: the former in $c$, the latter in $f$. Let the greater segments be $a.c.$ for the first, and $d.f.$ for the second. I say, therefore, that there is one [the same] proportion of both [whole lines] to their greater segments. Likewise, there is one proportion of both to their lesser segments, and also one [proportion] of the greater segments to the lesser segments, and conversely, and alternately, and jointly, and separately, and by conversion. For it is nothing else than whatever happens to one of them, the same also happens to the other. For it is established from the definition of a line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and from the first part of [Euclid] VI.16: that the [rectangle] which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ is equal to the square of $a.c.$; and in the same way, that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.f.$ is equal to the square of $d.f$. Therefore, the proportion of that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ to the square of $a.c.$ is as that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.f.$ to the square of $d.f.$, for both are a proportion of equality. Therefore, four times that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ to the square of $a.c.$ is as four times that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.f.$ to the square of $d.f.$, by [Euclid] V.15; and by alternating and equal proportionality, it is manifest that, jointly, four times that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ with the square of $a.c.$ to the square of $a.c.$ is as four times that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.f.$ with the square of $d.f.$ to the square of $d.f$. Let there be added in a straight line to line $a.b.$ one line which is equal to $b.c.$, which shall be called $b.g.$, and to $d.e.$ let there be added a line equal to $e.f.$, which shall be called $e.h$. [Note: OCR says $e.b.$, but context requires $e.h$]. It is manifest, therefore, from the eighth [proposition] of the second book [of Euclid] that four times that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.g.$ with the square of $a.c.$ is equal to the square of the line $a.g$. But truly, similarly, four times that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.h.$ with the square of $d.f.$ is equal to the square of $d.h$. But truly, from common knowledge, four times that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.c.$ is equal to four times that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $b.g.$, because $b.c.$ and $b.g.$ are equal. Similarly also, four times that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.f.$ is equal to four times that which is formed from $d.e.$ and $e.h.$, because $e.f.$ and $e.h.$ are also equal. Therefore, from the first part of V.7 and from V.11, the square of $a.g.$ is to the square of $a.c.$ as the square of $d.h.$ is to the square of $d.f$. Wherefore, from the second part of VI.21 [OCR says 21, likely 20 or 22 in standard numbering], the proportion of line $a.g.$ to line $a.c.$ is as line $d.h.$ to line $d.f.$, and jointly $a.g.$ and $a.c.$ to $a.c.$ as $d.h.$ and $d.f.$ to $d.f$. But truly, $a.g.$ with $a.c.$ are as double $a.b.$, and $d.h.$ with $d.f.$ as double $d.e$. Wherefore, double $a.b.$ is to $a.c.$ as double $d.e.$ to $d.f.$, and alternately double $a.b.$ to double $d.e.$ as $a.c.$ to $d.f$. But double $a.b.$ to double $d.e.$ is as $a.b.$ to $d.e.$ from V.15. Therefore, $a.b.$ is to $d.e.$ as $a.c.$ to $d.f$. Thus, by alternating, and by conversion, and by reversing, and by separating, and by joining: which was what was to be shown.

### Proposition 3

If the side of a hexagon is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, its greater part will be the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle circumscribing that same hexagon.

**[Demonstration]** Let line $a.b.$ be the side of the hexagon of some circle, and let it be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes at point $c$, and let its greater part be $b.c.$ I say that of whatever circle $a.b.$ is the side of the hexagon, $b.c.$ will be the side of the decagon of the same [circle]. For let there be added to line $a.b.$ the line $b.d.$, which is the side of the decagon of that circle of which $a.b.$ is the side of the hexagon. And from XIII.9, the line $a.d.$ will be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater part will be the line $a.b$. Since, therefore, each of the two lines $a.b.$ and $a.d.$ is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, therefore by the previous [proposition], there will be one proportion of both to their greater parts. Thus, $d.a.$ to $a.b.$ (which is its greater part) is as $a.b.$ to $b.c.$ (which is also its greater part). But $d.a.$ to $a.b.$ is as $a.b.$ to $b.d.$ from the definition of a line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes and its greater part. Therefore, from V.11, $a.b.$ is to $b.d.$ as $a.b.$ is to $b.c$. Wherefore, by the second part of V.9, $b.d.$ and $b.c.$ are equal. Since, therefore, $b.d.$ is the side of the decagon, from common knowledge $b.c.$ will also be the side of the decagon. Or otherwise: to line $a.b.$ add $b.d.$ equal to $b.c.$; and from XIII.4, the whole $a.d.$ will be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater part is line $a.b$. Thus, by the converse of XIII.9 (which we demonstrated immediately after it), of the circle of which line $a.b.$ is the side of the hexagon, the same line is $b.d.$ [side of decagon], and therefore line $b.c.$ (equal to it) is the side of the decagon. We can also demonstrate the same by another way if it pleases. For let $e.f.$ be equal to $a.b.$, which is also divided in $g$ according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and let its greater part be line $f.g$. It is established therefore from the preceding that just as $a.b.$ is equal to $e.f.$, so $a.c.$ is equal to $e.g.$ and $c.b.$ is equal to $g.f$. And when $b.d.$ is added to $a.b.$ as the side of the decagon of that circle of which $a.b.$ is the side of the hexagon, it will be (as said before) from XIII.9 that the whole $a.d.$ is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater part will be line $a.b$. Thus, by the preceding, $a.b.$ is to $b.d.$ as $f.g.$ to $g.e$. Wherefore, by the first part of VI.15 [likely VI.16], that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $g.e.$ is equal to that which is formed from $b.d.$ and $f.g$. And since $a.b.$ is equal to $e.f.$, it will be that which is formed from $e.f.$ and $g.e.$ is equal to that which is formed from $b.d.$ and $f.g$. But that which is formed from $e.f.$ and $g.e.$ is equal to the square of $f.g.$ from the definition of a line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes and from the first part of VI.16. Therefore, that which is formed from $b.d.$ and $f.g.$ is equal to the square of $f.g$. Therefore, from VI.1, line $b.d.$ is equal to $f.g$. And because $f.g.$ is equal to $c.b.$, $c.b.$ will also be equal to $b.d.$ and the side of the decagon, which was what was to be shown.

### Proposition 4

I pronounce that the square of the side of a pentagon inscribed in a circle, and the square of the line which subtends an angle of that pentagon, these both squares taken together, are five times the square of the half-diameter [radius] of the same circle.

**[Demonstration]** In circle $a.b.c.$, whose center is $d$, let there be inscribed one equilateral pentagon whose one side is $a.b.$, and let the diameter $c.d.e.$ be drawn out, dividing line $a.b.$ and its arc into equal parts. Therefore, arc $a.c.$ is half of a fifth part of the circumference of that circle, wherefore arc $a.c.$ is one fifth of the whole circumference [Note: text likely means arc $a.e.$]. Let two lines $a.e.$ and $a.c.$ be drawn out; $a.e.$ will be the side of an equilateral decagon because its arc is half of a fifth part of the circumference. Truly, line $a.c.$ will be that which subtends one of the angles of the aforesaid pentagon, because arc $a.c.$ is two-fifths of the circumference of the circle. I say, therefore, that the squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $a.c.$ taken together are five times the square of line $d.e$. For from II.4, the square of line $c.e.$ is four times the square of line $d.e$. Since, however, the angle $c.a.e.$ is a right angle from the first part of III.30, from the penultimate of the first [book] (Pythagorean theorem), the squares of the two lines $c.a.$ and $a.e.$ will be four times the square of $d.e$. Therefore, the squares of the three lines $c.a.$, $a.e.$, and $d.e.$ are five times the square of line $d.c$. And because from XIII.10 the square of $a.b.$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $a.e.$ and $d.e.$, it follows that the squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $c.a.$ are five times the square of $d.e.$, which is what was proposed.

**[Demonstration]** It is manifest, therefore, that the square of the side of a cube and the square of the side of the figure of twelve bases [dodecahedron], when the same sphere circumscribes the cube and the figure of twelve bases, both squares taken together are five times the square of the half-diameter of the circle which circumscribes the pentagon of that same figure of twelve bases.

**[Demonstration]** This corollary is truly manifest; for it is established from the demonstration of XIII.17 that the side of a cube subtends the angle of the pentagon of a dodecahedron when one and the same sphere circumscribes the cube and the dodecahedron. Thus, through this fourth [proposition], the corollary stands without obstacle, etc.

### Proposition 5

The pentagon of the figure of twelve bases [dodecahedron] and the triangle of the figure of twenty bases [icosahedron] which the same sphere circumscribes, are circumscribed by one and the same circle.

**[Demonstration]** Let there be a sphere whose diameter is $a.b.$, circumscribing two solid figures: namely, a dodecahedron of which one of the twelve pentagons is $c$, and an icosahedron of which one of the twenty triangles is $d$. For the pentagon $c$ and triangle $d$, let two circles be circumscribed upon two centers $d$ and $c$: for this one $f.c.$ from IV.14, and for that one $f.d.$ from IV.5. I say, therefore, that these two circles of the proposed spheres, of which one circumscribes pentagon $c$ and the other triangle $d$, are equal. For let two sides of pentagon $c$ containing one of its angles be marked with letters $e.f.$ and $f.g.$, and let line $e.g.$ be drawn out, which subtends angle $f$, and let the semi-diameter of the circle be $c.f$. Let each of the sides of triangle $d$ be marked with letters $k.h.$, and let the semi-diameter of its circle be $d.k$. Next, let line $l.m.$ be taken, to which line $a.b.$ (the diameter of the assigned sphere) is five-fold in power [$a.b.^2 = 5 \times l.m.^2$]. Let this $l.m.$ be divided in $n$ according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and let its greater part be line $l.n$. And according to the quantity of the whole $l.m.$, let circle $p.q.$ be lined out. Thus, the semi-diameter of circle $p.q.$ is equal to line $l.m$. Therefore, from the corollary of IV.15, line $l.m.$ is inscribed in circle $p.q.$ as the side of an equilateral hexagon. Therefore, by the third [proposition] of this [book], line $l.n.$ will be as the side of an equilateral decagon inscribed in the same circle. Therefore, from IV.11, let an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in circle $p.q.$ whose one side is $p.q$. From XIII.10, the square of $p.q.$ will be equal to the squares of the two lines $l.m.$ and $l.n.$ taken together. It is established, moreover, from the demonstration of XIII.16, that $b.k.$ [side of icosahedron] is equal to $p.q$. Therefore, the square of $b.k.$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $l.m.$ and $l.n.$ taken together. But truly, from the demonstration of XIII.17, it is manifest that $c.g.$ is the side of a cube circumscribable by the same sphere. Wherefore, by the corollary of XIII.14, $a.b.$ (the diameter of the sphere) is in power triple to $c.g.$ (the side of the cube). If, however, $e.g.$ is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, it is [shown] from the demonstration of XIII.17 that $e.f.$ is as its greater part. Therefore, by the second [proposition] of this [book], $c.g.$ is to $l.m.$ as $e.f.$ is to $l.n.$ [Correction: likely comparing the solids]. For as the whole is to the whole, so the greater part is to the greater part. Thus, by VI.21 [20/22], the square of $e.g.$ to the square of $l.m.$ is as the square of $c.f.$ to the square of $l.n$. Wherefore, by V.13, the squares of the two lines $e.g.$ and $e.f.$ taken together to the squares of the two lines $l.m.$ and $l.n.$ taken together are as the square of $e.g.$ to the square of $l.m$. Therefore, by V.15, and by alternating proportionality and equal, the triple of the two squares of the two lines $c.g.$ and $e.f.$ [Note: $c.g.$ and $e.g.$ are used interchangeably here in the OCR] taken together to the squares of the two lines $l.m.$ and $l.n.$ taken together is as the triple of the square of $e.g.$ to the square of $l.m$. The triple of the square $e.g.$ is as the square of $a.b.$ from the corollary of XIII.14. But the square of $a.b.$ is by hypothesis five-fold to the square of $l.m$. Therefore, the triple of the square of $e.g.$ is also five-fold to the square of $l.m$. Wherefore, also the triple of the squares of the two lines $e.g.$ and $e.f.$ taken together is five-fold to the squares of the two lines $l.m.$ and $l.n.$ taken together. It follows from common knowledge that the triple of the squares of $e.g.$ and $e.f.$ is five-fold to the square of $b.k$. It is established from XIII.8 that five times the square of $b.k.$ is fifteen times the square of $d.k.$, for the simple is triple. And from the fourth [proposition] of this [book], it is established that the triple of the squares of $e.g.$ and $e.f.$ is five times the square of $e.f.$, for the simple is five-fold. Thus, fifteen times the square of $c.f.$ is equal to fifteen times the square of $d.k$. Therefore, by V.15, the square of $c.f.$ is equal to the square of $d.k$. Wherefore, also line $c.f.$ is equal to line $d.k$. Therefore, from the definition of equal circles, the circle circumscribing pentagon $c$ is equal to the circle circumscribing triangle $d$, which was to be demonstrated from the beginning. For the semi-diameters of these circles are equal: namely, $c.f.$ and $d.k$.

### Proposition 6

The square, which is the triangle, or rather thirty times the rectangle which is contained under the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle circumscribing the pentagon of the figure of twelve bases to the side of the pentagon and under the side of the pentagon itself, is of necessity proved to be equal to all the surfaces of the body of twelve bases taken together.

**[Demonstration]** Let pentagon $a$ be one of the 12 bases of the figure of the dodecahedron, and let one of its sides be $b.c.$, and from IV.14 let a circle be circumscribed upon center $a$, and let lines $a.b.$, $a.c.$, and $a.d.$ (perpendicular to $b.c.$) be drawn out. I say, therefore, that thirty times that which is formed from $a.d.$ and $b.c.$ is equal to all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together. For it is established that pentagon $a$ is divisible into five triangles equal to triangle $a.b.c.$ from I.8. Thus, all 12 pentagons of the dodecahedron, since all are equal and similar to pentagon $a$, are divisible into 60 triangles, each of which by I.8 is equal to triangle $a.b.c$. Moreover, that which is from $a.d.$ and $b.c.$ is double, by I.41, to triangle $a.b.c$. Therefore, thirty times that which is from $a.d.$ and $b.c.$ is sixty times the triangle $a.b.c.$, for as the simple is to the simple, so the double to the double. Since, therefore, all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together are also sixty times triangle $a.b.c.$, it follows that thirty times that which is from $a.d.$ and $b.c.$ is equal to all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 7

The square, which is the triangle, or rather thirty times the rectangle which is contained under the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle to the side of the inscribed triangle of the figure of twenty bases and under the side itself of the triangle, is equal to all the surfaces of the figure of twenty bases taken together.

**[Demonstration]** Let this triangle $e$ be one of the 20 bases of the figure of the icosahedron, and let one of its sides be $f.g.$, and from IV.5 let a circle be circumscribed upon center $e$, and let lines $e.f.$, $e.g.$, and $e.h.$ (perpendicular to $f.g.$) be drawn out. I say, therefore, that thirty times that which is from $e.h.$ and $f.g.$ is equal to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together. For it is established that triangle $e$ is divisible into three triangles, each of which by I.8 is equal to triangle $e.f.g$. Thus, all 20 triangles of the icosahedron taken together, since they are all equal and similar to triangle $e$, are as sixty times the triangle $e.f.g$. And by I.14 [I.41], that which is from $e.h.$ and $f.g.$ is double triangle $e.f.g$. Therefore, thirty times this is equal to sixty times that. It follows that thirty times $e.h.$ by $f.g.$ is equal to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together, which was to be demonstrated.

**[Conclusion]** It is manifest, therefore, that the proportion of the surfaces of the figure of twelve bases [dodecahedron] in some containing sphere to the surfaces of the figure of twenty bases [icosahedron] concluded in the same sphere is as the proportion of the rectangle contained under the side of the pentagon of that figure of twelve bases and under the perpendicular drawn from the center of its circle to that side of the pentagon, to the rectangle contained under the side of the triangle of that figure of twenty bases and the perpendicular drawn from the center of its circle to the side of the triangle of the body of twenty *alchaidaz* [Note: "alchaidaz" is a medieval term, likely from Arabic *al-qa'idah*, meaning "bases" or "faces"]. Which, through that corollary, results in being so, whether the figure of 12 bases and the figure of 20 bases are circumscribable by the same sphere as proposed, or even if they were circumscribable by different spheres. But it is proposed according as these figures are circumscribable by the same sphere, because in this way it is valid and suffices for the proposition. Its common truth is proved thus: it is established from the 6th [proposition] of this [book] that thirty times $a.d.$ by $b.c.$ is equal to all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together, of which pentagon $a$ is one of the 12 surfaces; and from this 7th, it is established similarly that thirty times $e.h.$ by $f.g.$ is equal to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together, of which triangle $e$ is one of the 20 bases, whether the same sphere circumscribes that dodecahedron and this icosahedron or different [spheres]. Thus, the proportion of thirty times $a.d.$ by $b.c.$ to all the surfaces of that dodecahedron taken together is as thirty times $e.h.$ by $f.g.$ to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together: for on both sides there is a proportion of equality. Wherefore, alternately, thirty times $a.d.$ by $b.c.$ to thirty times $e.h.$ by $f.g.$ is as all the surfaces of that dodecahedron to all the surfaces of this icosahedron. And by V.15, thirty times to thirty times is as the simple to the simple. It is established, therefore, by V.11, that the proportion of all surfaces of that dodecahedron to all the surfaces of this icosahedron is as that which is from $a.d.$ and $b.c.$ to that which is from $e.h.$ and $f.g.$, and this is what is proposed from the corollary.

### Proposition 8

The proportion of all the surfaces of the body of twelve bases [dodecahedron] taken together to all the surfaces of the body of twenty bases [icosahedron] taken together, both of which are circumscribed by one sphere, is as the proportion of the side of the cube which the same sphere circumscribes to the side of the triangle of that body of twenty bases.

**[Demonstration]** That all ambiguity may depart from the process of the demonstration of this 8th [proposition] of the 14th book, it is necessary to know this beforehand: That if any line should be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and from its half as if half of its greater part is taken away: the half itself will also be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater part is as half of the greater part of its double. For example: let $a.b.$ be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes in $c$, and let its greater part be $a.c.$ And let $d.e.$ be as half of $a.b.$, and $d.f.$ as half of $a.c$. I say, therefore, that $d.e.$ is divided in $f$ according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater part is $d.f$. For it is established from V.15 that the proportion of $a.b.$ to $a.c.$ is as $d.e.$ to $d.f.$ (namely, double to double as simple to simple). Wherefore, alternately $a.b.$ to $d.e.$ is as $a.c.$ to $d.f$. Therefore, by V.19, $c.b.$ is to $f.e.$ as $a.b.$ to $d.e$. Thus $c.b.$ is double to $f.e.$, just as $a.b.$ is to $d.e$. Since, therefore, the whole $a.b.$ is double to the whole $d.e.$ and the individual parts of $a.b.$ to the individual parts of $d.e.$, wherefore from V.15 and V.11 for the division of a line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, the line $d.e.$ will be divided in $f$ just as is proposed. Now, therefore, we press on to the demonstration of that which was proposed. For this [proposition], in circle $a.b.c.$ with center $d$, let there be circumscribed the pentagon of the dodecahedron and the triangle of the icosahedron, which both together the same sphere circumscribes and concludes. For from the 5th [proposition] of this [book], it is manifest that the same circle circumscribes the pentagon of the one and the triangle of the other. Let line $a.b.$ be the side of the pentagon and line $a.c.$ the side of the triangle. And let line $b$ [Note: this represents a specific line segment] be as the side of the cube circumscribed by the same sphere. It is to be [shown] that the proportion of all surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together is as line $b$ to line $a.c$. Let there be produced from the center $d$ a perpendicular to $a.b.$ which shall pass through to the circumference, cutting $a.b.$ in point $e$ and its arc in point $f$. It is established that this perpendicular divides into equal parts both the line $a.b.$ and its arc: the chord $a.b.$ by the second part of III.3, the arc truly by I.4 and III.27. Therefore, arc $f.a.$ is a tenth part of the circumference. Let there be subtended to it the chord $a.f.$, which will be the side of the equilateral decagon of the same circle. Therefore, from XIII.9, the line consisting of $d.f.$ and $f.a.$ [joined together] is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater part will be line $d.f$. But truly from the first [proposition] of this [book], $d.e.$ is equal to half of $d.f.$ and half of $f.a.$ joined in length and straightness. Let $d.g.$ be the perpendicular to $a.c.$, and it will be from the corollary of XIII.8 that $g.d.$ is as half of $d.f$. Thus, if from line $d.e.$ (which is as half of $d.f.$ and $f.a.$ as one line) there is taken away [a line] equal to $d.g.$ (which is as half of $d.f.$), it will be by that which was proved before this that line $d.e.$ is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and the greater part will be as $g.d$. From the demonstration of XIII.17, it is established that if line $b$ (which is the side of the cube) is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, its greater part will be as $a.b.$, which is the side of the pentagon of the figure of 12 bases. Thus, by the second [proposition] of this [book], the proportion of $b$ to $a.b.$ is as $d.e.$ to $g.d$. Wherefore, by the first part of VI.15 [VI.16], that which results from $b$ and $g.d.$ is equal to that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $d.e$. From the corollary of the preceding [proposition], it is manifest that the proportion of all surfaces of the dodecahedron (whose side is $a.b.$) taken together to all surfaces of the icosahedron (whose side is $a.c.$) taken together is as that which is formed from $a.b.$ and $d.e.$ to that which is formed from $a.c.$ and $g.d$. Therefore, from the first part of V.7, the proportion of all surfaces of that dodecahedron to all [surfaces] of this icosahedron [is the same]. But truly, that which results from $b$ and $g.d.$ to that which results from $a.c.$ and $g.d.$ is, by VI.1, as $b$ to $a.c$. Thus, by V.11, the proportion of all the surfaces of that dodecahedron to all [surfaces] of this icosahedron is as $b$ to $a.c.$, which is what was proposed. We could prove this same thing in another way, if we first sent forth a necessary antecedent to it, which is:

**[Digression on Fractions]** If in any circle an equilateral pentagon is inscribed, the rectangle which is contained under three-quarters [*dodrans*] of the diameter of that circle and under five-sixths [*dextans*] of the line subtending an angle of that pentagon, must of necessity be equal to the same pentagon.

**[Conclusion]** Our ancestors divided each whole [integer] into 12 equal parts by intellect and reason, and called all of them together—that is, the whole itself—an *As*. Eleven of them they called a *Deunx*. Ten, a *Dextans*. Nine, a *Dodrans*. Eight, a *Bisse*. Seven, a *Septunx*. Six, a *Semis*. Five, a *Quincunx*. Four, a *Triens*. Three, a *Quadrans*. Two, a *Sextans*. One, they called an *Uncia* [ounce/inch]. And they designated them in order by such figures as are very often found in ancient books:

[Table of Roman Fractions: As, Deunx, Dextans, Dodrans, Bisse, Septunx / Semis, Quincunx, Triens, Quadrans, Sextans, Uncia]

**[Conclusion]** The *Uncia*, which we said to be the twelfth part of the *As*, they divided again into 12 fractions. But they divided by another way: for they called half of an *Uncia* a *Semuncia*. A third, a *Duella*. A fourth, a *Sicilicus*. A sixth, a *Sexcula*. An eighth, a *Dragma*. A twelfth, a *Semisicula*. An eighteenth, a *Tremissis*. A twenty-fourth, a *Scrupulus*. A forty-eighth, an *Obulus*. A seventy-second, a *Bissiliqua*. A ninety-sixth, a *Cerates*. The last, which is the 144th part of the *Uncia* itself, they named a *Siliqua*. To these 12 fractions of the *Uncia*, later men added the *Calcus*. The *Calcus* is the 192nd part of the *Uncia*. The reason for this addition was that it might descend or reach to the smallest extreme interval of the *diatessaron* and *diapente* harmonies, tones, and semitones distinguished by the denomination of these fractions. And they marked them all in order with such figures:

[Table of smaller fractions: Semuncia, Duella, Sicilicus, Sexcula, Dragma, Emmicecia (Hemiekton), Tremissis, Scrupulus, Obulus, Bissiliqua, Cerates, Siliqua, Calcus]

**[Conclusion]** Therefore, of that which is said, the sense is: that if in any circle an equilateral pentagon is inscribed, that which is formed from three-quarters of the diameter of the circle and five-sixths of the line subtending one of the angles of the inscribed pentagon is equal to the pentagon. For example: let the circle be $a.b.c.$ upon center $d$, and to it from IV.11 let there be inscribed an equilateral pentagon whose two sides containing one of its angles are $a.b.$ and $b.c.$, and to angle $b$ let line $a.c.$ be subtended, and let diameter $b.d.e.$ be drawn out cutting line $a.c.$ into equal parts at point $g$. And let $d.f.$ be half of $d.e.$ [Note: OCR says $d.c.$, likely $d.e.$], and $g.h.$ double to $b.g.$ [Note: OCR says $b.c.$, likely $b.g.$]. And $b.f.$ will be three-quarters [*dodrans*] of the diameter, for it is three-fourths of it; and $a.h.$ [Note: context suggests a segment of the diagonal] will be five-sixths [*dextans*]. Let line $a.d.$ be drawn out. I say that that which results from $b.f.$ and $a.h.$ is equal to the pentagon inscribed in the circle. For since $a.g.$ is perpendicular to $b.d.$, it will be from I.41 that that which results from $b.d.$ and $a.g.$ is double to triangle $a.b.d$. Therefore, what results from $b.f.$ and $a.g.$ will be triple to the same triangle, and what results from $b.f.$ and $b.g.$ double, and from $b.f.$ to the whole $a.h.$, five-fold. Since therefore the whole pentagon is five-fold to the same triangle, it is established that this which is from $b.f.$ and $a.h.$ [Note: OCR says $a.b.$] is equal to the pentagon, and that was to be demonstrated. That which was proposed from the beginning, let us now demonstrate by another way as we promised. There are, therefore, in the circle whose center is $d$ [Note: OCR says $b$], the inscribed pentagon of the dodecahedron and the triangle of the icosahedron which the same sphere circumscribes. For it is established from the 5th [proposition] of this [book] that the pentagon of this dodecahedron and the triangle of that icosahedron are circumscribed by the same circle. And let pentagon be $a.b.c.d.e.$ and triangle $a.f.g.$, and to angle $a$ of the pentagon let line $b.c.$ be subtended, which from the demonstration of XIII.17 will be the side of the cube which the same sphere concludes. Let diameter $a.h.k.$ be drawn out, cutting orthogonally and into equal parts both of the lines $b.c.$ and $f.g.$: this one in point $l$ and that one in point $m$. I say therefore that the proportion of all surfaces of the dodecahedron to all [surfaces] of the icosahedron, whose pentagon and triangle are inscribed in the proposed circle, is as line $b.c.$ (which is the side of the cube concluded by the same sphere) to line $f.g.$ (which is the side of the triangle of the icosahedron). For it is established from the corollary of XIII.8 that line $b.l.$ [Note: OCR says $b.m.$] is half of line $a.b.$ [Note: possibly $b.c.$], therefore $a.l.$ will be three-quarters [*dodrans*] of the diameter $a.k.$, for it is three-fourths of it. Let $l.n.$ be double to $n.c.$ [Note: unclear reading], $b.n.$ will be five-sixths [*dextans*] of $b.c$. Thus, by the preceding antecedent, what results from $a.l.$ [Note: OCR says $a.m.$] and $b.n.$ will be equal to the pentagon $a.b.c.d.e$. That which results from $a.l.$ and $l.f.$ [Note: OCR $m.f.$] is equal to triangle $a.f.g$. Therefore, from VI.1, the proportion of the pentagon to the triangle is as $b.n.$ to $l.f$. Wherefore, twelve-fold of that pentagon to twenty-fold of this triangle are as twelve-fold of line $b.n.$ to twenty-fold of line $l.f$. Which is manifest from V.15 and equal proportionality. Twelve-fold of $b.n.$ is as ten-fold of $b.c.$, for 12 *dextantes* equal 10 *asses* (that is, 10 wholes). Twenty-fold of $l.f.$ is as ten-fold of $f.g.$, for $f.g.$ is double to $l.f$. Therefore, twelve-fold of this pentagon to twenty-fold of this triangle is as ten-fold of $b.c.$ to ten-fold of $f.g$. And because twelve-fold of that pentagon is all the surfaces of the dodecahedron, and twenty-fold of this triangle is all the surfaces of the icosahedron, and because by V.15 ten-fold $b.c.$ to ten-fold $f.g.$ is as simple $b.c.$ to simple $f.g.$, it will be by V.11 that the proportion of all surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all surfaces of the icosahedron taken together is as $b.c.$ to $f.g$. And this is what was required for us to demonstrate.

### Proposition 9

If any line is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, the proportion of the line which is powerful [the side of the square] over the whole line and its greater part to the line which is powerful over the whole and its lesser part, will be as the proportion of the side of the cube to the side of the triangle of the body of twenty bases [icosahedron] contained with the cube itself in the same sphere.

**[Demonstration]** Let line $a.b.$ be divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and let its greater part be line $a.c$. Upon center $a$, according to the quantity of line $a.b.$, let circle $d.b.e.$ be described. In it, from IV.11, let an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, whose one side is $d.e.$, and from IV.2 an equilateral triangle whose one side is $d.f$. To one of the angles of the pentagon (which is $d$), let line $e.g.$ be subtended. It is established therefore from the 5th [proposition] of this [book] that the sphere circumscribing the dodecahedron whose pentagon side is $d.e.$ also circumscribes the icosahedron whose triangle side is $d.f$. And from the demonstration of XIII.17, it is manifest that the same sphere circumscribes the cube whose side is $e.g$. Therefore, let line $h$ [OCR says $b$] be taken, being powerful over the whole $a.b.$ and its greater part $a.c$. And let $k$ be taken, being powerful over the whole $a.b.$ and its lesser part $b.c$. I say, therefore, that the proportion of $e.g.$ to $d.f.$ (that is, of the side of the cube to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron) is as $h$ to $k$, or rather simply as $h$ to $k$. It is established indeed from the corollary of IV.15 that $a.b.$ is as the side of an equilateral hexagon inscribed in circle $b.d.e$. Therefore, from the third [proposition] of this [book], $a.c.$ is as the side of the equilateral decagon of the same circle. Thus, by XIII.10, $d.e.$ is powerful over the whole $a.b.$ and its greater part $a.c$. Wherefore, $d.e.$ is equal to $h$, for the square of each of them is as much as the squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $a.c.$ taken together. It is [shown] from XIII.8 that $d.f.$ is triple in power to $a.b$. [Correction: $d.f.^2 = 3 \times radius^2$]. But truly from XIII.5 it is clear that $k$ also is triple in power to $a.c$. Therefore, from the second part of VI.21, the proportion of $d.f.$ to $a.b.$ is as $k$ to $a.c$. Wherefore, alternately $d.f.$ to $k$ is as $a.b.$ to $a.c$. And because from the demonstration of XIII.17 it is manifest that if $e.g.$ is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, its greater part will be as $d.e.$, it will be by the second [proposition] of this [book] that the proportion of $e.g.$ to $d.e.$ is as $a.b.$ to $a.c$. Wherefore, by V.11, $e.g.$ to $d.e.$ will also be as $d.f.$ to $k$, and alternately $e.g.$ to $d.f.$ as $d.e.$ to $k$. And because by the first part of V.7, $d.e.$ to $k$ is as $h$ to $k$ (because $d.e.$ and $h$ are equal), it will be by V.11 that $e.g.$ to $d.f.$ is as $h$ to $k$, which is what was proposed. Not only is the proportion of $e.g.$ (side of cube) to $d.f.$ (side of triangle of icosahedron) as $h$ to $k$, but simply as any two lines, one to the other, of which one is powerful over any line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes and over its greater part, and the other truly over the whole and its lesser part. For of individual such lines there is one proportion. For example: let the previous hypotheses remain concerning lines $a.b.$, $h$, and $k$. And let any other line also be taken, which is $l.m.$, divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes in $n$, and let the greater part be $l.n$. And let line $p$ be powerful over the whole $l.m.$ and its greater part $l.n$, and line $q$ be powerful over the whole $l.m.$ and its lesser part $m.n$. I say, therefore, that the proportion of $p$ to $q$ is as $h$ to $k$. It is established from the second [proposition] of this [book] that $a.b.$ to $a.c.$ is as $l.m.$ to $l.n$. Therefore, by the first part of VI.21, the square of $b.a.$ to the square of $a.c.$ is as the square of $m.l.$ to the square of $n.l$. Wherefore, jointly the square of $h$ to the square of $a.c.$ is as the square of $p$ to the square of $l.n$, and alternately the square of $h$ to the square of $p$ as the square of $a.c.$ to the square of $l.n$. By the same kind of reasoning, it follows that the proportion of the square of $k$ to the square of $q$ is as the square of $c.b.$ to the square of $n.m$. Since from the second [proposition] of this [book] and from the first part of VI.21, the square of $a.c.$ is to the square of $l.n.$ as the square of $c.b.$ to the square of $m.n$, it will be from V.11 that the square of $h$ to the square of $p$ is as the square of $k$ to the square of $q$. Wherefore, by the second part of VI.21, $h$ to $p$ as $k$ to $q$. And alternately $h$ to $k$ as $p$ to $q$, which was to be demonstrated. And lest any place of doubt should obscure those things which remain to be demonstrated, we think certain things should still be sent beforehand, by which the following may remain unshaken with the firm strength of demonstration.

**[Lemma]** If any plane surface cuts any sphere, the common difference of the cutting plane surface and the curved surface of the sphere will be a circumference containing a circle.

**[Demonstration]** Therefore, let there be some plane surface cutting a sphere, and let line $a.b.$ be the common section of the cutting surface and the surface of the sphere. I say that line $a.b.$ is the circumference of a circle. For either the center of the sphere is in the cutting plane surface, or outside. If it is in it, let it be placed wherever it happens, and let it be $c$. Because therefore the whole line $a.b.$ is in the surface of the sphere, and because all lines drawn from the center of the sphere to its circumference are equal (as is established from the definition of a sphere), it follows that all lines drawn from point $c$ to line $a.b.$ are equal. Therefore, from the definition of a circle, the surface which line $a.b.$ contains is a circle and its center is $c$, namely the same as the center of the sphere. If, however, the center of the sphere is outside the cutting surface, let it be placed wherever you please, and let it be $d$; from which, according to the doctrine of XI.11, let line $d.c.$ be drawn perpendicular to the cutting surface. And let there be drawn from the same center $d$ two straight lines, however they happen, to line $a.b.$, which shall be $d.a.$ and $d.b.$, and join $c$ with $a$ and with $b$. The two lines $d.a.$ and $d.b.$ will be equal because they are from the center of the sphere to its surface. From the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface, it is manifest that angles $d.c.a.$ and $d.c.b.$ are right angles. Therefore, from the penultimate of the first [book] and this common knowledge—that those which are equal to equals are equal among themselves—the squares of the two lines $c.d.$ and $c.a.$ taken together will be equal to the squares of the two lines $d.c.$ and $c.b.$ taken together. Taking away therefore the square of $d.c.$ from both, the square of $c.a.$ will be equal to the square of $c.b.$, wherefore also line $c.a.$ to line $c.b$. By the same kind of reasoning, it is necessary that all lines drawn from point $c$ to line $a.b.$ are equal. Therefore, from the definition of a circle, the surface which line $a.b.$ contains is a circle and its center is $c$, which is what was proposed.

**[Corollary]** From this, therefore, it is manifest that when a surface cuts a sphere through its center, the section resulting on the surface of the sphere is a line containing a circle whose center is the center of the sphere. When, however, the surface cuts the sphere not through its center, the section resulting on the surface of the sphere is also a line containing a circle whose center is that point in which the perpendicular drawn from the center of the sphere to the cutting surface falls.

Furthermore, I say that:

**[Theorem]** If in any sphere there are equal circles, the perpendiculars drawn from the center of the sphere to the surfaces of those circles will be equal to each other.

**[Demonstration]** In a sphere whose center is $a$, let two equal circles $b$ and $c$ be marked, to the surfaces of which let perpendiculars be drawn from the center of the sphere (namely from point $a$) as XI.11 teaches: to this one $a.b.$, to that one $a.c$. I say that the two lines $a.b.$ and $a.c.$ are equal. For let there be drawn from points $b$ and $c$ individual straight lines to the circumferences of those circles as you please: in this one $b.d.$, in that one $c.e$. And join $a$ with $d$ and with $e$. From the definition of a line standing perpendicularly upon a surface, the angle $a.b.d.$ and $a.c.e.$ will be right on both sides. But truly from the second part of the preceding corollary, or rather it is manifest that the two points $b$ and $c$ are centers of circles $b$ and $c$; therefore, the two lines $b.d.$ and $c.e.$ are their semi-diameters. Since these circles are assumed equal, it follows from the definition of equal circles that these semi-diameters are equal. And because the two lines $a.d.$ and $a.e.$ are equal (for they are drawn from the center of the sphere to its surface), from the penultimate of the first [book], the two perpendiculars $a.b.$ and $a.c.$ will be equal, which was to be demonstrated. Now therefore let us return to the proposition.

### Proposition 10

The proportion of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, both of which one and the same sphere includes, is as the proportion of all its surfaces taken together to all the surfaces of that [other] taken together.

**[Demonstration]** This is what we commemorated above after the demonstration of the first [proposition] of this [book] by the authority of **Aristeus** and **Apollonius**, whose demonstration is evidently elicited from those things which have been sent before. From the 5th [proposition] of this [book] it is manifest that the circles of which one circumscribes the pentagon of the dodecahedron and the other the triangle of the icosahedron (which both bodies one sphere contains) are equal to each other. Thus, the perpendiculars from the center of the sphere to the surfaces of all the circles circumscribing the pentagons of this dodecahedron and the triangles of that icosahedron, falling into their centers, will be equal to each other, as is manifest from the preceding. For all these circles, by the witness of the 5th [proposition] of this [book] (as was said), are equal to each other. [The bodies are composed of] pyramids, therefore, of which the bases are the pentagons of the dodecahedron and their summits are the center of the sphere; and pyramids of which the bases are the triangles of the icosahedron and their summits similarly are the center of the sphere, are equally high. The perpendiculars falling from the summits to the bases measure or determine the altitude of all the pyramids. But it is necessary that equally high pyramids be proportional to their bases, as was proved in XII.6. Thus, the proportion of a pyramid whose base is a pentagon of the dodecahedron to a pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as [the area of] that pentagon to this triangle. Therefore, by V.24, the proportion of the twelve-fold of that pyramid whose base is a pentagon of the dodecahedron to [one] pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as the twelve-fold of that pentagon to this triangle. These 12 pyramids whose bases are the 12 pentagons of the dodecahedron are as the whole body of the dodecahedron itself. And the 12 pentagons are as all its surfaces. Thus, the proportion of the body of the dodecahedron to the pyramid whose base is the triangle of the icosahedron is as the proportion of all surfaces of the dodecahedron to the triangle of the icosahedron. Wherefore, again from V.24, the proportion of the body of the dodecahedron to the twenty-fold of that pyramid whose base is the triangle of the icosahedron is as all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to the twenty-fold of the triangle of the icosahedron. Since, therefore, the twenty-fold of this pyramid is as the whole body of the icosahedron, and the twenty-fold of this triangle is as all the surfaces of the icosahedron themselves, the proportion of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron (which both one and the same sphere concludes) will be as the proportion of all the surfaces of the body of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the body of the icosahedron taken together. This, however, is the opinion of the aforesaid philosophers concerning the proportion of these two bodies, fixed and solid, strengthened by demonstration.

Line AB: Since, therefore, each of the two lines AB and AD is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes <note>original: "proportionem habentem medium duoque extrema"; this refers to the Golden Ratio, where the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the larger segment to the smaller one</note>, it will be, by the previous proposition, that there is one proportion for both of them to their larger portions. Thus, DA is to AB (which is its larger portion) as AB is to BC (which is also its larger portion). Likewise, DA is to AB as AB is to BD, by the definition of a line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes and its larger portion. Therefore, from the eleventh [proposition] of the fifth [book], AB is to BD as AB is to BC; wherefore, by the second part of the ninth [proposition] of the fifth [book], BD and BC are equal. Since, therefore, BD is the side of a decagon <note>A ten-sided polygon</note>, BC will also be the side of a decagon by common knowledge. 

Or otherwise: let BD be joined to line AB, being equal to BC. Then, by the fourth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], the whole line AD is divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its larger portion is line AB. Thus, by the converse of the ninth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], which we demonstrated immediately after it, if line AB is the side of a hexagon <note>A six-sided polygon; in a circle, the side of an inscribed hexagon is equal to the radius</note> of a certain circle, then line BD (and therefore line BC, which is equal to it) is the side of a decagon. 

We can also demonstrate the same thing in another way if we wish. Let EF be equal to AB, and let it also be divided at G according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and let its larger portion be line FG. It is evident, therefore, from the previous [proposition], that just as AB is equal to EF, so AC is equal to EG and CB is equal to GF. And when BD is added to AB as the side of the decagon of that circle of which AB is the side of the hexagon, it will be, as was said before from the ninth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], that the whole line AD is divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its larger portion will be line AB. Thus, by the previous [proposition], AB is to BD as FG is to GE. Therefore, by the first part of the fifteenth [proposition] of the sixth [book], the product of AB and GE is equal to the product of BD and FG. And since AB is equal to EF, the product of EF and GE will be equal to the product of BD and FG. But the product of EF and GE is equal to the square of FG, by the definition of a line divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes and from the first part of the sixteenth [proposition] of the sixth [book]. Therefore, the product of BD and FG is equal to the square of FG, and so, from the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], line BD is equal to FG. And because FG is equal to CB, CB will also be equal to BD, which is the side of the decagon, as was to be shown.

**XIV**

The squares of the two lines *a.b* and *c.a* are five times the square of *d.e*, which is what was proposed.

¶ It is manifest, therefore, that the square of the side of the cube and the square of the side of the figure of twelve bases <note>the dodecahedron</note>—when the same sphere circumscribes both the cube and the dodecahedron—both squares taken together are five times the square of the radius <note>literally "half the diameter"</note> of the circle that circumscribes the pentagon of that same dodecahedron.

¶ This corollary is truly manifest; for it is established from the seventeenth demonstration of the thirteenth book <note>referring to Proposition 17 of Book XIII of Euclid's Elements</note> that the side of the cube subtends the angle of the pentagon of the dodecahedron when one and the same sphere circumscribes both the cube and the dodecahedron. Thus, by this fourth proposition, the corollary stands established without obstacle.

The <term>ounce</term> <note>Latin: *uncia*; the standard unit of measurement here, representing one-twelfth of a whole</note>, which we have previously stated is the twelfth part of the <term>as</term> <note>Latin: *as*; the primary unit of weight or value in the Roman system</note>, was divided by others again into twelve further fractions. For they called half of an ounce a <term>semiuncia</term> <note>meaning "half-ounce"</note>; the third part, a <term>duella</term>; the fourth part, a <term>sicilicus</term>; the sixth part, a <term>sextula</term> <note>OCR reads *sexcula*</note>; the eighth part, a <term>drachma</term> <note>a term borrowed from the Greek weight system</note>; the twelfth part, a <term>semisextula</term> <note>OCR reads *semissiclam*; literally "half a sextula"</note>; the eighteenth part, a <term>tremissis</term>; the twenty-fourth part, a <term>scrupulum</term> <note>the "scruple," a tiny unit of weight</note>; the forty-eighth part, an <term>obolus</term>; the seventy-second part, a <term>bissiliqua</term> <note>meaning "two siliquae"</note>; the ninety-sixth part, a <term>ceratium</term> <note>OCR reads *cerace*; the root of the word "carat"</note>. The very last part, which is the 144th part of the ounce itself, they named the <term>siliqua</term> <note>originally the seed of the carob tree, used as the smallest Roman weight</note>.

# **BOOK**

->[A geometric diagram is positioned here. It shows a large circle representing a sphere. Inside, two smaller circles are depicted in perspective as ellipses. A vertical line passes through the center of the large circle, labeled **a**. This line also passes through the centers of the two ellipses, labeled **b** and **c**. Let there be two equal circles, **b** and **c**, marked within a sphere whose center is **a**. To the surfaces of these circles, perpendicular lines are drawn from the center of the sphere—namely from point **a**—according to the instructions in the eleventh proposition of the Eleventh Book <note>This refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book XI, which deals with solid geometry</note>: one line being **ab** and the other **ac**. I say that these two lines, **ab** and **ac**, are equal. 

To prove this, let straight lines be drawn from points **b** and **c** to the circumferences of those circles as one pleases: specifically **bd** in the first circle and **ce** in the second. Then, let lines **ad** and **ae** be joined. By the definition of a line standing perpendicularly above a surface, both of the two angles **abd** and **ace** will be right angles. Furthermore, from the second part of the previously mentioned corollary, it is manifest that the two points **b** and **c** are the centers of the circles **b** and **c**; therefore, the two lines **bd** and **ce** are their <term>semidiameters</term> <note>radii</note>. Since these circles are posited as being equal, it follows from the definition of equal circles that these semidiameters are equal. And because the two lines **ad** and **ae** are equal (as they are drawn from the center of the sphere to its surface <note>they are both radii of the sphere</note>), it follows from the second-to-last proposition of the First Book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Book I, Prop. 47</note> that the two perpendiculars **ab** and **ac** are equal, which is what was required to be demonstrated. Now, therefore, let us return to the main proposition.

### **Proposition 10**

**P**he ratio of the body of a <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>a 12-faced solid</note> to the body of an <term>icosahedron</term> <note>a 20-faced solid</note>, when both are enclosed by one and the same sphere, is the same as the ratio of the sum of all the dodecahedron's surfaces to the sum of all the icosahedron's surfaces.

This is what we mentioned earlier, following the demonstration of the first [proposition], on the authority of Aristaeus and Apollonius <note>Aristaeus the Elder and Apollonius of Perga, Greek mathematicians who studied conic sections and regular solids</note>, the demonstration of which is clearly drawn from the premises already established. 

From the fifth proposition of this book, it is manifest that the circles circumscribing the pentagonal face of the dodecahedron and the triangular face of the icosahedron (where both bodies are contained by one sphere) are equal to one another. Therefore, the perpendiculars falling from the center of the sphere to the centers of all the circles circumscribing the pentagons of this dodecahedron and the triangles of that icosahedron will be equal to one another, as is clear from the previous proofs. For all these circles, as stated in the fifth proposition, are equal to one another. 

The <term>pyramids</term> <note>The author envisions the solids as being composed of pyramids whose bases are the faces of the solid and whose apexes meet at the center of the sphere</note> whose bases are the pentagons of the dodecahedron, and whose apexes are the center of the sphere, and the pyramids whose bases are the triangles of the icosahedron, and whose apexes are likewise the center of the sphere, are all of equal height. This height is measured or determined by the perpendiculars falling from the apexes to the bases. 

It is necessary for pyramids of equal height to be proportional to their bases, as was proved in the sixth proposition of the Twelfth Book. Thus, the ratio of a pyramid whose base is a pentagon of the dodecahedron to a pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as the ratio of that pentagon to that triangle. Therefore, by the twenty-fourth proposition of the Fifth Book, the ratio of the twelve-fold sum of those pyramids (whose bases are the twelve pentagons of the dodecahedron) to the pyramid of the icosahedron is as the twelve-fold sum of those pentagons to the triangle. 

These twelve pyramids, whose bases are the twelve pentagons, constitute the entire body of the dodecahedron itself. Similarly, the twelve pentagons constitute all of its surfaces. Thus, the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to a pyramid of the icosahedron is as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to one triangle of the icosahedron. 

Wherefore, again by the twenty-fourth proposition of the Fifth Book, the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the twenty-fold sum of those pyramids (whose bases are the triangles of the icosahedron) is as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to the twenty-fold sum of the triangles of the icosahedron. Since the twenty-fold sum of these pyramids is the same as the whole body of the icosahedron, and the twenty-fold sum of the triangles is the same as all the surfaces of the icosahedron, it follows that the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron (both enclosed by the same sphere) is as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together. 

This was the settled opinion of the aforementioned philosophers regarding the proportion of these two bodies, now strengthened by a solid demonstration.
