To which this must also be added: for since the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the side of a cube to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron [**ꝯ**] concluded within the same sphere together with the cube itself is as the ratio [**ꝓ**] of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron itself concluded in the same sphere, as has been demonstrated from the 8th [proposition] of this [book]: it will follow from the 11th of the Fifth [Book of Euclid] that the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, both of which are revolved by one sphere, is as the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the side of the cube inscribable in the same sphere to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron. Furthermore, because when any line is divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes [the Golden Ratio], the ratio of the line powerful over [whose square is equal to] the whole and its greater portion to the line powerful over the whole and its lesser portion is as the side of a cube inscribed in some sphere to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron circumscribed by the same sphere, as demonstrated from the 9th [proposition] of this [book], it will also be from the 11th of the Fifth that, with any line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes, the ratio of the line powerful over the whole and its greater portion to the line powerful over the whole and its lesser portion is as the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, both of which one and the same sphere circumscribes. 

From what has been said, therefore, the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the side of the cube inscribed in some sphere to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron circumscribed by the same sphere is manifest; and likewise the ratio [**ꝓ**] of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to all the surfaces of the icosahedron, both of which are circumscribed upon the same sphere. And again, the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the line powerful over any line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes and over its greater portion, to the line powerful over the same and over its lesser portion, and also the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, which one and the same sphere constrains, is a single ratio. Wondrous, therefore, is the power of a line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes: for which, while many things worthy of the admiration of philosophers agree, this principle or chief thing proceeds from the aforesaid by an invariable nature, so that it rationally reconciles solids so diverse, as much in magnitude as in the number of bases, as well as in their irrational figure, by a certain symphony. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that the ratio [**ꝓ**] of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, which both fit within one sphere, is as the ratio [**ꝓ**] of a line powerful over any line divided according to the aforementioned ratio over its greater part, to any line powerful over the same and its lesser part. Since, however, nothing has been said concerning the three other regular bodies, I shall strive to say something about them.

### Proposition 11

In every equilateral triangle, if a perpendicular is drawn from one of its angles to the base, it will be found that the side of the same triangle is sesquitertial [ratio of 4:3] in power to that perpendicular.
For let there be an equilateral triangle $a.b.c.$, and let the line $a.d.$ be drawn from angle $a$ perpendicular to the base: I say that $a.b.$ is sesquitertial in power to $a.d.$ Indeed, from the 5th of the First, the two angles $b$ and $c$ are equal, and because the angles at $d$ are right, the line $b.c.$ will be divided into equal parts at point $d$ by the 26th of the First. Thus, from the 4th of the Second, the square of $b.c.$ is quadruple to the square of $b.d.$, and therefore the square of $a.b.$ is also quadruple to the square of $b.d.$ Since it is an equilateral triangle, therefore by the penultimate [proposition] of the First, the squares of the two lines $a.d.$ and $b.d.$ taken together are quadruple to the square of $b.d.$ Thus the square of $a.d.$ is triple to the square of $b.d.$ The proposition [**ꝓ**] therefore stands.

### Proposition 12

Every equilateral triangle whose side is rational is proved to be a medial surface. Let there be, as before, an equilateral triangle $a.b.c.$, and let its side $a.b.$ be rational [**ronnale**] either in length or in power only; I say therefore that the triangle itself is a medial surface. For I shall draw the perpendicular $a.d.$ from angle $a$ to the base: and from the premise and from the 6th of the Tenth... of the rational surface, the square of line $a.d.$ will be rational and line $a.d.$ rational in power. However, from the last part of the Tenth, by means of the premise, it will be incommensurable to line $a.b.$, and likewise to line $b.d.$ which is as its half. Thus the two lines $a.d.$ and $b.d.$ are rational, communicating in power only. Therefore, from the 19th of the Tenth, the surface of one of them into the other is medial. And since the surface of one into the other is equal to the triangle $a.b.c.$, it is established that what we have said is true.

**[Page LIBER]**

### Proposition 13

All the surfaces of either of two solids, of which one is a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases [tetrahedron] and the other is a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases [octahedron], taken together: if the diameter of the sphere circumscribing them be rational, they compose a medial surface.
For if the diameter of the sphere circumscribing either of the two proposed bodies be rational either in length or in power only: from the corollary of the 13th of the Thirteenth book, the side of the pyramid will be rational in power, and from the corollary of the 15th of the same, the side of the body of eight bases will also be rational in power. Wherefore, by [**ꝑ**] the premise, the triangles which are the bases of either body will be medial surfaces. And because the triangles of either body are equal to one another: from the 21st of the Tenth, all the surfaces of either body taken together compose a medial surface, as is proposed [**ꝓ**], etc.

### Proposition 14

If a tetrahedron and an octahedron are circumscribed by one and the same sphere, one of the bases of the tetrahedron will be sesquitertial [4:3] to one of the bases of the octahedron; it is necessary, however, that all the bases of the octahedron taken together have a sesquialter [3:2] ratio [**ꝓ**] to all the bases of the tetrahedron taken together.
Let there be some sphere whose diameter is $a$, circumscribing a pyramid whose side is $b$ and an octahedron whose side is $c$. I say therefore that the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is sesquitertial to the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$, and that the surface which the eight equilateral triangles (each of whose side is $c$) produce is sesquialter to the surface which the four equilateral triangles (each of whose side is $b$) compose. For it is established from the corollary of the 13th of the Thirteenth that the square of $a$ is to the square of $b$ as 6 is to 4; therefore, conversely, the square of $b$ is to the square of $a$ as 4 is to 6. From the corollary of the 15th of the same, it is manifest that the square of $a$ is to the square of $c$ as 6 is to 3; thus by [**ꝑ**] equal proportionality, the square of $b$ is to the square of $c$ as 4 is to 3. But the square of $b$ is to the square of $c$ as the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is to the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$, for in both cases it is as the duplicate ratio of $b$ to $c$ from the second part of the 18th of the Sixth: therefore the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is to the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$ as 4 is to 3; wherefore the first part of the proposition is established. From which the second part is evidently drawn: for by converse proportionality, the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$ will be to the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ as three is to four. Therefore, the octuple of the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$ to the quadruple of the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is as the octuple of three to the quadruple of four. This, however, is as 24 to 16. And since the octuple of the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$ is all the bases of the octahedron whose side is $c$, and the quadruple of the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is all the bases of the pyramid whose side is $b$, and since the ratio of 24 to 16 is sesquialter, it follows that the surface which all the bases of the octahedron whose side is $c$ compose, regards the surface which all the bases of the pyramid whose side is $b$ compose in a sesquialter ratio, as we have said.

**[Page XIIII]**

### Proposition 15

When a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases is placed within any sphere, if a straight line is drawn from any of its angles through [**ꝑ**] the center of the sphere to the base, it is necessarily proved to fall into the center of the circle circumscribing the base and to stand perpendicularly upon the same base.
Let there be a pyramid $a.b.c.d.$ of triangular and equilateral bases placed within some sphere whose center is $f$. And since any of the four angles of this pyramid can be its vertex [**conus**] and any of the four triangles its base, let us now imagine its solid angle $a$ to be the vertex and imagine the triangle $b.c.d.$ to be the base, and let us understand the circle $b.c.d.$ to be circumscribed about this base. Then, from point $a$, which we have imagined as the vertex of the pyramid, let us draw to the base $b.c.d.$ a straight line passing through [**ꝑ**] point $f$, which is the center of the sphere circumscribing the pyramid about which we dispute, and let this line meet the surface $b.c.d.$ (which we imagined as the base of the pyramid) at point $e$. I say therefore that point $e$ is the center of the circle $b.c.d.$ and that the line $a.f.e.$ is perpendicular to the surface $b.c.d.$ For I shall produce the lines $f.b., f.c., f.d.$: and since the four points $a.b.c.d.$ are on the surface of the sphere whose center is $f$, because it was posited that that sphere circumscribes this pyramid, all four lines $f.a., f.b., f.c., f.d.$ will be equal to one another, for they are drawn from the center of the sphere to its surface. Therefore, since the two sides $a.f.$ and $f.b.$ of triangle $a.f.b.$ are equal to the two sides $a.f.$ and $f.c.$ of triangle $a.f.c.$, and base $a.b.$ to base $a.c.$ (for the pyramid is posited as equilateral), from the 8th of the First, angle $a.f.b.$ will be equal to angle $a.f.c.$ Thus by [**ꝑ**] the 13th of the First, angle $b.f.e.$ will also be equal to angle $c.f.e.$ In the same way, you will prove angle $d.f.e.$ to be equal to angle $c.f.e.$, for it is necessary from the 8th of the First that angle $a.f.e.$ [transcription note: likely $a.f.d$ intended] be equal to angle $a.f.d.$; wherefore by [**ꝑ**] the 13th of the First, angle $c.f.e.$ will also be equal to angle $d.f.e.$ Thus the three angles $b.f.e., c.f.e., d.f.e.$ are equal to one another. Therefore, having drawn the lines $e.b., e.c., e.d.$, it follows from the 4th of the First, twice assumed, that they are equal to one another. And therefore, by [**ꝑ**] the 9th of the Third, point $e$ is the center of the circle $b.c.d.$ And since the perpendicular drawn from the center of the sphere to the surface of any circle cutting it falls upon the center of the same circle—as you have learned from those things which were premised, namely from those which immediately precede the 10th [proposition] of this [book]—it convinces that the line $a.f.e.$ is perpendicular to the surface of the circle $a.b.c.$ [transcription note: likely $b.c.d$ intended], just as is proposed [**ꝓ**]. Otherwise, there would be two centers of the same circle, which nature abhors as impossible.

### Proposition 16

A solid of eight triangular and equilateral bases which is circumscribed by some sphere is divisible into two pyramids of equal height, whose height is equal to the semidiameter [radius] of the sphere; the base of each, however, is a square which is half of the square of the diameter of the sphere.
Let there be a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases whose six angles are $a, b, c, d, e, f$, circumscribed by a sphere whose center is $g$. It is established, therefore, that the six points $a, b, c, d, e, f$ are on the surface of the sphere whose center is $g$. If, therefore, the center $g$ is joined to any of these six points, the lines joining it will be equal to one another, since they are from the center of the sphere to the surface. But since from the corollary of the 15th of the Thirteenth, the diameter of the sphere is in power double to the side of this body, it follows from the 4th of the Second that the side of this body is in power double to the semidiameter of the sphere. Therefore, the square of $e.f.$ is double to the square of $c.g.$, and thus equal to the two squares of the two lines $c.g.$ and $g.f.$ Thus, by [**ꝑ**] the penultimate of the First, angle $c.g.f.$ is a right angle. By the same reasoning, each of the triangles $f.g.d.,$

**[Page LIBER]**

$d.g.c.,$ and $c.g.e.$ is a right [triangle], since by [**ꝑ**] the 14th of the First, $c.g.d.$ and $f.g.e.$ is one line: therefore from the second part of the 11th, the five points $c, f, d, e, g$ are in one surface. It is manifest, however, from the 5th of the First and the 32nd of the same, that each of the four angles $c, e, d, f$ is right: therefore from the definition of a square, the surface $c.e.d.f.$ is square. Since its side is the side of the proposed body, it is established from the corollary of the 15th of the Thirteenth that this square is half the square of the diameter of the sphere. By similar reasoning, it is established that each of the two lines $a.g.$ and $g.b.$ with any of the four lines $c.g., f.g., d.g., e.g.$ contains a right angle: therefore from the 4th of the Eleventh, each of them is perpendicular to the surface $c.e.d.f.$, and both (namely $a.g.$ and $g.b.$), by [**ꝑ**] the 14th of the First, compose one line. The proposed body is therefore divided into pyramid $a.c.f.d.e.$, whose base is the square $c.e.d.f.$ (which is half the square of the sphere's diameter) and also the height of line $a.g.$ (which is the semidiameter of the sphere), and into pyramid $b.c.f.d.e.$, whose base is the aforesaid square and its height line $g.b.$ (which is the semidiameter of the sphere); and this is what it was necessary to show.

### Proposition 1 (of Book XV)

Within a proposed cube, to describe a body having four triangular bases of equal sides [a tetrahedron]. 
It will be convenient to fabricate the cube itself by this art: with a square of the base described according to any line from the 45th of the First, let a perpendicular [**cathecus**] be erected upon each of its angles from the 12th of the Eleventh according to the measure of the side of the square itself... ### Proposition 2

Within a given body having four triangular and equilateral bases [tetrahedron], to distinguish a body of eight triangular bases of equal sides [octahedron].

We intend to inscribe an octahedron in a cube... In the assigned body of eight bases, inscribe a cube according to the precepts of the premise, and in the inscribed cube, inscribe as the first [proposition] teaches, a pyramid... it is manifest from the definition that we have done what was sought.

Within a given body of twenty bases and equal sides [icosahedron], to regularly compose a body of twelve pentagonal bases of equal sides and equal angles [dodecahedron].

### Notes on Abbreviations and Terms:
*   **ꝓ (proportio):** Ratio or proportion.
*   **ꝯ (corporis):** Of the body/solid.
*   **ꝑ (per):** Through or by (often referring to a Proposition).
*   **Potentialiter:** "In power," meaning the square of the line.
*   **Sesquitertia:** A ratio of 4:3.
*   **Sesquialtera:** A ratio of 3:2.
*   **Ypothemisa / Apothemisa:** Non-standard terms likely referring to "apothem" or "hypotenuse" (lines connecting centers to edges or vertices).
*   **Ronale / Ronnale:** *Rationale* (Rational).
*   **Medium duoque extrema:** The "mean and extreme ratio," i.e., the Golden Ratio.

**Proposition 15.**

**P**yramid of four triangular and equilateral bases <note>A regular tetrahedron.</note> placed within any sphere: if from any of its angles a straight line is drawn through the center of the sphere to the base, it is necessarily proven that it falls into the center of the circle circumscribing that base and stands perpendicularly to that same base.

Let there be a pyramid *a.b.c.d.* of triangular and equilateral bases placed within a sphere whose center is *f*. Since any of the four angles of this pyramid can be its apex <note>The text uses "conus," referring to the vertex or point of the pyramid.</note> and any of the four triangles its base, let us now imagine its solid angle *a* to be the apex and triangle *b.c.d.* to be the base. Let us understand that a circle *b.c.d.* is circumscribed around this base. Then, from point *a*, which we have imagined as the apex of the pyramid, let us draw a straight line to the base *b.c.d.* passing through point *f*, which is the center of the sphere circumscribing the pyramid under discussion. Let this line meet the surface *b.c.d.* (which we imagined as the pyramid's base) at point *e*. I say, therefore, that point *e* is the center of circle *b.c.d.* and that line *a.f.e.* is perpendicular to the surface *b.c.d.*

For I shall extend the lines *f.b.*, *f.c.*, and *f.d.* Since the four points *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d* are on the surface of the sphere whose center is *f* (because the sphere is positioned to circumscribe this pyramid), all four lines *f.a.*, *f.b.*, *f.c.*, and *f.d.* will be equal to one another, for they are drawn from the center of the sphere to its surface. Therefore, because the two sides *a.f.* and *f.b.* of triangle *a.f.b.* are equal to the two sides *a.f.* and *f.c.* of triangle *a.f.c.*, and the base *a.b.* is equal to the base *a.c.* (since the pyramid is defined as equilateral), it follows from the eighth [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Euclid's Elements, Book I, Prop. 8 regarding Side-Side-Side congruence.</note> that angle *a.f.b.* is equal to angle *a.f.c.* Therefore, by the 13th [proposition] of the first [book], angle *b.f.e.* will also be equal to angle *c.f.e.* In the same way, you will prove that angle *d.f.e.* is equal to angle *c.f.e.* It is necessary from the eighth of the first that angle *a.f.e.* be equal to angle *a.f.d.*, whereby through the 13th of the first, angle *c.f.e.* will also be equal to angle *d.f.e.*

Thus, the three angles *b.f.e.*, *c.f.e.*, and *d.f.e.* are equal to one another. Otherwise, there would be two centers for the same circle, which nature shrinks from as impossible.

**[Decorative Initial D]**ouble the square of the diameter of the sphere circumscribing a cube is equal to the sum of all the surfaces of that same cube. It is also necessarily proven that the <term>perpendicular</term><note>A line at a right angle (90 degrees) to a surface.</note> drawn from the center of the sphere to any of the surfaces of the cube is equal to half of the side of that same cube. 
¶ It is indeed evident from the corollary of the 14th proposition of the thirteenth book that the diameter of a sphere enclosing a cube is triple in <term>power</term><note>original: "potentia"; in Greek geometry, a line is "triple in power" to another if its square is three times the square of the other.</note> to the side of the cube. Since, therefore, the square of the diameter of the sphere is triple the square of the side of the cube—and thus three times as great—it follows that double the square of the diameter of the sphere is equal to six times the square of the side of the cube. Furthermore, all the surfaces of a cube are six squares which are produced by multiplying the side by itself. Therefore, double the square of the diameter of the sphere is equal to all the surfaces of the cube. The first part is thus established; the second part you will easily prove from the 18th, 19th, and 40th propositions of the eleventh book.
¶ From these things, it must necessarily happen that the <term>solidity</term><note>The volume or three-dimensional content.</note> of the cube is produced from half the side of the cube multiplied by two-thirds of the square produced from the diameter of the sphere surrounding that cube. 
¶ **Here ends the fourteenth book. Here begins the Fifteenth Book.**

¶ **Proposition .1.**
**[Decorative Initial I]**nscribe a body having four triangular bases of equal sides <note>A regular tetrahedron.</note> within a given cube.
¶ Let there be a cube whose base is the square **a.b.c.d.** and whose top surface is the square **e.f.g.h.** It is convenient to construct this using the following method: on the square of the base, described according to any line from the 45th proposition of the first book, a <term>cathetus</term><note>A vertical line or perpendicular height.</note> according to the measure of the side of that square should be erected upon each of its corners according to the 12th proposition of the eleventh book. It is established from the 6th proposition of the eleventh book that these lines are parallel. Let these lines then be joined two by two at the top by lines placed parallel to the side of the square. It is therefore established that a cube is composed; for its four lateral surfaces are squares from the 33rd and 34th propositions of the first book and the definition of a square. Regarding the top surface, it is also manifest that it is a square from the 10th (or rather 24th) proposition of the eleventh book, and by this common principle: "things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other," and by the definition of a square. 
If, therefore, one wishes to inscribe in this cube a body of four triangular and equilateral bases: let two diameters <note>Diagonal lines.</note> be drawn in the base and in its top surface, one of which connects two bottom extremities of two vertical lines, and the other connects the top extremities of the other two vertical lines—which you will understand in your mind to be **a.c.** and **b.f.** Then, from the two points **b.** and **f.** terminating the diameter of the top surface, drop <term>hypothenuses</term><note>original: "ypothemisaliter"; here meaning diagonal lines across the faces of the cube.</note> in pairs which divide the lateral surfaces. You will imagine these to be from **b.**, namely **b.a.** and **b.c.**; and from **f.**, namely **f.a.** and **f.c.** I have declined to draw these diameters in this flat figure lest a multitude of lines confuse the understanding. If, therefore, you complete this figure as is proper—either in reality or in your mind—you will see that from the six diagonal lines dividing the six surfaces of the cube, a <term>pyramid</term><note>A tetrahedron.</note> of four triangular bases is perfected, which is clearly inscribed in the proposed cube by definition. That the bases of this pyramid are equilateral is established by the fact that, from the 4th proposition of the first book, all these six diagonals are equal to one another.

XV

For example <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>, join the center of the front face with the center of the right and with the center of the left; you will also join the center of the last [back] face with the same. This one, indeed, with the center of the right and the center of the left. Thus you have a body of eight triangular bases <note>an octahedron</note> contained by these 12 lines that continue the centers of the cube's surfaces. If you then wish to prove these bases are equilateral: from the centers of the cube's bases, draw perpendicular lines to all of its sides. These must divide all sides of the cube into equal parts according to the second part of the third [proposition] of the third [book] <note>Euclid's Elements, Book III, Prop. 3</note>. This is clear if you circumscribe a circle around each of the cube's bases, and thus it is established that pairs of these lines meet at the same point on the sides of the cube's bases. And from the second part of the 13th [proposition] of the third [book], it is evident they are equal to each other and equidistant from the sides of the cube, according to the second part of the 28th [proposition] of the first [book]. Therefore, each is also equal to half the side of the cube. It is manifest from the 10th [proposition] of the eleventh [book] that these lines, meeting in pairs upon the same side of the cube at its midpoint, contain a right angle, because all surfaces of the cube are square. Therefore, those 12 lines connecting the centers of the cube's surfaces, and the angles which these lines contain when meeting in pairs at the midpoints of the cube's sides, will be equal to each other by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book]—or even, if you prefer, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>the Pythagorean Theorem, Euclid I.47</note>. Therefore, in the proposed cube, a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases has been designated, which was what was required to be done, etc.

### Proposition 4

-> To figure a cube within a given body of eight triangular and equilateral bases. <-

Do not doubt that you can construct a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>an octahedron</note> by a certain rule in this manner: take any straight line erected orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> upward upon some plane, divide it into equal parts, and from its midpoint draw out two perpendicular lines on either side which together form one line. These two lines intersecting each other—namely the first which is erected orthogonally upon the given plane and the other which intersects it orthogonally at its midpoint—are situated in the same surface according to the first part of the second [proposition] of the eleventh [book]. Therefore, upon the surface in which they are situated, at their common point of intersection, erect a perpendicular as the 12th [proposition] of the eleventh [book] teaches, making it penetrate that same surface on both sides. Set all six portions of these three lines to be equal from the point in which they intersect each other. In this way, any one of them will divide any other into equal parts and orthogonally. Thus, since there are three lines, any two of them will contain the venerable sign of the saving cross <note>a reference to the X, Y, and Z axes forming a cross shape</note> at right angles. Therefore, from the top point of the line erected upon the given plane, drop four hypotenuses <term>ypothemisas</term> <note>the slanted edges of the top pyramid</note> to the extremities of the two lines intersecting it. Then, from the bottom point of the same erected line, raise four other hypotenuses to the same extremities of the two intersecting lines. Finally, connect the extremities of these hypotenuses with four straight lines containing a square. These twelve lines—namely the four hypotenuses descending from the top point of the vertical perpendicular, the four raised upward from its bottom point, and the remaining four lines connecting the extremities of these hypotenuses—will be equal to each other according to the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], the point of joining having been repeated many times. Thus it is established that the body bounded by them is contained by eight triangular and equilateral bases. If it then pleases you to inscribe a cube within this body, labor to find the centers of the eight triangles surrounding it from the 5th [proposition] of the fourth [book]. Once these are found, connect them with 12 straight lines by this rule: that the center of each of these triangles be joined by a straight line to the center of each of the three [triangles] that share its sides. It is not suitable to depict a figure of this thing in a plane <note>it is difficult to draw this 3D concept in 2D</note>; therefore, it remains for you to conceive in your mind what is said, and if it pleases you, complete it with actual work and effort.

# BOOK [XIV]

->**In this book, we intend to demonstrate the relationships and proportions of the regular solids.**<-

### PROPOSITION 5
If a regular solid is inscribed within a sphere, the lines of its sides are related in a specific ratio to the diameter of that sphere. We must consider the nature of the <term>equilateral</term> <note>A shape where all sides are of equal length; original: "equilater"</note> faces that compose these bodies. When we compare the surfaces of these figures, we find that the ratio of the areas <note>original: "arearum"</note> follows the square of the ratio of their sides. 

### PROPOSITION 6
<margin>Calculation of the diameter</margin>
**Therefore** <note>original: "igitur"</note>, if we consider the construction of the <term>icosahedron</term> <note>A 20-sided regular solid made of equilateral triangles.</note> and the <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>A 12-sided regular solid made of regular pentagons.</note> within the same sphere, we may observe their shared symmetries. Let the lines be drawn out <note>original: "protrahantur"</note> from the center of the sphere to the vertices of the solid. 

By this arrangement, it is shown that:
1. The perpendiculars from the center are equal.
2. The edges of the solids <gloss>the lengths of the sides</gloss> are in a fixed proportion to the radius.

It follows that the ratio of the side of the cube to the side of the octahedron is as the square root of two is to one. **And** <note>represented by the "et" abbreviation ꝛ</note> this relationship is fundamental to the division of the sphere.

...in the [proposition] previously set forth, by joining the centers of all the triangles bounding the whole icosahedron with 30 straight lines, such that you join the center of each to the centers of all surrounding ones with which it shares a side by straight lines. When, therefore, you have done this, you will see that from those 30 lines, twelve pentagons are constituted, opposite the 12 solid angles of the given icosahedron. These [OCR: *bos* → *hos*] pentagons, therefore, just as you did in the [proposition] previously set forth concerning the bases of the cube, you shall prove to be equilateral. For it is necessary that for any two triangles having the same side, their centers are distant by the same space. It remains, therefore, that you should syllogize [deduce] that they are also equiangular. Moreover, it is manifest from the reasoning of the 16th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book] that the given body of twenty bases [the icosahedron] is circumscriptible by the same sphere whose diameter is, as it were, the diameter of this body—namely, the lines which contain its two opposite angles. If, therefore, this diameter is cut through the middle, the point of the section will be the center of the sphere circumscribing it. Therefore, from that [point], draw lines perpendicular to the surfaces of all the pentagons. From the point where they meet each of the pentagons, according to the 11th [proposition] of the eleventh [book], direct straight lines to each of their angles. Then, join the center of the sphere with each of the angles of those pentagons. Therefore, prove that they are equiangular in this manner. For since all the circles circumscribing the triangles of the icosahedron are equal, all the perpendiculars coming from the center of the sphere to them, falling into their centers, will be equal. Therefore, all lines coming from the center of the sphere to the angles of any pentagon are equal. For the angles of the pentagons are the centers of the circles circumscribing the triangles of the icosahedron themselves. Since, therefore, from the hypothesis and from the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], by the same kind of argumentation as we used above in the 14th, the result follows [unclear: *sectore* / *rectore*] that when any plane surface cuts a sphere not through its center, the circumference containing the circle is on the surface of the sphere. It is necessary that the five lines coming from the meeting point of the perpendicular drawn from the center of the sphere to the surfaces of all the pentagons to the five angles of each pentagon be mutually equal. Thus, for all twice-twelve [sic, likely meaning all twelve] pentagons, there is a circumscriptible circle. Since, therefore, they are equilateral, it follows that they are also equiangular, which was to be shown.

### Proposition .7.

**Within a given body of twelve pentagonal, equilateral, and equiangular bases [a dodecahedron], to construct a body of twenty triangular and equilateral bases [an icosahedron]:**
How it behooves one to compose a body of twelve pentagonal, equilateral, and equiangular bases, seek from the 17th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book]. But how a body of twenty triangular and equilateral bases is fit to be inscribed in it, learn here: the centers of its pentagons having been found, as is done in the 14th [proposition] of the fourth [book], connect them to each other with 30 lines by this law: that the center of each pentagon be joined to the center of each pentagon communicating with it at a side, so that, namely, the center of each pentagon is contained [connected] by the centers of the five pentagons bounding or surrounding it. When, therefore, you have done this, there will appear to you twenty triangles contained by these 30 lines connecting the centers of the pentagons. And these twenty triangles will be opposite the twenty solid angles of the dodecahedron itself, embracing a body of twenty triangular bases, which we shall demonstrate to be equilateral. The 12 solid angles of this body of 20 bases will be in the centers of the 12 pentagons bounding the body of the given dodecahedron. Prove that these 20 triangles are equilateral thus: from the centers of the pentagons, let perpendiculars be drawn to the sides, and all the perpendiculars will be equal. Therefore, you shall prove, two by two, from 

**[Page: LIBER (XV)]**

the eighth [proposition] of the first [book], that they contain equal angles. Because the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons are subtended by these angles contained by the perpendiculars taken two by two, since all the perpendiculars are equal, all the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons will be equal, according to the fourth [proposition] of the first [book]; which is what was proposed. Moreover, gather that the perpendiculars contain equal angles two by two, and that all of them are mutually equal, thus: from the fifth [proposition] of the first [book] and the 26th of the same, it is established that each of them divides the sides of the pentagons upon which they fall into equal parts; and that they are mutually equal, lines having been drawn from the centers of the pentagons to each of their angles. Wherefore, those falling two by two upon the same side will meet at the same point of that side, because each divides that side, common to the two pentagons from whose centers they come, into equal parts. Therefore, these perpendiculars, having been produced two by two through the centers of the pentagons as far as the angles to which the common side in which they meet is opposite, subtend two lines to those same angles, which from the demonstration of the 17th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book] it is manifest are as the side of a cube circumscriptible by the same sphere as the proposed dodecahedron. And therefore it is clear they are equal, because all sides of a cube are equal. And it is clear from the ninth [proposition] of the eleventh [book] that they are parallel, because both are parallel to the common side in which the perpendiculars meet two by two. But indeed, it is established that these same [lines] are divided into equal parts by these perpendiculars. Thus, by the 33rd [proposition] of the first [book], all lines connecting the points in which the perpendiculars meet two by two upon these lines (which we said would be as the sides of the cube) are mutually equal. For all are as the side of the cube. Therefore, from the eighth [proposition] of the first [book], the angles contained by the perpendiculars two by two are equal; wherefore, by the fourth [proposition] of the same, the lines also connecting the centers of the pentagons are mutually equal to each other. Therefore, there has been inscribed in the proposed dodecahedron a body of twenty triangular bases of equal sides, as we were commanded.

### Proposition .8.

**A solid of twelve pentagonal and equilateral bases being proposed, to distinguish a cube within it.**
Since [OCR: *Lū* → *Cum*] a dodecahedron is constructed upon the sides of a cube, as is established from the 17th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], it is fitting for a cube to be inscribed in it. For since there are twelve pentagons, if for each one of them you subtend one chord at one angle (as you will see the figure of the cube requires), from those twelve chords you will complete six equilateral and rectangular surfaces embracing the body of the cube. That they are equilateral is established from the fourth [proposition] of the first [book]; that they are rectangular, however, [is proven] by the same kind of argumentation by which, in the sixth [proposition] of this [book], we demonstrated the bases of the dodecahedron [sic, should be icosahedron] inscribed in a given icosahedron to be equiangular. It is established indeed from the seventeenth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book] that the proposed dodecahedron is inscribable in a sphere. From the center of that sphere, draw perpendiculars to all the quadrilateral base surfaces, as the eleventh [proposition] of the eleventh [book] teaches; from the point of meeting, direct straight lines to the individual angles of those quadrilateral surfaces. And join those same angles of the quadrilateral surfaces with the center of the sphere; and these lines connecting the center of the sphere with the angles of the quadrilateral surfaces will be the radii of the sphere. Because, when the square of the perpendicular is taken away from their squares, there remain, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], the squares of the lines connecting the point of meeting of the perpendiculars with the angles of the quadrilateral surfaces, it is necessary that circles be circumscriptible for all these quadrilateral surfaces,

**[Page: XV]**

and thus it is necessary that they be equiangular since they are equilateral. And because from the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], the angles of each of them taken together are equal to four right angles, it follows that they are rectangular. Therefore, nothing is lacking to the inscribed body regarding the nature of a cube.

### Proposition .9.

**Given a dodecahedron, finally to include an octahedron within it.**
The dodecahedron having been composed [OCR: *Lōposito* → *Composito*] as in the 17th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], divide its sides [unclear: *fciij* / *secundi?*] into equal parts, namely those which... [text describing technical line construction involving the cube]... they shall cut each other into equal parts through the middle point of the diameter of the cube, according to the 48th [proposition] of the eleventh [book]; and it will be that two of those three also divide each other at right angles. If, therefore, you connect the extremities of these three lines by 12 straight lines, there will result for you a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases, by the fourth [proposition] of the first [book], or more so from the penultimate of the first; which was to be shown.

### Proposition .10.

**Within an assigned dodecahedron, it still remains to distinguish a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases [a tetrahedron].**
In the assigned [OCR: *Lassignato* → *Cassignato*] dodecahedron, inscribe a cube according to the eighth [proposition] of this [book], and in the cube, a pyramid according to the first [proposition]. Since, therefore, the angles of the pyramid are in the angles of the cube, as is clear from the reasoning of the first [proposition], and the angles of the cube are in the angles of the dodecahedron from the reasoning of the eighth [proposition], the angles of the pyramid will also be in the angles of the dodecahedron. Thus, what we want is established.

### Proposition .11.

**A proposed icosahedron being given, to figure a cube within it.**
In the icosahedron [OCR: *Lycocedro* → *Icocedro*], a dodecahedron is inscribed by the sixth [proposition], and in the dodecahedron, a cube by the eighth. Moreover, it is established from the demonstration of the sixth [proposition] that all angles of the dodecahedron fall upon the center of the bases of the icosahedron, and the angles of the cube are in the angles of the dodecahedron; thus, the angles of the cube are in the centers of the bases of the icosahedron. Therefore, we have what was proposed.

### Proposition .12.

**A given icosahedron requires a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases to be inscribed within itself.**
If in a given icosahedron you inscribe a cube by the preceding [proposition], and in the cube you include a pyramid by the first [proposition], it will not be doubted that you have satisfied the requirement of the icosahedron. It must be known, however, that since there are five regular bodies, concerning whose mutual inscription in each other this 15th book determines, if each of them were inscribable in any of the others, 20 inscriptions would occur. For since any five of them would have the other four inscribable [within them], therefore four times five inscriptions, which is 20, would necessarily result. But indeed, for the pyramid, only the octahedron is fit to be inscribed. For there are not in the pyramid bases or angles or sides in which the angles of the cube or the icosahedron or even the dodecahedron might touch the extremities of the pyramid itself.

**[Page: LIBER (XV)]**

Likewise, the cube is only for the reception of the pyramid and the octahedron, just as the octahedron is only for the reception of the pyramid and the cube. For how will you place the 12 angles of the icosahedron, or the 20 angles of the dodecahedron, in either of them, so that they fall individually into each of theirs? The icosahedron, moreover, although it can embrace others with a suitable surrounding, cannot be a receptacle for the icosahedron [itself]. For the six angles of the octahedron regard each other in pairs by semidiametrical opposition, and the lines connecting them divide each other into equal parts orthogonally. Thus, let them return that [unclear: *glosū* / *glossy?*] sign [the cross/octahedron] at the sight of which demons are confounded, tripled under right angles. Thus, neither the bases nor angles nor sides of the icosahedron can receive these triangles in their position; for you will not find in it six bases or six angles or six sides containing themselves by this diametrical and orthogonal opposition. The dodecahedron, however, has denied the hospitality of its embrace to none of the others; rather, it stands as the receiver of all. Whence, not inconveniently, the disciples of ancient Plato ascribed the figure of the dodecahedron to heaven, just as they ascribed the form of the pyramid to fire, because it flies upward in a pyramidal figure. And that of the octahedron to air; for just as air follows fire in the lightness of its motion, so the form of the octahedron follows the form of the pyramid in its suitability for motion. But the figure of twenty bases [icosahedron] they assigned to water; for since it, by the plurality of its bases, is more circular than the others, it seemed more suited to the motion of a flowing thing than a climbing one. Some indeed gave the figure of the cube to the earth. For what among figures needs more violence for motion than a *tessera* [a die/cube]? And among the elements, what is found more fixed and constant than earth? If, therefore, from the 20 inscriptions, you reject the 3 which the pyramid does not sustain, and the pairs from which the nature of the cube and octahedron are alien, and again the one which the figure of the icosahedron rejects, there will remain only 12: for the pyramid only one; for the cube and octahedron two each; for the icosahedron three; for the dodecahedron four; concerning all of which, as I judge, it has been sufficiently disputed elsewhere.

### Proposition .13.

**Having fabricated any of the five regular bodies, to inscribe a sphere within it.**
From the thirteenth book, it is manifest that each of these five bodies is inscribable in a sphere. Now, therefore, it shall be established conversely that a sphere is inscribable in each of them. For from the center of the circumscribing sphere, let perpendiculars go out to all the bases of any of them, which must necessarily fall within the centers of the circles circumscribing those bases. And since all the circles circumscribing them are equal, these perpendiculars will be equal. Thus, if you describe a circle with the quantity of one of them upon the center of the circumscribing sphere, and lead its semicircle around until it returns to the place from which it began to move, because it must necessarily pass through the extremities of all the perpendiculars, you will prove from the corollary of the 15th [proposition] of the third [book] that the sphere described by the motion of this semicircle touches all the bases of the assigned body at the meetings of the perpendiculars. For a sphere cannot touch more of the bases of the body than the circumducted semicircle touched while it was being moved; wherefore, it is established that we have inscribed a sphere in the assigned bodies just as had been proposed.

> **The work of the Elements of Euclid of Megara in the art of Geometry, and also the Commentaries of the most perspicacious Campanus upon it, here end. Erhard Ratdolt of Augsburg, most skillful printer, printed this at Venice. In the year of salvation 1482, on the eighth Calends of June [May 25].**

### Notes on Abbreviations and Unclear Readings:
*   **OCR Errors**: Many leading letters (initials) were misread by OCR (e.g., *Lū* for *Cum*, *Lassignato* for *Cassignato*, *Lubon* for *Cubum*). These have been corrected based on the standard Latin text of the Ratdolt edition.
*   **glosū signū**: Likely *glossis signum* or *gloriosum signum*. In the medieval context, the octahedron's internal axes form a cross, which was often referenced as a "sign" that put demons to flight.
*   **fciij**: Likely a garbled reference to a specific section or proposition number (perhaps *secundi* or *decimi*).
*   **cōrausti**: Likely *exhausti* or *conhausti*, referring to the drawing or exhaustion of lines in the geometric construction.
*   **yocedron/duodecedron**: Standard medieval/Renaissance spellings for icosahedron and dodecahedron.
*   **tessera**: Used here to mean a die or a cube, emphasizing its stability on the ground.

**BOOK**

<note>original: "octaua primi"</note> the eighth proposition of the first book <note>This refers to Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 8, which deals with the congruence of triangles based on their sides.</note> contains equal angles, and because the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons are subtended by these angles, which are contained by pairs of perpendiculars: since all the perpendiculars are equal, then by the fourth proposition of the first book, all the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons will be equal, which is what was proposed. 

That the pairs of perpendiculars contain equal angles and are all equal to one another can be gathered as follows: From the fifth and twenty-sixth propositions of the first book, it is established that each of them divides the sides of the pentagons upon which they fall into equal parts. These perpendiculars are equal to one another when lines are drawn from the centers of the pentagons to each of their angles. Therefore, those that fall in pairs upon the same side will meet at the same point of that side, because each divides that side—which is common to the two pentagons from whose centers they come—into equal parts. 

Therefore, extend these pairs of perpendiculars through the centers of the pentagons to the angles opposite the common side where they meet, and subtend two lines to those same angles. It is clear from the demonstration of the seventeenth proposition of the thirteenth book that these lines are like the <term>edge of a cube</term> <note>The "latus cubi" or edge of a cube that shares the same circumscribing sphere as the dodecahedron.</note> circumscribed by the same sphere as the proposed <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>A 12-faced regular solid where each face is a pentagon.</note>. For this reason, it is clear they are equal, because all edges of a cube are equal. 

It is also clear from the ninth proposition of the eleventh book that they are parallel, because both are parallel to the common side where the pairs of perpendiculars meet. Furthermore, it is established that these same lines are divided into equal parts by these perpendiculars. Thus, by the thirty-third proposition of the first book, all the lines connecting the points where the pairs of perpendiculars meet on these lines (which we said would be the edges of the cube) are equal to one another. For they are all like the edge of a cube. 

Therefore, from the eighth proposition of the first book, the angles contained by the pairs of perpendiculars are equal. For this reason, by the fourth proposition of the same book, the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons are also equal to one another. Thus, a body of twenty triangular bases and equal sides <note>This "body of twenty bases" is an icosahedron.</note> has been inscribed in the proposed dodecahedron, just as we were commanded.

->**Proposition 8**<-

**S**ince a solid of twelve pentagonal and equilateral bases is proposed, to distinguish a cube within it.

Since the <term>dodecahedron</term> is built upon the edges of a cube, as is established from the seventeenth proposition of the thirteenth book, it is appropriate that a cube be inscribed within it once it is built. Since there are twelve pentagons, if you subtend one <term>chord</term> <note>original: "chordam"; in this context, a diagonal line across the face of a pentagon.</note> in each of them at one of its angles (as you will see the figure of the cube requires), you will complete the six equilateral and rectangular surfaces of a cube from these twelve chords, and the body will be enclosed. 

That these surfaces are equilateral is established by the fourth proposition of the first book. That they are rectangular is proven by the same kind of reasoning we used in the sixth proposition of this book, where we demonstrated that the bases of a dodecahedron inscribed in a given <term>icosahedron</term> <note>A 20-faced regular solid.</note> are equiangular. 

It is established from the seventeenth proposition of the thirteenth book that the proposed dodecahedron can be inscribed in a sphere. Therefore, from the center of that sphere, draw perpendiculars to all the quadrilateral surfaces, as the eleventh proposition of the eleventh book teaches. From the point of intersection, direct straight lines to each angle of those quadrilateral surfaces. Then join those same angles of the quadrilateral surfaces with the center of the sphere. These lines connecting the center of the sphere with the angles of the quadrilateral surfaces will be the radii of the sphere. Because the squares of the lines connecting the intersection point of the perpendiculars with the angles of the quadrilateral surfaces remain when the square of the perpendicular is subtracted from the squares of the radii (by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Euclid I.47).</note>), it is necessary that circles can be circumscribed around all these quadrilateral surfaces.

...and therefore it is necessary for them to be equiangular since they are equilateral. ### Proposition 9.
**D**iven a dodecahedron <note>A 12-faced solid where each face is a pentagon.</note>, to finally include an octahedron <note>An 8-faced solid where each face is a triangle.</note> within it.
¶ Having composed the dodecahedron as in the 17th [proposition] and the 16th [proposition] of the second [part] of the tenth book, divide its sides—namely those which are perpendicular <term>cathecos</term> <note>From the Greek "kathetos," meaning a perpendicular line.</note> over the six lines cutting the opposite sides of the surfaces of the cube into equal parts—into equal segments, as if they were their centers. These, joined two by two to one another, will cut each other continuously through three lines which intersect at the middle point of the diameter of the cube, according to the 48th proposition of the eleventh book. It follows that any two of these three lines will also divide each other at right angles. If, therefore, you join the extremities of these three lines with 12 straight lines, there will result a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases—from the 4th proposition of the first book, or if greater, from the penultimate of the first—which is what was required to be shown.

### Proposition 10.
**I**t still remains to delineate a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases <note>A tetrahedron, the simplest Platonic solid.</note> within an assigned dodecahedron.
¶ Inscribe a cube in the assigned dodecahedron according to the 8th proposition of this book, and in that cube, inscribe a pyramid according to the 1st proposition. Since, therefore, the angles of the pyramid are at the angles of the cube—as is clear from the reasoning of the 1st proposition—and the angles of the cube are at the angles of the dodecahedron—from the reasoning of the 8th—the angles of the pyramid will also be at the angles of the dodecahedron. Thus, what we desired is established.

### Proposition 11.
**P**roposed: to fashion a cube within an icosahedron <note>A 20-faced solid where each face is a triangle.</note>.
¶ A dodecahedron is inscribed in an icosahedron according to the 6th proposition, and a cube in a dodecahedron according to the 8th. It is established from the demonstration of the 6th that all angles of the dodecahedron fall upon the center of the bases of the icosahedron, and the angles of the cube are at the angles of the dodecahedron; thus, the angles of the cube are at the centers of the bases of the icosahedron. We have therefore achieved what was proposed.

### Proposition 12.
**A** given icosahedron demands that a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases be inscribed within it.
¶ If you inscribe a cube in the given icosahedron according to the preceding proposition, and include a pyramid in that cube according to the 1st proposition, there will be no reason to hesitate in satisfying the icosahedron's demand. One ought to know, however, that since there are five regular bodies whose mutual inscriptions within one another are determined in this 15th book, if every one of them were inscribable in any other, 20 such inscriptions would occur. Indeed, for each of the five, the other four would be inscribable; therefore four times five inscriptions, which is 20, would necessarily result. But in truth, only the octahedron is suitable to be inscribed in the pyramid. For there are no bases, angles, or sides in a pyramid upon which the angles of a cube, or an icosahedron, or even a dodecahedron could touch the extremities of that pyramid.

The cube is also suited for the reception of the pyramid <note>The author uses "pyramid" to refer to the four-sided tetrahedron.</note> and the octahedron, just as the octahedron is suited to the reception of the pyramid and the cube alone, for in either of them you may arrange the 12 angles <term>vertices</term> of the icosahedron, or the 20 angles of the dodecahedron, so that each one falls upon the individual parts of the others. Concerning all of these, I believe enough has been discussed elsewhere.

### EUCLID. *Elements.* <insert>With notes by Campanus of Novara.</insert>
<note>Pencil note: Q 402 <unclear>illegible</unclear></note>
May 25, 1482.

Hain *6693; B.M.C., part V, p. 285. <note>These are standard reference numbers used by librarians to identify early printed books (incunabula).</note>

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Printed with gothic type, the "propositions" in larger and the "demonstrations" <term>demonstrations (the step-by-step mathematical proofs)</term> in smaller size. A complete copy has 138 leaves, the last blank. In the Library's copy the first leaf, containing Ratdolt's dedicatory letter to the Doge <note>The chief magistrate and leader of the Republic of Venice.</note> Mocenigo, is missing; in its place | a vellum <note>High-quality parchment made from animal skin.</note> leaf is inserted, covered with writing in a fifteenth-century hand. The size of a leaf is 302 X 206 mm., and the text measures 206 X 118 mm. There are many decorative initials and marginal diagrams. The binding is contemporary: oak boards half-covered with sheepskin. |

This is the first printed edition of Euclid's "*Elements*." The Latin translation was made about 1120 by Adelard (Aethelard) of Bath, an early English scholastic philosopher. It was based on the Arabic version of the work. However, it is probable that Adelard, who lived for a time in the Norman kingdom of Sicily and knew Greek, used also the Greek original. His translation was revised about 1260 by Campanus of Novara, a chaplain to Pope Urban IV, who, following the Greek text more closely, rendered the "demonstrations" clearer and more complete.

The first translation made directly from the Greek text was by Bartolomeo Zamberti, and was published in 1505 at Venice. Zamberti had the worst opinion of Campanus's style and scientific observations; the first he described as "barbarous" and the latter he called "scarecrows, nightmares, and phantasies." His own translation, in its turn, was severely criticised by the defenders of Campanus. The Greek original of the "*Elements*" was first printed in 1533.

The Library has several of the sixteenth-century editions of the work, among them the one published by Henri Étienne in 1516 in Paris, containing both Campanus's and Zamberti's versions. But of the greatest interest to us is the first English edition in the translation of Sir Henry Billingsley, printed in 1570 by John Daye. This monumental work of 464 leaves, with its hundreds of illustrations, is one of the finest products of the early English press.

The 1482 Venice edition of the "*Elements*" was the first important printed mathematical book. As the German printer pointed out in his dedicatory letter to the Doge, "although books by ancient and modern authors were published at Venice every day, little or nothing mathematical had appeared." But the volume is remarkable also from a typographical point of view. The letters are well-cut and the printing is neat. Beautiful initials decorate almost every page and, placed on the wide margins, hundreds of diagrams illustrate the text. There has been a considerable controversy among bibliographers about these diagrams. Ratdolt refers to them in his dedicatory letter: "After much labor I had discovered," he wrote, "a method by which geometrical figures may be as easily reproduced as letters printed." According to some, this means that Ratdolt cut his figures in soft metal instead of wood; that he used <term>clichés (metal printing plates cast from a mold)</term> and not woodcuts. The use of metal would also account for the perfection of his initials and border ornaments, in which he attained a delicacy of line unknown to any previous printer.

Ratdolt was born about 1443 at Augsburg, where he lived till 1474. His whereabouts during the next two years are unknown. He may have worked at Nuremberg with Regiomontanus, who had a private press there, thus acquiring a taste for the publishing of mathematical books by the side of the great mathematician and astronomer. In 1476 he established himself at Venice, where some fifty German printers were already at work. For two years he was in partnership with two of his countrymen, Bernhard Maler and Peter Löslein, then continued alone till 1486. After these ten years at Venice he returned to his native city. Enjoying a high reputation as a craftsman and a prosperous business man, he worked steadily till his death in 1528.

There is no need of commenting here on Euclid or the "*Elements*." Euclid lived in Alexandria, during the reign of the first Ptolemy. In the early editions of his work he is often called <note>original: "Megarensis," meaning "of Megara"</note> "of Megara," confusing him with another Euclid, a disciple of Socrates, who was born at Megara in Greece. Even to-day little is known about the life of the great Alexandrian mathematician. The "*Elements*," on the other hand, is known to every schoolboy. The geometry, both plane and solid, that is taught in the secondary schools is nothing else but Euclid's work as he wrote it. The arrangement of the axioms, postulates, theorems, problems, and propositions in the modern textbooks on geometry largely follows the work of the old Alexandrian.

It is difficult to determine now to what extent Euclid was a discoverer and to what extent a compiler. Geometrical knowledge in Egypt and in Greece was considerable before his time. Possibly, his main share in the work was the logical arrangement of the material and the clearer development of the proofs. But even if he was merely an editor, he deserves his fame. He succeeded in making geometry — within limits, of course — an attractive science.

Bought in April, 1916.
